封底，我们印上了我在祖母海岛拍的那张日偏食（eclipse）照片——缺了一口的太阳——底下是林老师的一行字：“你正在呼吸的大气（atmosphere），正翻开这一页的微风（breeze），还有被喝过雨水的树做成的纸张——它们本来就是同一个课题。这就是我们把它叫作‘地球研究’的原因。”

quiz.q: The sea evaporates into vapour, which travels and then falls as rain. Vapour is —
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S7 一滴水的旅程 → 本篇杂志"水的版面"）：水循环四部曲 evaporate（蒸发）→ vapour（水汽）→ condense（凝结成云）→ precipitate（降落为雨雪）。换个故事，词还是那个词——这正是情境复现的意义。

quiz.q: In the magazine, rivers build deltas where —
o: they rise from a mountain spring
they meet the sea and drop their mud
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S8 从小溪到大海）：delta 三角洲——河流入海口流速骤降，silt 淤积成陆，形似希腊字母 Δ。本篇说河流"走累了似的卸下泥沙"，把 S8 的搬运工比喻又推进了一步。

quiz.q: Rivers erode valleys in the mountains. To erode is to —
o: build something up layer by layer
wear something away gradually, bit by bit
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S13 变灰的河流里是"河岸被侵蚀"，本篇是"河流侵蚀出峡谷"）：erode 本义就是流水与风对岩石的缓慢磨损——soil erosion 水土流失；引申义 erode confidence 逐渐削弱信心。一词贯穿两个故事，两个语境。

quiz.q: The oasis turned green again after three years of drought. An oasis is —
o: a fertile, watered spot in the middle of a desert
a lake high in the mountains
the mouth of a great river
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S6 通往绿洲的路）：oasis 绿洲，复数 oases；引申义 a peaceful oasis in the city 都市中的一片宁静。与 drought（干旱）是天敌——两篇故事里它们都成对出现。

quiz.q: In Antarctica, the windows grow frost flowers on the inside. Frost is —
o: rain that falls when it is freezing
a thin layer of ice crystals that forms on cold surfaces
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S3 气象站的银白田野 → S11 南极的霜花）：frost 霜是水汽直接凝华成的冰晶；对比 dew 露（液态水珠）。搭配：a hard frost 严霜、frost damage 霜冻灾害（农业话题）。

quiz.q: The club gathered pebbles from the stream on their climb. A pebble is —
o: a mineral rich enough to mine
a small, smooth stone worn round by water
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S1 林老师的石头课 → S9 登山捡石）：pebble 鹅卵石，被水流长期打磨得圆滑的小石头；pebble beach 卵石滩。近义梯度：stone 泛指 → rock 岩块 → pebble 小圆石。

quiz.q: "Some damage is irreversible, so prevention is always the cheaper choice." Irreversible means —
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S13 消失的河蚌 → 本篇杂志的警告页）：irreversible damage / irreversible climate change 是环境类雅思阅读的最高频搭配。故事里那句"预防永远比修复便宜"（prevention is cheaper than cure）可直接搬进雅思大作文结论段。

quiz.q: "The breeze turning this page..." A breeze is —
quiz.ex: 跨篇复习（S4 追风的人里的"第一缕微风" → 本篇杂志结尾的抒情句）：风力阶梯 breeze < gust < gale < storm < hurricane。林老师用 breeze 收束全刊——轻的词放在重的位置，这正是本篇杂志的编辑美学。

title: The Glass Laboratory
text:
Mei had always thought plants were quiet furniture. Then she spent a morning in Dr Weber's laboratory, and never looked at a leaf the same way again.

"Welcome to the glasshouse," said Dr Weber, leading her past benches of green {{vegetation}}. "I teach {{botany}} here — the science of plants — but what I really want to show you is how a leaf makes its living."

The first room held a row of small sealed chambers, each containing one young wheat plant. "This is where we watch {{photosynthesis}} at work," she said. "The leaf {{absorb}}s sunlight, takes in carbon {{dioxide}}, and uses the captured {{energy}} to build sugar. As a by-product, it {{release}}s oxygen — the very gas you are breathing now." Beside each chamber, sensors recorded the {{uptake}} of carbon dioxide going in and the {{emission}} of oxygen coming out; the numbers {{fluctuate}}d gently with the light, peaking at noon and sliding towards evening.

"Behind all of this is chemistry," she added. "Inside every cell, an {{enzyme}} called rubisco works as a {{catalyst}}, making the sugar-building reaction run fast enough to matter. Without it, a leaf would be a kitchen with no cook."

"At night the story turns around," she went on. "In darkness, every plant must {{respire}} — burning its own sugar to stay alive, taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide. A whole forest breathes in and out like a slow green animal."

In the corner, tubes carried a pale liquid to plants growing with no soil at all. "Our {{nutrient}} system," Dr Weber said. "The {{circulation}} {{mechanism}} keeps the mineral solution moving past the roots. If the salt level should {{exceed}} a safe limit, an alarm rings — too much of a good thing kills a plant as surely as too little."

The next room was warm and smelled of earth. On the bench stood three trays of seedlings: one green, one pale yellow, one with strangely curled leaves. "This pale one carries a {{mutation}} in a single gene," she explained. "{{genetics}} is the study of how such instructions pass from parent to offspring. That small {{variation}} between individuals is the raw material of everything: cross two plants and you get {{hybridisation}}; keep crossing for a hundred generations and the species slowly {{evolve}}s. {{diversity|Diversity}}, in the end, is a plant's only real insurance policy."

"And how do you keep track of them all?" Mei asked.

"We {{classify}} them — family, genus, species — and watch how each one {{reproduce}}s. Some need insects; some manage alone. That is half of {{ecology}}, the study of how living things fit together. The other half is in that tank." She pointed at a glass tank of water plants and tiny swimming creatures. "A small {{ecosystem}}: every {{organism}} inside it eats, and is eaten, and nothing is wasted."

Before Mei left, Dr Weber walked her past the outdoor trial beds, where an {{herb}} garden met rows of experimental flowers. "These are {{perennial}}s — they die down each winter and return each spring, no replanting needed. We garden the {{eco-friendly}} way here: no poison, just patience. People call it {{horticulture}}; I call it arguing politely with nature."

On the bus home, Mei caught herself watching the trees along the road — breathing, feeding, quietly working — and understood that she would never see them as furniture again.
tr:
梅一直觉得植物是安静的家具。直到在韦伯博士的实验室里度过一个上午之后，她再也不用从前的眼光看一片叶子了。

“欢迎来到玻璃温室。”韦伯博士领着她走过一排排绿色的植被（vegetation），“我在这里教植物学（botany）——研究植物的科学——但我真正想给你看的是：一片叶子如何谋生。”

第一间屋里放着一排密封小培养箱，每箱一株小麦苗。“我们在这里观察光合作用（photosynthesis），”她说，“叶片吸收（absorb）阳光，摄入二氧化碳（dioxide），用捕获的能量（energy）制造糖分，并作为副产品释放（release）氧气——正是你此刻呼吸的气体。”每个培养箱旁的传感器记录着流入的二氧化碳摄取量（uptake）与排出的氧气排放量（emission）；数字随光照轻轻波动（fluctuate），正午达峰，傍晚回落。

“这背后全是化学，”她补充道，“每个细胞里都有一种酶（enzyme）——rubisco——充当催化剂（catalyst），让造糖反应快到有意义。没有它，叶片就是一间没有厨师的厨房。”

“夜里故事就倒过来了，”她接着说，“黑暗中每株植物都必须呼吸（respire）——燃烧自己的糖分维持生命，吸入氧气、呼出二氧化碳。整片森林就这样像一头缓慢的绿色巨兽，日夜吞吐呼吸。”

角落里，管道把淡色液体送往完全无土栽培的植物。“营养（nutrient）系统，”韦伯博士说，“循环（circulation）机制（mechanism）让矿物溶液不停流过根部。一旦盐分超过（exceed）安全上限，警报就会响——好事过了头，和太少一样会杀死植物。”

隔壁房间很暖，有泥土的气息。台子上摆着三盘幼苗：一盘翠绿，一盘淡黄，一盘叶片怪异地打卷。“这盘黄的带有一个单基因突变（mutation），”她解释道，“遗传学（genetics）研究的正是这类指令如何从亲代传给后代。个体间这种细微的变异（variation）是一切的原材料：把两种植物杂交（hybridisation）得到杂种；连续培育一百代，物种就会慢慢进化（evolve）。多样性（diversity）说到底是植物唯一真正的保险单。”

“那你们怎么把它们都分清楚？”梅问。

“我们分类（classify）——科、属、种——再观察它们各自如何繁殖（reproduce）。有的靠昆虫，有的自己就行。这是生态学（ecology）的一半：研究生物如何彼此咬合。另一半在那个水箱里。”她指着一只养着水草和微小游动生物的玻璃缸，“一个小型生态系统（ecosystem）：里面每个生物（organism）都在吃，也都被吃，什么都不浪费。”

临别前，韦伯博士带她走过户外试验苗圃，香草（herb）园连着一排排实验花卉。“这些是多年生（perennial）植物——每年冬天枯萎，来年春天自己回来，不用重种。我们在这里用环保（eco-friendly）的方式做园艺（horticulture）：不下药，只靠耐心。人们叫它园艺学；我管它叫‘礼貌地跟自然讲道理’。”

回程的公交上，梅发现自己一路望着路边的树——它们在呼吸、在进食、在安静地干活——她知道自己再也不会把它们看成家具了。

quiz.q: The leaf absorbs sunlight, takes in carbon dioxide, and builds sugar. This process is photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is —
o: the movement of mineral solution past a plant's roots
the burning of sugar to release energy during the night
the process by which plants use light to make food from carbon dioxide and water
the transfer of pollen between two flowers
quiz.ex: photosynthesis = 光合作用：光吸收 + 二氧化碳 + 水 → 糖 + 氧气。记构词：photo-（光）+ synthesis（合成）。反义过程是 respiration（呼吸作用）：消耗氧气、分解糖分释放能量，日夜都在进行，只是白天被光合作用掩盖。

quiz.q: In darkness, every plant must respire, burning its own sugar to stay alive. To respire is to —
o: breathe; take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide
grow towards a source of light
quiz.ex: respire = 呼吸（动植物吸入氧气、释放二氧化碳的生理过程）。名词 respiration。植物白天光合作用产氧大于呼吸耗氧，所以净放氧；夜里只剩呼吸。雅思考题常考 respiration vs photosynthesis 的昼夜对比。

quiz.q: The leaf absorbs sunlight and takes in carbon dioxide. To absorb is to —
o: take in or soak up something
quiz.ex: absorb = 吸收（液体、光线、热量、信息等）。常见搭配：absorb water / nutrients / knowledge。对比 release / emit = 释放、排放。名词 absorption。

quiz.q: An enzyme called rubisco works as a catalyst, making the sugar-building reaction run fast enough. A catalyst is —
o: a gene that carries a mutation
a machine that pumps liquid around a laboratory
a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up
a sensor that records gas levels
quiz.ex: catalyst = 催化剂：加速化学反应而自身不被消耗。引申义也常考：a catalyst for change（变革的催化剂）。相关词 catalytic（催化的）。文中 enzyme（酶）本身就是生物体内的催化剂，rubisco 是地球上含量最多的酶。

quiz.q: This pale seedling carries a mutation in a single gene. A mutation is —
o: a chemical used to feed the roots
a change in the genetic material of an organism
quiz.ex: mutation = 突变：基因序列发生的改变，可遗传给后代。多数突变无影响或有害（如文中的 pale 叶色），少数带来有利变异。mutation 是 variation（变异/差异）的来源之一，而自然选择挑选有利变异，推动物种 evolve（进化）。

quiz.q: Cross two plants and you get hybridisation; keep crossing for a hundred generations and the species slowly evolves. Hybridisation is —
o: breeding two different varieties or species to produce mixed offspring
removing all variation from a population
the natural death of old leaves
the study of how organisms fit together
quiz.ex: hybridisation = 杂交（英式拼法；美式 hybridization）：不同品种/物种间繁殖，产生 hybrid（杂种）。现代农业的杂交水稻、杂交小麦都源于此。构词记忆：hybrid（杂种）+ -isation（…化）。

quiz.q: A small ecosystem: every organism inside it eats, and is eaten, and nothing is wasted. An ecosystem is —
o: a community of living things interacting with each other and their environment
a glass tank used for growing plants without soil
a family tree showing parent and offspring
a machine that circulates mineral solution
quiz.ex: ecosystem = 生态系统：生物群落 + 非生物环境（水、土、光）构成的自我维持整体。对比 ecology（生态学，学科名）与 organism（单个生物体）。雅思阅读常考 ecosystem services（生态系统服务）一词。

quiz.q: These are perennials — they die down each winter and return each spring, no replanting needed. A perennial plant is one that —
o: completes its whole life in a single year
lives for many years, reappearing each growing season
quiz.ex: perennial = 多年生的（per- 通过 + enn- 年，即"年复一年"）。反义词 annual = 一年生的。引申义 a perennial problem = 长期反复出现的老问题（雅思阅读高频用法）。

title: Grandfather's Garden
text:
My grandfather's garden was small, but it ran on a strict {{seasonal}} {{pattern}}: every plant had its month, and he knew them all by heart.

In March, the first green {{bud}}s broke open on the plum tree. By April the branches were white with {{blossom}}, and the {{scent}} drifted through the {{surroundings}} so sweetly that neighbours stopped at the gate. "Not just decoration," Grandpa said, watching a bee stumble from {{flower}} to flower. "That's {{pollen}} on the move. The bee is a deliveryman with wings."

Under the tree, purple {{violet}}s opened in the shade — truly {{shade-tolerant}} little plants, perfectly happy where the {{sunlight}} never fully reached. Along the path, the {{tulip}}s stood up like painted cups, and the {{mint}} by the tap grew so fast you could almost watch it. Grandpa pinched a leaf and held it to my nose: {{aromatic}}, sharp and cool. "Nature's chewing gum," he said. The roses by the bench would {{bloom}} on and on until November, and on the kitchen table there was always a {{vase}} of them.

Along the back wall climbed a grape {{vine}} older than my father; beside the gate stood an {{olive}} tree with silver leaves, and beyond it two tall {{pine}}s that dropped needles all year round.

In June, small hard green fruits hung where the blossoms had been. All summer they drank the sun and quietly {{ripen}}ed. When I finally picked one, still warm, the juice ran down my wrist. "A {{fruit}}," said Grandpa, "is a flower's second act." Each autumn he also saved the fattest bean {{seed}}s in a paper bag; sown in spring, they would {{germinate}} in the dark soil within a week, sending up pale shoots that {{burgeon}}ed into seedlings by May. The chrysanthemums were the patient ones — {{short day|short-day}} plants, he explained, that refused to open until the nights grew long.

After the harvest came the slow ending. Petals dropped, leaves yellowed and {{wither}}ed. Grandpa never burned them; he raked them onto the compost heap at the bottom of the garden, where they would {{decompose}} and {{rot}}, slowly settling into dark, crumbly earth. {{decay|Decay}}, he insisted, was "not dying, just changing address". White threads of {{fungus}} ran through the heap like tiny roads. And in his kitchen nothing was wasted: whatever bread went {{stale}} went out to the birds, and if they missed a piece, blue {{mould}} would claim it within a week.

I left that garden when I grew up. But every April, wherever I am, I catch the scent of plum blossom on some street corner and stand still — the whole cycle starting over, exactly as he planned it.
tr:
祖父的花园不大，却按一套严格的季节性（seasonal）规律（pattern）运转：每种植物都有属于自己的月份，而他全都记在心里。

三月，李树上第一批绿色的新芽（bud）绽开。到四月，枝头已开满白色的花朵（blossom），香气（scent）在四周（surroundings）飘散，甜得让邻居们在门口驻足。“这不光是好看，”祖父望着一只蜜蜂在花与花（flower）之间跌跌撞撞地说，“那是花粉（pollen）在赶路。蜜蜂就是长了翅膀的快递员。”

树下，紫色的紫罗兰（violet）在荫蔽处开放——真正耐阴（shade-tolerant）的小植物，在阳光（sunlight）照不透的地方也活得自在。小径旁，郁金香（tulip）像涂了颜色的杯子一样挺立，水龙头边的薄荷（mint）长得快得几乎能看着它长。祖父掐下一片叶子递到我鼻子前：芳香扑鼻（aromatic），清冽沁凉。“大自然的口香糖，”他说。长椅边的玫瑰会一直开放（bloom）到十一月，厨房桌上永远为它们摆着一只花瓶（vase）。

后墙上爬着比父亲年纪还大的葡萄藤（vine）；门边立着一棵银灰色叶子的橄榄树（olive），再远处是两棵整年掉针叶的松树（pine）。

六月，曾经开花的地方挂上了又小又硬的绿果子。整个夏天它们饮着阳光，悄悄成熟（ripen）。等我终于摘下一颗，还带着温度，果汁顺着我的手腕流下来。“果子（fruit），”祖父说，“不过是花的第二幕。”每年秋天他还把最饱满的豆子种子（seed）收进纸袋；春天播下，一周之内就在黑暗的泥土里发芽（germinate），抽出苍白的嫩枝，到五月便蓬勃生长（burgeon）成幼苗。菊花最有耐心——它们是短日照（short day）植物，他解释说，夜不够长就不肯开花。

收获之后是缓慢的谢幕。花瓣落了，叶子变黄、枯萎（wither）。祖父从不烧它们，而是把它们耙到花园尽头的堆肥堆上，在那里分解（decompose）、腐烂（rot），慢慢沉成黑褐色、一捏就碎的泥土。腐朽（decay），他坚持说，“不是死，只是换个住址”。白色的真菌菌丝（fungus）像细小的道路在肥堆里穿行。他的厨房里也从不浪费：面包一旦不新鲜（stale）就拿去喂鸟；鸟若没吃掉，一周之内蓝色霉菌（mould）就会认领它。

长大后我离开了那座花园。但每年四月，无论身在何处，我总会在某个街角闻到李子花香，然后站定——整个轮回又从头开始，一如他所安排的那样。

quiz.q: Watching a bee stumble from flower to flower, Grandpa says: 'That's pollen on the move.' Pollen is —
o: the silver skin on an olive leaf
the sweet liquid that fruits produce when ripe
the green insect that eats rose leaves
the fine powder made by flowers that fertilises other flowers
quiz.ex: pollen = 花粉：花的雄性生殖细胞，由风或昆虫带到另一朵花上完成授粉。搭配：be allergic to pollen（花粉过敏，雅思听力生活场景常见）。

quiz.q: Sown in spring, the bean seeds would germinate within a week. To germinate is to —
o: begin to grow, as a seed sprouts into a shoot
produce flowers at the end of summer
quiz.ex: germinate = （种子）发芽、开始生长。名词 germination（萌发）。对比 burgeon = 抽枝、蓬勃生长（多用于植物生长和抽象事物兴起，如 burgeoning demand 日益增长的需求）。

quiz.q: All summer the small green fruits drank the sun and quietly ripened. To ripen is to —
o: become fully grown and ready to eat
fall from the branch onto the ground
turn hard and dry in winter
change colour from purple to white
quiz.ex: ripen = 成熟（果实变得可以食用）。搭配：ripen in the sun。反义联想：rot / decay = 熟过头之后的腐烂。ripe（成熟的）即 a ripe banana 熟香蕉。

quiz.q: Petals dropped, leaves yellowed and withered. To wither is to —
quiz.ex: wither = 枯萎、凋谢（因缺水或季节结束而干缩死去）。习语 a withering look（令人难堪的眼神）为引申用法。对比：bloom（开花）是它的反方向。

quiz.q: On the compost heap, the leaves would decompose and rot, settling into dark earth. To decompose is to —
o: be carried away by the wind
break down naturally into simpler substances
be eaten by birds and insects
quiz.ex: decompose = 分解（有机物在微生物作用下分解为简单物质）。de-（分开）+ compose（组成），即"组成的逆过程"。近义词：decay、rot。decompose 强调化学过程，decay 强调渐坏，rot 强调结果腐烂发臭。

quiz.q: Whatever bread went stale went out to the birds. Bread that has gone stale is —
o: no longer fresh — dry and hard to eat
quiz.ex: stale = （食物）不新鲜的、变味走气的（如面包变硬、啤酒走气）。引申义：stale air 不流通的浊气；a stale joke 听腻了的笑话；stale news 过时消息。反义 fresh。

quiz.q: The scent drifted through the surroundings so sweetly that neighbours stopped at the gate. A scent is —
o: a smell, usually a pleasant one
the sound bees make in spring
quiz.ex: scent = 香味、气味（多指好闻的）。搭配：the scent of roses；a bottle of scent（一瓶香水，英式旧用法）。近义辨析：smell 中性、odour 偏书面（可好可坏）、fragrance/aroma 明确好闻。

quiz.q: The violets were shade-tolerant little plants, perfectly happy where the sunlight never fully reached. A shade-tolerant plant —
o: needs full sun all day long
can grow well with little direct light
only opens its flowers at night
quiz.ex: shade-tolerant = 耐阴的：能在弱光下正常生长。构词法记忆：shade（荫）+ tolerant（容忍的）。反义 sun-loving / light-demanding（喜阳的）。雅思阅读植物类文章常见此构词，如 drought-tolerant（耐旱的）、salt-tolerant（耐盐的）。

title: Harvest Week at Green Valley
text:
Every September I go back to Green Valley to help my uncle bring in the {{harvest}}, and every September I relearn how little I remember from the year before.

The farm sits on a slope of {{arable}} land — soil so deep and dark that, my uncle likes to say, "you could {{cultivate}} umbrellas here and they'd grow." The lower {{field}}s carry maize; the orchard climbs the hill in grassy {{terrace}}s; and beside the stream runs a strip of {{experimental}} rows where he trials new seed varieties with the agricultural college.

Harvest week starts at dawn. We {{pick}} apples by hand — "no machine can judge ripeness like fingers," he insists — and {{pluck}} the last tomatoes from the vines before the first frost claims them. Between the crop rows, the season's long war against {{weed}}s never truly ends; the old {{spade}} and the wooden {{rake}} hang in the shed, still trusted for corners the machines cannot reach, while the {{plough}} waits behind the tractor for its brief autumn moment of glory: once the maize is off, he will turn the soil over and {{sow}} winter wheat in a single breath of days.

By noon the yard has become a busy map of order: crates of fruit {{stack}}ed three high by the gate, a {{heap}} of stones cleared from the far corner, a {{bundle}} of bean poles tied with red string, a {{bunch}} of carrots saved for the neighbours' supper. The {{grass}} cut from the {{meadow}} twice each summer dries into sweet-smelling {{hay}}; the maize stalks, stripped of their cobs, are bundled into {{straw}} for the animals' winter beds. "Hay is food," my uncle recites, as he does every year, "straw is bedding. Never mix them up in front of a farmer." The most {{productive}} tree in the whole orchard, he points out, is the crooked old one by the gate — it has never once missed a year.

While we work, his wife {{rear}}s free-range chickens at the top of the yard, and the dog supervises everything from a patch of sun.

At supper he does the arithmetic. This year's {{yield}}, he reckons, will be {{considerable}} — the rain fell kindly in June and August stayed warm, the most {{favourable}} season in a decade. "Weather is the one partner you can't divorce," he says. The {{outcome}} of the experimental rows will decide next spring's seed order; a small trial, but its {{impact}} on the whole farm is real. He farms the way he cooks: {{optimal}} ingredients, {{minimal}} waste. The old combine harvester is slow but {{effective}}, he says; the new one is more {{efficient}} but "eats money". And a farm, he warns me, should never chase {{maximal}} output at the price of taste.

On the last evening we walk down to the bottom field, the one my great-grandfather {{reclaim}}ed from the marsh a hundred years ago, stone by stone. "Every farm is borrowed," my uncle says, kicking the good dark earth. "We only hold it for the next harvest."
tr:
每年九月我都会回绿谷帮叔叔收（harvest）庄稼，而每年九月我都会重新发现，自己把上一年的事忘得一干二净。

农场坐落在一片可耕种（arable）的坡地上——土壤深厚乌黑，叔叔喜欢说：“在这儿你就算种（cultivate）雨伞，它都能发芽。”下面的田（field）里种着玉米；果园顺着山坡修成一层层长草的梯田（terrace）；溪边还有一排试验（experimental）田，他和农学院一起试种新的种子品种。

收获周从黎明开始。我们用手摘（pick）苹果——“没有机器能像手指一样判断熟度，”他坚持说——赶在初霜之前，把最后一批番茄从藤上摘下（pluck）。庄稼行间的地里，整个季节与杂草（weed）的漫长战争从未真正结束；旧铁锹（spade）和木耙（rake）挂在棚里，机器够不到的角落还信得过它们；犁（plough）跟在拖拉机后面，等着它秋天短暂的荣耀时刻：玉米一收完，他就翻地，一鼓作气把冬小麦播（sow）下去。

到中午，院子成了一幅井然有序的作战图：水果箱在门口摞（stack）了三层，远处角落堆（heap）着清出来的石头，一捆（bundle）豆架用红绳扎着，一把（bunch）胡萝卜留给邻居的晚餐。每年夏天从草甸（meadow）上割两次的草（grass）晒成甜香的干草（hay）；褪掉玉米的秸秆扎成稻草（straw），给牲畜铺冬天的床。“干草是饲料，”叔叔像每年一样背诵，“稻草是铺草。别在农民面前搞混。”他还指着说，全果园产量最高（productive）的树是门口那棵歪脖子老树——它一年都没缺席过。

我们干活时，婶婶在院子尽头养（rear）着一群散养鸡，狗在一块阳光地里监督一切。

晚饭时他开始算账。今年的收成（yield），他估计会相当可观（considerable）——六月雨水下得正好，八月一直暖和，是十年来最顺遂（favourable）的季节。“天气是你唯一离不了的合伙人，”他说。试验田的结果（outcome）将决定明年春天订哪种种子；试验虽小，对整个农场的影响（impact）却是实打实的。他种地和做菜一个道理：用最佳（optimal）的原料，制造最少（minimal）的浪费。旧联合收割机慢是慢，但管用（effective）；新机器更有效率（efficient），可“它吃钱”。而一座农场，他警告我，永远不该为了最大（maximal）的产量牺牲味道。

最后一个傍晚，我们散步走到最底下的田地——那是曾祖父一百年前一块石头一块石头从沼泽里开垦（reclaim）出来的。“每座农场都是借来的，”叔叔踢了踢乌黑的好土，“我们只是替下一次收获看管它。”

quiz.q: The farm sits on a slope of arable land — soil so deep and dark. Arable land is land that —
o: is covered by buildings and roads
is too rocky for any use
quiz.ex: arable = 适于耕种的（land 即农田、耕地）。arable farming = 耕作农业，对比 pastoral farming（畜牧）。来源拉丁语 arare（犁地）。雅思农业类阅读高频词。

quiz.q: Once the maize is off, he will turn the soil over and sow winter wheat. To sow is to —
quiz.ex: sow = 播种（注意读音 /səʊ/，与"母猪"sow /saʊ/ 同形不同音）。reap/sow 连用：As you sow, so shall you reap 种瓜得瓜。搭配：sow the seeds of… 播下……的种子（也用于抽象义）。

quiz.q: This year's yield, he reckons, will be considerable. A yield is —
o: the money paid for new machines
the number of workers on a farm
quiz.ex: yield = 产量、收成（名词）；作动词时 = 屈服（yield to pressure）或让路。农作物语境：a high-yield variety 高产品种。注意与 production 区分：yield 强调单位产出的比例概念，是农业阅读核心词。

quiz.q: His wife rears free-range chickens at the top of the yard. To rear animals is to —
o: keep them in cages all winter
sell them at the spring market
raise and care for them until they are grown
quiz.ex: rear = 饲养、养育（动植物或孩子）。英式常用 rear livestock；美式多说 raise。搭配：be reared on… 吃……长大。rear 作名词还有"后部"义：the rear of the house 房屋后部。

quiz.q: The grass cut from the meadow twice each summer dries into sweet-smelling hay. Hay is —
o: the stalks left after grain has been removed
a pile of stones cleared from a field
grass that has been cut and dried for animal food
quiz.ex: hay = 干草（割下晒干的草，做饲料）。Make hay while the sun shines 趁晴晒草/抓紧时机（谚语）。务必与 straw（稻草/麦秆，做铺垫）区分——文中叔叔的原话正是考点。

quiz.q: The maize stalks are bundled into straw for the animals' winter beds. Straw is —
o: red string used to tie bean poles
grass cut and dried to feed animals
green leaves eaten by chickens in summer
dry stalks of grain crops, used mainly for bedding
quiz.ex: straw = 稻草、麦秆（脱粒后的干茎，铺牲畜圈或编草帽）。a straw in the wind 迹象；the last straw 压垮骆驼的最后一根稻草。与 hay（干草饲料）相对：straw 管"住"，hay 管"吃"。

quiz.q: The bottom field was the one my great-grandfather reclaimed from the marsh, stone by stone. To reclaim land is to —
o: cover it with a new building
give it up to the neighbouring farm
bring it back into useful condition
rent it out for one summer
quiz.ex: reclaim = 开垦、开拓（把荒地/沼泽变为可用之地）；也常考"回收"：reclaim materials 回收材料。re-（重新）+ claim（声称占有）→ 重新拿回来用。文中"从沼泽开垦田地"是最经典用法。

quiz.q: We pluck the last tomatoes from the vines before the first frost claims them. To pluck is to —
o: water the plants late at night
cover the vines with white sheets
pull something off quickly with the fingers
quiz.ex: pluck = 摘、采、拔（迅速用手拽下）。pluck a chicken 拔鸡毛；pluck up courage 鼓起勇气（固定搭配）。与 pick 相比，pluck 更强调"拽、拔"的动作力度，pick 是中性的"采摘"。

title: The Keeper of Miller's Wood
text:
The first thing Ranger Silva told me was that a forest is not a photograph. "People think it should stay the same forever," she said, walking me into Miller's Wood. "But a living wood is always moving. Our job is to steer it, not to freeze it."

She had spent ten years in Brazil before this. Out there, she said, the {{rainforest}} is so vast and so loud with life that scientists still find unnamed birds in it. Her first job had been marking trees in a {{jungle}} camp; her second, measuring a pine {{plantation}} the size of a small country; and before all that, two damp years counting {{alga|algae}} on a coral {{reef}} for a coastal survey. "The jungle and the plantation taught me {{forestry}} — the craft of caring for forests — and both broke my heart a little."

Here the work was smaller, but the arithmetic was the same. "We cut {{timber}} from this wood," she said, patting a tall straight beech, "but only as fast as it grows. For every {{trunk}} we take, we plant three. The books must {{counterbalance}} — a forest that spends more than it earns goes bankrupt, same as a shop." The oldest oaks had trunks so wide that three people joining hands could just reach around one; their lowest {{bough}}s sagged with age, and every smaller {{branch}} carried its own little world of moss. "Half the tree is underground," she added, stamping the soil. "Damage a {{root}}, and the whole thing starts to lean."

By the pond, {{reed}}s bowed in the wind, and a hedge of blackthorn stood armed with {{thorn}}s — "the best fence birds ever had." Near the station grew the only mown {{lawn}} in the reserve ("for morale," she said), and on the gate hung a painted {{logo}}: a green circle holding one oak leaf, the mark of the {{conservation}} trust whose whole purpose is to {{preserve}} what the ice age left behind and to {{protect}} it from what the present keeps trying to do to it.

From the thinnings, the trust burns {{charcoal}} in old kilns and sells it to pay the rangers' wages. One fallen {{log}} lies exactly where it fell, on purpose. "A dead log feeds more lives than a living tree," she said. "Beetles, fungi, moss — a whole city."

Her face changed when we reached the ridge. "In 2019, a {{bush fire}} started up there — one campfire, one dry spring. We fought it for three days before a helicopter could {{extinguish}} it." The {{destruction}} had been {{massive}}: a third of the wood {{ruin}}ed, thousands of young trees {{perish}}ed, and the heat was so {{immense}} that it cracked the stones of the old visitor bridge, which later had to be {{demolish}}ed. The investigation found that campers had been breaking the rules for years — quietly {{infringe|infringing}} the reserve's no-fire zone — while the long droughts before had {{undermine}}d the trees' resistance. For the dormouse, she said quietly, that one summer pushed the local population to the very edge of {{extinction}}.

"So we plant," she said at last, nodding towards a slope of knee-high oaks. "People ask when the wood will be back to normal. I tell them: a forest is not a photograph. It's a film — and we've only just pressed play again."
tr:
护林员席尔瓦对我说的第一句话是：森林不是一张照片。“人们以为它该永远保持原样，”她边说边领我走进米勒树林，“可一片活着的林子始终在移动。我们的工作是掌舵，不是冻结。”

在这之前，她在巴西待过十年。她说，那里的雨林（rainforest）广袤无边、生命喧腾，科学家至今还能在里面发现没有名字的鸟。她的第一份工作是在丛林（jungle）营地给树木做标记；第二份是丈量一座小国那么大的松树种植园（plantation）；更早以前，还在一项海岸调查里度过两年潮湿的时光，数珊瑚礁（reef）上的海藻（alga）。“丛林和种植园教会了我林学（forestry）——照料森林的手艺——也都让我有点心碎。”

在这里，事情小得多，算术却一样。“我们从这片林子里伐木（timber），”她拍着一棵笔直的山毛榉说，“但只按它生长的速度砍。每取走一根树干（trunk），就补种三棵。账目必须相互抵消（counterbalance）——一座入不敷出的森林会破产，跟商店没有区别。”最老的橡树树干粗得三人合抱才能围拢；最低处的大枝（bough）被岁月压弯，每根较小的枝条（branch）上都长着一个苔藓的小世界。“树的一半在地下，”她跺了跺土，“伤了根（root），整棵树就开始倾斜。”

池塘边，芦苇（reed）在风里弯腰；一道黑刺李树篱浑身是刺（thorn）——“鸟儿用过的最好的栅栏”。护林站旁长着保护区里唯一一块修剪的草坪（lawn）（“为了士气，”她说）；大门上挂着徽标（logo）：绿色圆圈里一片橡树叶，那是保护（conservation）信托的标记。信托的全部使命，是保存（preserve）冰川时代留下的遗产，并保护（protect）它免遭当下一次次的觊觎。

信托用间伐的小树在旧窑里烧炭（charcoal），卖了钱支付护林员的工资。一根倒下的原木（log）被特意留在它倒下的地方。“一根死木头养活的生命比活树还多，”她说，“甲虫、真菌、苔藓——一整座城市。”

走到山脊时，她的神情变了。“2019年，一场丛林大火（bush fire）从那儿烧起来——一堆篝火，一个干燥的春天。我们扑了三天，直到直升机把它扑灭（extinguish）。”破坏（destruction）是巨大（massive）的：三分之一林子被毁（ruin），数千棵幼树枯死（perish）；热度大得（immense）连老游客桥的石头都崩裂了，后来只能整座拆除（demolish）。调查发现，露营者多年来一直在悄悄违反（infringe）保护区的禁火区规定；而此前连年的干旱也早已削弱（undermine）了树木的抵抗力。她声音很轻地说：对睡鼠而言，那个夏天把本地种群推到了灭绝（extinction）的边缘。

“所以我们种树，”她最后朝一片齐膝高的橡树苗点了点头。“有人问林子什么时候能恢复原样。我告诉他们：森林不是照片，是电影——而我们才刚刚重新按下播放键。”

quiz.q: We cut timber from this wood, but only as fast as it grows. Timber is —
o: the seeds of the oldest oaks
the paper made from young trees
wood prepared for building and other uses
quiz.ex: timber = 木材、木料（已砍伐备用的建筑用材）；英式英语也指"树林"。timber wolf 大灰狼为固定名称。与 lumber 近义（美式多叫 lumber）。雅思议题常考 sustainable timber 可持续木材。

quiz.q: For every trunk we take, we plant three — the books must counterbalance. To counterbalance is to —
o: offset one thing with an equal opposite effect
count the trees twice a year
sell the wood at a higher price
cut down more than you plant
quiz.ex: counterbalance = 抵消、平衡（counter- 相反 + balance 平衡）。名词用法：act as a counterbalance to… 对……起制衡作用。写作可用：Benefits are counterbalanced by risks. 利弊相抵。

quiz.q: We fought the fire for three days before a helicopter could extinguish it. To extinguish is to —
o: start a fire in dry grass
watch a fire from a safe distance
quiz.ex: extinguish = 扑灭（火）；引申义：extinguish hope 扼杀希望。名词 extinguisher 即"灭火器"（fire extinguisher）。形近词 distinguish（区分）勿混。

quiz.q: Campers had been quietly infringing the reserve's no-fire zone. To infringe is to —
o: report a crime to the rangers
break a rule, law or agreement
pay a fine at the station gate
quiz.ex: infringe = 违反、侵犯（规则、法律、权利）。搭配：infringe the law / on someone's rights。名词 infringement（侵权）。雅思法律类文章高频。与 violate 近义。

quiz.q: The long droughts before had quietly undermined the trees' resistance. To undermine is to —
o: dig beneath the roots of a tree
quiz.ex: undermine = 逐渐削弱、暗中破坏（under 下面 + mine 挖矿 → 从下面挖空）。高频学术用法：undermine confidence / authority / health。引申链：under-（在下）系列：underestimate 低估、underpay 少付。

quiz.q: A third of the wood was ruined and thousands of young trees perished. To perish is to —
o: die, especially suddenly or in large numbers
quiz.ex: perish = 死亡、暴毙（书面语，常用于灾难中大量死亡）。形容词 perishable = 易腐的（perishable goods 易腐货物，物流场景常考）。勿与 parish（教区）混淆。

quiz.q: The heat cracked the old visitor bridge, which later had to be demolished. To demolish is to —
o: pull down a building or structure completely
move something to a new location
quiz.ex: demolish = 拆除、摧毁（建筑）；引申：demolish an argument 驳倒论点。名词 demolition。近义辨析：demolish 拆建筑；destroy 泛指毁坏；ruin 强调"毁掉价值"；demolition derby 撞车赛是趣味联想。

quiz.q: That one summer pushed the local dormouse population to the very edge of extinction. Extinction is —
o: the protection given to rare animals
the state of a species dying out completely
quiz.ex: extinction = 灭绝（形容词 extinct 灭绝的/熄灭的）。搭配：be on the edge/brink of extinction 濒临灭绝；drive a species to extinction 使物种灭绝。恐龙经典句：Dinosaurs are extinct. 议论文常与 biodiversity（多样性）成对出现。

title: The Morning Round
text:
At six in the morning, before the gates open, the zoo belongs to the animals and to the people who look after them. I was allowed to follow the head {{keeper}}, Mr Ade, on his morning round.

He had once planned to be a {{zoologist}}, he told me as we walked, and had ended up as something between a nurse, a chef and a diplomat. The science was handled by Dr Nabi, the zoo's resident {{biologist}}; an old friend of hers, now an {{ecologist}}, advised on the design of the enclosures; and each spring a visiting {{botanist}} checked every plant that shared the animals' quarters. "A zoo is a small world," Mr Ade said. "You need all of biology to run one."

We started in the reptile house, where the {{reptile}}s were still cool and slow from the night. In the next room the {{amphibian}}s sat half in water, half out, breathing through their skins. "People forget," he said, "that {{creature}}s like these were the first to leave the ancient seas. Every {{vertebrate}} you will meet today — everything with a backbone — is their distant cousin."

The primate house smelled of fruit and warm fur. A young chimpanzee pressed its whole face against the glass to look at us. "Every {{mammal}} in this building feeds its young milk," said Mr Ade, "and most of them would rather be anywhere else. Homesickness is not a human monopoly."

The big cats were awake and pacing. "A {{carnivore}} eats meat and a {{herbivore}} eats plants," he recited, "but both spend their lives thinking about food. We {{feed}} the lions at nine — late enough to keep them keen, early enough to keep them calm."

On every enclosure hung a small sign with the animal's name and {{species}}. "It just means 'a kind'," he said. "But each sign is also a promise. Some of the kinds on these signs now survive better here than out there."

He paused by the wolf enclosure, where a new litter had been born in March. "People ask if zoo animals are sad. It's a fair question. A {{captive}} animal born here can't simply be released — it has never learned to hunt. But a well-kept one grows calm enough to {{breed}}, {{tame}} enough for the vet to examine without fear, and every birth here is a small victory for {{wildlife}}."

The enclosures themselves, he pointed out, were half the job. Each one copies the animal's natural {{habitat}}: sand or snow, pond or rock, with nesting boxes tucked where a bird would build its {{nest}}. The old iron {{cage}}s of the 1930s are long gone. Even the modern {{barrier}}s are disguised — a strip of water, a slope of glass — so that no {{bar}} crosses the visitor's view and the wolf seems free. Between the areas run the {{stable}} block for the ponies, the {{barn}} where the winter hay is kept, and a green {{hedge}} that hides the service paths. "In his day," Mr Ade said of his grandfather, "a zoo was a row of small boxes. People called the animals {{beast}}s, treated the strongest like a {{brute}}, and thought it funny. It was {{cruel}}, and we are still paying for it."

In the classroom by the offices, Dr Nabi was teaching {{anatomy}} — the map of bones and organs inside a body — to the new volunteers. Outside her window, the peacocks screamed like rusted hinges. "Remember," she called after us, "in the wild every animal out there is either {{prey}} or {{predator}} — often both in the same afternoon. Here, they are neither. That is the whole point."

As the first visitors came through the gates at nine, Mr Ade looked back once at the wolf cubs tumbling in the grass. "A zoo," he said, "is a promise that the world's {{fauna}} and {{flora}} outlast us. The rest is housekeeping."
tr:
清晨六点，大门还没开，动物园只属于动物和照料它们的人。我获准跟着管理员（keeper）阿德先生走了一趟晨巡。

他一边走一边告诉我，他年轻时想当动物学家（zoologist），最后却成了护士、厨师和外交家的混合体。科学研究交给园里的生物学家（biologist）纳比博士；她的一位老朋友现在是生态学家（ecologist），负责兽舍的设计顾问；每年春天还有一位植物学家（botanist）来检查与动物同住的每一株植物。“动物园是个小世界，”阿德先生说，“要经营它，得用上全部的生物学。”

我们从爬行动物馆开始，夜里变凉的爬行动物（reptile）还缓慢迟钝。隔壁房间里，两栖动物（amphibian）半坐水中、半露水面，用皮肤呼吸。“人们忘了，”他说，“正是这样的生物（creature）最先离开远古的海洋。你今天见到的每一只脊椎动物（vertebrate）——一切有脊椎的动物——都是它们的远亲。”

灵长类馆里满是水果和暖毛皮的气味。一只小黑猩猩把整张脸贴在玻璃上看我们。“这栋楼里的每只哺乳动物（mammal）都用乳汁哺育幼崽，”阿德先生说，“而且它们大多更愿意待在别处。想家可不是人类的专利。”

大猫们醒着，来回踱步。“食肉动物（carnivore）吃肉，食草动物（herbivore）吃草，”他背诵道，“但两者一辈子都在想吃的。我们九点喂（feed）狮子——晚一点让它们保持敏锐，早一点让它们保持安静。”

每个兽舍外挂着小牌子，写着动物的名字和物种（species）。“意思就是‘一种’，”他说，“但每块牌子也是一份承诺。牌子上的一些物种，如今在这里比在外面活得更好。”

他在狼舍前停下，三月里那里新添了一窝幼崽。“有人问动物园里的动物难不难过。这问题问得对。在这里出生的圈养（captive）动物不能直接放归——它从没学过捕猎。但照料得好的动物会平静到足以繁殖（breed），驯服（tame）到能让兽医检查而不恐惧。这里每一次新生命，都是野生动物（wildlife）的一次小小胜利。”

他指着兽舍本身说，设计就占了一半的功夫。每一座都在模仿动物的自然栖息地（habitat）：沙或雪、池塘或岩石，筑巢箱藏在鸟儿会筑巢（nest）的地方。上世纪三十年代的铁笼（cage）早已拆除；连现代的屏障（barrier）都做了伪装——一道水沟、一面斜玻璃——视线里没有任何栅栏（bar），狼看起来是自由的。各区之间是矮种马的马厩（stable）区、存放过冬干草的谷仓（barn），还有一条挡住后勤小路的绿篱（hedge）。“在我祖父那个年代，”阿德先生说起旧事，“动物园就是一排小盒子。人们管动物叫野兽（beast），把最强壮的当作蛮兽（brute）对待，还觉得有趣。那很残忍（cruel），我们至今仍在偿还这笔账。”

办公室旁的教室里，纳比博士正给新志愿者讲解解剖学（anatomy）——身体里骨骼与器官的地图。她窗外，孔雀叫得像生锈的铰链。“记住，”她在我们身后喊，“在野外，那里的每只动物不是猎物（prey）就是捕食者（predator）——常常同一个下午两者都是。在这里，它们两者都不是。这正是全部意义所在。”

九点，第一批游客进门。阿德先生回头望了一眼草地上翻滚的小狼崽。“动物园，”他说，“是一个承诺：让世界的动物群（fauna）与植物群（flora）活得比我们更久。剩下的，都是家务事。”

quiz.q: He had once planned to be a zoologist, and ended up as something between a nurse and a diplomat. A zoologist is a scientist who studies —
quiz.ex: zoologist = 动物学家。构词规律：-ologist = "……学家"，词根 zoo-（动物）。同族词：biologist（生物学家）、ecologist（生态学家）、botanist（植物学家）。雅思听力Part 4讲座中常出现这类职业词。

quiz.q: Every vertebrate you will meet today — everything with a backbone — is their distant cousin. A vertebrate is an animal that —
quiz.ex: vertebrate = 脊椎动物（vertebr- 脊椎）。反义词 invertebrate 无脊椎动物。分类链：脊椎动物下分哺乳类 mammal、鸟类、爬行类 reptile、两栖类 amphibian、鱼类。"用乳汁哺育幼崽"是 mammal（哺乳动物）的定义，别与 vertebrate 混淆。

quiz.q: A carnivore eats meat and a herbivore eats plants. A carnivore is —
o: an animal that eats only fruit
quiz.ex: carnivore = 食肉动物（carni- 肉 + vor- 吃）。herbivore 食草动物；omnivore 杂食动物（omni- 全部）。人类是 omnivore。形近词 herbivorous / carnivorous 为形容词形式。

quiz.q: A captive animal born here can't simply be released — it has never learned to hunt. A captive animal is one that —
o: is kept enclosed and not free
quiz.ex: captive = 被圈养的、被俘的（名词指俘虏/被圈养的动物）。搭配：captive breeding 圈养繁殖（保护生物学核心概念）。captivity 名词：be born / held in captivity 圈养出生/被囚。

quiz.q: A well-kept animal grows calm enough to breed, and every birth here is a small victory. To breed is to —
quiz.ex: breed = 繁殖（动词）；名词指"品种"（a rare breed of sheep）；breeder 指饲养者。过去式 bred。注意与 brood（一窝幼鸟；孵蛋）拼写仅一字母之差。

quiz.q: Each enclosure copies the animal's natural habitat: sand or snow, pond or rock. A habitat is —
o: the country where a zoo is located
the cage designed by zoo architects
the natural home of a plant or animal
quiz.ex: habitat = 栖息地（拉丁语 habitare 居住）。高频搭配：habitat loss / destruction 栖息地丧失（物种灭绝头号原因）；natural habitat 自然栖息地。雅思阅读环保话题核心词。

quiz.q: In the wild every animal is either prey or predator, often both in the same afternoon. Prey is —
o: the meat sold at the zoo shop
an animal hunted and eaten by another
quiz.ex: prey = 猎物（名词）；动词 prey on = 捕食、（引申）坑害：prey on the elderly。搭配 fall prey to… 沦为……的猎物。与 predator（捕食者）构成一对。

quiz.q: Dr Nabi was teaching anatomy — the map of bones and organs inside a body. Anatomy is —
o: the behaviour of animals in groups
the history of an old zoo
the scientific study of body structures
quiz.ex: anatomy = 解剖学、（动植物的）结构（ana- 分开 + tomy 切割）。形容词 anatomical。引申义：the anatomy of a crisis 一场危机的剖析（雅思阅读标题常见）。

title: One Week at the Wildlife Hospital
text:
The Wildlife Hospital takes in about two thousand hurt animals a year. I spent a week there with Dr Reyes, and every morning began with the same question on the whiteboard: who is worse today?

Monday brought a {{fox}} with a torn {{fur}} coat and a trap mark on one {{paw}}. "Look at the {{claw}}s," said Dr Reyes, gently extending a foot; they {{curl}} like hooks. "Made for gripping, not for glass." The fox watched us with yellow eyes and did not {{bite}} — "a good sign; fear is tiring, and calm patients heal faster." While she worked, its whiskers kept {{bristle|bristling}}, the only part of it that admitted any fear.

Tuesday was bird day. A {{swan}} had flown into a power line; a young {{crow}} with a bent {{beak}} was learning to eat from a spoon; a {{pigeon}} — the hospital's most frequent customer — had met a car. "A {{flock}} of starlings can turn a whole sky dark," Dr Reyes said, resetting the broken {{wing}} with two flat sticks and tape, "but a single pigeon can't argue with a bus." She gathered the loose {{feather}}s from the towel. "Every one is a page from a bird's diary," she said, and indeed the swan's {{plume}}s, snow-white and slightly oily, told her it had been healthy until the evening it met the wire.

Wednesday brought a shoebox with a {{swarm}} of bees rescued from a garage — nobody stung, "they only {{sting}} when the hive is threatened" — and a hedgehog caught by a dog. The hedgehog had rolled into a ball: fully {{defensive}}, every spike saying don't touch. "Hedgehogs {{creep}} along the ground at night, slow and low, eating worms," she explained. "They can't run from danger, so they curl — an {{instinct}} older than roads. Against foxes it works beautifully. Against cars, not at all." He was a {{victim}} of the rush hour, one of dozens each autumn; the road-casualty records were how the hospital learned which species {{suffer}} most from our traffic, and which were simply too {{vulnerable}} to keep living near us at all. "Half our job," she said quietly, "is counting."

Thursday began with a bat found unconscious on an office carpet; on the ground bats can only {{crawl}}, and the paper-thin {{skin}} of its wing had torn on a chair leg. The afternoon's bigger cases were a {{seal}} pup from the coast, a fishing line wound deep near its left {{fin}}, and an old sheepdog kicked by a cow, yelping in a thin {{bark}}, who {{rub}}bed his bandaged side against the kennel wall until Dr Reyes moved his bed to the cool end. He would {{undergo}} an operation on Friday and, she expected, complain through all of it.

The week's loudest guest arrived Friday evening: a young red deer stag, separated from its {{herd}} in the fog. In October, she told me, the park rumbles all night — the stags {{roar}} to warn off rivals — and every autumn a few wanderers end up in towns, dazed by streetlights, with a {{throng}} of onlookers gathering. "A {{crowd}} makes everything worse," she said. "People mean well. But noise is stress, and stress is shock."

Saturday was release day. The fox went back to the field behind the hospital, wearing a small radio collar. "Now the real work starts," Dr Reyes said, watching the screen that would {{track}} it. "Surgery is craft. What happens after — whether it eats, whether it hides, whether it survives — that's the {{trace}} we follow for months." Her hands, I had noticed all week, moved before her words did: she felt a fracture, or a fever, or a lie, and only then explained it. "You learn the theory," she said, "and then your hands learn the rest. The second part isn't in books — it's {{intuitive}}."

On my last evening I asked her how she kept doing it, given how many did not make it. She thought for a while. "Because the ones that do make it wouldn't {{exist}} without this place. The hedgehog with the fixed leg has no opinion about statistics." She smiled. "Neither have I, after eight years. You just keep fixing legs."
tr:
野生动物医院每年收治约两千只受伤的动物。我在那里跟着雷耶斯博士待了一周，每天早晨都是从白板上的同一个问题开始：今天谁的情况更糟？

周一送来一只狐狸（fox），毛皮（fur）外套撕裂，一只爪子（paw）上有兽夹的痕迹。“看看这些爪子（claw），”雷耶斯博士说着，轻轻扳开一只脚；爪子像钩子一样卷曲（curl）着。“天生是用来抓握的，不是用来对付玻璃的。”狐狸用黄眼睛看着我们，没有咬（bite）人——“这是个好迹象；恐惧很耗体力，安静的病人好得快。”她处理伤口时，狐狸的胡须一直竖着（bristle），那是它全身唯一承认害怕的部位。

周二是鸟类日。一只天鹅（swan）撞上了电线；一只喙（beak）撞弯的年轻乌鸦（crow）正在学用勺子进食；还有一只鸽子（pigeon）——医院最常来的顾客——被汽车撞了。“一群（flock）椋鸟能让整片天空变黑，”雷耶斯博士用两根平木条和胶带固定好折断的翅膀（wing），“但一只鸽子争不过一辆公交车。”她把毛巾上散落的羽毛（feather）收拢起来。“每一根都是鸟类日记里的一页，”她说。确实，天鹅雪白、略带油光的翎羽（plume）告诉她：在撞上电线的那晚之前，它一直很健康。

周三带来一只鞋盒，里面是从车库救出的一群（swarm）蜜蜂——没有人被蜇，“只有蜂巢受到威胁时它们才蜇（sting）人”——还有一只被狗咬伤的刺猬。刺猬蜷成了球：完全处于防御（defensive）状态，每根尖刺都在说“别碰”。“刺猬夜里贴着地面缓慢爬行（creep），又慢又低，找虫子吃，”她解释道。“遇到危险它们跑不掉，所以只能蜷起来——一种比道路古老得多的本能（instinct）。对付狐狸，这招非常好用。对付汽车，毫无用处。”它是晚高峰的受害者（victim），每年秋天都有几十只；道路伤亡记录让医院得以了解哪些物种在我们的车流中受苦（suffer）最深，哪些则实在太脆弱（vulnerable），根本无法继续生活在人类身边。“我们一半的工作，”她轻声说，“是数数。”

周四先是从办公室地毯上救起一只昏迷的蝙蝠；蝙蝠在地面上只能爬行（crawl），它翅膀上薄如纸张的皮肤（skin）被椅子腿划破了。下午的重头戏是一只从海边送来的海豹（seal）幼崽，鱼线在它左鳍（fin）附近割出了深深的伤口；还有一只被奶牛踢伤的老牧羊犬，发出细细的吠叫（bark），不停地把缠着绷带的一侧身子在犬舍墙上蹭（rub），直到雷耶斯博士把它的床挪到阴凉的那头。它周五要接受（undergo）一场手术，而她预计，整个过程它都会抱怨个不停。

本周嗓门最大的客人是周五傍晚到的：一只在大雾中与鹿群（herd）走散的年轻雄赤鹿。她告诉我，每年十月，公园整夜轰鸣——雄鹿咆哮（roar）着警告对手——每年秋天总有几只迷路的鹿出现在城镇里，被路灯晃得发懵，身边围起一群（throng）看热闹的人。“围观人群（crowd）只会让一切更糟，”她说。“大家都是好意。但噪音就是压力，压力就是休克。”

周六是放归日。狐狸回到了医院后面的田野，脖子上戴着小型无线电项圈。“真正的工作现在才开始，”雷耶斯博士望着即将追踪（track）它的屏幕说。“手术是手艺。之后发生的事——它吃不吃、藏不藏、活不活得下来——那才是我们要追寻几个月的踪迹（trace）。”这一周里我注意到，她的手总是先于她的话行动：她先摸到骨折、发烧或谎言，然后才解释。“理论可以学，”她说，“然后你的手学会剩下的部分。第二部分书上没有——它靠直觉（intuitive）。”

最后一个晚上，我问她，这么多动物没能活下来，她是怎么坚持下来的。她想了一会儿。“因为活下来的那些，没有这个地方就不复存在（exist）了。腿接好的刺猬对统计数字毫无意见。”她笑了。“八年之后，我也没有。你只管接腿就是了。”

quiz.q: While she worked, the fox's whiskers kept bristling — the only part of it that admitted any fear. When hair or whiskers bristle, they —
quiz.ex: bristle = （毛发）竖起；（人）怒气冲冲：The idea made him bristle. 这个念头让他火冒三丈。名词 bristle = 硬毛、鬃毛（猪鬃刷）。

quiz.q: The swan's plumes, snow-white and slightly oily, told her it had been healthy. A plume is —
quiz.ex: plume = 大羽毛、羽饰。引申义高频：a plume of smoke / steam 一缕烟/蒸汽（烟柱）。plumage = （一只鸟的）全身羽毛（集合名词）。

quiz.q: Wednesday brought a shoebox with a swarm of bees rescued from a garage. A swarm is —
o: a large group of insects moving together
quiz.ex: swarm = 蜂群、一大群（飞行昆虫）。动词搭配：swarm with = 挤满、充满：The garage swarmed with bees. 类似量词群：a flock of birds、a herd of cattle、a school of fish。

quiz.q: The hedgehog had rolled into a ball: fully defensive, every spike saying don't touch. If an animal is defensive, it is —
quiz.ex: defensive = 防御的、戒备的。体育场景：defensive player 防守队员。引申略带贬义：a defensive attitude 辩解的、随时准备自我开脱的态度。动词 defend + -sive。

quiz.q: They can't run from danger, so they curl — an instinct older than roads. An instinct is —
o: a memory of a past injury
a skill learned by watching others
natural behaviour one is born with
a plan made the night before
quiz.ex: instinct = 本能、直觉。搭配：by instinct 凭本能；instinct for survival 求生本能。形容词 instinctive 本能的；近义 intuitive 直觉的（凭感觉、不假思索）。

quiz.q: The records showed which species suffer most from our traffic, and which were too vulnerable to live near us. Vulnerable means —
quiz.ex: vulnerable = 易受伤害的、脆弱的。高频搭配：vulnerable to attack / disease / criticism 易受攻击/患病/批评。环保话题：vulnerable species 易危物种（IUCN保护级别，介于近危与濒危之间）。

quiz.q: You learn the theory, and then your hands learn the rest — the second part is intuitive. Intuitive means —
o: known by feeling rather than by logic
quiz.ex: intuitive = 直觉的。反义高频词：counter-intuitive 反直觉的（雅思阅读常见：a counter-intuitive finding 出人意料的发现）。名词 intuition 直觉。

quiz.q: He would undergo an operation on Friday and complain through all of it. To undergo is to —
quiz.ex: undergo = 经历、接受（正式用语，多指不愉快的事）。不规则变化：undergo – underwent – undergone。高频搭配：undergo surgery / tests / training / a transformation 接受手术/检测/培训；经历转变。

title: The Station on the Point
text:
The research station on the point has two jobs: rescue whatever the sea sends ashore, and understand what is still swimming out there. I arrived in June, when both were busy at once.

That week, a {{calf}} — a young pilot {{whale}} — had stranded on the sand below the cliff. She was thin and dehydrated, and the vet's first act was to {{derive}} her weight from a tape measure, length times girth, because no scale in the county could hold a whale. Blood samples went to the lab, where a technician counted white blood {{cell}}s and read the levels of {{protein}} and {{vitamin}} in her plasma. "Her {{metabolism}} is running on empty," the vet said. "She has been burning her blubber for weeks."

Whales, the station director told me, {{originate}}d — in the deepest sense — on land. Their oldest {{ancestor}} was a small hoofed animal that waded into warm estuaries fifty million years ago; every whale in the ocean is its {{descendant}}, carrying a {{gene}} kit that is still recognisably mammalian. "Which means," she said, "that when we treat one, half of veterinary medicine applies. The other half we are still writing."

While the calf swam in the rehabilitation pool, the field team took me out to watch the colony of elephant seals on the far beach. A {{bull}} lay like a mountain among his females, scarred from a hundred {{courtship}} battles; two fat {{pup}}s slept beside their mothers. In the water, a male was showing off for a possible {{mate}} — a young female who would be {{mature}} enough to breed next season, and who watched him with what I can only describe as indifference.

The seals' {{behaviour}} changes completely between land and sea, the biologist explained. On shore they are slow and quarrelsome; underwater they dive for half an hour at a time, hunt fish at depth, and {{swallow}} their prey whole. Every animal is logged: a {{subgroup}} of the colony carries satellite tags, so the team knows which individuals hunt where, and which ones are drifting toward busy shipping lanes.

Back at the lab, an intern was listening to hydrophone recordings. "The whale side of our work runs on {{acoustic}} data," she said. Whale song travels hundreds of kilometres, and the instruments that record it are {{sensitive}} enough to hear a ship crossing an ocean. Nobody who listens for long doubts whale {{intelligence}}, the intern added: the songs change between years, the calves learn them slowly, and mothers in a pod take turns babysitting one another's young. The {{optical}} side was less romantic: a machine measured how far light penetrates the water, because clarity decides where plankton can grow — and where the fish that {{spawn}} in the bay will find food for their {{offspring}}.

The bay itself was changing. Warm years brought jellyfish that {{proliferate}} in the new temperatures. {{Turtle}}s that {{lay}} their eggs on the island beach — females {{alternate}} between flippers as they dig the nest chamber, a rhythm that has survived millions of years — now return to sand that is too hot. "The sex of a turtle is decided by the temperature of the egg," the director said. "Hot sand makes females. It is a slow problem, and one with the {{potential}} to end the colony." A turtle at sea drinks seawater and stays fresh, she added: glands near her eyes {{secrete}} concentrated salt, which she then {{excrete}}s — which is why stranded turtles always look as if they are crying. In a normal year, the eggs would {{hatch}} about sixty days later, at night, and the hatchlings would run straight for the brightest horizon — the moon on the water.
tr:
海角上的研究站有两项工作：救助海浪送上岸的一切，并理解仍在海里游动的一切。我是六月到的，那时两项工作正同时繁忙。

那一周，一头幼崽（calf）——一头小领航鲸（whale）——搁浅在悬崖下的沙滩上。它又瘦又脱水，兽医做的第一件事是用一条卷尺推算（derive）它的体重——体长乘以体围——因为全县没有一台秤能称下一头鲸。血样送进实验室，技师在那里数白血球（cell）的数量，读出血浆中蛋白质（protein）和维生素（vitamin）的水平。“它的新陈代谢（metabolism）已经空转了，”兽医说。“它燃烧自己的鲸脂已经烧了好几个星期。”

站长告诉我，从最根本的意义上说，鲸是起源于（originate）陆地的。它们最古老的祖先（ancestor）是一种五千万年前走进温暖河口的小型有蹄动物；海里的每一头鲸都是它的后代（descendant），携带着一套仍然明显属于哺乳动物的基因（gene）。“也就是说，”她说，“我们治疗一头鲸时，一半的兽医学可以直接套用。另一半，我们还在边写边学。”

幼鲸在康复池里游动期间，野外小组带我出海，去看远处海滩上的象海豹群。一头雄海豹（bull）像一座山一样卧在它的雌性中间，身上留着上百场求偶（courtship）争斗的伤疤；两只肥硕的幼崽（pup）睡在母亲身边。水里，一头雄性正在向一位可能的配偶（mate）炫耀——那是一头明年才到性成熟（mature）年龄的年轻雌性，而它看他的眼神，我只能形容为漠不关心。

生物学家解释说，海豹的行为（behaviour）在陆地和海里完全不同。在岸上它们迟缓又爱吵架；在水下它们一次能潜半小时，在深处捕鱼，把猎物整个吞下（swallow）。每一只都有记录：群体里的一个小群（subgroup）佩戴着卫星标签，这样团队就知道哪些个体在哪里捕猎，哪些正在漂向繁忙的航道。

回到实验室，一名实习生正在听水听器的录音。“我们的鲸类研究靠声学（acoustic）数据运转，”她说。鲸歌能传播数百公里，录制它的仪器灵敏（sensitive）到能听见一艘船横穿一片大洋。实习生还说，凡是长时间听过录音的人，都不会怀疑鲸的智力（intelligence）：鲸歌年年在变，幼鲸要慢慢学唱，鲸群里的母亲们还会轮流照看彼此的孩子。工作中光学（optical）的那一半则不那么浪漫：一台机器测量光线能穿透水面多深，因为水的清澈度决定浮游生物能在哪里生长——也决定在海湾里产卵（spawn）的鱼能否为它们的后代（offspring）找到食物。

海湾本身也在变化。暖水年份带来成群的水母，它们在新的水温里大量繁殖（proliferate）。在岛上沙滩产卵（lay）的海龟（turtle）——雌龟挖产卵巢穴时两只前鳍交替（alternate）使用，这种节奏已经延续了数千万年——如今回到的沙子却热得发烫。“海龟的性别由孵化温度决定，”站长说。“热沙孵出雌龟。这是个慢问题，也是一个有潜力（potential）终结整个种群的问题。”她还说，海里的海龟喝海水却保持体内清淡：它眼睛附近的腺体分泌（secrete）高浓度盐分，再将其排出（excrete）——这就是搁浅的海龟看起来总像在哭的原因。在正常的年份，蛋大约六十天后会在夜里孵化（hatch），小海龟径直奔向最亮的地平线——月光洒在水面上的方向。

quiz.q: Her metabolism is running on empty — she has been burning her blubber for weeks. Metabolism is —
o: the speed at which a whale swims
the total weight of an animal
all the chemical processes in a living body
the fat layer under the skin
quiz.ex: metabolism = 新陈代谢。派生词：metabolic 代谢的。雅思健康类高频：a fast / slow metabolism 快/慢代谢；boost your metabolism 促进代谢。blubber（鲸脂）是鲸的能量储备。

quiz.q: Their oldest ancestor was a small hoofed animal that waded into warm estuaries fifty million years ago. An ancestor is —
o: a family member from long ago
the plant an animal feeds on
a fossil with no living relatives
quiz.ex: ancestor = 祖先。反义词 descendant 后代。形容词 ancestral 祖传的：ancestral home 祖籍。同义表达：forebear（正式）。

quiz.q: The vet's first act was to derive her weight from a tape measure, length times girth. To derive something is to —
o: ask another station for the number
quiz.ex: derive = 取得、源自。高频搭配：derive sth from sth 从……获得；derive from 源于（= originate from / stem from）。名词 derivative 派生物；（数学）导数。

quiz.q: Warm years brought jellyfish that proliferate in the new temperatures. To proliferate is to —
quiz.ex: proliferate = 激增、大量繁殖。名词 proliferation 扩散/激增：the proliferation of plastic waste 塑料垃圾的激增（雅思环保高频）。近义：multiply、mushroom（比喻用法）。

quiz.q: Glands near her eyes secrete concentrated salt, which she then excretes. To secrete is to —
quiz.ex: secrete = 分泌（se- 分开 + crete 筛出）。名词 secretion 分泌物。形近辨析：secrete（分泌）与 secret（秘密）发音相同、拼写仅差一个 e；excrete = 排泄（排废物），一对高频易混词。

quiz.q: Females alternate between flippers as they dig the nest chamber. To alternate is to —
o: use both at the same time
use first one and then the other in turn
stop digging in order to rest
quiz.ex: alternate v. 交替；adj. 交替的/轮流的：on alternate days 每隔一天。名词 alternative 可供选择的事物；副词 alternatively 另外、换个做法（写作高频衔接词）。注意 alternate 与 alternative 的分工。

quiz.q: The fish that spawn in the bay will find food for their offspring. Offspring are —
o: the eggs left on the seabed
the young of a person or animal
the oldest members of a group
quiz.ex: offspring = 后代、幼崽。单复数同形：one offspring, two offspring。同族表达：young（集合名词）、cub（食肉/熊科幼崽）、chick（雏鸟）、kitten（幼猫）。

quiz.q: A bull lay among his females, scarred from a hundred courtship battles. Courtship is —
o: the behaviour by which animals attract a mate
the fight for territory between two males
the seasonal move to colder water
quiz.ex: courtship = 求偶（court 追求 + -ship 表状态/身份）。动词 court = 追求；引申 court disaster 招致灾难。构词规律：-ship 结尾名词：friendship、leadership、membership。

title: A Year on the Hill Farm
text:
Marta's farm sits at twelve hundred metres, where the road ends and the footpaths begin. It is close to a {{subsistence}} farm — "we eat what we grow, and sell whatever is left" — with twenty sheep, six {{cattle}}, two water {{buffalo}} who love the wet meadow, an old {{ox}} too patient for words, a grey {{donkey}}, and a {{horse}} called Bianca who believes the whole farm belongs to her.

The day is arranged around animals. At five the {{cock}} announces the sunrise, whether or not the sun agrees. A {{goose}}, Marta says, guards better than a dog — nothing crosses her yard unseen. In the corner pen a hen is {{brood|brooding}}, sitting tight on ten eggs, and woe to anyone who reaches beneath her. In the granary the war is permanent: the {{mouse}} lives behind the flour sacks and the barn {{rat}} under the floorboards, and both are hunted by a cat who works for her supper, while the hens scratch for their {{worm}}s outside the door.

"Sheep first." Marta is a {{shepherd}} the way her grandmother was: the flock goes up the hill in the morning and comes home at dusk. Lambs born in March can stand within the hour; by June a {{lamb}} is a small jumping engine. But spring is also the season of worry. A {{wolf}} came out of the forest in April and took two of them. "When my grandmother was young," Marta said, "the government paid for wolf skins. They nearly managed to {{exterminate}} them in this whole valley. Now the wolves are protected, and we are learning to live together again — with dogs, fences, and fewer grudges."

The garden has its own enemies. {{Pest}}s — slugs and aphids — {{devour}} the bean seedlings overnight, so the beds are ringed with ash. A {{hare}} lives in the alfalfa and is tolerated; the {{sparrow}}s of the yard are welcome because they feed their chicks on insects; the {{squirrel}}s in the oaks are not welcome at all, since they steal the walnuts before they fall. At the garden's slow end lives an ancient {{tortoise}} — the fourth generation of the family to be called Pietro — who disappears in October into {{hibernation}} under the compost heap and reappears in April with the first warm rain.

Even the non-animal problems are animal-adjacent. The old water pipe used to freeze; the new plastic one is {{flexible}} enough to bend where the frost heaves the ground. The new barn is purely {{functional}} — straight walls, no carving, none of the romance of the old one — but it holds heat far better. In February, when the hay runs low, the sheep get pressed {{cube}}s of alfalfa. And in the lean-to hang two kinds of leather: Bianca's {{saddle}}, used once a year at the fair, and the ox's {{harness}}, used twice a week all winter, hauling wood.

Does anything on the farm turn a profit? Marta shrugs. "All my problems {{stem}} from the same root: the farm is big enough to be work, and too small to be a business." Her neighbours try different routes. One {{hybridise}}s his beans — crossing his own line with an imported one, then saving seed for years to fix the mix. Another keeps wolfish-looking dogs and only shrugs when the vet reminds him that dogs and wolves {{interbreed}} freely wherever forest touches farmland. And up at the top pasture, where the fence ends, the summer left its proof: a {{bear}} had broken the apple tree in September, before the long sleep. "He was fat and in a hurry," said Marta, hammering the post back in. "We were all young once."
tr:
玛尔塔的农场坐落在海拔一千二百米的地方，公路到此为止，剩下的只有小径。这几乎是自给自足（subsistence）的农场——“我们吃自己种的，剩下的才拿去卖”——养着二十只羊、六头牛（cattle）、两头喜欢湿草甸的水牛（buffalo）、一头耐心得无话可说的老阉牛（ox）、一头灰驴（donkey），还有一匹名叫比安卡的马（horse），它坚信整个农场都归它所有。

一天的日程围着动物安排。五点，公鸡（cock）宣布日出，不管太阳同不同意。玛尔塔说，鹅（goose）比狗还会看家——院子里发生的任何事都逃不过它的眼睛。角落的围栏里，一只母鸡正在孵窝（brood），死死坐在十枚蛋上，谁敢把手伸到它肚子底下谁倒霉。粮仓里，战争是永恒的：小鼠（mouse）住在面粉袋后面，谷仓大鼠（rat）住在地板下面，追捕它们的那只猫靠晚餐付工资，母鸡们则在门外刨虫子（worm）吃。

“先管羊。”玛尔塔当牧羊人（shepherd）的方式和她祖母一样：羊群清早上山，黄昏回家。三月出生的羊羔（lamb）一小时内就能站立；到了六月，羊羔成了一台小小的跳跃机器。但春天也是担忧的季节。四月，一只狼（wolf）从森林里出来，叼走了两只羊羔。“我祖母年轻的时候，”玛尔塔说，“政府收购狼皮。他们几乎把整个山谷的狼都消灭（exterminate）干净了。如今狼受保护，我们重新学着共存——靠狗、围栏，还有少记一点仇。”

菜园有菜园的敌人。害虫（pest）——蛞蝓和蚜虫——一夜之间吞食（devour）掉豆苗，所以苗床四周撒了一圈草木灰。一只野兔（hare）住在苜蓿地里，被默许留下；院子里的麻雀（sparrow）受欢迎，因为它们用昆虫喂雏鸟；橡树上的松鼠（squirrel）则完全不受欢迎，因为核桃还没落地就被它们偷走了。菜园最里头住着一只老陆龟（tortoise）——已经是家里第四代叫它皮耶罗的了——它十月钻进堆肥堆下冬眠（hibernation），四月的头一场暖雨里重新露面。

连那些和动物无关的麻烦，也和动物沾边。旧水管总冻裂；新的塑料管足够柔韧（flexible），冻土拱起哪里它就弯到哪里。新谷仓纯粹讲实用（functional）——直上直下的墙，没有雕花，没有老谷仓的浪漫——但保温好得多。二月干草告急时，羊群能吃到压缩成方块（cube）的苜蓿饲料。杂屋里挂着两副皮具：比安卡的马鞍（saddle），一年只在集市上用一次；阉牛的挽具（harness），整个冬天每周两次，拉木头。

农场有什么能赚钱的吗？玛尔塔耸耸肩。“我所有的麻烦都源于（stem）同一个根子：这农场大到够干一辈子活，又小到做不成一门生意。”邻居们各显神通。有一位给菜豆杂交（hybridise）——用自家的品系和进口的杂交，然后花好几年留种把特性固定下来。另一位养着长得像狼的狗，兽医提醒他森林挨着农田的地方狗和狼可以自由异种交配（interbreed）时，他只是耸耸肩。而在最高处的牧场、围栏到头的地方，夏天留下了它的证据：九月里，一只熊（bear）折断了苹果树，就在它的长觉之前。“它吃得肥，走得急，”玛尔塔一边把桩子敲回去一边说，“我们也都年轻过。”

quiz.q: It is close to a subsistence farm — we eat what we grow, and sell whatever is left. A subsistence farm is one that —
o: produces just enough to feed the family
quiz.ex: subsistence = 生存、生计；自给自足。高频搭配：subsistence farming 自给农业；subsistence level 温饱水平；live below subsistence 生活在温饱线以下。雅思农业与发展类话题核心词。

quiz.q: In the corner pen a hen is brooding, sitting tight on ten eggs. To brood over eggs is to —
o: sit on them to keep them warm
feed the chicks in the yard
quiz.ex: brood n. 一窝幼崽：a brood of chicks 一窝小鸡；v. 孵蛋；引申义高频：brood over / on sth 郁郁沉思：He sat brooding over his failure. 他坐着反复琢磨失败。一词两义都是考点。

quiz.q: Pests — slugs and aphids — devour the bean seedlings overnight. To devour is to —
o: eat something up quickly and completely
cut the stems with a blade
quiz.ex: devour = 吞食、狼吞虎咽。引申用法：devour a book 如饥似渴地读书；be devoured by jealousy 被嫉妒吞噬。同根词 voracious 贪吃的（carnivore 食肉动物同根 vor- 吃）。

quiz.q: The government paid for wolf skins — they nearly managed to exterminate them in the whole valley. To exterminate is to —
o: kill all of a group of animals or pests
quiz.ex: exterminate = 根除、消灭（exterminator 灭虫公司）。近义辨析：exterminate 人为根除；extinct 灭绝（状态）：go extinct；eradicate 连根铲除（也用于疾病、恶习）：eradicate poverty。

quiz.q: The tortoise disappears in October into hibernation under the compost heap. Hibernation is —
o: the laying of eggs in autumn
the state of sleeping through the winter
the search for food before winter
quiz.ex: hibernation = 冬眠（hibern- 冬）。动词 hibernate。雅思动物话题高频：bears / tortoises / dormice hibernate。相关词：migration 迁徙；estivation 夏眠。

quiz.q: All my problems stem from the same root: the farm is too small to be a business. To stem from is to —
quiz.ex: stem v. 起源于：stem from = derive from = originate from；另一高频义"阻止"：stem the flow of blood 止血；stem the tide of migration 遏制移民潮。名词 = 茎、词干。多义词，阅读需看搭配。

quiz.q: One neighbour hybridises his beans, crossing his own line with an imported one. To hybridise is to —
o: breed from two different varieties or species
save seeds from a single old line
quiz.ex: hybridise = （使）杂交（hybrid + -ise，美式拼写 hybridize）。名词 hybrid 杂交种：hybrid car 混合动力车。冷知识：骡 mule 是马 horse 与驴 donkey 的杂交后代，通常不育。

quiz.q: Pests — slugs and aphids — devour the bean seedlings overnight. A pest is —
o: a machine for spraying the fields
a plant growing where it is not wanted
a small animal or insect that harms crops
quiz.ex: pest = 害虫、有害生物。搭配：pest control 害虫防治；pesticide 杀虫剂（pest + -cide 杀）。构词规律：-cide = 杀：insecticide 杀虫剂、genocide 种族灭绝、suicide 自杀。

title: A Day with the Zoo Vet
text:
Dr Okafor's day starts at seven, before the heat and before the visitors. First stop: the {{elephant}} house, where the oldest female, aged fifty-one, is having her morning {{trunk}} examination. "Fifty thousand muscles," the keeper says, while the vet checks the tip the way a dentist checks a child's tooth. Outside, the sun catches the worn stumps where her tusks used to be. {{Ivory}} is why there are so few of her kind left: her grandmother was born wild and survived the poaching years. In the next enclosure the rhino snores; his {{horn}} is keratin, the same material as fingernails, and still people pay more for it than for gold.

The laboratory is the vet's real office. On the bench sits a rack of samples from a young elephant with a fever. "Two years ago we nearly lost him to a {{virus}}," she says. "Herpes, elephant version — it moves fast." The team screens every sample for {{bacteria}} as well; on the wall hangs a chart of every {{parasite}} found in the zoo in the past decade. "The public calls them {{germ}}s," she says. "The lab calls them {{microbe}}s. Either way, they don't care how rare the animal is. One bad season, one {{epidemic}}, and a breeding programme forty years deep is gone. And they are patient — some bacteria can lie {{dormant}} in the soil for decades and still wake up hungry."

At nine we move to the insect house, where breakfast is alive. The lizards get a box of {{cricket}}s; the {{spider}}s get flies; and every {{insect}} in the building is also food for something else. In the education centre, a glass-walled {{hive}} lets schoolchildren watch ten thousand bees at work. The butterfly room is warm as a greenhouse — a new {{butterfly}} was emerging from its chrysalis, wet and slow, and a class of seven-year-olds held its breath for it. The only animal the zoo kills on purpose is the {{mosquito}}: every pot of standing water is emptied, because mosquitoes carry bird malaria, and the {{penguin}}s in the pool next door catch it badly.

At ten, the birds of prey fly. A {{falcon}} slices the air like a thrown knife; a {{hawk}} takes the glove for a dead chick; the old {{eagle}}, half-blind in one eye, still insists on the highest post. At eleven we cross to the dark wing — the {{nocturnal}} house — where the lights run backwards: night inside, day outside. An {{owl}} with a healed wing watches us pass without turning its head.

The afternoon is checks and paperwork. A {{primate}} health screen: the old chimpanzee puts his arm through the bars for a blood-pressure cuff, having learned that cooperation earns grapes. A {{kangaroo}} with a joey half out of the pouch; a {{zebra}} with a scraped hip; a {{camel}} who needs his teeth floated; a Komodo {{dragon}} who needs two keepers and a shield. In the frog room, the {{frog}} collection sits behind misted glass — a third of the world's amphibians, a sign says, are disappearing because of one fungus carried everywhere by boots and trade.

At six, as the gates close, we stop at the {{panda}} house. The twins are asleep in the fig tree, and their story is the zoo's favourite: after six years of nothing, the pair were separated, reintroduced, and their long {{sterility}} ended — nobody is quite sure why — with a single afternoon of squealing. "We manage diets, temperatures, lights," Dr Okafor says, packing her bag. "Then the animals decide. That's the job: you prepare everything, and you control almost nothing."
tr:
奥卡福博士的一天从七点开始，赶在暑气和游客之前。第一站：象（elephant）馆，五十一岁的最年长母象正在做晨间象鼻（trunk）检查。“五万块肌肉，”饲养员说，兽医检查鼻尖的样子，像牙医检查孩子的牙。外面，阳光照在它象牙磨旧的残根上。象牙（ivory）正是它同类如此稀少的原因：它的祖母生在野外，熬过了盗猎的年代。隔壁兽舍里犀牛打着呼噜；它的角（horn）是角蛋白，和指甲是同一种材料，可人们为它出的价钱仍然比黄金还高。

实验室才是兽医真正的办公室。台子上摆着一架样本，来自一头发烧的幼象。“两年前我们差点因为一种病毒（virus）失去它，”她说，“大象版本的疱疹——来得非常快。”团队对每个样本同时筛查细菌（bacteria）；墙上挂着一张表，列出过去十年在园里发现的每一种寄生虫（parasite）。“公众管它们叫病菌（germ），”她说，“实验室管它们叫微生物（microbe）。不管叫什么，它们可不在乎这种动物多稀有。一个糟糕的季节、一场流行病（epidemic），四十年的繁育计划就没了。而且它们有耐心——有些细菌能在土壤里休眠（dormant）几十年，醒来照样胃口大开。”

九点，我们来到昆虫馆，这里的早餐是活的。蜥蜴分到一盒蟋蟀（cricket）；蜘蛛（spider）分到苍蝇；这栋楼里的每一种昆虫（insect），同时也是别的动物的食物。教育中心里，一面玻璃墙的蜂巢（hive）让小学生们看着一万只蜜蜂干活。蝴蝶室暖得像温室——一只新生的蝴蝶（butterfly）正从蝶蛹里钻出来，湿漉漉、慢吞吞，一班的七岁孩子替它屏住了呼吸。动物园唯一故意杀死的动物是蚊子（mosquito）：每一盆积水都被倒空，因为蚊子传播禽疟疾，而隔壁池子里的企鹅（penguin）最经不起它。

十点，猛禽开始飞行。一只隼（falcon）像掷出的刀一样切开空气；一只鹰（hawk）落到手套上领走一只死雏鸡；一只眼睛半盲的老雕（eagle），仍然坚持要站最高的那根栖木。十一点，我们穿过黑暗的那一侧——夜行（nocturnal）馆——这里的灯光是反着来的：里面是夜，外面是昼。一只翅膀痊愈的猫头鹰（owl）目送我们走过，头都不转一下。

下午是体检和文书。灵长类（primate）健康筛查：老黑猩猩把胳膊伸出栏杆量血压，它早就学会了合作换葡萄。一只袋鼠（kangaroo），育儿袋里的小袋鼠探出了半个身子；一只斑马（zebra），胯上蹭破了皮；一只骆驼（camel）需要磨牙；一只科莫多巨蜥（dragon）需要两名饲养员加一面盾牌。蛙类室里，蛙（frog）们藏在起雾的玻璃后面——告示牌上写着，全世界三分之一的两栖动物正在消失，起因是一种被靴子和贸易带到世界各地的真菌。

六点，大门关闭，我们在熊猫（panda）馆前停下。双胞胎在无花果树上睡着了，它们的故事是全园最爱讲的：在整整六年毫无动静之后，这对熊猫被分开、重新合笼，长期的不育（sterility）忽然结束了——没人说得清为什么——以一个尖叫的下午告终。“我们管理饲料、温度、灯光，”奥卡福博士收拾着包说，“然后动物们自己决定。这就是这份工作：你准备好一切，却几乎控制不了什么。”

quiz.q: The public calls them germs; the lab calls them microbes. A germ is —
o: a seed kept for next season
a young insect before it changes form
a very small organism that causes disease
quiz.ex: germ = 病菌、胚芽。日常口语中 germ 泛指病菌（wash your hands to kill germs）；另一义"萌芽"：the germ of an idea 想法的萌芽（雅思阅读出现过）。近义辨析：germ（口语）、microbe（微生物，较学术）、bacteria（细菌，具体类别）、virus（病毒，比细菌更小）。

quiz.q: Some bacteria can lie dormant in the soil for decades and still wake up hungry. Dormant means —
quiz.ex: dormant = 休眠的、蛰伏的（dorm- 睡眠，同根 dormitory 宿舍）。高频搭配：a dormant volcano 休眠火山；lie dormant 潜伏。名词 dormancy 休眠状态。

quiz.q: On the wall hangs a chart of every parasite found in the zoo in the past decade. A parasite is —
o: an animal kept in a zoo enclosure
a creature that lives on or in another and feeds off it
a plant that grows without soil
quiz.ex: parasite = 寄生虫、寄生生物（para- 旁边 + site 食物 = 旁坐吃饭者）。引申义：a social parasite 吃白食的人。形容词 parasitic。相关词：host 宿主、symbiosis 共生。

quiz.q: One bad season, one epidemic, and a breeding programme forty years deep is gone. An epidemic is —
o: the yearly health check of a zoo
a medicine that cures many animals
the rapid spread of a disease through a population
quiz.ex: epidemic = 流行病（epi- 之中 + dem- 人民 = 在人民中间）。搭配：an epidemic of flu 流感疫情。扩展：pandemic 大流行（跨洲全球）；endemic 地方性流行的（也指某地特有）。雅思健康类高频三兄弟。

quiz.q: After six years of nothing, the pair were reintroduced, and their long sterility ended. Sterility is —
o: the state of being completely clean
the state of being unable to produce young
quiz.ex: sterility 两义：①不育、不结果（sterile 不育的/贫瘠的）；②无菌（sterile instruments 无菌器械；sterilise 消毒/绝育）。一词多义，看上下文。反义：fertility 肥沃、生育力。

quiz.q: At eleven we cross to the dark wing — the nocturnal house — where the lights run backwards. Nocturnal animals are active —
quiz.ex: nocturnal = 夜行性的、夜的（noct- 夜）。反义：diurnal 昼行性的。高频搭配：nocturnal habits 夜间习性。词根 nox/noct = 夜：equinox 昼夜平分点。

quiz.q: Ivory is why there are so few of her kind left: her grandmother survived the poaching years. Ivory is —
o: the hard white material of elephant tusks
the fur of a rare wild cat
a medicine made from animal bones
quiz.ex: ivory = 象牙；（引申）象牙色、乳白色：ivory tower 象牙塔（脱离现实的学术圈）。高频语境：the ivory trade 象牙贸易（国际禁令话题）。注意 rhino horn 犀牛角是 keratin 角蛋白，与象牙是两种东西。

quiz.q: The only animal the zoo kills on purpose is the mosquito: every pot of standing water is emptied. A mosquito is —
o: a worm that lives in standing water
a small bird that hunts at night
a type of tick that lives on mammals
a flying insect whose females bite and suck blood
quiz.ex: mosquito = 蚊子（西班牙语借词，-o 结尾类似 tomato）。高频语境：mosquito-borne diseases 蚊媒疾病（malaria 疟疾、dengue 登革热）；insecticide-treated nets 经杀虫剂处理的蚊帐（雅思公益话题）。

title: The Comet Summer
text:
The {{observatory}} stands on a dry hill two hours from the city, where the nights are cold and the {{celestial}} light arrives undimmed. I went up in July, the summer of the {{comet}}, and stayed ten days.

Dr Inés runs the place with two engineers and a dog. She studied {{astronomy}}, not {{astrology}} — "one is a science," she says, "the other is a newspaper column" — and as a girl she had wanted to be an {{astronaut}}. "Then I understood you can touch the planets with mathematics and never leave the chair."

The comet was that year's {{spectacle}}: a pale brushstroke above the pines, visible even from the light-polluted city. Through the {{telescope}} it had already grown an {{envelope}} of glowing gas a hundred thousand kilometres wide, and a {{tail}} of {{dust}} that pointed away from the Sun, as comets' tails always do — pushed, Dr Inés explained, by nothing more than the {{pressure}} of sunlight. Its heart was a {{chunk}} of ice and rock, a {{diameter}} of perhaps eight kilometres, dirty as a snowball dragged behind a truck. Every eighty thousand years it made this trip; the last time it passed, humans were just learning to farm.

On the chart table she traced its {{orbit}}: a long flat {{curve}}, tilted out of the {{ecliptic}} — the invisible plate on which the planets circle. "Everything obeys the same laws," she said. "Orbital {{dynamics}} is Newton's laws of {{motion}} plus patience. Where it will be in the year 3000, we know to the metre." The {{galaxy}}, she liked to say, holds perhaps a hundred billion such wanderers; the {{universe}}, two trillion galaxies; and {{cosmos}} — "that is the word the poets borrow when they want to sound calm about it." That week the four inner planets, the {{terrestrial}} ones, were baking in the summer heat, while the gas giants rode their slow circles outside.

Her office wall carried the timeline of space {{exploration}}. Her favourite page was Rosetta: a European {{spacecraft}} — "a {{probe}}, or a {{spaceship}}, depending on who you write for" — that spent ten years catching a comet. It borrowed speed from Mars and Earth, performed a {{flyby}} of two asteroids, dropped a landing {{module}} named Philae onto the comet itself, and then followed it around the Sun for two years. Its {{propulsion}} was mostly patience, burning fuel the way a miser spends money. "The best {{expedition}} ever mounted," she said. "Nobody went anywhere. Everyone travelled."

That Saturday the Earth crossed the comet's old dust trail, and we watched meteors from the balcony: grains no heavier than {{ash}}, burning seventy kilometres up. "In the sky it's a meteor," she said. "On the ground, if it survives, it's a {{meteorite}} — and it arrives with a calling card: the {{crater}} in Arizona, nearly six hundred metres in {{radius}}, is one of them." Sometimes, she added, a comet grows {{vent}}s — jets of gas erupting through the crust when the ice below turns straight to vapour; one in her photographs looked like a kettle deciding to leave. And twice in recorded history, telescopes have caught true {{interstellar}} visitors — objects from another star entirely, passing through without stopping, like travellers who never learn the local language. Down in the basement lab, a student named Amara was grinding a fragment of the meteorite that had fallen in the valley the winter before — but that is the second half of this story.
tr:
天文台（observatory）坐落在离城市两小时车程的干燥山丘上，那里夜晚寒冷，天上的（celestial）光线毫无遮拦地抵达地面。彗星（comet）之年的七月，我上山待了十天。

伊内丝博士带着两名工程师和一条狗管理着这里。她学的是天文学（astronomy），不是占星术（astrology）——“一门是科学，”她说，“另一门是报纸专栏”——少女时代的她曾想当宇航员（astronaut）。“后来我明白了，你可以用数学触摸行星，一步也不用离开椅子。”

那颗彗星是那年夏天的奇观（spectacle）：松林上方一道苍白的笔痕，连光污染严重的城里都看得见。在望远镜（telescope）里，它已经长出一个十万公里宽的、发光气体的包层（envelope），还有一条尘埃（dust）彗尾（tail），永远背向太阳——伊内丝博士解释说，推动它的不过是阳光的压力（pressure）。它的核心是一大块（chunk）冰和岩石，直径（diameter）也许有八公里，脏得像被卡车拖了一路的雪球。它每八万年完成一次这样的旅行；上一次它经过时，人类刚刚学会耕种。

她在图桌上描出它的轨道（orbit）：一条又长又扁的曲线（curve），倾出黄道（ecliptic）之外——黄道是行星们环绕的那块看不见的圆盘。“一切都服从同样的定律，”她说。“轨道动力学（dynamics）就是牛顿的运动（motion）定律加上耐心。到公元3000年它在哪儿，我们能精确到米。”她喜欢说，银河系（galaxy）里也许有一千亿个这样的流浪者；宇宙（universe）里有两万亿个星系；至于 cosmos（宇宙整体）——“那是诗人们想显得平静时借用的词。”那个星期，四颗内侧的类地（terrestrial）行星正在夏天的热浪里烘烤，气态巨行星们在更外面骑着它们缓慢的圆圈。

她办公室的墙上挂着太空探索（exploration）的时间线。她最喜欢的一页是罗塞塔号：一艘欧洲航天器（spacecraft）——“叫探测器（probe）还是宇宙飞船（spaceship），取决于你为谁写作”——花了十年时间去追一颗彗星。它借火星和地球加速，飞掠（flyby）了两颗小行星，把一个名叫菲莱的着陆舱（module）投放到彗星上，然后跟着这颗彗星绕太阳转了两年。它的推进（propulsion）方式主要是耐心，烧燃料的方式像守财奴花钱。“史上最了不起的远征（expedition），”她说。“没有一个人去任何地方，所有人都完成了旅行。”

那个周六，地球穿过彗星古老的尘埃带，我们在露台上看了流星：颗粒轻得像灰烬（ash），在七十公里的高空烧尽。“在天上它叫流星，”她说，“落到地面还活着，它就叫陨石（meteorite）——而且它自带名片：亚利桑那那座半径（radius）近六百米的陨石坑（crater）就是其中一张。”她还说，有时彗星会长出喷口（vent）——冰直接升华成气体时，从壳里喷出的气流；她照片里的一处喷口，像一把决定出走的水壶。有记录以来，望远镜还抓到过两次真正的星际（interstellar）访客——来自另一颗恒星的天体，路过而不停留，像从不学习当地语言的旅人。地下实验室里，一个叫阿玛拉的学生正在研磨一块冬天落进山谷的陨石碎片——但那是这个故事的下半篇。

quiz.q: She studied astronomy, not astrology — one is a science, the other is a newspaper column. Astrology is —
o: the science of stars and galaxies
the belief that star positions influence human affairs
quiz.ex: astrology = 占星术（astro- 星）。astronomy = 天文学（-nomy 法则、测量）。同根词：astronaut 宇航员（naut- 航行者）、astronomer 天文学家。这对近形词是雅思听力的经典陷阱。

quiz.q: Through the telescope it had grown an envelope of glowing gas a hundred thousand kilometres wide. Here, envelope means —
o: a paper cover for a letter
quiz.ex: envelope = 信封；科学技术语境指"包层、包络"。彗星的彗发（coma）就是一层气体包层。动词 envelop = 包裹。一词多义在雅思阅读中很常见。

quiz.q: A tail of dust pointing away from the Sun — pushed by nothing more than the pressure of sunlight. Pressure is —
o: the force pushing on an area
quiz.ex: pressure = 压力、压强。高频搭配：air pressure 气压；under pressure 承受压力；peer pressure 同辈压力；pressure sb into doing 施压。物理与心理双场景高频。

quiz.q: A long flat curve, tilted out of the ecliptic — the invisible plate on which the planets circle. The ecliptic is —
o: the plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun
the brightest star in the sky
the edge of the Milky Way
the belt between Mars and Jupiter
quiz.ex: ecliptic = 黄道（eclipt- 蚀，因日月食只发生在黄道附近而得名）。黄道十二宫（zodiac signs）沿黄道分布。天文类阅读的加分词。

quiz.q: The four terrestrial planets were baking in the summer heat. Terrestrial means —
o: of the land or the planet Earth
quiz.ex: terrestrial = 陆地的、地球的（terr- 土地，同根 territory 领土）。extraterrestrial = 外星的（外星人 ET 的全称）。四大类地行星：水星、金星、地球、火星。

quiz.q: It performed a flyby of two asteroids. A flyby is —
o: a flight passing close to something without landing
a failure of a rocket engine
a landing on a comet's surface
a photograph taken from the ground
quiz.ex: flyby = 飞掠（fly + by）。航天高频：gravity-assist flyby 借力飞掠。同类合成词：flyover 立交桥；takeoff 起飞；touchdown 着陆。

quiz.q: The best expedition ever mounted, she said — nobody went anywhere, everyone travelled. An expedition is —
o: an organised journey for exploration or research
a walk to the nearest village
quiz.ex: expedition = 远征、探险（ex- 向外 + ped- 脚）。搭配：mount / lead / join an expedition。go on an expedition。同根词：pedal 踏板、pedestrian 行人。

quiz.q: In the sky it's a meteor; on the ground, if it survives, it's a meteorite. A meteorite is —
o: a space rock that reaches the ground
a streak of light burning in the air
a piece of a comet's tail
a hole made by an impact
quiz.ex: 陨石三兄弟只差后缀：meteoroid 流星体（在太空）→ meteor 流星（在大气中燃烧）→ meteorite 陨石（落到地面）。雅思阅读天文类曾专门考过这条链。

title: The Basement Lab
text:
Downstairs from the telescope, the observatory keeps a basement laboratory, and for three weeks that summer it belonged to Amara, a doctoral student with a deadline and a {{fragment}} of meteorite no bigger than a walnut. The valley stone — as everyone called the meteorite that had fallen in February, punching a small {{crater}} into a sheep field — had been divided between six laboratories. Hers was the piece with the interesting mass-spectrometer results.

Her {{method}} was patient and physical. Half of the fragment stayed whole — the museum {{specimen}}, pretty as a geode — and the other half became {{sample}} powder, a few grams in a glass vial. First question: {{composition}}. Iron and nickel, as expected; silicates; carbon {{compound}}s nobody had looked for; and, deep inside certain grains, {{substance}}s older than the Sun itself.

The instruments were a chemistry lesson wearing a lab coat. A {{molecule}} is two or more {{atom}}s holding hands; an {{ion}} is an atom that has lost or gained an {{electron}}; and inside the atoms, smaller {{particle}}s — quarks and the rest — obey rules written in {{quantum}} mechanics. "Half my work," she said, "is persuading ions to march in single file."

Each element prints its signature. Heat the sample, and the light it gives off splits — by {{refraction}}, through a prism, the way Newton split sunlight — into a {{spectrum}} of lines, {{distinct}} as fingerprints. Under {{ultraviolet}} light, certain grains glowed faintly. What was {{invisible}} to the eye was loud to the machine: a weak but {{discernible}} {{signal}}, rising out of the noise at exactly the {{frequency}} her model had predicted. On the roof above her, the radio {{antenna}} played the same trick for louder things: satellites, storms, the Sun.

Part of her work was about heat, because a meteorite remembers. A {{solid}} holds its shape; a {{liquid}} takes the shape of its container; a {{fluid}}, the engineers liked to remind her, is anything that flows, gases included — and the early solar system was a fluid cloud. {{Radioactive}} isotopes inside the stone decay at known rates, so the sample can be dated: a clock that started before the Earth existed. Some of her grains were {{fossil}}s in the strict sense — material that survived the {{formation}} of the solar system unchanged, dust welded into stone by gentle {{collision}}s four and a half billion years ago. The Moon itself, the theory goes, was born in a {{cataclysmic}} collision between the young Earth and something the size of Mars.

The third week began badly. The mass spectrometer died on Monday — a {{circuit}} fault, deep in the rack — and the month before had been {{overwhelming}} enough: twelve-hour days, a supervisor on another continent, a visa form that refused to save. Tuesday brought {{despair}}, the clean kind, the kind with nothing left to do but continue. On Wednesday she was {{desperate}} enough to open the instrument herself, against every rule, and found the fault with a torch and a mirror: a scorched board, one failed joint. The situation had seemed {{hopeless}}; it turned out to be merely boring. On Thursday the signal came back, and that evening she cleared her head the way the engineers had taught her — {{squash}}, badly, on the village court. On Friday she {{synthesise}}d a reference standard in the fume hood, and by Saturday the numbers stood up straight.

That evening she climbed to the balcony, where the comet hung over the pines, and tried to explain what she had found: grains older than the Sun, welded into stone before the Earth existed. The story had four {{dimension}}s, she said — three of space and one of deep time — and every instrument in the basement was only a way of listening to it.
tr:
望远镜楼下，天文台有一个地下实验室，那年夏天的三个星期里，它属于阿玛拉——一名有截止日期的博士生，和一块不比核桃大多少的陨石碎片（fragment）。山谷之石——大家都这么叫那块二月落下的陨石，它在一片牧场上砸出一个小小的陨石坑（crater）——被分给了六家实验室。她分到的，是质谱结果有意思的那一块。

她的方法（method）需要耐心和体力。碎片的一半保持完整——那是博物馆的标本（specimen），像晶洞一样漂亮——另一半被磨成样品（sample）粉末，几克，装在小玻璃瓶里。第一个问题：构成（composition）。铁和镍，意料之中；硅酸盐；没人找过的碳化合物（compound）；而在某些颗粒深处，藏着比太阳本身更古老的物质（substance）。

那些仪器就是一件穿着白大褂的化学课。分子（molecule）是两个以上手拉手的原子（atom）；离子（ion）是失去或得到一个电子（electron）的原子；而在原子内部，更小的粒子（particle）——夸克等等——服从量子（quantum）力学写下的规则。“我一半的工作，”她说，“是说服离子排成单行前进。”

每种元素都会留下自己的签名。加热样品，它发出的光经过折射（refraction），穿过棱镜——像牛顿分解阳光那样——分离成一条光谱（spectrum），一条条谱线像指纹一样彼此有别（distinct）。在紫外（ultraviolet）光下，某些颗粒微微发光。眼睛看不见（invisible）的东西，机器听得很响：一个微弱但可辨别（discernible）的信号（signal），从噪声里升起来，频率（frequency）分毫不差，正是她的模型预言的那个。她头顶的屋顶上，无线电天线（antenna）为更响的东西变着同样的把戏：卫星、风暴、太阳。

她的一部分工作是关于热的，因为陨石记得温度。固体（solid）保持自己的形状；液体（liquid）取容器的形状；流体（fluid）——工程师们喜欢提醒她——是任何会流动的东西，气体也算；而早期的太阳系就是一团流体云。石头内部的放射性（radioactive）同位素以已知的速率衰变，所以样品可以断代：一座在地球存在之前就开始走的钟。她的某些颗粒，严格意义上是化石（fossil）——在太阳系的形成（formation）中未经改变地幸存下来的物质，四十五亿年前被轻柔的碰撞（collision）焊进石头。至于月球本身，理论认为，它诞生于一场灾难性的（cataclysmic）碰撞——年轻的地球，和一个火星大小的天体。

第三周开局不利。质谱仪周一死了——电路（circuit）故障，在机架深处——而之前的一个月已经够让人喘不过气（overwhelming）：每天十二小时，导师在另一个大陆，一份怎么也保存不上的签证表。周二带来了绝望（despair），干净的那种，除了继续没有别的事可做的那种。周三她不顾一切（desperate）到亲手打开了仪器——违反所有规矩——用手电和一面镜子找到了故障：一块烧焦的板子，一个失效的焊点。局面看起来毫无希望（hopeless）；结果只是无聊而已。周四信号回来了，那天傍晚她用工程师教的办法清空脑袋——在村里的球场打壁球（squash），打得很烂。周五她在通风橱里合成（synthesise）了一个参考标准品用来校准；到周六，数字站直了。

那天傍晚她登上露台，彗星悬在松林上方，她试着向我解释她发现了什么：比太阳更古老的颗粒，在地球存在之前就被焊进石头。她说，这个故事有四个维度（dimension）——三个属于空间，一个属于深时——而地下实验室里的每一台仪器，不过是聆听它的方式。

quiz.q: Half of the fragment stayed whole — the museum specimen; the other half became sample powder. A specimen is —
o: a small amount of powder for testing
an individual example kept for study or display
a reading taken from a machine
a theory used as a model
quiz.ex: specimen = 标本、样品（完整的个体）。sample = 样品（取来的一部分）。医学场景：blood sample 血样；生物场景：specimen jar 标本瓶。近义辨析是考点。

quiz.q: An ion is an atom that has lost or gained an electron. An ion is —
o: the smallest unit of an element
quiz.ex: ion = 离子（带电的原子）。cation 阳离子 / anion 阴离子；ionic bond 离子键。同族词：electron 电子、isotope 同位素、neutron 中子。化学类听力讲座常见。
