quiz.ex: outline = 提纲、大纲。in outline 概括地。动词 outline 概述。写作题里 outline your essay 列提纲。

quiz.q: To cite a source is to say where an idea was born. To cite means —
o: to cut forty slides to twelve
to photocopy an extract for a box
to recite results like a report
to mention a source of information formally
quiz.ex: cite = 引用、引证。citation 引文；引证格式。cite your sources 标注出处。注意与 site（地点）、sight（视力）同音。

quiz.q: To revise, in the English of universities, means to re-see — cut the weak paragraph, move the strong one. To revise means —
o: to memorise notes before an exam
to read again and change in order to improve
to submit the final printed copy
to dictate the week into a phone
quiz.ex: revise = 修改、修订（英式也指复习）。revision 修改/复习。美式复习用 review。

title: The Sandwich Mystery
text:
Every Tuesday at eleven-fifteen, the staff-room sandwiches vanished. By the third week, Dr Feng had a case, and by the fourth she had a seminar: "Today," she announced, "we learn how knowledge works. Someone has been eating the staff's lunch. You will {{analyse}} the evidence, and you will be wrong in public, which is how every science begins."

The evidence went on the table: crumbs under the window (not by the door), a plate moved two metres from the fridge, the thefts always on Tuesdays, never on Thursdays, and a faint smell of tuna near the recycling bin.

"First, the words," said Dr Feng, "because the words are the method. To {{assume}} is to accept something as true with no evidence at all. To {{presume}} is to suppose it is more likely than not. To {{suppose}} is to imagine a case and see where it leads. Now: who assumed, who presumed, and who supposed?"

"I {{presume}} the thief has a key," said Tomas. "Only staff can open that door."

"I {{assume}} the thief was hungry," said Ada.

"I {{suppose}} the sandwiches were never there at all," said Dani. "Maybe the person who brings them changed her day."

"Three positions," said Dr Feng. "Tomas, your presumption has evidence and can be tested. Ada, your assumption is comfortable and worth nothing — nice people steal sandwiches too. Dani, your supposition is the interesting one, because it attacks the crime itself. Write all three down; you will need them."

A {{hypothesis}}, she explained, is a presumption promoted to a testable guess: "Tomas suspects the caretaker. That is hypothesis one. It predicts behaviour: if the caretaker is guilty, the thefts will stop when he is on holiday. We {{speculate}}d this morning in the staff room — a fox, the ghost of the fourth floor, a secret second sandwich maker — but speculation is only hypothesis with its evidence missing. Miss Adeyemi went further and {{postulate}}d a propped-open door: a thing we have not seen but which would explain everything we have. A postulate is what you must believe for the story to work."

"Now {{predict}}," she said. "Next Tuesday, eleven-fifteen. If our story is true, something will happen. Watch."

The watching was the lesson. To {{perceive}} is to take the world in through the senses; to {{detect}} is to notice what most people miss — the smell of tuna, the crumbs under the window; to {{discern}} is to see a pattern in what you have detected; to {{recognize}} is to match it against something already known. "The class detected crumbs," said Dr Feng. "Dani discerned that they lay under the window, not the door. The caretaker, if he were the thief, would have left them by the door. Hypothesis one is wounded."

They laid the two timetables side by side to {{compare}} them, then to {{contrast}} them — the same exercise, different verb: compare looks for likeness, contrast looks for difference. The caretaker's walk and the bin collection {{overlap}}ped at eleven-fifteen exactly, and only on Tuesdays. "The overlap is not proof," Dr Feng warned. "Two things happening together is a coincidence until the third thing arrives. This is {{inductive}} reasoning — from many Tuesdays to one rule — and induction is generous: it hands you conclusions with holes in them. Sherlock Holmes {{deduce}}s: from the crumbs he would {{infer}} the direction the eater faced, from the direction the window, from the window the height of the visitor. We do it backwards: from the rule we {{conclude}} the case. Deduction is strict; give it one false crumb and it will lie to you elegantly."

By Thursday the class had a diagnosis. "We {{diagnose}} this like an illness," said Ada, "and the illness is an open door." The {{detail}} that solved it was the smallest: a door wedge, borrowed from the music room, appearing in photographs of every Tuesday. The bin lorry was loud, the door was propped, and at eleven-sixteen a dog — the caretaker's spaniel, walked at eleven-ten, fed on schedule at noon — performed the only crime of its career. "I {{reckon}} you earned your marks," said Dr Feng, who was {{conscious}} of having enjoyed herself. The head teacher, {{deem}}ing the matter "a serious breach of sandwich security", bought the staff a new plate; the empty plate under the window seemed to {{imply}} an accomplice, until the cleaner pointed out it was the same spaniel, twice.

"Understand the case, and you {{comprehend}} the method," said Dr Feng at the door. "Assume nothing, presume carefully, suppose freely, and be {{thorough}}: it is always the smallest detail that turns a mystery into a fact."
tr:
每周二十一点一刻，教师休息室的三明治会消失。到第三周，冯博士手上有了案子；到第四周，她开了一堂研讨课。“今天，”她宣布，“我们学习知识是如何运作的。有人一直在吃教职员工的午餐。你们将分析（analyse）证据，并且当众犯错——每一门科学都是这么开始的。”

证据摆上桌面：窗下的面包屑（不在门边），一只从冰箱挪出两米的盘子，失窃永远在周二、从不在周四，回收箱附近一丝淡淡的吞拿鱼味。

“先讲词，”冯博士说，“因为词就是方法。假定（assume）是完全没有证据就当作真；推定（presume）是认定它多半为真；设想（suppose）是想像一种情形，看它通向哪里。现在：谁在假定，谁在推定，谁在设想？”

“我推定（presume）小偷有钥匙，”托马斯说，“只有教职工能开那扇门。”

“我假定（assume）小偷饿了，”阿达说。

“我设想（suppose）三明治根本没送到，”丹妮说，“也许带三明治的人换了日子。”

“三个立场，”冯博士说，“托马斯，你的推定有证据，可以检验。阿达，你的假定很舒服，但一文不值——好人也偷三明治。丹妮，你的设想最有意思，因为它攻击的是罪案本身。三个都记下来，待会儿用得上。”

假设（hypothesis），她解释道，是被提升为可检验猜测的推定：“托马斯怀疑门卫。这是假设一。它预言行为：如果门卫有罪，他休假时失窃就该停止。今天早上休息室里我们瞎猜（speculate）了一通——狐狸、四楼的鬼、一个秘密的第二三明治人——但瞎猜只是缺了证据的假设。阿德耶米小姐更进一步，设定（postulate）了一扇被撑开的门：一件我们没见过、却能解释一切已有事实的东西。公设是为了让故事成立而必须相信的东西。”

“现在预测（predict），”她说，“下周二，十一点一刻。如果我们的故事是真的，某件事就会发生。看着。”

“看”本身就是课。感知（perceive）是用感官把世界收进来；察觉（detect）是注意到多数人错过的东西——吞拿鱼味、窗下的碎屑；辨明（discern）是从察觉到的东西里看出规律；辨认（recognize）是把它与已知的东西对上号。“全班察觉了碎屑，”冯博士说，“丹妮辨明了它们在窗下而非门边。门卫若是小偷，碎屑该留在门边。假设一负伤了。”

他们把两张时间表并排放好做比较（compare），再作对比（contrast）——同一个练习，两个动词：compare 找相似，contrast 找差异。门卫的遛狗时间和垃圾清运恰好重叠（overlap）在十一点一刻，且只在周二。“重叠不是证明，”冯博士警告，“两件事同时发生，在第三件事到来之前都只是巧合。这是归纳（inductive）推理——从许多个周二推出一条规则——归纳是慷慨的：它递给你的结论带着洞。夏洛克·福尔摩斯靠演绎（deduce）：从碎屑推断（infer）进食者面朝的方向，从方向推到窗，从窗推到访客的身高。我们反着来：从规则结案（conclude）。演绎是严格的：喂它一粒假碎屑，它会对你说一个优雅的谎。”

到周四，全班有了诊断。“我们像诊断（diagnose）疾病一样诊断此案，”阿达说，“病名是一扇敞开的门。”破案的是最小的细节（detail）：一个从音乐室借来的门楔，出现在每个周二的监控照片里。垃圾车很吵，门被撑开，十一点十六分，一条狗——门卫的 spaniel 猎犬，十一点十分遛，十二点准时开饭——完成了它一生中唯一的罪案。“我估摸（reckon）你们挣到了分数，”冯博士说，她清楚自己（conscious）玩得很开心。校长认定（deem）此事“严重违反三明治安全条例”，给教职员买了一副新盘子；窗下那只空盘子似乎暗示（imply）有共犯，直到清洁工指出，那是同一条猎犬，作案两次。

“理解了这个案子，你们就领会（comprehend）了方法本身，”冯博士在门口说，“不凭空假定，谨慎推定，大胆设想，并且要彻底（thorough）：把谜团变成事实的，永远是最小的那个细节。”

quiz.q: From the crumbs Holmes would infer the direction the eater faced. To infer means —
o: to compare two timetables side by side
to state a rule before any evidence exists
to notice a smell with the senses
to work something out from evidence, without being told directly
quiz.ex: infer = 推断（由证据推结论）。infer sth from sth。名词 inference。对比 imply（暗示）：说话者 imply，听者 infer。

quiz.q: Sherlock Holmes deduces: from crumbs, direction; from direction, the window; from the window, the height. To deduce means —
o: to reach a conclusion by strict logical steps from general rules
to guess freely without any evidence
to presume something is more likely than not
to detect a smell of tuna
quiz.ex: deduce = 演绎、推论。deduce A from B 从B推出A。deduction 演绎法。对比 induction 归纳法。

quiz.q: To assume is to accept something as true with no evidence at all — nice people steal sandwiches too. To assume means —
o: to test a guess against next Tuesday
to take something as true without proof
to notice what most people miss
to work out a thief's height from a window
quiz.ex: assume = 假定、想当然。assume responsibility 承担责任；assuming that... 假定…。名词 assumption 假设。

quiz.q: To perceive is to take the world in through the senses. To perceive means —
o: to conclude the case from a rule
to match a pattern against something known
to become aware of something through sight, hearing or other senses
quiz.ex: perceive = 察觉、感知。perceive a change/difference。名词 perception 知觉、看法。近义 detect 侧重"发现易被忽略的"。

quiz.q: This is inductive reasoning — from many Tuesdays to one rule — and induction hands you conclusions with holes. Inductive reasoning —
o: starts from many observed cases and generalises to a rule
starts from a general rule and applies it strictly
assumes the thief has a key
quiz.ex: inductive = 归纳的（由个案到一般）。inductive reasoning 归纳推理；对比 deductive reasoning 演绎推理（由一般到个案）。

quiz.q: The class detected crumbs; Dani discerned that they lay under the window, not the door. To discern means —
o: to buy the staff a new plate
to smell tuna near the recycling bin
to presume the thief is hungry
to work out a pattern in what you have noticed
quiz.ex: discern = 辨明、看出（细微差别或规律）。discern a pattern/difference。形容词 discerning 有辨识力的。

quiz.q: We speculated this morning — a fox, the ghost, a secret second sandwich maker. To speculate means —
o: to form guesses without enough evidence
to compare and contrast two timetables
quiz.ex: speculate = 猜测、推测；另一高频义：投机（speculate in shares 炒股）。名词 speculation 猜测/投机。

quiz.q: I presume the thief has a key — only staff can open that door. To presume means —
o: to accept something as true with no evidence at all
to suppose something is probably true, based on some evidence
quiz.ex: presume = 推定、（有依据地）假定。presume innocent until proven guilty 无罪推定。对比 assume（无依据地假定）。

title: Results and Prizes
text:
The results arrived on the third Thursday of August: by text at nine, by post at noon. Dani had promised herself she would be calm, and she was — for about four seconds, which is how long it took to read the {{grade}}s.

Each subject came with a {{mark}} out of a hundred and a letter beside it; the {{score}} in mathematics was the number her father would quote at family dinners for a year. The school, to its lasting embarrassment, also {{rank}}ed every subject from first to last, and Dani was first in Portuguese and comfortably last in swimming.

Tomas could not {{understand}} his chemistry {{grade}} at all: he had topped every class {{test}} that year and walked out of the examination smiling. So he filed a {{query}} — a formal question about a mark — with the exams office, and waited. The office {{resolve}}d the query within a fortnight and {{confirm}}ed what he already suspected: a page of his paper had gone unmarked. The C became an A, and it carried its own lesson: never accept a number you cannot see the back of.

In September, the teachers wrote {{feedback}} letters — half a page each, more useful than the grades, because feedback tells you what to do next and a grade only tells you where you stand. "Results are like weather reports," Miss Adeyemi offered by way of {{analogy}}. "Accurate about yesterday, vague about Friday, and no use at all for deciding what to plant." Exams, she said, {{determine}} what a university knows about you; only you can {{decide}} what you know about yourself.

The money came separately. The university offered Dani a small {{grant}} — money given once, never repaid. The engineering faculty advertised a {{scholarship}} for its top applicant. And the travelling {{fellowship}}, worth a whole year abroad, went — the school bulletin noted with pride — to a former student who had failed her first set of exams entirely and retaken every one.

At the leaving assembly, Mr Okafor gave the leavers three verbs. "You {{attain}} a level — a standard that other people set. You {{achieve}} a goal — one you set yourself. And occasionally you {{accomplish}} something that was not on anybody's list until you did it. Most of what matters in a life is in the third category, and no examination has ever gone looking there."

Prize night came in December. The {{award}} for progress went to Sam from Floor C, who nearly dropped it. The {{prize}} for physics went, to nobody's surprise, to Ada. The {{reward}} — the envelope with actual money in it — went to the robotics club, who had beaten the robot arm that had beaten everyone else.

The head teacher kept her speech short. "Let me {{illustrate}} what I mean," she said, "with two {{example}}s. First: the year's examinations {{demonstrate}}d what this cohort can do under pressure — timed, silent, and alone. Second {{instance}}: the flood in February, when the same students moved two thousand books to the upper floor in forty minutes, unpaid, unasked, and mostly unphotographed. The second event is what I mean by {{manifest}} talent: ability that shows itself without being examined. Do not let one measurement {{prove}} to you that the other one never happened."

She gave {{credit}} where it was due — to the caretaker, the kitchen, and above all the librarian — and her {{praise}} for the students was brief and precise. "To {{appreciate}} something," she reminded the hall, "means both to be grateful for it and to understand its true worth. Do both tonight."

Her final warning was the one the leavers wrote down. "The world will {{underestimate}} some of you because of where you come from, and {{overestimate}} the rest of you for exactly the same reason. Both errors are the same error. Correct it wherever you meet it, beginning with yourselves."

After the ceremony, the hall emptied quickly. Dani, holding her own small prize for progress in Portuguese — "{{achieve}}d with visible reluctance", the citation had said — stayed behind to help stack the chairs: a task no examination has ever measured and no prize has ever paid for, and which was, as Miss Adeyemi would certainly have said, the whole point.
tr:
成绩在八月的第三个周四到达：九点发短信，中午寄信件。丹妮向自己保证过要冷静，她也确实冷静了——大约四秒钟，也就是读完所有等级（grade）所需的时间。

每门课都附有一个百分制的分数（mark）和一个字母；她的数学得分（score）是她父亲将在未来一年的家宴上反复引用的数字。学校还以各科名次（rank）从第一排到最后——这件事让它自己长久地难为情——而丹妮的葡萄牙语第一，游泳稳居倒数第一。

托马斯完全不能理解（understand）他的化学等级（grade）：那一年每次课堂测验（test）他都是第一，走出考场时还在微笑。于是他向考试办公室提交了一份查询（query）——对一个分数的正式质询——然后等待。办公室两周内处理（resolve）了这份查询，并证实（confirm）了他已有的怀疑：他试卷的一页漏判了。C变成了A，还附赠一课：永远不要接受一个你看不到背面的数字。

九月，老师们写了反馈（feedback）信——每人半页纸，比等级有用得多，因为反馈告诉你接下来做什么，而等级只告诉你现在站在哪里。“成绩就像天气预报，”阿德耶米小姐打了个比方（analogy），“对昨天很准确，对星期五含含糊糊，对决定种什么毫无用处。”考试，她说，决定（determine）一所大学对你的了解；只有你自己能决定（decide）你对自己的了解。

钱是另外来的。大学给了丹妮一小笔助学金（grant）——一次性发放、无需偿还的钱。工学院为最优申请者设了奖学金（scholarship）。而那份价值一整年海外访学的研究员基金（fellowship）——校刊自豪地注明——给了一位头一回考试全部挂科、后来每门重考的往届学生。

毕业典礼上，奥卡福先生送给毕业生三个动词。“你们达成（attain）一个水平——那是别人定下的标准。你们实现（achieve）一个目标——那是你们自己定下的。偶尔，你们会完成（accomplish）一件在你做到之前不在任何人清单上的事。人生中真正重要的东西大多属于第三类，而从来没有哪场考试去那里找过。”

颁奖夜在十二月到来。进步奖（award）颁给了C层的山姆，他差点没接住。物理奖（prize）毫无悬念地给了阿达。而那份报酬（reward）——装着真钞票的信封——给了机器人社，他们造出了击败过所有人的那条机械臂。

校长的致辞很短。“让我用两个例子（example）来说明（illustrate）我的意思，”她说，“第一：今年的考试展示了（demonstrate）这届学生在压力之下的能力——限时、安静、独自一人。第二个事例（instance）：二月的洪水，同一批学生在四十分钟内把两千本书搬上二楼——无报酬、没人要求、也基本没人拍照。第二件事才是我所说的显露（manifest）出来的才华：无需考试便会自己显形的能力。别让一次测量向你证明（prove）另一件事从未发生。”

她把功劳（credit）归于应得之人——门卫、厨房，尤其是图书管理员——她对学生的赞扬（praise）简短而精确。“珍视（appreciate）一件事，”她提醒全场，“既意味着对它心怀感激，也意味着理解它真正的价值。今晚两样都做。”

最后的警告是毕业生们记进笔记本的那句。“这个世界会因为你来自哪里而低估（underestimate）你们中的一些人，也会因为完全相同的原因高估（overestimate）另一些人。两个错误是同一个错误。在哪里遇到，就在哪里纠正它——从你们自己开始。”

典礼结束后，礼堂很快空了。丹妮拿着她自己那份小小的葡萄牙语进步奖——颁奖词写着“以肉眼可见的不情愿取得（achieve）”——留下来帮忙摞椅子：一件从来没有考试测量过、也没有奖品付过钱的差事。而这，正如阿德耶米小姐必然会说的，才是全部的意义。

quiz.q: 'Results are like weather reports' — Miss Adeyemi offered this by way of analogy. An analogy is —
o: a comparison between two things that are alike in some way
a formal question about an exam mark
money given once and never repaid
a ranking from first to last
quiz.ex: analogy = 类比。draw/make an analogy 打比方。by analogy with sth 通过与…类比。对比 metaphor（暗喻）。

quiz.q: You attain a level — a standard that other people set. To attain means —
o: to finish a task that was on nobody's list
to reach a level or standard, usually after effort
to give credit where it is due
quiz.ex: attain = 达到、获得（标准/水平）。attain a goal/target/level。近义 achieve；名词 attainment 造诣。

quiz.q: The university offered a small grant — money given once, never repaid. A grant is —
o: a formal query about a mark
money given for a purpose, which does not have to be paid back
quiz.ex: grant = 助学金、拨款（n.）；授予（v.）。take sth for granted 视为理所当然。对比 scholarship 奖学金、fellowship 研究基金。

quiz.q: The school ranked every subject from first to last. To rank means —
o: to award a letter grade to each student
to put people or things in order of position or quality
to write half a page of feedback
quiz.ex: rank = 排名、名次（n./v.）。rank first/second 名列第一/第二。top-ranked 首屈一指的。

quiz.q: The world will underestimate some of you because of where you come from. To underestimate means —
o: to think something is smaller or less important than it really is
to think something is greater than it really is
to resolve a query within a fortnight
quiz.ex: underestimate = 低估。反义 overestimate 高估。前缀 under-/over- 一对：underpaid/overpaid。

quiz.q: Tomas filed a query — a formal question about a mark. A query is —
o: an envelope with money in it
a question, especially a formal or doubtful one
quiz.ex: query = 质询、疑问（n.）；质疑（v.）。query the results 质询成绩。数据库高频：database query 查询。

quiz.q: Manifest talent: ability that shows itself without being examined. Here manifest means —
o: hidden until an exam reveals it
quiz.ex: manifest = 明显的、显露的（adj.）；显现（v.）。manifest itself 显露出来。manifesto 宣言与之同根。

quiz.q: To appreciate something means both to be grateful for it and to understand its true worth. To appreciate means —
o: to rank it from first to last
to value and be thankful for something
quiz.ex: appreciate 一词两义：感激；理解/欣赏（其价值）。I appreciate your help 感激；appreciate the difference 体会差别。名词 appreciation。

title: The Inventor's Attic
text:
Number 14 had stood empty for a month when Mr Novak moved in: a small man with a walking stick, three crates of papers, and a piano the removal men refused to carry. Dani helped with the crates, and by teatime had earned the only tour of the attic Mr Novak ever gave anyone.

The attic was a museum with a workbench. "I trained at the {{polytechnic}} in 1968," he said, "when a {{technology}} course meant valves, solder and drawing boards. Technology is a whole way of making things work. A {{technique}} is one clever move inside it — how you hold the iron, how you read a circuit. People confuse the two, and then they confuse both with luck."

He had spent forty years as an {{engineer}}; his wife, he said, had been an aircraft {{mechanic}}, which was a harder job and a better paid one. "She said engineering was thinking with a pencil and mechanics was thinking with your hands. Between us, we thought with everything."

"Did you invent things?" asked Dani.

"Three patents," he said, pulling a folder from a crate. "A {{patent}} is a deal you make with the state. You {{disclose}} exactly how your machine works — every screw, every secret — and in exchange the state promises that for twenty years nobody else may sell it. Most inventors hate that part. Secrecy feels safer than disclosure. It isn't."

"How is disclosing different from just... telling people?"

"Four words, four jobs," said Mr Novak. "You {{disclose}} to the patents office, because the law requires it. You {{reveal}} to the world, when you choose to. You {{uncover}} something that was hidden — a fact, a fraud, an old well under the kitchen floor. And journalists {{expose}} what powerful people would rather keep dark. Disclosure, revelation, uncovering, exposure: the same action, watched from four different directions."

"And what did you invent?"

He opened the folder. "A water-level alarm for boilers. Small, brass, honest. And here is the lesson, since you are still standing: to {{invent}} is to make something that was never there. To {{discover}} is to find something that always was — America, penicillin, the well under the kitchen. And to {{devise}} — the quiet third verb — is to work out a way of doing something: a method, a trick. I have done one of each, and only the first one paid."

On the bench lay a half-built brass machine. "A {{prototype}}," he said. "The first rough body of an idea, built to be doubted. This one worked for six weeks and then educated me by failing. Beside it is the {{mould}} for its plastic case — a mould is the hollow shape you pour things into, and the reason your telephone looks like everybody else's."

"Was it a breakthrough?"

"A {{breakthrough}}," said Mr Novak, "is what newspapers call the one good year in twenty. The other nineteen you {{advance}} an inch at a time, and if you are lucky you {{innovate}} once — do something genuinely new. People use the three words interchangeably, which is how you can tell they have never done any of them."

Optics, he admitted, was never his {{domain}}. "A {{domain}} is the territory you own or work in — the patents office files everything by domain. A {{field}} is the profession's own word for the same ground: my field was hydraulics. A {{realm}} is grander — a kingdom of ideas rather than a street of workshops. Choose your word according to the size of your ambition."

Inside those territories he had {{specialise}}d in valves, and for six years his job title had been {{tester}}. "A tester's job is to be cruel politely. You try to break what your colleagues love. The good ones write reports the designers read twice."

The brass machine had a switch with two positions. "Eco and boost — even kettles have {{mode}}s now," he said. "Modes are what happens when a machine offers to think for you."

"And the {{foundation}} of the whole business?" he added, as they went down the narrow stairs. "Arithmetic. Every trick upstairs is standing on it." At the bottom he pressed a small object into Dani's hand: a brass disc that rang when the pressure dropped. "A {{gizmo}}," he said. "A small mechanism with a silly name that solves a problem nobody knew they had. It is the best word in engineering, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise."

It rang that night, at two in the morning, in Dani's kitchen, when nobody had touched it. She never found out why. Mr Novak, asked the next day, only looked pleased.
tr:
14号宅子空了一个月后，诺瓦克先生搬了进来：一个拄着手杖的小个子男人，带着三箱文件，和一架搬运工拒绝抬上楼的钢琴。丹妮帮忙搬了箱子，到喝茶时间，她赢得了诺瓦克先生一生中唯一一次带人参观阁楼的机会。

那间阁楼是一座带工作台的博物馆。“我1968年在理工学院（polytechnic）受训，”他说，“那时一门技术（technology）课意味着电子管、焊锡和绘图板。技术是让事物运转的一整套方法。技巧（technique）是其中聪明的一手——怎么握烙铁，怎么读电路。人们混淆这两个词，接着又把两者都和运气混为一谈。”

他做了四十年工程师（engineer）；他的妻子，他说，曾是飞机机械师（mechanic），活儿更累，钱也更多。“她说工程是用铅笔思考，机械是用双手思考。我们俩加起来，用全身思考。”

“你发明过东西吗？”丹妮问。

“三项专利，”他从箱子里抽出一个文件夹。“专利（patent）是你和国家做的一笔交易。你披露（disclose）你的机器究竟如何运转——每颗螺丝、每个秘密——作为交换，国家承诺二十年内别人不得售卖它。多数发明人讨厌这一步。保密感觉比公开安全。其实不然。”

“披露和直接告诉别人有什么区别？”

“四个词，四份工作，”诺瓦克先生说。“你向专利局披露（disclose），因为法律要求。你向世界揭示（reveal），时机由你选。你揭开（uncover）本被隐藏的东西——一个事实、一场骗局、厨房地板下的一口老井。而记者们曝光（expose）权势者希望继续黑暗下去的勾当。披露、揭示、揭开、曝光：同一个动作，从四个方向看过去。”

“那你发明了什么？”

他打开文件夹。“一台锅炉水位警报器。小巧，黄铜，诚实。既然你还站着，就再听一课：发明（invent）是造出世上原本没有的东西。发现（discover）是找到世上一直存在的东西——美洲、青霉素、厨房底下那口井。而设计（devise）——安静的第三个动词——是想出做事的办法：一种方法、一个巧计。三样我各干过一件，只有第一件挣到了钱。”

工作台上躺着一台半成品的黄铜机器。“样机（prototype），”他说，“一个念头的第一具粗糙身体，造出来就是让人怀疑的。这台运转了六周，然后用失败给我上了一课。旁边是它塑料外壳的模具（mould）——模具就是你往里浇注东西的空腔形状，也是你的电话和别人长得一模一样的原因。”

“这算突破吗？”

“突破（breakthrough），”诺瓦克先生说，“是报纸对二十年里那一个好年份的称呼。其余十九年，你一寸一寸地推进（advance），运气好的话创新（innovate）一次——做出真正新的东西。人们把这三个词换着用，由此你就能断定，这三件事他们一件也没做过。”

光学，他承认，从来不是他的领域（domain）。“领域（domain）是你拥有或耕耘的领地——专利局一切归档都按领域分。行业（field）是行当自己对同一块地盘的说法：我的行业是液压。领域（realm）则宏大得多——是思想的王国，而非一条作坊街。按你野心的大小挑你的词。”

在这些领地里，他专门化（specialise）研究阀门，而且有六年，他的职位头衔是测试员（tester）。“测试员的工作是礼貌地残忍。你去弄坏同事们心爱的东西。干得好的，写出的报告设计师会读两遍。”

那台黄铜机器有个两档开关。“节能档和强力档——如今连水壶都有模式（mode）了，”他说，“模式就是机器主动替你思考时发生的事。”

“那这一切的地基（foundation）是什么？”下楼时他又补了一句。“算术。楼上的每个花样都站在它上面。”到了楼下，他把一件小东西塞进丹妮手里：一个气压下降时会响的黄铜圆盘。“小玩意儿（gizmo），”他说，“一个名字傻气、解决没人知道自己有的问题的小机械。这是工程学里最好的词，谁反驳都别听。”

当晚凌晨两点，那东西在丹妮的厨房里响了，没有任何人碰过它。她始终没弄清原因。第二天去问，诺瓦克先生只是露出一副得意的样子。

quiz.q: A small mechanism with a silly name that solves a problem nobody knew they had. A gizmo is —
o: a job title for someone who breaks machines politely
a legal deal with the state lasting twenty years
the hollow shape you pour plastic into
a small gadget or device, often with a silly name
quiz.ex: gizmo = 小装置、小玩意儿（口语）。近义 gadget。雅思口语描述发明类话题可用。

quiz.q: You disclose exactly how your machine works, and in exchange the state protects it for twenty years. A patent is —
o: a legal right to be the only seller of an invention for some years
a rough first body of an idea
a way of thinking with your hands
a file kept by the patents office only
quiz.ex: patent = 专利。apply for a patent 申请专利。形容词 patented 获专利的。注意区别 parent（父母）。

quiz.q: The first rough body of an idea, built to be doubted. A prototype is —
o: the mould for the plastic case
the first working model made to test a design
quiz.ex: prototype = 样机、原型。prototype testing 样机测试。前缀 proto-（最初的）。

quiz.q: To devise — the quiet third verb — is to work out a way of doing something. To devise means —
o: to tighten valves for forty years
to find something that always existed
to file papers with the patents office
to invent a method, plan or system by thinking
quiz.ex: devise = 设计、想出（方法/方案）。devise a plan/scheme。名词 device 装置。两词同根不同义。

quiz.q: A breakthrough is what newspapers call the one good year in twenty. A breakthrough is —
o: a failure that educates the inventor
an inch of progress per year
an important discovery that suddenly advances a field
a mode on a modern kettle
quiz.ex: breakthrough = 突破。a major/scientific breakthrough 重大/科学突破。动词短语 break through 突围。

quiz.q: Optics was never his domain; hydraulics was his field; ideas are a grander realm. A domain is —
o: a wooden workbench in an attic
a folder in a crate of papers
an area of activity, knowledge or ownership
quiz.ex: domain = 领域、领地。public domain 公有领域；the domain of science 科学领域。近义 field（行业）、realm（王国、境界）。

quiz.q: A tester's job is to be cruel politely — try to break what your colleagues love. A tester is —
o: someone whose job is to test products for faults
someone who trains at a polytechnic
an aircraft mechanic paid better than an engineer
quiz.ex: tester = 测试员。动词 test + -er。game tester 游戏测试员。同构：designer 设计师、repairer 修理工。

quiz.q: Technology is a whole way of making things work; a technique is one clever move inside it. A technique is —
o: a particular method of doing something skilfully
a deal with the patents office
quiz.ex: technique = 技巧、手法。technique for doing sth 做某事的技巧。区分 technology（技术、技术体系）。

title: The Repair Café
text:
On the last Saturday of the month, the community hall becomes a Repair Café. You bring anything broken; a table of volunteers tries to save it. Repairs are free, donations buy the tea, and the house rule is the oldest thing in the building: nothing leaves this room worse than it arrived.

The hall is a public {{facility}} — a building with a job — and once a month it fills with {{equipment}}. "Learn the family tree," says Mr Novak, who runs the electrical table. "A {{tool}} is held in the hand and does one job — a screwdriver, a file. An {{appliance}} plugs into the wall and does domestic work — a toaster, a washing machine. A {{device}} is any clever made thing, from a wristwatch to a missile. An {{instrument}} measures, or makes music. And equipment is the collective word — the whole kit you would load into a van. Five words, one family, and the family argues at Christmas."

At the watch table sits Miss Okonkwo, who taught physics for thirty years. Hers is the vocabulary of measurement. "You {{gauge}} by eye — thickness, distance, mood. You {{measure}} with a ruler and write the number down. You {{count}} what can be counted — screws, teeth, beads. You {{estimate}} what cannot — age, the weight of a suitcase, the hour of the day. You {{calculate}} on paper, and you {{compute}} when a machine does the arithmetic for you. Then come the two judges: you {{assess}} a situation — is it safe, is it worth it? — and you {{evaluate}} the repair itself: cost, hope, and history. People bring their grandmothers' clocks here. You are not evaluating an object. You are evaluating an inheritance."

An old radio arrived at eleven, wrapped in a tea towel. Inside: dust, a loose wire, a capacitor gone grey. The young volunteers {{gather}}ed round; screws {{accumulate}}d in the magnetic dish; nothing new was {{add}}ed, and nothing should have been. "Repair is the art of taking something apart honestly," said Miss Okonkwo. "You {{assemble}} it back the way it came apart, {{attach}} the last screw, and only then look up."

The {{accessory}} box held straps, springs and caps — things the machine could live without but would look undressed without. The {{auxiliary}} speaker was the spare one, kept for emergencies; and the {{byproduct}} of every repair session was a box of orphan parts that nobody would ever claim. "Everything {{belong}}s somewhere," said Miss Okonkwo, labelling the box. "We just don't always know where yet."

At the bike table, a boy was praising his screwdriver to the roof. "It's {{versatile}}," he said. "Opens machines, tightens hinges, and in an emergency opens paint tins." — "Which is also," said Mr Novak, "why you {{utilise}} it for everything. To utilise is to use, with a shirt and tie on. It is what you do when the proper tool is at home and the job is now."

A manual was taped under the toaster's lid, listing its {{usage}}: how often, how long, how hard. "Usage is what the maker intended," said Mr Novak. "Use is what actually happens. The gap between them is why we are all here."

"You must {{concentrate}} in this room," Miss Okonkwo told the newest volunteer, whose eyes kept drifting to the tea urn. "Concentration is the whole ticket: eyes, hands, one radio. And when you find the fault, you will {{focus}} — the whole world narrowing down to one wire. Focus is concentration with its elbows on the table."

The new volunteers {{absorb}}ed the tricks without noticing: which way a thread turns, which smell means trouble, which customer should be given tea before the bad news. Absorption is what learning is called when it is happening to someone else.

"And where does the house rule {{apply}}?" someone asked, as the afternoon ended. "Everywhere," said Mr Novak. "Rules apply everywhere; tools only where they fit." He tightened the last screw of a lamp, and the lamp, for no reason anyone could explain, worked.

By four o'clock the old radio sang — a Polish station, faint but proud — and its owner, an old man who had said nothing all afternoon, stayed behind to help stack the chairs. The café's record is painted on the wall of the hall: six hundred and forty objects saved, twelve given up. Every entry, in Miss Okonkwo's handwriting, ends with the same four words: it belongs somewhere.
tr:
每月最后一个周六，社区会堂就变成一家维修咖啡馆。你带来任何坏掉的东西，一桌志愿者会设法救活它。修理免费，捐款买茶，而馆规是这栋楼里最老的东西：任何东西离开这间屋子时，都不许比来的时候更糟。

会堂是一处公共设施（facility）——一栋有职责的建筑——每月一次，它会被各种设备（equipment）填满。“学会这棵家谱树，”负责电工桌的诺瓦克先生说。“工具（tool）握在手里，干一件事——螺丝刀、锉刀。家电（appliance）插在墙上，干家务活——烤面包机、洗衣机。装置（device）是任何人造的巧妙物件，从手表到导弹。仪器（instrument）用来测量，或者演奏音乐。而设备（equipment）是集合词——你往面包车里装的那一整套。五个词，一家人，而且这家人圣诞节还吵架。”

钟表桌旁坐着教了三十年物理的奥孔科沃小姐。她拥有的是测量的词汇。“你用眼估（gauge）——厚度、距离、心情。你用尺量（measure），并写下数字。你能数的就数（count）——螺丝、齿、珠子。不能数的就估（estimate）——年龄、一只手提箱的重量、此刻的钟点。你在纸上算（calculate），机器替你算时叫计算（compute）。然后是两位裁判：你评估（assess）局面——安全吗，值得吗？——你再评判（evaluate）这次修理本身：成本、希望，和历史。人们把祖母的座钟送到这里来。你评判的不是一件物品，是一笔遗产。”

十一点，一台老收音机送到，裹在茶巾里。拆开：灰尘，一根松了的电线，一个发灰的电容器。年轻志愿者围（gather）拢过来；螺丝在磁性盘里越积（accumulate）越多；没有添加（add）任何新东西，本来也不该加。“修理是一门诚实拆解的艺术，”奥孔科沃小姐说。“你把它按拆开的原样装（assemble）回去，固定（attach）最后一颗螺丝，然后才抬头。”

附件（accessory）盒里放着背带、弹簧和帽盖——机器离了它们能活，但光着身子不好看。那台辅助（auxiliary）音箱是备用的，留作急用；而每场维修的副产品（byproduct），是一盒永远无人认领的孤儿零件。“每样东西都属于（belong）某个地方，”奥孔科沃小姐给盒子贴标签时说，“只是我们不一定知道是哪里。”

自行车桌边，一个男孩对着天花板赞美他的螺丝刀。“它多才多艺（versatile），”他说，“拆机器、紧铰链，紧急时还能开油漆罐。”“这也是为什么，”诺瓦克先生说，“你会拿它利用（utilise）于一切。utilise 就是 use，只是穿了衬衫打了领带。合适的工具在家里、活儿却在眼前时，你干的就是这件事。”

烤面包机盖子内侧贴着说明书，列出它的用法（usage）：多频繁、多长时间、多用力。“用法是制造者的本意，”诺瓦克先生说，“使用是实际发生的事。两者的差距，就是我们大家今天坐在这儿的原因。”

“在这个房间里你必须专注（concentrate），”奥孔科沃小姐对最新的志愿者说，后者的眼睛老往茶炉那边飘。“专注是全部的入场券：眼睛、手、一台收音机。等你找到故障，你就会聚焦（focus）——整个世界缩窄成一根电线。focus 就是把手肘撑上桌的 concentration。”

新志愿者不知不觉地吸收（absorb）着各种窍门：螺纹朝哪边拧、哪种气味意味着麻烦、哪种顾客该在坏消息之前先上茶。吸收，是学习发生在别人身上时的名字。

“那馆规适用于（apply）哪里？”下午快结束时有人问。“所有地方，”诺瓦克先生说，“规则处处适用；工具只在合适的地方。”他拧紧一盏台灯的最后一颗螺丝，那盏灯出于无人能解释的原因，亮了。

四点整，那台老收音机唱了起来——一个波兰电台，微弱却骄傲——它的主人，一位整个下午一言不发的老人，留下来帮忙摞椅子。会堂墙上刷着咖啡馆的战绩：六百四十件物品获救，十二件放弃。每一条记录，奥孔科沃小姐的笔迹，结尾都是同样的四个字：它属于某处。

quiz.q: An appliance plugs into the wall and does domestic work — a toaster, a washing machine. An appliance is —
o: any clever made thing, from watch to missile
a machine for household use, usually electrical
a hand tool with one job
a collective word for all the kit
quiz.ex: appliance = 家用电器。household appliances 家电。区分 device（泛指装置）、instrument（仪器/乐器）、tool（手持工具）。

quiz.q: You gauge by eye — thickness, distance, mood. To gauge means —
o: to count screws in a magnetic dish
to measure with a ruler and write it down
to judge a size or amount by looking, without exact measuring
quiz.ex: gauge = 估计、目测（v.）；计量器（n.）。a fuel/pressure gauge 油/压力表。美式拼写 gage 少见。

quiz.q: You assess a situation, and you evaluate the repair itself: cost, hope, and history. To evaluate means —
o: to gather volunteers round a table
to judge the value or worth of something carefully
quiz.ex: evaluate = 评估、评价。evaluate performance/risks 评估表现/风险。名词 evaluation。近义 assess（评估局面）。

quiz.q: The byproduct of every repair session was a box of orphan parts. A byproduct is —
o: something produced as a secondary result of a process
the spare speaker kept for emergencies
a strap or spring in the accessory box
the house rule of the café
quiz.ex: byproduct = 副产品。by-（次要的）+ product。引申义：意外结果。同构：byroad 小路、byway 偏僻小径。

quiz.q: Opens machines, tightens hinges, opens paint tins — the screwdriver is versatile. Versatile means —
o: able to be used for many different purposes
quiz.ex: versatile = 多才多艺的、多用途的。a versatile tool/actor 万能工具/多面手演员。名词 versatility。

quiz.q: You assemble it back the way it came apart, attach the last screw, then look up. To assemble means —
o: to fit the parts of something together
to gather screws in a dish
to wrap a radio in a tea towel
quiz.ex: assemble = 组装、装配。assembly line 装配线。反义 disassemble 拆解。近义 gather（人的聚集）。

quiz.q: The hall is a public facility — a building with a job. A facility is —
o: a building or service provided for a purpose
the whole kit loaded into a van
a manual taped under a lid
quiz.ex: facility = 设施、场所。sports/medical facilities 运动/医疗设施。另一义：能力（a facility for languages 语言天赋）。

quiz.q: The auxiliary speaker is the spare one, kept for emergencies. Auxiliary means —
quiz.ex: auxiliary = 辅助的、备用的。auxiliary staff/verb 助手/助动词（语法术语）。名词指辅助设备、辅助人员。

title: Signals and Screens
text:
The rain cancelled Saturday's match, so Tomas spent the afternoon in his grandfather's study, where four generations of machines lived on the same shelves and none of them agreed about anything.

Top shelf: a pair of naval binoculars. "{{Optics}}," his grandfather said, "is the physics of light — the science behind everything from spectacles to telescopes. Each barrel holds a {{lens}}; grind it a hair wrong and the whole world smears." Tomas's school {{microscope}} lived on the same shelf, on loan to the house, its three little lenses mounted in a brass turret.

"{{Radar}}," the old man went on, "works like shouting at a cliff. You send out a pulse and wait for the {{echo}} — the reflected shout. Time the gap, multiply by the speed of the pulse, halve it, and you know how far the cliff is. At sea, the cliff might be a ship, a coastline, or weather. The machine listens for its own voice coming back. A {{sensor}} is anything that feels the world and tells a machine about it: a thermometer, a camera, the smoke alarm upstairs. Your generation is surrounded by sensors and calls it convenience."

The middle shelf held the sound machines: a valve radio with a glowing {{dial}}, a reel-to-reel {{tape}} recorder, and a shoebox of {{cassette}}s labelled in his grandmother's handwriting. At the bottom sat an honest {{microcomputer}} from 1982 — "a keyboard with pretensions," his grandfather called it — and beside it, Tomas's own {{laptop}}, thin as a magazine.

On the microcomputer, programs arrived as instructions typed laboriously on its {{keyboard}}; its {{screen}} showed green letters on black, and it saved nothing unless you remembered to save it. On the laptop, the {{software}} did the remembering. "{{Digital}} means counted in numbers," the old man said. "Everything in there — every photograph, every song, this afternoon's weather — is stored as {{binary}}: nothing but ones and zeros, on and off, yes and no. Your grandmother's tape is different. It is a wave — a copy of the shape of her voice. The wave is fragile; the numbers are patient."

That evening they carried the shoebox downstairs. The laptop's {{wireless}} found the home {{network}}; Tomas opened a {{browser}} to check one fact on the {{high-definition}} screen and stayed an hour. They plugged the cassette player into the machine and let the software listen, and through the {{loudspeaker}}s, faint under the rain, his grandmother began to sing.

"You can hear the difference between her tape and a digital file," the old man said. "The file is cleaner. The tape is warmer. Neither is wrong; they are two kinds of honest."

Tomas recorded his grandfather's voice on the laptop's {{microphone}} — the radar story, the binoculars, the names of the cassettes — while the words still came easily. "Why record it?" he asked. "Because your children will want to hear it," said his grandfather, "and because I will not always be this talkative."

On the bottom shelf, paperbacks: Verne, Wells, Le Guin. "{{Science fiction}} is the literature of what might happen if we go on," his grandfather said, "and {{fantasy}} is the literature of what never will. Both begin with a {{vision}} — a picture of a world not yet built. Everything in this room was somebody's science fiction first: the radar, the laptop, the microphone that is recording me saying so. Even the {{multimedia}} evening you are having — {{audio}}, moving pictures, text and links, all at once — was a prophecy with a library stamp on it."

Before Tomas left, they labelled the new files. "The tape remembered her as a wave," he wrote on the box. "The numbers will remember you as numbers. Both, apparently, remember."
tr:
大雨取消了周六的比赛，托马斯便在祖父的书房里度过这个下午。四代机器住在同一排架子上，彼此对什么都不服气。

最上层：一副海军双筒望远镜。“光学（optics），”祖父说，“是光的物理学——从眼镜到望远镜，一切背后的学问。每个镜筒里有一片透镜（lens）；研磨差一根头发丝，整个世界就花了。”托马斯学校的显微镜（microscope）也在同一层，借住在这间屋子里，三枚小透镜装在黄铜转塔上。

“雷达（radar），”老人继续说，“原理就像对着悬崖喊话。你发出一个脉冲，等回声（echo）——被反射回来的那声喊回来。掐算间隔，乘以脉冲的速度，除以二，就知道悬崖有多远。在海上，那道‘悬崖’可能是一艘船、一段海岸，或者一场天气。机器听的，是自己的声音回不回来。传感器（sensor）就是任何能感知世界并告诉机器的东西：温度计、相机、楼上的烟雾报警器。你们这代人被传感器包围，还管它叫便利。”

中层住着声音的机器：一台指针发亮的刻度（dial）式电子管收音机，一台开盘磁带（tape）录音机，还有一鞋盒祖母手写标签的盒式磁带（cassette）。最下层坐着一台1982年产的正经微机（microcomputer）——“一台有野心的键盘，”祖父这么叫它——旁边是托马斯自己的笔记本电脑（laptop），薄得像本杂志。

在微机上，程序靠键盘（keyboard）上辛辛苦苦敲进去的指令到来；它的屏幕（screen）是黑底绿字，你忘了存盘它就什么都不留。在笔记本电脑上，软件（software）替你记着。“数字（digital）的意思是用数字来计数，”老人说，“那里面的一切——每张照片、每首歌、今天下午的天气——都以二进制（binary）存储：只有一和零，开和关，是和否。你祖母的磁带不一样，它是一道波——她声音形状的拷贝。波是脆弱的，数字是有耐心的。”

当晚他们把鞋盒搬下楼。笔记本电脑的无线（wireless）连上了家庭网络（network）；托马斯在高清（high-definition）屏幕上打开浏览器（browser）核实一个事实，一待就是一个小时。他们把卡带机接上电脑，让软件听着，然后透过音箱（loudspeaker），在雨声底下，祖母开始唱歌，微弱却清晰。

“你能听出她的磁带和数字文件的区别，”老人说，“文件更干净，磁带更温暖。两个都没错；它们是两种诚实。”

托马斯用笔记本电脑的麦克风（microphone）录下祖父的声音——雷达的故事、双筒望远镜、一盒盒磁带的名字——趁这些话现在还说得出。“为什么要录？”他问。“因为你的孩子会想听，”祖父说，“也因为我不会永远这么健谈。”

最底层是平装书：凡尔纳、威尔斯、勒古恩。“科幻（science fiction）小说是‘如果我们继续走下去，可能发生什么’的文学，”祖父说，“奇幻（fantasy）是‘永远不会发生什么’的文学。两者都始于一个愿景（vision）——一幅尚未建成的世界的图景。这间屋里的每样东西，起初都是某人的科幻小说：雷达、笔记本电脑、此刻正在录音说这句话的麦克风。连你今晚这场多媒体（multimedia）——音频（audio）、活动画面、文字和链接同时进行——也曾是一份盖着图书馆印章的预言。”

临走前，他们给新文件贴上标签。“磁带以波的形式记住她，”他在盒子上写，“数字将以数字记住你。两种方式，显然都记得住。”

quiz.q: Send out a pulse and wait for the echo — the reflected shout. An echo is —
o: a device that feels the world and tells a machine
a sound that comes back after hitting a surface
a binary code of ones and zeros
quiz.ex: echo = 回声。radar works like shouting at a cliff and timing the echo。引申义：echo sb's views 附和某人观点。

quiz.q: A sensor is anything that feels the world and tells a machine about it. A sensor is —
o: a screen showing green letters on black
a device that detects light, heat, motion etc. and reports it
a lens ground a hair wrong
quiz.ex: sensor = 传感器。motion/smoke/temperature sensor 运动/烟雾/温度传感器。动词 sense 感知。

quiz.q: Everything in there is stored as binary: nothing but ones and zeros, on and off. Binary means —
o: using only two symbols or states
quiz.ex: binary = 二进制的。bi-（二）+ nomen。binary code/number 二进制代码/数。binary star 双星。

quiz.q: Optics is the physics of light — behind everything from spectacles to telescopes. Optics is —
o: the science of light and lenses
quiz.ex: optics = 光学。fiber optics 光纤。形容词 optical 光学的/视力的（optical illusion 视错觉）。

quiz.q: A shoebox of cassettes labelled in his grandmother's handwriting. A cassette is —
o: a small flat tape for recording sound or video
quiz.ex: cassette = 盒式磁带。cassette player/tape recorder 磁带播放机。同根 cassettetes 无此拼法，注意双 s。

quiz.q: The laptop's wireless found the home network. Here wireless means —
o: a radio connection that needs no cables
a glowing dial in the dark
a microphone built into the screen
quiz.ex: wireless = 无线的（adj.）；无线电（n.，英式旧称 radio 为 wireless）。wireless network 无线网络。构词：wire + -less（无）。

quiz.q: Audio, moving pictures, text and links, all at once — a multimedia evening. Multimedia means —
o: science fiction with a library stamp
using several forms of media together
quiet and warm like a cassette
quiz.ex: multimedia = 多媒体。multi-（多）+ media（媒介）。multimedia presentation 多媒体演示。

quiz.q: Science fiction begins with a vision — a picture of a world not yet built. Here a vision is —
o: a faint song under the rain
a mental picture of a possible future
quiz.ex: vision 一词多义：愿景/远见（a leader with vision）；视力（blurry vision 视力模糊）；幻象。本文为"愿景"。

title: The City Underneath
text:
On careers day the engineering firm opens its doors, and Ms Osei takes six students down a spiral staircase into the city beneath the city. "Everything visible up there," she says, "is standing on everything invisible down here."

The first chamber smells of rain. "This is the {{drainage}} network," she says — "the system that carries storm water away from the streets. When it rains, thirty thousand litres a minute arrive in this room. When it does not rain, the room waits." Steel gates the size of doors turn on a single {{pivot}}, opened by {{hydraulic}} rams — water, pushing water — while above them, the street carries on not knowing.

The pump hall is the cathedral of the underworld: fourteen {{pump}}s in a row, a back-up {{generator}} in the corner, and one {{gear}} wheel the size of a dinner table. "We {{convert}} electricity into motion, and motion into flow," says Ms Osei. "Every machine in this hall {{transform}}s one thing into another; that is the whole of engineering. {{Ventilation}} shafts keep the air breathable down here — the first thing a miner's canary ever taught us."

The treatment works is quieter and smells, honestly, of itself. "{{Sewage}} is not a rude word," says Ms Osei firmly. "It is simply used water. First it is screened; then it settles; then it passes through a {{filter}} bed; then chemicals and sunlight {{purify}} it. To purify is to remove what harms; to {{refine}} is to remove what merely coarsens; and in the laboratory upstairs they {{distil}} samples — boil them and catch the steam — to test them. The whole art is subtraction. And when we improve the plant, we {{simplify}} it: every good system is a simplification of a worse one. Complexity is what a design looks like before it is finished."

In the plant room the compressors {{compress}} air for the tools, and the chillers {{condense}} steam back into water for the boilers. "Compress and condense," she says. "One squeezes, one settles. Most of engineering is knowing which to do when."

The control room is a wall of screens. "The works {{operate}}s twenty-four hours a day, and this room {{facilitate}}s everything — it makes the whole plant easier to run, coordinating pumps, gates and alarms. The current upgrade runs on a {{framework}} — an overall structure of plans — with every {{aspect}} of the works considered, from noise to wildlife, and it will be delivered in three {{phase}}s. The city {{alter}}s every decade: demand {{shift}}s southward, the river {{turn}}s its moods, the rules change. The plant {{adapt}}s slowly, like a whale, and we {{adjust}} the pumps hourly, like a heartbeat."

On her screen, a map of the city glows with green threads. "Acoustic loggers. A leak announces itself by singing, and the network can {{pinpoint}} it within a metre."

"Is that accurate?" asked a student.

"Careful," said Ms Osei, delighted. "{{Accurate}} means close to the truth. {{Precise}} means finely divided — you can be precisely wrong. {{Correct}} means exactly right, the whole answer. Three words, three standards. Engineers who mix them up build very confident bridges."

By the door hung a photograph: a flooded street, a paper boat floating past a shop window. "In 1998, this room failed," she said. "An {{error}} in a calculation — a wrong number. A {{mistake}} in a decision — the gates were held open. A {{flaw}} in the design — the overflow was sized for a smaller storm. And a {{fault}} in a weld that no inspection caught. Four words, four doors into the same flood. An error is a wrong number; a mistake is a wrong action; a flaw is built into the drawing; a fault is where the world finally gives way. And the fifth word—" she tapped the photograph — "a {{stumble}}: the small trip that teaches a city to walk. Everything rebuilt after 1998 is better than what it replaced. Every plan we write now carries a {{contingency}} — a plan for the plan going wrong — because you cannot choose your {{circumstance}}s, only your answers to them."

At six o'clock she unlocked her own front door, three neighbourhoods away, into a hallway that said, in a warm synthetic voice, "{{welcome home}}" — and switched on the lights, the heating and, for reasons known only to itself, the kettle. "Every one of those words," she told the kettle, "is a sensor, a network and a pump. And somebody, somewhere, is still on the night shift, keeping it all invisible."
tr:
职业开放日，工程公司敞开大门，奥塞女士带着六名学生沿一道旋转楼梯，走进城市之下的城市。“上面一切看得见的东西，”她说，“都站在下面一切看不见的东西上。”

第一间屋子闻得到雨。“这是排水（drainage）管网，”她说，“把雨水从街道带走的系统。下雨时，每分钟三万升水涌进这个房间。不下雨时，房间等着。”门板大小的钢闸在单根枢轴（pivot）上转动，由液压（hydraulic）柱塞推开——用水推水——而头顶上，街道照常运转，一无所知。

泵房是地下世界的大教堂：十四台泵（pump）排成一列，角落里一台备用发电机（generator），还有一只餐桌大小的齿轮（gear）。“我们把电转化（convert）为运动，再把运动转化为流量，”奥塞女士说。“这个大厅里的每台机器都在把一种东西变成（transform）另一种；这就是工程的全部。通风（ventilation）竖井让地下的空气可以呼吸——这是矿工的金丝雀教给我们的第一课。”

处理厂安静些，气味嘛，说实话，像它自己。“污水（sewage）不是个粗俗的词，”奥塞女士语气坚定，“它只是用过的水。先隔栅拦污，再沉淀，然后经过滤（filter）床，最后由化学品和阳光净化（purify）。净化是去除有害的；精炼（refine）是去除只是粗粝的；楼上实验室里，他们蒸馏（distil）水样——煮沸再接住蒸汽——来检测。这门艺术的全部就是减法。我们改进这座厂时，是在把它简化（simplify）：每个好系统都是一个更坏系统的简化版。复杂，是设计完工之前的样子。”

机房里，压缩机把空气压缩（compress）供工具使用，冷水机组把蒸汽冷凝（condense）回锅炉用水。“压缩和冷凝，”她说，“一个挤，一个沉。工程学的大半，是知道什么时候用哪个。”

控制室是一整面墙的屏幕。“处理厂一天二十四小时运转（operate），而这个房间促成（facilitate）一切——让整座厂更易于运转，协调水泵、闸门和警报。眼下的升级改造按一个框架（framework）进行——一整套计划结构——方方面面（aspect）都考虑到了，从噪音到野生动物，并将分三个阶段（phase）交付。城市每十年都会改变（alter）：需求向南转移（shift），河流变脸（turn），规章更迭。处理厂像鲸鱼一样缓慢地适应（adapt），而我们像心跳一样，每小时调节（adjust）一次水泵。”

她的屏幕上，一张城市地图亮着绿色的细线。“声学记录仪。漏水会以唱歌的方式自我暴露，网络能把泄漏点精确定位（pinpoint）到一米之内。”

“这算准确吗？”一个学生问。

“小心，”奥塞女士很高兴。“准确（accurate）指接近真相。精确（precise）指刻度分得细——你可以精确地错。正确（correct）指完全对，整个答案。三个词，三种标准。混淆它们的工程师，会造出信心十足的桥。”

门边挂着一幅照片：一条被淹的街，一只纸船漂过商店橱窗。“1998年，这个房间失守了，”她说。“计算里的一个错误（error）——一个错的数字。决策中的一个失误（mistake）——闸门被保持敞开。设计上的一个缺陷（flaw）——溢流道是按小一号的暴雨设计的。还有一处焊缝的故障（fault），检验没查出来。四个词，通向同一场洪水的四扇门。错误是错的数字，失误是错的行动，缺陷是画在图纸里的，故障是世界最终让步的地方。还有第五个词——”她敲了敲照片，“一次绊倒（stumble）：教会一座城市走路的那一小跤。1998年后重建的一切，都比被它替换的好。我们现在写的每份计划都带着应急预案（contingency）——为计划的落空准备的计划——因为你无法选择境遇（circumstance），只能选择对它的回答。”

六点整，她在三个街区外打开自家前门，门厅用一个温暖的合成声音说：“欢迎回家（welcome home）”——然后打开灯、暖气，还出于只有它自己知道的原因，烧上了水壶。“这句话里的每个字，”她告诉水壶，“都是一台传感器、一张网络和一台泵。而某个人，在某个地方，还在值夜班，让这一切保持隐形。”

quiz.q: Steel gates turned on a single pivot, opened by hydraulic rams — water, pushing water. Hydraulic means —
o: powered by electricity from a generator
quiz.ex: hydraulic = 液压的。hydraulic ram/pump 液压柱塞/泵。名词 hydraulics 水力学。词根 hydra = 水。

quiz.q: Sewage is not a rude word — it is simply used water. Sewage is —
o: waste water carried away in drains
quiz.ex: sewage = 污水。sewage system/treatment 污水系统/处理。区分 sewer 下水道（管道）、sewerage 排污系统。

quiz.q: Chemicals and sunlight purify it; to refine is to remove what merely coarsens. To purify means —
o: to boil and catch the steam
to remove harmful substances and make clean
to make a system more complex
quiz.ex: purify = 净化。purify water/air 净化水/空气。名词 purity 纯度；形容词 pure 纯的。对比 refine（精炼、提纯去粗）。

quiz.q: This room facilitates everything — makes the whole plant easier to run. To facilitate means —
o: to operate twenty-four hours a day
to make a process easier or help it happen
to pinpoint a leak within a metre
to hold the gates open in a storm
quiz.ex: facilitate = 促进、使便利。facilitate communication/discussions 促进沟通/讨论。名词 facility 设施（词义已分化）。

quiz.q: A leak announces itself by singing, and the network can pinpoint it within a metre. To pinpoint means —
o: to sing quietly through a green thread
to make a mistake in a decision
to locate something exactly and precisely
quiz.ex: pinpoint = 精确定位（v.）；极小的/精确的（adj.）。pin（针）+ point（点）。a pinpoint location 精确位置。

quiz.q: Precise means finely divided — you can be precisely wrong. Precise means —
o: exact in detail or measurement, though not necessarily true
quiz.ex: precise = 精确的（刻度细）。区分 accurate（准确、接近真相）。可以 precise but not accurate：刻度很细但整体偏了。

quiz.q: A flaw in the design — the overflow was sized for a smaller storm. A flaw is —
o: a wrong number in a calculation
a weakness built into the design itself
a wrong action taken in the moment
the place where a weld gives way
quiz.ex: flaw = 缺陷、瑕疵（设计/性格中的）。a fatal flaw 致命缺陷。flawless 无瑕的。区分 fault（故障）、error（数值错误）、mistake（行为失误）。

quiz.q: Every plan now carries a contingency — a plan for the plan going wrong. A contingency is —
o: a flooded street with a paper boat
a possible future event you prepare for in advance
a heartbeat adjustment to the pumps
a spiral staircase into the underworld
quiz.ex: contingency = 意外情况、应急事项。contingency plan 应急预案。contingent on sth 视…而定。

title: The Museum Basement
text:
Every {{museum}} keeps two collections: the one you pay to see upstairs, and the one in the basement that pays nobody. Noor volunteered on Saturdays, and Dr Reyes, the conservator, had promised her Box 47 — a crate from a dig that ended before either of them was born.

"{{Archaeology}}," said Dr Reyes, prising the lid, "is the art of listening to objects. Historians read what people wrote; we {{excavate}} what they dropped." Inside, wrapped in 1962 newspaper: {{pottery}} — three bowls, a cracked jug — a bronze ring {{engrave}}d with a name too worn to read, and a string of glass beads that had once {{decorate}}d somebody's neck, or hair, or god.

"An {{antique}}," said Dr Reyes, holding the ring to the light, "is anything over a hundred years old that someone wants to sell you. This is not for sale; this is {{heritage}} — what a whole group inherits, whether it wants to or not. You {{inherit}} your grandmother's ring; a nation inherits its ruins. One is personal, one is public, and both arrive without instructions."

The bowls raised the big words. "A {{culture}} is a whole way of life — food, language, manners, gods. A {{civilisation}} is a culture with infrastructure: cities, writing, taxes, and usually an army. And a {{renaissance}} is what happens when a civilisation rereads its own old books and decides it used to be clever. The word means rebirth, and every country claims one."

"Some words in this room are heavy," she added. "{{Feudalism}} — the system where land, labour and loyalty all belonged to the same lord. {{Slavery}} — the system where people themselves were property. Both are gone here, and both ended recently; these bowls are older than their endings."

"And an {{epic}}?" asked Noor, who had seen the word on a poster.

"A long poem about heroes — war, exile, homecoming — old enough that nobody remembers who wrote it. Every culture with a coastline has one. Epics are how people remembered who they were before they could all read."

The beads raised the people words, and Dr Reyes drew her famous ladder on the packing paper. "A {{tribe}} is a group bound by kin and custom. The {{aboriginal}} inhabitants are the first ones — the people who were there before the histories started. An {{inhabitant}} is anyone who lives somewhere, full stop. A {{native}} was born there. A {{local}} merely lives there now — I am a local; my grandmother was a native of somewhere else. And from the outside looking in: {{exotic}} means excitingly foreign — a word the West has applied to almost everyone, including itself, from the right angle. A {{foreigner}} is a person from another country; an {{alien}} is the legal word for one, and also, if you prefer, an illegal word for a Martian."

"Who studies all this?"

"An {{anthropologist}} studies living cultures; an archaeologist studies dead ones; the two professions argue at conferences. And the {{humanitarian}} — the one whose concern is simply human welfare, wherever the humans are from — is the person both professions secretly want to become."

On the second tray lay objects with gods on them, and Dr Reyes slowed down, as conservators do. "{{Religion}} is the system: beliefs and practices organised around what a people holds sacred. A {{ritual}} is one repeated, formal act within it — a baptism, a festival, a burial. {{Etiquette}} is ritual's little sister: the polite forms of everyday life, no gods required. People defend all three harder than they defend their borders.

"A {{belief}} is a thing held true without demanding proof. The {{soul}} is the self that religion says survives the body. {{Spirit}} covers everything from ghost to mood to national character; and where the three words overlap, wars have started.

"And the adjectives. {{Holy}} belongs to a god. {{Sacred}} is set apart for anything worthy of reverence — a text, a mountain, a silence. {{Hallowed}} is holy grown old: hallowed ground, hallowed be thy name. Use them carefully; people can tell."

They worked until five, matching bowls to cards, and Noor earned the ring's last secret. "The {{engrave}}d name," said Dr Reyes, tilting it under the lamp, "spells the oldest signature in this collection. Someone loved this person enough to order the letters. That is a {{ritual}} too, you know — the smallest one we have."

Then Noor asked about the difference between a {{custom}} and a tradition, and got the answer Dr Reyes gave every volunteer, the one written on the basement wall in pencil: "A {{tradition}} is what your family does at Christmas. A {{custom}} is what your street does. A {{convention}} is what your profession does — gloves in a laboratory, silence in a courtroom. And an {{ideology}} is what a movement wants everybody to do. The first three keep society warm; the fourth keeps it arguing. And when a custom harms someone," she added, packing the beads away, "it stops being charming. That is the {{ethical}} question — the {{moral}} one too: moral is the private judgement of right and wrong; ethical is that judgement written down as rules for a profession. A conservator's first rule is honesty about what is old and what is new. Which is why," she said, tapping the 1962 newspaper, "we keep the wrapping too."
tr:
每座博物馆（museum）都养着两套藏品：楼上那套你付钱看，地下那套谁也不给钱看。努尔周六来做志愿者，修复师雷耶斯博士答应让她开第47号箱——一只木箱，来自一场在她们俩出生前就结束的挖掘。

“考古学（archaeology），”雷耶斯博士撬开箱盖说，“是倾听器物的艺术。历史学家读人们写下的话；我们发掘（excavate）人们丢下的东西。”箱内裹着1962年的报纸：陶器（pottery）——三只碗、一只裂了的壶——一枚刻着（engrave）磨损得无法辨认的名字的青铜戒指，还有一串曾装饰（decorate）过某人脖颈、头发或神明的玻璃珠。

“古董（antique），”雷耶斯博士把戒指举向光，“是任何超过一百年、又有人想卖给你的东西。这一件不出售；它是遗产（heritage）——一整群人共同继承的东西，想不想要都得要。你继承（inherit）祖母的戒指；一个国家继承它的废墟。前者是私人的，后者是公共的，而且都不附说明书。”

这几只碗引出了大词。“文化（culture）是一整套生活方式——食物、语言、礼仪、神明。文明（civilisation）是有基础设施的文化：城市、文字、税收，通常还有一支军队。而文艺复兴（renaissance）是文明重读自己的旧书、发现自己从前很聪明时发生的事。这个词的意思是重生，每个国家都宣称自己有过一次。”

“有些词很沉重，”她补充道。“封建制度（feudalism）——土地、劳役与效忠都归属同一位领主的制度。奴隶制（slavery）——人本身就是财产的制度。两者在这里都已终结，而终结并不久远；这几只碗比它们的终结更古老。”

“那史诗（epic）呢？”努尔问，她在海报上见过这个词。

“写英雄的长诗——战争、流亡、还乡——古老到没人记得作者是谁。每种临海的文化都有一部。在人人识字之前，史诗就是人们记住自己是谁的方式。”

珠子引出了关于人的词，雷耶斯博士在包装纸上画起她那道著名的梯子。“部落（tribe）是由血缘和习俗结成的群体。原住（aboriginal）居民是第一批人——历史开始之前就在那里的人。居民（inhabitant）是住在某处的任何人，仅此而已。本地人（native）生在那里。当地人（local）只是现在住在那里——我是当地人，我祖母是别处的本地人（native）。再从外往里看：异域（exotic）意思是‘外国得令人兴奋’——西方用这个词形容过几乎所有人，角度对了，连自己也包括。外国人（foreigner）是来自另一国的人；外侨（alien）是法律用语，如果愿意，也可以指火星人。”

“研究这些的是谁？”

“人类学家（anthropologist）研究活着的文化；考古学家研究死去的文化；两个职业在学术会议上吵架。而人道主义者（humanitarian）——那个只关心人类福祉、不管人类来自哪里的人——是这两个职业私下都想成为的人。”

第二层托盘上摆着带神的器物，雷耶斯博士放慢了语速，修复师都会这样。“宗教（religion）是体系：围绕一个民族奉为神圣之物组织起来的信仰与践行。仪式（ritual）是其中一个重复的、正式的行为——洗礼、节庆、下葬。礼节（etiquette）是仪式的小妹妹：日常生活的礼貌形式，不需要神。人们捍卫这三样的劲头，比捍卫边境还足。

“信仰（belief）是不要求证据便信以为真的东西。灵魂（soul）是宗教所说肉体死后仍在的那个自我。精神（spirit）从鬼魂到心情到民族性格无所不包；而这三个词重叠的地方，战争已经开始过。

“再看形容词。神圣（holy）属于神。圣洁（sacred）是为任何值得敬畏之物而设——一段文本、一座山、一种沉默。受尊崇的（hallowed）是变老的神圣：hallowed ground 圣地，hallowed be thy name 愿人皆尊你的名为圣。用的时候小心些，人们分辨得出来。”

她们一直干到五点，把碗和卡片一一对应，努尔也赢得了戒指的最后一个秘密。“这刻着的名字，”雷耶斯博士把它侧到灯下，“拼出的是这套藏品里最古老的签名。有人爱这个人，爱到肯去订这些字母。这也是一种仪式（ritual），你知道的——我们所拥有的最小的一种。”

然后努尔问了习俗（custom）和传统的区别，得到了雷耶斯博士给每个志愿者都讲过的答案，就是用铅笔写在地下室墙上的那句：“传统（tradition）是你们家圣诞节做的事。习俗（custom）是你们那条街做的事。惯例（convention）是你们那个行业做的事——实验室戴手套，法庭保持安静。而意识形态（ideology）是一场运动想让所有人做的事。前三种让社会保暖；第四种让社会争吵。”她把珠子收好，又补了一句：“当一种习俗伤害了谁，它就不再可爱。这就是伦理的（ethical）问题——也是道德的（moral）问题：道德是个人对是非的私下判断；伦理是写成行业规则的判断。修复师的第一条规则，是对什么是旧的、什么是新的保持诚实。这也是为什么，”她敲了敲1962年的报纸，“连包装我们也留着。”

quiz.q: This is not for sale; this is heritage — what a whole group inherits. Heritage is —
o: things passed down to a group from the past, worth preserving
an antique over a hundred years old with a price tag
the first inhabitants of a land
quiz.ex: heritage = 遗产（集体）。cultural/national heritage 文化/民族遗产。UNESCO World Heritage 世界遗产。对比 inherit（v. 继承）。

quiz.q: Historians read what people wrote; we excavate what they dropped. To excavate means —
o: to engrave a name on a ring
to dig out buried objects from the ground
quiz.ex: excavate = 发掘、挖出。名词 excavation 挖掘/发掘现场。考古学高频词。

quiz.q: The aboriginal inhabitants are the first ones — before the histories started. Aboriginal means —
o: relating to the earliest known inhabitants of a place
quiz.ex: aboriginal = 原住的、土著的。Aboriginal Australians 澳大利亚原住民。近义 indigenous（本土的）。大写 Aboriginal 特指澳洲原住民。

quiz.q: A ritual is one repeated, formal act — a baptism, a festival, a burial. A ritual is —
o: a system of beliefs organised around the sacred
a polite everyday form requiring no gods
a formal act done in the same way every time
quiz.ex: ritual = 仪式、例行程序。religious rituals 宗教仪式。引申义：日常惯例（my morning ritual）。

quiz.q: Exotic means excitingly foreign — a word the West has applied to almost everyone. Exotic means —
o: strikingly unusual because it comes from far away
quiz.ex: exotic = 异域的、奇异的。exotic plants/food 异国植物/食物。词义自带'外来视角'：所谓异域，取决于你站在哪。

quiz.q: Hallowed is holy grown old: hallowed ground, hallowed be thy name. Hallowed means —
o: honoured as sacred over a long time
quiz.ex: hallowed = 受尊崇的、奉为神圣的。hallowed ground 圣地。动词 hallow 使神圣。语气比 holy 更庄重古雅。

quiz.q: An ideology is what a movement wants everybody to do. Ideology is —
o: a professional convention like gloves in a lab
a system of ideas and beliefs of a group or movement
quiz.ex: ideology = 意识形态。political ideology 政治意识形态。形容词 ideological。对比 custom（习俗）、convention（惯例）。

quiz.q: Moral is the private judgement of right and wrong; ethical is that judgement written down as rules for a profession. Ethical means —
o: relating to professionally accepted standards of right conduct
quiz.ex: ethical = 伦理的、合乎职业道德的。ethical standards/conduct 伦理标准/行为。ethics 伦理学/伦理准则。

title: Cathedrals and Kings
text:
Mrs Kowalski gave her last tour of St Aldhelm's on a cold bright Saturday in October, after twenty-two years of explaining the same stones. Six visitors came; by the end, all six were telling her to keep going.

"A {{cathedral}}," she began, in the place she always began, "is a church that houses a bishop's chair — a cathedra. A {{church}} is any building for Christian worship; the {{priest}} serves at its altar; the {{bishop}} oversees a region; and the {{pope}}, in Rome, oversees the bishops. Hierarchy is not architecture, but in a cathedral the two look identical." She pointed out the {{choir}} stalls — "the singers, and also the place where they sing; language recycles itself here" — and the worn slab where the {{monk}}s of the old priory had knelt to copy the {{bible}}, letter by letter, for three hundred years.

"And this is Father Joseph," she said, indicating a dark portrait, "the {{missionary}} who left this town in 1701 to explain us to the tropics, and the tropics to us, with mixed success both ways. A {{temple}}, he wrote home, is the general word for a house of gods — and a {{pagoda}}, he learned, is the many-storeyed kind. His letters are in the county archive, next to his debts."

The tour moved to the windows, and to history. "Now, the {{chronology}} — the order of events, which is history's spine. The {{empire}} of Rome built the first road through here; the {{imperial}} administration taxed it; then the empire fell and the road grew grass. A {{king}} granted the town its charter in 1123 — one {{king}}, one signature, and every {{royal}} visit since has merely re-borrowed the idea. The {{dynasty}} that followed quarrelled for three generations: an {{emperor}} on the continent, a {{queen}} regnant here for once, a {{prince}} who drowned, a {{princess}} who married badly. 'His {{majesty}}', 'Her Majesty' — the titles change less than the families wearing them. The {{nobility}} sat in the north transept; the {{lord}} of the manor had his own pew; the {{knight}}s were buried under the floor you are standing on — walk softly — and the {{guardian}} of the gate, the lowest title in this story, is the only one whose job still exists. I hold it now, and it comes with a set of keys."

One visitor, a teacher, asked about the poet buried by the font, the town's one {{celebrity}}. "Famous for a hundred years, forgotten for fifty, and now on the school syllabus — {{status}}, you see, is weather, not climate. It changes. My own {{background}} — a mill town, two languages, no books — would have predicted none of this. My {{experience}} is the only evidence I trust: that people become what they practise, including kindness."

She told them her three stories, the ones every tour guide keeps for the end. The {{anecdote}}: the bishop who lost his crozier in the river and it was returned by a fisherman, and both families still claim the miracle. The {{incident}}: the German plane that landed in the churchyard in 1941, harmlessly, and the pilot who came back in 1991 to apologise to the organ. And the {{accident}}: the fire of 1874, which began with a candle and ended with the new roof — "because an accident is an unplanned event with damage, an incident is an event officially noted, and an anecdote is a small true story told for the pleasure of it. Keep the three apart and you can read any newspaper."

Outside, the town glittered. "This place has {{thrive}}d twice — wool in the fifteenth century, insurance in the twentieth — and {{prosperity}}, when it comes, always arrives looking permanent and never is. Between the two booms: plague, flood, the collapse of the mill — {{setback}}s, every one of them, which is the polite word; {{adversity}} is the honest one, and the town's best stonework all dates from the decades straight after it. Draw your own conclusions."

At the west door she was asked the question she liked least, and answered it anyway. "Do I ever feel {{nostalgia}} — homesickness for a time rather than a place? Every day. I was {{homesick}} for my first town for ten years, and then one morning I was homesick for this one instead, and I have lived here ever since. Homesickness is how a place becomes yours."

She locked the west door, the way the {{guardian}} of the gate has done since 1123, and gave each visitor a postcard of the {{cathedral}} at dusk. "Everyone here was a foreigner once," she said, "including the stones."
tr:
十月一个晴冷周六，科瓦尔斯卡夫人做完了圣奥尔德海姆教堂的最后一场导览。二十二年来她一直解释着同一批石头。来了六位游客；到结束时，六个人都在劝她继续讲下去。

“大教堂（cathedral），”她从每次开始的地方开始，“是设有主教座位的教堂——cathedra，座位。教堂（church）是任何基督教崇拜建筑；神父（priest）在祭坛侍奉；主教（bishop）统辖一个地区；而罗马的教皇（pope）统辖众主教。等级制度不是建筑，但在大教堂里，两者看上去一模一样。”她指出唱诗班（choir）的席位——“既指歌者，也指他们唱歌的地方；语言在这里自我回收”——还有旧修院修士（monk）们跪着抄写圣经（bible）的那块磨平的石板，一个字母一个字母，抄了三百年。

“这是约瑟夫神父，”她指着一幅深色的画像，“那位传教士（missionary），1701年离开本镇，去向热带解释我们，也向我们解释热带，两个方向都成败参半。神庙（temple），他在家信里写道，是神之居所的统称；而宝塔（pagoda），他后来学到，是多层的那种。他的信件存放在郡档案馆，旁边是他的欠债单。”

导览走向彩窗，走向历史。“现在讲年代学（chronology）——事件的顺序，历史的脊柱。罗马帝国（empire）修通了穿过这里的第一条路；帝国（imperial）的行政机构对它征税；然后帝国倾覆，路上长满草。一位国王（king）在1123年颁给本镇特许状——一位国王，一个签名，此后每一次王室（royal）驾临都只是把同一个主意再借回去一次。其后的王朝（dynasty）吵了三代人：大陆上有一位皇帝（emperor），这里难得有一位在位的女王（queen），一位溺水的亲王（prince），一位所嫁非人的公主（princess）。‘陛下（majesty）’、‘女王陛下’——头衔的变化，远小于佩戴它们的家族的变化。贵族（nobility）坐在北耳堂；庄园领主（lord）有自己的专座；骑士（knight）们就埋在你们脚下这块地板下——脚下留情——而门卫（guardian），这个故事里最低的头衔，是唯一延续至今的职位。现在这个职位归我，还配一串钥匙。”

一位游客是教师，问起圣水盆旁安葬的诗人，本镇唯一的名人（celebrity）。“红了一百年，被忘了五十年，如今进了学校教学大纲——地位（status），你们看，是天气，不是气候，会变的。我自己的背景（background）——一座磨坊镇、两种语言、没有书——什么也预见不了。经验（experience）是我唯一信任的证据：人会变成他所练习的东西，包括善良。”

她讲起每份导游都留到最后的三段故事。趣闻（anecdote）：主教把权杖掉进河里，被渔夫送回，两家人至今都在争夺这个奇迹的所有权。事件（incident）：1941年一架德国飞机无害地降落在教堂墓地，飞行员1991年回来向管风琴道了歉。事故（accident）：1874年的大火，起于一根蜡烛，止于新屋顶——“因为事故是有损害的意外事件，事件是被正式记录的事件，而趣闻是为了愉悦而讲的小真事。分清这三个词，你就能读懂任何一份报纸。”

门外，小镇闪闪发光。“这个地方兴旺（thrive）过两次——十五世纪的羊毛，二十世纪的保险——而繁荣（prosperity）来临时总显得永久，从来都不是。两次高潮之间：瘟疫、洪水、磨坊倒闭——挫折（setback），每一个都是，这是客气说法；逆境（adversity）是诚实的说法，而本镇最好的石雕，全都出自紧接着逆境之后的几十年。结论你们自己下。”

西门边，有人问了她最不喜欢的问题，她还是答了。“你会怀旧（nostalgia）吗——对一个时代而不是一个地方的乡愁？每天都怀。头十年我想念我的第一座城，后来某天早晨起，我开始想念这一座，从此再没离开。乡愁（homesick）是一个地方变成你的方式。”

她锁上西门，像1123年以来历任门卫（guardian）做过的那样，并送给每位游客一张暮色中大教堂（cathedral）的明信片。“这里的每一个人都曾是个外来者，”她说，“包括这些石头。”

quiz.q: A cathedral is a church that houses a bishop's chair — a cathedra. A cathedral is —
o: the residence of the lord of the manor
the principal church of a bishop's area
quiz.ex: cathedral = 大教堂（主教座堂）。词源 cathedra（主教座）。对比 church（教堂）、chapel（小礼拜堂）。

quiz.q: Father Joseph, the missionary who left in 1701 to explain us to the tropics. A missionary is —
o: a guardian of the gate with keys
a monk who copies the bible
someone sent to spread a religion in another place
quiz.ex: missionary = 传教士。词根 mission（使命）。missionary work 传教工作。形容词：missionary zeal 传教般的热忱。

quiz.q: The dynasty that followed quarrelled for three generations. A dynasty is —
o: a sequence of rulers from the same family
the emperor's administration on the continent
a royal visit that re-borrows a charter
the nobility seated in the north transept
quiz.ex: dynasty = 王朝。the Ming dynasty 明朝。形容词 dynastic。体育引申：a sports dynasty 体育豪门。

quiz.q: Now the chronology — the order of events, which is history's spine. Chronology is —
o: the study of saints and miracles
a list of the town's celebrities
the arrangement of events in order of time
quiz.ex: chronology = 年代学、年表。chrono-（时间）+ -logy（学科）。chronological order 时间顺序。同根：chronic 慢性的。

quiz.q: An anecdote is a small true story told for the pleasure of it. An anecdote is —
o: a short amusing account of a real event
quiz.ex: anecdote = 趣闻、轶事。anecdotal evidence 轶事证据（非系统）。区分 incident（事件）、accident（事故）。

quiz.q: Setbacks — the polite word; adversity is the honest one. Adversity means —
quiz.ex: adversity = 逆境、厄运。in the face of adversity 面对逆境。形容词 adverse 不利的。近义 hardship。

quiz.q: Nostalgia — homesickness for a time rather than a place. Nostalgia is —
o: a mixed feeling of longing for the past
the pain of missing one's home town
a church's west door at dusk
quiz.ex: nostalgia = 怀旧、乡愁（对往昔）。nostalgic 怀旧的。区分 homesickness（对当下家乡的思念）。词源：nostos（返乡）+ algos（痛）。

quiz.q: The guardian of the gate, the lowest title in this story, is the only job that still exists. A guardian is —
o: a knight buried under the floor
the lord with his own pew
someone who protects or watches over something
quiz.ex: guardian = 守卫者、监护人。legal guardian 法定监护人。guardian angel 守护天使。动词 guard 守卫。

title: The Story of Language
text:
On the last Friday of the summer term, Miss Ferreira, who had taught {{language}}s for thirty-one years, put no books on her desk. Instead: a ball of string, a photograph of a Chinese street sign, a lump of modelling clay, and her grandmother's letters.

"I am going to tell you where your words come from," she said. "{{Linguistics}} is the science of language — its sounds, its structures, its history — and today you get the whole subject in one hour."

"Before writing, we had the body. A {{sign}} is anything that carries meaning — a red flag, a raised hand, a wet umbrella by the door. A {{gesture}} is a meaning made with the body: the wave, the shrug, the two fingers that mean different things in different countries. And a {{symbol}} is a sign that means by agreement rather than resemblance: the dove, the cross, the arrow. Humans are the animal that agreed."

She held up the string. "The Inca kept records in knots — a {{knot}} for a number, a coloured cord for a category. No paper, no alphabet, and an empire administered in string. Meanwhile—" she showed the photograph — "Chinese writing still uses {{logogram}}s: one character standing for one word. And the first writing of all, in Mesopotamia, pressed a reed into clay and left a {{wedge}} — which is why we call it cuneiform, 'wedge-shaped'. The very first {{pictograph}}s were pictures: a sun meant the sun. Then the pictures grew lazy and abstract, and became letters."

"An {{alphabet}} is the great economy: twenty-six shapes that spell every word we have. And how you make those shapes is your {{handwriting}} — the last portrait a person draws of themselves. My grandmother's letters say as much about her as her sentences do."

"Now the sounds. {{Phonetics}} is the study of them. The smallest unit of sound that changes meaning is a {{phoneme}}: pat and bat differ by one. Open your {{vowel}}s — a, e, i, o, u — where the air flows free. Close a {{consonant}} — t, k, m — where something blocks it. String them together into a {{syllable}} and you can {{pronounce}} a word. But listen—" she said the same word twice, once flat, once rising "—the {{intonation}} carries a meaning no letters record. And when a word changes its shape to do its work — sing, sang, sung — that is an {{inflection}}. Languages age in their inflections."

"The spoken word came first: {{oral}} tradition, poems held in memory for a thousand years before any alphabet. Anything put into words is {{verbal}} — the word means 'in words', spoken or written, though people use it to mean spoken. And a single stretch of speech — one sentence, one cry, one apology — is an {{utterance}}."

"Then the rules. {{Grammar}} is the whole system. {{Syntax}} is the order of words — 'the dog bit the man' versus 'the man bit the dog': same words, different universes. {{Semantic}}s is meaning itself — what the words are actually about. Grammar without syntax is a bag of words; semantics without grammar is a cry."

"And the variety. My {{accent}} tells you where I learned English — Lisbon, with an echo. My {{dialect}} is my English itself: its words, its rhythms, its little grammars. An accent is how you sound; a dialect is how you speak. Nobody speaks language in general; everyone speaks a dialect of something."

She pressed one letter into the clay and stood it up. "Your {{vocabulary}} is every word you own — and you own more than you think; the {{dictionary}} merely lists them, as a museum lists its objects. A {{phrase}} is a small group of words behaving as one — 'at the drop of a hat'. An {{idiom}} is a phrase whose meaning has left its words behind: no hat is available for inspection. A {{clause}} is a sentence within a sentence, with its own subject and verb. An {{expression}} is any fixed way of saying something. A {{tense}} puts the action in its time — past, present, future — and English marks time more rudely than most languages. And every word has a {{root}} — the seed it grew from. 'Dictionary' comes from dictare, 'to say again and again'. Now you know why it sounds tired."

The bell went. "Homework," she said over the noise. "Ask your grandparents for one word they used that nobody uses now, and bring it in on Monday. A language is only alive while people are still changing it."
tr:
夏季学期的最后一个周五，教了三十一年语言（language）的费雷拉小姐没有在讲台上放任何书。取而代之的是：一团绳子、一张中国路牌的照片、一块黏土，还有她祖母的信。

“我要告诉你们，你们的词是从哪里来的，”她说。“语言学（linguistics）是关于语言的科学——它的语音、它的结构、它的历史——今天一小时，你们得到整个学科。”

“在文字之前，我们有身体。符号（sign）是任何携带意义的东西——一面红旗、一只举起的手、门边一把湿伞。手势（gesture）是用身体做出的意义：挥手、耸肩、那两根在不同国家含义不同的手指。而象征（symbol）是凭约定而非相似来表意的符号：鸽子、十字、箭头。人类，就是那个达成约定的动物。”

她举起绳子。“印加人用绳结记账——一个结（knot）记一个数，一条彩绳记一个类目。没有纸，没有字母，一个帝国靠绳子治理。与此同时——”她出示照片——“中文至今使用语标文字（logogram）：一个字对应一个词。而最早的文字出现在美索不达米亚，芦苇杆压进黏土，留下一个楔形（wedge）——所以我们叫它 cuneiform，‘楔形的’。最早的象形文字（pictograph）就是图画：画一个太阳，指的就是太阳。后来图画渐渐变懒、变抽象，成了字母。”

“字母表（alphabet）是伟大的节省：二十六个形状，拼出我们拥有的每一个词。而你怎么写这些形状，是你的笔迹（handwriting）——一个人为自己画的最后一幅肖像。我祖母的信，说的关于她的事，不比她的句子少。”

“再说声音。语音学（phonetics）是研究声音的学问。能改变意义的最小语音单位是音位（phoneme）：pat 和 bat 只差一个。打开元音（vowel）——a、e、i、o、u——气流自由通过。闭合辅音（consonant）——t、k、m——有东西挡住气流。把它们串成音节（syllable），你就能发音（pronounce）一个词。但是听——”她把同一个词说了两遍，一遍平，一遍升“——语调（intonation）承载着任何字母都记录不下的意义。而当一个词为了完成工作而改变形状——sing、sang、sung——那就是屈折变化（inflection）。语言就老在屈折变化里。”

“先有口语：口传（oral）传统，诗歌在记忆里保存了一千年，早于任何字母。凡是诉诸词语的都是口头的/言语的（verbal）——这个词的意思是‘用词语的’，说和写都算，虽然人们用它指口说。而单独的一段话语——一个句子、一声喊、一句道歉——是一次话语（utterance）。”

“然后是规则。语法（grammar）是整个体系。句法（syntax）是词的顺序——“狗咬了人”对“人咬了狗”：同样的词，不同的宇宙。语义（semantic）学是意义本身——词究竟在说什么。没有句法的语法是一袋子词；没有语法的语义是一声喊。”

“还有多样性。我的口音（accent）告诉你我在哪里学的英语——里斯本，带一点回声。我的方言（dialect）是我说的这套英语本身：它的词汇、节奏、小小的语法。口音是你听上去怎样；方言是你怎样说话。没有人说‘一般的语言’；每个人说的都是某种东西的方言。”

她把一个字母压进黏土，立起来。“你的词汇量（vocabulary）是你拥有的每一个词——你拥有的比你以为的多；词典（dictionary）只是列出它们，像博物馆列出藏品。短语（phrase）是一小组结伴而行的词——“at the drop of a hat”（立刻）。习语（idiom）是意义已经离开字面词语的短语：现场并没有帽子可供查证。从句（clause）是句中之句，有自己的主语和动词。表达（expression）是任何固定的说法。时态（tense）把动作放进时间里——过去、现在、将来——而英语标记时间的方式，比多数语言都粗鲁。每个词都有词根（root）——它生长自的那粒种子。dictionary 来自 dictare，‘反复地说’。现在你知道它为什么听起来累了。”

铃响了。“作业，”她在喧闹声里喊，“去向你们的祖父母要一个他们用过、如今没人用的词，周一带来。一门语言，只在人们还在改变它的时候活着。”

quiz.q: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning has left its words behind: no hat is available for inspection. An idiom is —
o: any small group of words behaving as one
a fixed phrase whose meaning cannot be built from its words
quiz.ex: idiom = 习语、成语。'kick the bucket' 字面无帽子可查。对比 phrase（短语，意义可从字面组合）。

quiz.q: 'The dog bit the man' versus 'the man bit the dog': same words, different universes. This is because of —
o: intonation — the rise and fall of the voice
syntax — the order of words in a sentence
quiz.ex: syntax = 句法。词序规则：主谓宾。形容词 syntactic。区分 semantics（语义学）。

quiz.q: The smallest unit of sound that changes meaning: pat and bat differ by one. A phoneme is —
o: a knot in an Inca cord
a group of sounds forming a word part
the smallest sound unit that distinguishes one word from another
quiz.ex: phoneme = 音位。/p/ 与 /b/ 之差。phonemic/phonetic 之分：音位学的 vs 语音的。

quiz.q: An accent is how you sound; a dialect is how you speak. A dialect is —
o: a written symbol standing for a word
a variety of a language with its own words and grammar
the root a word grew from
quiz.ex: dialect = 方言。regional dialect 区域方言。区分 accent（口音）：dialect 含词汇语法差异，accent 只关发音。

quiz.q: Sing, sang, sung — when a word changes shape to do its work, that is an inflection. An inflection is —
o: the order of words in a sentence
a change in a word's form to mark tense, number or case
quiz.ex: inflection = 屈折变化。词尾变化表时态、单复数、格：-ed、-s、-ing。inflected language 屈折语（如拉丁语）。

quiz.q: The very first pictographs were pictures: a sun meant the sun. A pictograph is —
o: a symbol that represents an object by drawing it
an agreed sign like the dove
quiz.ex: pictograph = 象形文字。picto-（图画）+ graph（写）。汉字多源于象形。对比 logogram（语标，表词）。

quiz.q: Chinese writing still uses logograms: one character standing for one word. A logogram is —
o: a picture of the thing it means
a written symbol representing a whole word
quiz.ex: logogram = 语标文字。logo-（词）+ gram（写）。汉字是典型的语标文字体系。

quiz.q: A tense puts the action in its time — past, present, future. Tense is —
o: the seed a word grew from
the melody carried by the voice
a fixed way of saying something
the verb form that locates an action in time
quiz.ex: tense = 时态。the past/present/future tense 过去/现在/将来时。tensile 同根（绷紧）——时态就是时间的绷紧。

title: The Translation Workshop
text:
The translation workshop met on Wednesdays: six students, one Polish short story, and Miss Ferreira's standing rule — a translator is a person paid to make decisions.

The first hour was anatomy. She put a sentence on the board and dissected it. "The {{noun}} is the thing itself — river, Tuesday, courage. The {{verb}} is what it does — flows, arrives, fails. The {{adjective}} describes the noun: a cold river. The {{adverb}} modifies everything else: it flows coldly. The {{pronoun}} stands in for a noun — it, we, nobody — and the moment it is unclear, wars of interpretation begin. The {{preposition}} positions — in, under, despite — the smallest words doing the heaviest lifting. The {{conjunction}} connects — and, but, because — and a translated story lives or dies by its 'buts'. A noun is {{singular}} when there is one of it and {{plural}} when there are more — and the Polish story's first problem was that its river was plural in a way English refuses to be."

Then they built words. "A {{prefix}} goes in front — un-, re-, mis- — and changes the meaning. A {{suffix}} goes behind — -ness, -ful, -ly — and changes the job. Un-hope-ful-ness: four pieces, one feeling. An {{abbreviation}} shortens — Dr, BBC — and laser, which began life as an abbreviation and ended as a word. For every word there are {{synonym}}s — near-twins with different shadows: big, large, enormous — and an {{antonym}} or two to define it by opposition. 'Big' only means anything because 'small' is standing behind it."

The story was two pages long and took six weeks. "We have three {{version}}s now," said Karol, who had found it in his grandmother's anthology: "a literal one, a literary one, and one that makes sense." — "The three do overlap," said Miss Ferreira, "but only the third one reads." The students {{compile}}d a shared glossary of the hard words — to compile is to gather into a single document — and argued about every entry.

The verbs had to be sorted early. "To {{translate}} is to carry across — the word itself admits the strain. To {{paraphrase}} is to say the same thing in different words, within one language. To {{interpret}} is to explain a meaning — and also to translate speech aloud: a translator works with texts, an interpreter with people. To {{narrate}} is to tell the story, in the order it deserves. To {{decipher}} is to read what is barely readable — a code, a smudged postcard. And to {{illuminate}}—" she showed them a photograph of a medieval manuscript, its margins gold — "is to shed light: on a text, or literally on a page, which is why painted manuscripts are called illuminated. Both meanings are true at once, which is the mark of a good word."

The workshop's house rules were short. Be {{consistent}}: if the boatman's name is Jan on page one, it is Jan on page twenty. Prefer the {{complex}} to the {{complicated}}: complex means many parts fitting together; complicated means tangled for no reason. "A translation," said Miss Ferreira, "should be complex the way an engine is complex, not complicated the way insurance is."

And then the arguing, which was the point. The Wednesday {{discussion}} was followed by a {{brainstorm}} — everyone's worst ideas at once, on the wall, so that the good ones could hide among them — and then the {{debate}}: two readings, one comma, forty minutes. Miss Ferreira refereed. "A {{contention}} is a claim you are prepared to defend: state yours and hold it politely.
