And to {{negotiate}} is to reach agreement by giving things up — you will negotiate with this story, because it will not surrender its meaning on the first date." At the end of each session one student delivered a {{commentary}} on the week's decisions, line by line, explaining why the river had become rivers and why the ending had been allowed to keep its Polish weather.

In June they read the finished translation aloud to the Polish class two doors down. Karol's grandmother came, and heard her story in English for the first time. "It's not the same," she said — which everyone had feared — and then: "It's the same the way a sister is the same."

That, said Miss Ferreira afterwards, was the whole art of translation in one sentence. "{{Eloquence}}," she added, packing her bag, "is saying the truest thing in the fewest words that will hold it. And to {{communicate}} means to share — to make common. Everything else — the grammar, the glossaries, the six weeks — is only the wrapping."
tr:
翻译工作坊每周三碰头：六个学生，一篇波兰语短篇小说，还有费雷拉小姐的常年守则——译者，就是靠做决定领薪水的人。

第一小时是解剖课。她在黑板上放了一个句子，把它剖开。“名词（noun）是事物本身——河、星期二、勇气。动词（verb）是它做的事——流、到达、失败。形容词（adjective）描述名词：一条冷的河。副词（adverb）修饰其余一切：它冷冷地流。代词（pronoun）代替名词——它、我们、没有人——而只要它一含糊，阐释的战争就开始。介词（preposition）负责位置——in、under、despite——最小的词干最重的活。连词（conjunction）负责连接——and、but、because——而一篇译文，生死全在那些‘但是’上。名词只有一个时是单数（singular），多于一个时是复数（plural）——而这篇波兰小说的第一个难题，就是它的河是复数的，英语死也不肯这样。”

然后是构词。“前缀（prefix）在前——un-、re-、mis-——改变意义。后缀（suffix）在后——-ness、-ful、-ly——改变词性。un-hope-ful-ness：四块零件，一种心情。缩写（abbreviation）负责缩短——Dr、BBC——还有 laser，它生下来是缩写，长大后成了词。每个词都有同义词（synonym）——影子不同的近义孪生子：big、large、enormous——还有一两个反义词（antonym），靠对立来划定边界。big 之所以有意义，是因为 small 站在它身后。”

小说只有两页，却花了六周。“现在我们有三版（version）了，”卡罗尔说，这篇小说是他在祖母的选集里找到的：“一个直译版，一个文学版，一个读得懂的版本。”“三版确有重叠，”费雷拉小姐说，“但只有第三版读得下去。”学生们把难词汇编（compile）成一份共享词汇表——compile 就是搜集进一份文件——然后为每一个词条争吵。

动词们早早地就得分类。“翻译（translate）的本义是‘搬运过去’——这个词本身就承认了吃力。意译（paraphrase）是在同一种语言里换词重说。阐释（interpret）是解释意义——也指口头传译：translator 面对文本，interpreter 面对人。叙述（narrate）是按它应得的顺序讲故事。破译（decipher）是读出几乎不可读的东西——密码、一封字迹模糊的明信片。而照亮（illuminate）——”她给他们看一幅中世纪手稿的照片，页边烫金——“是投下光亮：照在文本上，或者当真照在纸页上，这就是为什么彩绘手稿叫 illuminated manuscript。两个意义同时为真，这是一个好词的标志。”

工作坊的馆规很短。保持一致（consistent）：船夫第一页叫 Jan，第二十页也得叫 Jan。宁取复杂（complex）而弃繁难（complicated）：complex 指许多零件彼此咬合；complicated 指无缘无故地缠成一团。“一篇译文，”费雷拉小姐说，“应该像发动机那样复杂，而不是像保险条款那样繁难。”

然后是争吵，而这正是意义所在。周三的讨论（discussion）之后是头脑风暴（brainstorm）——所有人最糟的主意同时上墙，好让好主意能藏在里面——然后是辩论（debate）：两种读法，一个逗号，四十分钟。费雷拉小姐当裁判。“论点（contention）是你准备好为之辩护的主张：说出你的，礼貌地守住它。而谈判（negotiate）是通过让步达成一致——你们将和这篇小说谈判，因为它不会在第一次约会就交出自己的意义。”每次课结束，一名学生对本周的决定做一篇评注（commentary），逐行解释：河为什么变成了河们，结尾为什么获准保留它的波兰天气。

六月，他们把完成的译文朗读给两扇门之外的波兰语班听。卡罗尔的祖母来了，头一次听到她的故事的英文。“不是原来那篇了，”她说——所有人都怕这句——然后是：“是妹妹那种一样。”

这一句，费雷拉小姐后来说，就是翻译艺术的全部。“雄辩（eloquence），”她一边收拾包一边补充，“是用最少的词托住最真的话。而沟通（communicate）的意思是分享——使成为共同。其余的一切——语法、词汇表、这六个星期——都只是包装纸。”

quiz.q: To paraphrase is to say the same thing in different words, within one language. To paraphrase means —
o: to carry a text across into another language
to translate speech aloud for people
to express the same meaning using other words
quiz.ex: paraphrase = 意译、改述（同语言内换词）。para-（旁边）+ phrase。雅思写作高频要求：paraphrase the question。

quiz.q: To decipher is to read what is barely readable — a code, a smudged postcard. To decipher means —
o: to succeed in reading something unclear or encoded
to tell a story in the order it deserves
to shed light on a page with gold margins
quiz.ex: decipher = 破译、辨认（难读的文字）。de-（去除）+ cipher（密码）。名词 decipherment。

quiz.q: To illuminate is to shed light — on a text, or literally on a page, which is why painted manuscripts are illuminated. To illuminate means —
o: to light up; to make something clear to understand
to argue over one comma for forty minutes
quiz.ex: illuminate = 照亮；阐明。illuminated manuscripts 泥金装饰手稿；illuminate a point 阐明观点。名词 illumination。

quiz.q: Complex means many parts fitting together; complicated means tangled for no reason. Complex means —
o: consisting of many connected parts (often neutral)
quiz.ex: complex = 复杂的（多部件精密组合，中性）；complicated = 繁难的（不必要地纠缠，贬义）。complex system 复杂系统。

quiz.q: Be consistent: if the boatman's name is Jan on page one, it is Jan on page twenty. Consistent means —
quiz.ex: consistent = 前后一致的。consistently ranked 名列前茅。名词 consistency 一致性。反义 inconsistent。

quiz.q: A contention is a claim you are prepared to defend: state yours and hold it politely. A contention is —
o: a storm of worst ideas on a wall
a gathering of hard words into one document
an opinion or claim argued for
the smallest word doing the heaviest lifting
quiz.ex: contention = 论点；争论。points of contention 争议点。动词 contend 竞争、主张。

quiz.q: Near-twins with different shadows: big, large, enormous. A synonym is —
o: a word part added to the front
a word with the opposite meaning
a word with a similar meaning to another
a shortened form of a word
quiz.ex: synonym = 同义词。syn-（同）+ onym（名）。近义词有 shadow 差异：big 口语、large 一般、enormous 程度强。

quiz.q: A prefix goes in front — un-, re-, mis- — and changes the meaning. A prefix is —
o: letters added to the beginning of a word
letters added to the end of a word
a word standing in for a noun
quiz.ex: prefix = 前缀。pre-（前）+ fix（固定）。对比 suffix 后缀（改词性）。unhappy/rewrite/misread。

title: A Week at the Herald
text:
The Herald has been {{publish}}ed every Thursday since 1882, and Noor spent her work-experience week learning what that sentence hides. The {{press}} lives in one building on Fore Street: four rooms, a printing press in the basement — the machine the whole profession is named after — and a permanent smell of coffee and toner.

"A newspaper," said Mr Byrne, the {{editor}}, "is only a {{medium}} — a means of carrying something. Singular: medium. Plural: media. Radio is a medium; this paper is a medium; the town's noticeboard is a medium. What we carry is Thursday." He ran the place from a desk visibly made of two other desks.

The staff were five. Rita, the veteran {{journalist}}, was the county's leading {{exponent}} of the long interview — an exponent being someone who practises and promotes a thing — and knew everyone's grandmother by name. The young {{correspondent}} covered the council: a correspondent is the one who writes back from wherever the news is. The {{critic}} came in on Fridays to review the amateur dramatics, mercilessly and, the dramatists agreed, fairly. The {{commentator}} on local radio was a separate species, paid to hold opinions at speed. The {{announcer}} read the death notices each morning in a voice Noor's grandmother called "the sound of a warm bath". And the {{messenger}} — the last title in the building — was a boy on a bicycle who still carried copy down to the printer whenever the internet was "having one of its days". Mrs Adeyemi, the {{typist}}, had worn the office's one typewriter into legend and now typed with two fingers at the speed of most people's ten.

On Tuesday, Rita taught her the ethics of information. "A {{handout}} is what an organisation gives you, already written, hoping you will print it as news. A {{leaflet}} is the same thing without the hope. And {{propaganda}} is information with an army behind it: one side, all the answers, no questions. Our job is to publish what happened. Their job is to {{disseminate}} what they wish had happened — to scatter it as widely as the budget allows. Dissemination is not lying; it is aiming. Learn to see which one you are holding."

Wednesday brought the future. "Four verbs, one tomorrow," said Rita, laying them out like cutlery. "You {{foresee}} the flood before the rain — you see it coming, on evidence. You {{anticipate}} the roadworks — you expect them and get ready. You {{expect}} the mayor's resignation the way you expect rain in April: probable, not certain. And you {{await}} a statement, formally, the way a lawyer awaits a verdict. Same future, four certainties. The front page forgives nothing, so choose carefully."

On Thursday the paper came out with Noor's name at the bottom of one story: two hundred words about the {{festival}} committee's new {{program|programme}}. "Not bad," said Mr Byrne — which she would later learn was the paper's highest honour. "Next week," he added, "we'll teach you why 'local' is the most ambitious word in journalism."
tr:
《先驱报》自1882年以来每周四出版（publish），努尔在职业体验周里学到的，正是这句话藏起来的东西。新闻界（press）住在前街的一栋楼里：四个房间，地下室一台印刷机——整个行业因它得名——以及一种永不散去的咖啡和碳粉味。

“一份报纸，”主编（editor）伯恩先生说，“只是一种媒介（medium）——运载某样东西的手段。单数是 medium，复数是 media。广播是一种媒介；这份报纸是一种媒介；镇上的公告板也是一种媒介。我们运载的东西，叫星期四。”他办公用的那张桌子，一看便知是由另外两张桌子拼成的。

员工一共五位。资深记者（journalist）丽塔是本郡长篇访谈的头号倡导者（exponent）——exponent 指亲身实践并推广某事的人——她叫得出每个人祖母的名字。年轻的本报记者（correspondent）跑市政新闻：correspondent 就是从新闻发生的地方写信回来的人。评论员（critic）每周五来评论业余剧社的演出，毒舌而公道——剧社的人承认后者。地方电台的时事评论员（commentator）是另一个物种，靠快速发表观点领薪水。播音员（announcer）每天早晨用努尔祖母称之为“热水澡的声音”的嗓音播报讣告。而信使（messenger）——楼里最后一个头衔——是个骑自行车的男孩，每当互联网“闹脾气”，仍负责把稿子送去印刷厂。打字员（typist）阿德耶米夫人把办公室仅剩的一台打字机用成了传奇，如今用两根手指打出大多数人十根手指的速度。

周二，丽塔给她上了信息伦理课。“新闻稿（handout）是机构写好递给你的东西，指望你把它当新闻登出来。传单（leaflet）是同一种东西，只是不抱指望。而宣传（propaganda）是有军队撑腰的信息：只有一方，全是答案，没有问题。我们的工作是出版发生的事。他们的工作是散布（disseminate）他们希望发生的事——在预算允许的范围内撒得越广越好。散布不等于说谎；它是一种瞄准。你要学会分辨手里拿的是哪一种。”

周三讲未来。“四个动词，一个明天，”丽塔像摆餐具一样把它们摆开。“你预见（foresee）洪水先于下雨——凭证据看见它来。你预计（anticipate）道路施工——料到它并做好准备。你预期（expect）市长辞职，就像预期四月下雨：很可能，不确定。而你等待（await）一份声明，正式地，像律师等待判决。同一个未来，四种确定程度。头版不原谅任何失误，所以选词要小心。”

周四，报纸出刊，努尔的名字排在一条新闻末尾：两百字，写的是节庆（festival）委员会的新节目单（program）。还行——伯恩先生说。她后来才知道，这是这家报社的最高荣誉。“下周，”他补了一句，“我们教你为什么‘本地’是新闻业里最有野心的词。”

quiz.q: A newspaper is only a medium — a means of carrying something. Singular: medium; plural: media. A medium is —
o: a printing press in the basement
a person who types with two fingers
a means or channel of carrying information
quiz.ex: medium = 媒介、手段（复数 media）。mass media 大众传媒。另一义：中间的（medium size）；灵媒。

quiz.q: Their job is to disseminate what they wish had happened — to scatter it as widely as the budget allows. To disseminate means —
o: to type at the speed of ten fingers
quiz.ex: disseminate = 传播、散布。dis-（散开）+ semin（种子）。disseminate information/knowledge 传播信息/知识。

quiz.q: Propaganda is information with an army behind it: one side, all the answers, no questions. Propaganda is —
o: one-sided information spread to influence opinion
a leaflet handed out at the gate
the noticeboard outside the town hall
quiz.ex: propaganda = 宣传（贬义，单向灌输）。political propaganda 政治宣传。对比 publicity（ publicity 宣传，中性）。

quiz.q: You foresee the flood before the rain — you see it coming, on evidence. To foresee means —
o: to know something will happen before it does
to get ready for expected roadworks
quiz.ex: foresee = 预见。fore-（前）+ see。foreseeable consequences 可预见的后果。对比 anticipate（预料并准备）。

quiz.q: Rita, the county's leading exponent of the long interview — someone who practises and promotes a thing. An exponent is —
o: a printing machine in the basement
a boy on a bicycle carrying copy
a person who advocates and practises a skill or idea
quiz.ex: exponent = 倡导者、阐述者；指数（数学）。a leading exponent of jazz 爵士乐大师。对比 advocate（只主张，未必实践）。

quiz.q: A handout is what an organisation gives you, already written, hoping you will print it as news. A handout is —
o: the smell of coffee and toner
a prepared text given out, hoping for publication
the front page that forgives nothing
quiz.ex: handout = 新闻稿；散发材料；施舍物。另一义：政府救济（live on handouts 靠救济过活）。

quiz.q: You await a statement, formally, the way a lawyer awaits a verdict. To await means —
o: to wait for, in a formal register
to see something coming on evidence
to read death notices on the radio
quiz.ex: await = 等候（正式）。await the results/decision。await + 名词，不用 await for。对比 wait for。

quiz.q: Mr Byrne, the editor, runs the place from a desk made of two other desks. An editor is —
o: the one paid to hold opinions at speed
the one who writes back from the news
the person in charge of a newspaper's content
quiz.ex: editor = 主编、编辑。chief editor 主编。动词 edit 编辑；edition 版本。区分 editorial 社论。

title: The Circus Comes to Town
text:
For three days before it arrived, the {{circus}} was the only subject in town. The {{gossip}} ran ahead of it — gossip being news about people, told for pleasure rather than accuracy — and the {{rumour}}s ran ahead of the gossip: there would be elephants; there would be no elephants; the trapeze artist was famous; the trapeze artist had retired. By Tuesday the town had reached a {{consensus}} — a general agreement nobody remembers voting for — that the circus would be the best or the worst thing since the flood, and nothing it actually did could shift either verdict.

A circus is an old answer to a permanent question: what shall we do with our evenings? Every {{pastime}} — every hobby that pleasantly fills the hours — competes for the same attention. The council provided {{recreation}}: organised leisure — the park, the pool, the chess club. Television provided {{amuse}}ment without leaving the sofa. But only a circus {{entertain}}ed in a field, with diesel, canvas and danger, and that was the difference people came for. Recreation is what you do yourself; entertainment is what is done, magnificently, in front of you.

The tent went up on Thursday. On Friday afternoon Noor was allowed in to watch the {{rehearsal}} — the performance before the performance, where everything is done at half speed and twice the danger. The ringmaster practised his voice. The clown {{imitate}}d him mercilessly, and then explained the difference, because clowns are the only performers who teach. "You {{imitate}} a person by copying what they do," he said, wiping off one eyebrow. "You {{mimic}} them by copying how they do it — the walk, the pause, the little wave. And the third one, {{simulate}}, is what the second half of tonight's show will do to a storm: wind machine, thunder sheet, no weather at all. The audience knows, and doesn't care, which is the definition of theatre." The {{drama}} of the evening, he said, lived in the trapeze; the {{magic}} act would fool everyone twice; and he himself would fall over eleven times, professionally.

Outside the tent, the fair food was its own {{feast}} — toffee apples, fried dough, a wheel of cheese won in a raffle — and the queue was longer than the one for the tickets.

The rivals had also posted their season. The town hall's autumn programme offered a {{concert}} of string quartets, one full {{symphony}} from the visiting philharmonic, the youth {{orchestra}}'s December {{ballet}} with real snow machines, and — the rowdiest night of the calendar — the pantomime. "A circus and a concert hall are in the same trade," said Noor's grandmother, studying both posters. "Turning an ordinary Tuesday into something you remember. The circus does it with muscle; the concert hall does it with strings."

The first performance was full. The elephants (there were elephants) paraded at eight. The simulated storm brought actual rain, which the ringmaster announced as a personal favour, and the trapeze artist — famous, not retired — caught everything thrown at her, including the evening.

When the circus left on Monday it took the gossip with it, and the town returned to its pastimes, its recreations and its sofa. The field kept a rectangle of flattened grass, a receipt for the weekend. And Noor, who had watched both the rehearsal and the show, kept the difference between them: the performance was perfect; the rehearsal was true.
tr:
马戏团（circus）到来前的三天里，它是镇上唯一的话题。流言（gossip）跑在它前头——流言是关于人的新闻，讲它图的是快乐而非准确——而谣言（rumour）又跑在流言前头：会有大象；不会有大象；空中飞人很有名；空中飞人已经退役。到周二，全镇达成了共识（consensus）——一种谁也不记得投过票的普遍一致——马戏团将是洪水以来最好或最糟的事，而它实际做什么都撼动不了这两条判决中的任何一条。

马戏团是对一个永恒问题的古老回答：我们的晚上该怎么办？每一项消遣（pastime）——每一种愉快填满时光的爱好——争夺的都是同一份注意力。镇议会提供娱乐活动（recreation）：有组织的休闲——公园、泳池、棋社。电视提供不必离开沙发的逗乐（amuse）。但只有马戏团肯在一片场地上，用柴油、帆布和危险来表演（entertain），而这正是人们前来寻找的区别：娱乐消遣是你自己做的事；而 entertainment 是在你面前，壮观地替你做的事。

帐篷周四立起。周五下午，努尔获准进场观看排练（rehearsal）——演出之前的演出，一切动作以一半的速度、两倍的危险完成。 ringmaster 练他的嗓音。小丑毫不留情地模仿（imitate）他，然后解释起区别来，因为小丑是唯一会授课的演员。“模仿（imitate）一个人，是照抄他做的事，”他一边擦掉一边眉毛一边说，“而学他（mimic），是照抄他做事的样子——走路的姿态、停顿、那个小小的挥手。至于第三个词，模拟（simulate），是今晚下半场要对一场暴雨做的事：鼓风机、雷皮，一点天气都没有。观众知道，但不在乎，这就是戏剧的定义。”晚上的戏剧性（drama），他说，在空中飞人身上；魔术（magic）表演会把每个人骗上两回；而他自己将以专业姿态摔倒十一次。

帐篷外，集市小吃自成一场盛宴（feast）——太妃苹果、炸面团、抽奖赢来的一整轮奶酪——排队的人比买票的还多。

对手们也贴出了自己的演出季。镇政厅的秋季节目单里有弦乐四重奏音乐会（concert）、来访爱乐乐团的一整部交响曲（symphony）、青年管弦乐团（orchestra）十二月配真雪机的芭蕾（ballet），还有——全年日历上最喧闹的一晚——哑剧。“马戏团和音乐厅是同行，”努尔的祖母研究着两张海报说，“都是把一个普通的星期二变成你记得住的东西。马戏团靠肌肉，音乐厅靠琴弦。”

首演满座。大象（确实有大象）八点巡游。模拟的暴雨带来了真的雨，ringmaster 宣称这是他个人的面子，而空中飞人——有名，没退役——接住了抛给她的一切，包括这个夜晚。

马戏团周一离开时把流言也带走了，小镇回到它的消遣、娱乐活动和沙发中间。场地留下一块压平的草地，算作这个周末的收据。而看过排练也看过演出的努尔，记住了两者的区别：演出是完美的；排练是真实的。

quiz.q: Gossip being news about people, told for pleasure rather than accuracy. Gossip is —
o: a general agreement nobody voted for
casual talk about other people's lives
a wheel of cheese won in a raffle
quiz.ex: gossip = 流言蜚语、闲话。office gossip 办公室八卦。对比 rumour（无来源的传言）。

quiz.q: A general agreement nobody remembers voting for. A consensus is —
o: a rumour about retired trapeze artists
an opinion shared by most of a group
organised leisure provided by the council
a storm made of wind machines
quiz.ex: consensus = 共识、一致意见。reach a consensus 达成共识。consensus politics 共识政治。词根 sens（感觉）。

quiz.q: Every pastime — every hobby that pleasantly fills the hours — competes for the same attention. A pastime is —
o: the programme of a concert hall
an activity done regularly for enjoyment
quiz.ex: pastime = 消遣、娱乐。pass（度过）+ time。an enjoyable pastime。近义 hobby、recreation。

quiz.q: You imitate a person by copying what they do; you mimic them by copying how they do it. To mimic means —
o: to perform at twice the danger
to copy someone's manner or behaviour closely
quiz.ex: mimic = 模仿（神态/方式）。名词 mimic 模仿者。模仿声音/动作用 mimic，模仿行为用 imitate。

quiz.q: Simulate is what the show will do to a storm: wind machine, thunder sheet, no weather at all. To simulate means —
o: to produce the appearance of something artificially
to copy what a person does
to catch everything thrown at you
to flatten a field of grass
quiz.ex: simulate = 模拟、假装。simulated exam 模拟考试；simulated conditions 模拟环境。名词 simulation。形容词 simulated。

quiz.q: The rehearsal — the performance before the performance, at half speed and twice the danger. A rehearsal is —
o: a practice session before a public performance
the first night with a full tent
a joke told by a clown
quiz.ex: rehearsal = 排练。dress rehearsal 彩排。动词 rehearse。对比 performance（正式演出）。

quiz.q: Only a circus entertained in a field, with diesel, canvas and danger. To entertain means —
o: to reach a consensus about elephants
to organise the park, the pool, the chess club
to amuse an audience; to hold their attention
quiz.ex: entertain = 娱乐、款待。entertain guests 招待客人；entertaining 有趣的。名词 entertainment。

quiz.q: There would be elephants; there would be no elephants — the rumours ran ahead of the gossip. A rumour is —
o: talk about people told for pleasure
information spread without a reliable source
quiz.ex: rumour = 谣言、传闻。rumour has it that... 据传……。对比 gossip（闲话，可无恶意）。

title: The Friday Gallery
text:
Every Friday after four, the Marlowe {{gallery}} — a room built for looking at art, and, if the guard likes your face, for buying it — opens its back door to students. For one winter I was the student who came.

Mrs Okafor, who ran the place, was strict about words. "A museum keeps things forever," she told me on my first afternoon. "A {{gallery}} shows them and sells about a third of them. Write that down." She was a {{patron}} of the arts in the old sense — a person who gives money so that art can go on existing — and she tolerated, barely, the modern word for the same job, {{sponsor}}, which she said sounded like a racehorse.

That winter we were preparing the spring {{exhibition}}: a public showing of many works under one roof. My task was to help her {{select}} from the store-room — to choose, but with reasons. "Anybody can pick," she said. "To {{select}} is to pick and then survive the question 'why that one?'"

The store-room held forty years of the city. There were {{painting}}s of streets that no longer existed. There was one {{sculpture}} — a bronze horse — that three men could not move and one man, refusing all help, did. There were {{photograph}}s of the 1974 floods, so sharp you felt the cold coming off them. And there was a {{portrait}} of Mrs Okafor's grandmother, painted by a {{painter}} who had been merely {{well-known}} in her lifetime — known by the right people — and became properly {{famous}} afterwards: known by everyone, including people who dislike art.

"You {{describe}} a thing in words," Mrs Okafor said, dusting the frame. "A painting never describes. It {{depict}}s — it shows its subject in line and colour, without sentences. And {{draw}} is the honest verb underneath everything: to make marks. Every picture in this building began as somebody's marks on paper."

The frames came from Mr Aziz, the last {{craftsman}} on the street — a man who could {{carve}} oak into leaves — who called himself the only honest man in the art trade. "An {{artist}} has ideas," he said, tapping his chisel. "I have measurements. Their customers {{collect}} — they gather objects on purpose, like magpies with chequebooks — and every spring they come to me to have their habits framed."

The {{aesthetic}} of the show — the whole idea of what counted as beautiful in it — was settled in March, in an argument Mrs Okafor won by leaving the room. In April the labels were written, the bronze horse was positioned where it could watch the door, and a small dark room off the corridor was given over to {{animation}}: films built from thousands of hand-drawn pictures that walk when you spin them past a light. Visitors could {{opt}} for the paper guide or the recorded one — to {{opt}} is to choose freely between the things offered — and most, out of politeness, took the paper and left it folded.

The largest canvas depicted a {{scene}} from the old Theatre Royal: a stage inside the picture, actors frozen mid-argument. On opening night this was convenient, because the real {{stage}} — a platform of crates by the window — stood right beside it, and Mrs Okafor, having assigned herself a {{role}} she took very seriously, {{perform}}ed the welcome speech. Halfway through, her notes slid off the crate and she {{improvise}}d — made the rest up as she went, better than the written half — while the frozen actors in the canvas watched her do it.

"That," she said afterwards, "is the whole of art. Prepared, then rescued."
tr:
每周五下午四点后，马洛画廊（gallery）——一间专为观看艺术而设的房间，若是门卫喜欢你，也可以买点什么——会为学生打开后门。整个冬天，我就是那个来的学生。

经营这地方的奥卡福女士对用词很严格。“博物馆把东西永远留住，”我来的第一个下午她告诉我，“而画廊（gallery）是展示它们、并卖掉其中三分之一的地方。记下来。”她是旧意义上的艺术赞助人（patron）——一个出钱让艺术得以延续的人——而对这份差事的现代同义词赞助商（sponsor），她勉强忍着，说这词听着像一匹赛马。

那年冬天我们在筹备春季展览（exhibition）：把许多作品放在同一屋檐下公开展出。我的任务是帮她从库房里做挑选（select）——带着理由去选。“谁都会挑，”她说，“select（挑选）是挑了之后，还能经得住‘为什么是这件’的追问。”

库房装着这座城市四十年。有画着已不复存在的街道的画作（painting）。有一件雕塑（sculpture）——一匹铜马——三个男人搬不动，一个拒绝了所有帮忙的人搬动了。有一九七四年洪水的照片（photograph），清晰得让你感到寒气扑面。还有奥卡福女士祖母的肖像（portrait），出自一位画家（painter）之手，生前只是颇有名气（well-known）——被对的人知道——身后才真正出名（famous）：被所有人知道，包括不喜欢艺术的人。

“用词语来描述（describe）一样东西，”奥卡福女士擦着画框说，“画从不描述。它描绘（depict）——用线条和色彩展示对象，不用句子。而画（draw）是一切底下最诚实的动词：留下笔迹。这栋楼里的每一幅画，都始于某人在纸上的笔迹。”

画框来自阿齐兹先生，街上最后一位工匠（craftsman）——一个能把橡木雕刻（carve）成叶子的人——他自称艺术行当里唯一诚实的人。“艺术家（artist）有想法，”他敲着凿子说，“我有尺寸。买家们收藏（collect）——有目的地聚拢物件，像揣着支票簿的喜鹊——每年春天都来找我，给他们的习惯装框。”

这场展览的美学（aesthetic）——关于什么算美的整套理念——是三月份定下的，在一场奥卡福女士靠离席获胜的争论里。四月，标签写好，铜马摆到能盯住门口的位置，走廊旁一间小黑屋让给了动画（animation）：由成千上万张手绘图片构成、放到光前转动就会走路的影片。参观者可以选择（opt）纸质导览或录音导览——opt（选择）就是在提供的选项之间自由挑选——大多数人出于礼貌拿了纸的，原样折好放在手里。

最大的那幅画布描绘了老皇家剧院的一幕（scene）：画中有个舞台，演员们凝固在争吵中途。开幕之夜这很方便，因为真正的舞台（stage）——窗边几个货箱搭的平台——就立在旁边，奥卡福女士给自己派了个她非常当回事的角色（role），表演（perform）了欢迎致辞。讲到一半，讲稿滑下货箱，她便即兴（improvise）发挥——后半段边走边编，比写好的那半还好——画布上凝固的演员们看着她做完这一切。

“这就是艺术的全部，”她后来说，“先准备好，再被拯救。”

quiz.q: A museum keeps things forever; a gallery shows them and sells about a third. A gallery is —
o: a room or building for displaying (and often selling) works of art
a storeroom where paintings are hidden from the public
a theatre where actors perform on a stage
a dark room for showing animation films
quiz.ex: gallery = 画廊、美术馆（常含展销性质）。National Gallery 国家美术馆。对比 museum（博物馆，永久收藏）。

quiz.q: She was a patron of the arts in the old sense — a person who gives money so that art can go on existing. A patron is —
o: a person who visits a gallery on Fridays
a person who supports an activity or artist with money
an artist with ideas but no measurements
quiz.ex: patron = 赞助人、资助者（旧义，个人出资支持艺术）。现代商业同义词 sponsor。patronage 资助、惠顾。

quiz.q: That winter we were preparing the spring exhibition: a public showing of many works under one roof. An exhibition is —
o: a private argument settled by leaving the room
a public display of works for people to view
a bronze horse that watches the door
quiz.ex: exhibition = 展览。hold/mount an exhibition 举办展览。exhibit 展品/展出。对比 collection（收藏）。

quiz.q: A painting never describes; it depicts — it shows its subject in line and colour, without sentences. To depict means —
o: to show something, especially in a picture
to buy a third of what is shown
quiz.ex: depict = 描绘、刻画（用图画表现）。The painting depicts a rural scene. 近义 portray。对比 describe（用语言描述）。

quiz.q: The aesthetic of the show — the whole idea of what counted as beautiful in it. Aesthetic means —
o: connected with the weight of bronze horses
connected with the price of frames
connected with beauty and artistic taste
connected with the length of speeches
quiz.ex: aesthetic = 美学的、审美的。aesthetic value 审美价值。名词 aesthetics 美学。

quiz.q: Mr Aziz, the last craftsman on the street, could carve oak into leaves. A craftsman is —
o: a guard who decides whom to like
a person who collects objects on purpose
a skilled worker who makes things by hand
quiz.ex: craftsman = 工匠、手艺人。craft 手艺；handicraft 手工艺品。对比 artist（艺术家，重创意）。

quiz.q: A small dark room was given over to animation: films built from thousands of hand-drawn pictures that walk when you spin them past a light. Animation is —
o: the art of improvising a speech
the carving of oak into leaves
the technique of making films from a series of drawn images
quiz.ex: animation = 动画（制作）。animated film/cartoon 动画片。animate 使有生命。

quiz.q: Her notes slid off the crate and she improvised — made the rest up as she went. To improvise means —
o: to perform a written speech seriously
to make or do something without preparation
to leave an argument by exiting the room
to fold a paper guide politely
quiz.ex: improvise = 即兴创作、临时凑成。improvised performance 即兴表演。形容词 improvised 临时拼凑的。

title: The Music Shop
text:
Duda's Music, between the baker and the closed cinema, sells instruments nobody can play and records nobody wants, and has been failing cheerfully since 1979.

Mr Duda sorted all music into four drawers, and made you listen to a minute of each before you were allowed to buy anything. {{Classical}}: music that is written down before it is played — symphonies, quartets, the great dead Germans. {{Jazz}}: music that thinks while it plays, argues with itself, and wins. {{Rock}}: guitars turned up until they become weather. {{Pop}}: music built to be loved by everybody for exactly six weeks. He kept the {{hip-hop}} in a fifth drawer he refused to label, because his filing system was forty years old and had never met it: words spoken in {{rhythm}} over drum machines — poetry with a pulse.

"When you are ready," he said, "you will join a {{band}} — musicians who play together, each hiding a little behind the others — or you will go {{solo}} — alone, visible, and unable to blame anybody. Most people are band people. They just don't know it yet."

The instruments hung from ceiling hooks like drying laundry. The {{piano}} filled the whole back wall: eighty-eight keys, the orchestra one family can afford. Under it, leaning, the {{violin}} — small, held at the chin — and behind the counter the {{cello}}, its serious older brother, played seated, half-embraced. On the wall hung six {{guitar}}s, a {{harmonica}} small enough for a pocket, a {{trumpet}} that had been bright once, and a single {{drum}} that Mr Duda struck whenever a customer lied about a price. The {{flute}} he kept in the till, wrapped in cloth, "so the metal doesn't get ideas."

"Four words," he said on my first afternoon, tapping the counter in time. "The {{rhythm}} is this: the pattern of time underneath, the pulse you clap to. The {{melody}} is the tune's journey: the line of notes you hum in the bath. A {{tune}} is a melody small enough to whistle — a souvenir you can carry. And the {{tone}} is the colour of the sound: this drum dark, that trumpet bright. Rhythm is the feet, melody is the road, tune is what you bring home, tone is the weather. Now you know more than the radio does."

In a crate by the door he sold old {{disc}}s — flat black records the size of dinner plates — for one pound each, "because they are heavier than downloads, and therefore more real."

His daughter Irene had managed the cinema two doors down, and her vocabulary had infected the shop. An {{opera}}, she had decided, was "a play sung all the way through, in which nobody dies of embarrassment"; a {{musical}} was "a play that talks until it feels something, and then sings." A {{comedy}} ended with a wedding; a {{tragedy}} ended with a funeral; a {{sketch}} — a sketch being the short comic piece, five minutes, one laugh, and no plot to speak of — ended whenever the actors ran out of nerve; and the difference between those two endings, said Mr Duda, was also the difference between jazz and classical, though he never explained how. The {{film}} — the British word — and the {{movie}} — the American one — were the same object, and every Friday Irene brought round the week's posters, marked 15, 18, and once, in red, {{x-rated}}: forbidden to the young, because what was inside was not for them yet.

Under glass on the counter, Mr Duda kept a notebook in which he wrote down the {{lyric}}s customers sang while trying instruments — the words of songs, the part people actually remember — and said it was the only honest poetry being written in the city.

"The hands I can teach," he said, when I finally bought the harmonica. "The rhythm I can teach. The tone, the taste, the nerve — those you grow into. Come back in ten years and we'll see."
tr:
达达乐器行夹在面包店和歇业的电影院之间，卖没人会弹的乐器和没人想要的唱片，自1979年以来一直快乐地经营失败着。

达达先生把所有音乐分进四个抽屉，而且在你买任何东西之前，先让你每样听一分钟。古典（classical）：演奏之前先写下来的音乐——交响曲、四重奏、伟大的已故德国人。爵士（jazz）：边演奏边思考的音乐，与自己争论并且获胜。摇滚（rock）：音量调大直到变成天气的吉他。流行（pop）：被造出来让所有人恰好爱六周的音乐。他把嘻哈（hip-hop）放在第五个拒绝贴标签的抽屉里，因为他的分类法已有四十年，从没见过它：跟着鼓机节奏（rhythm）说出的词——带脉搏的诗。

“等准备好了，”他说，“你会加入一支乐队（band）——一起演奏、各自躲一点在别人身后的音乐人——或者你会单飞（solo）——独自一人，醒目，也没法怪罪任何人。大多数人都是乐队型的人，只是自己还不知道。”

乐器挂在天花板的挂钩上，像晾着的衣物。钢琴（piano）占满整面后墙：八十八个键，一个家庭负担得起的管弦乐团。琴身下面斜靠着小提琴（violin）——小，夹在下巴处——柜台后面是大提琴（cello），它严肃的哥哥，坐着演奏，半拥在怀里。墙上挂着六把吉他（guitar）、一支小得能进口袋的口琴（harmonica）、一支曾经明亮过的小号（trumpet），还有一面鼓（drum），每当有顾客在价格上撒谎，达达先生就敲它。长笛（flute）他收在钱柜里，裹着布，“免得金属起念头。”

“四个词，”头一个下午，他敲着柜台打拍子说，“节奏（rhythm）是这个：底下的时间模式，你跟着拍手的那个脉搏。旋律（melody）是曲子的旅程：你在浴缸里哼的那串音符。曲调（tune）是小到能吹口哨的旋律——一件带得走的纪念品。而音色（tone）是声音的颜色：这面鼓暗，那支小号亮。节奏是脚，旋律是路，曲调是你带回家的东西，音色是天气。现在你比电台懂得多了。”

门边的木箱里，他卖旧唱片（disc）——晚餐盘子大小的黑色圆盘——一镑一张，“因为它们比下载重，所以更真实。”

他女儿艾琳曾管理隔两家的电影院，她的词汇感染了这家店。她断定歌剧（opera）是“从头唱到尾的戏剧，剧中没人会尴尬致死”；音乐剧（musical）是“说着说着有了感受、然后唱起来的戏剧”。喜剧（comedy）以婚礼收尾；悲剧（tragedy）以葬礼收尾；小品（sketch，sketch 指那种五分钟、一个笑点、谈不上情节的短喜剧）以演员胆气用尽收尾；达达先生说，这两种结局的差别也是爵士与古典的差别，虽然他从不解释怎么个差法。电影（film）——英国词——和 movie（电影的美式说法）是同一个东西，每周五艾琳把这一周的海报带过来，上面标着15、18，有一回用红色写着x级（x-rated）：禁止年轻人观看，因为里面的内容还不到给他们看的时候。

柜台玻璃板下面，达达先生放着一个笔记本，记下顾客试乐器时唱的歌词（lyric）——歌里的词，人们真正记得住的部分——他说这是城里唯一诚实的诗歌。

“手我可以教，”当我最终买下那支口琴时他说，“节奏我可以教。音色（tone）、品位、胆量——这些要长进去。十年后回来，我们看看。”

quiz.q: The melody is the tune's journey: the line of notes you hum in the bath. A melody is —
o: the pattern of time you clap to
the main line of notes in a piece of music
the colour of a drum's sound
a flat black record the size of a dinner plate
quiz.ex: melody = 旋律。主旋律 the main melody。对比 rhythm（节奏）、tone（音色）。

quiz.q: The rhythm is this: the pattern of time underneath, the pulse you clap to. Rhythm is —
o: the line of notes you hum
the regular pattern of beats in music or speech
a group of musicians playing together
quiz.ex: rhythm = 节奏、韵律。the rhythm of the drums 鼓的节奏。形容词 rhythmic。对比 melody（旋律）。

quiz.q: The tone is the colour of the sound: this drum dark, that trumpet bright. Tone is —
o: the quality or character of a sound
quiz.ex: tone = 音色、语气。a warm tone 温暖的音色；a friendly tone 友好的语气。

quiz.q: Or you will go solo — alone, visible, and unable to blame anybody. To perform solo means —
o: to speak words over drum machines
to play while hiding behind others
to perform alone, without the group
to argue with yourself and win
quiz.ex: solo = 独奏（的）、单独（的）。a solo performance 独奏演出。反义 ensemble（合奏）。乐队 band vs 单飞 solo。

quiz.q: A musical is 'a play that talks until it feels something, and then sings.' A musical is —
o: a play sung all the way through
a play combining spoken dialogue with songs
a comedy that ends with a wedding
a film forbidden to the young
quiz.ex: musical = 音乐剧。对比 opera（歌剧，从头唱到尾）。名词 music 音乐；musical instrument 乐器。

quiz.q: A comedy ended with a wedding; a tragedy ended with a funeral. A tragedy is —
o: a play of spoken rhythm and drum machines
a play that everybody loves for six weeks
a serious play with an unhappy ending
quiz.ex: tragedy = 悲剧。对比 comedy（喜剧）。引申义 tragedy 灾难、不幸事件。

quiz.q: The lyrics customers sang — the words of songs, the part people actually remember. Lyrics are —
o: a list of prices customers lie about
quiz.ex: lyric = 歌词（常用复数 lyrics）；形容词 抒情的。lyric poetry 抒情诗。

quiz.q: Old discs — flat black records the size of dinner plates — one pound each. A disc is —
o: a flat circular disc for storing music or data
quiz.ex: disc = 唱片、圆盘。compact disc (CD) 光盘。disc jockey (DJ) 打碟师。

title: A Week at the Riverside Centre
text:
The Riverside Sports Centre opened in October with a free trial week, and Kofi, fifteen, arrived on Monday morning with a plan: try everything before Sunday, decide nothing, enjoy all of it.

The building sorted sport by roof. The {{indoor}} games — the ones played inside — filled the warm halls: six {{badminton}} courts, where a feathered shuttlecock argues backwards and forwards until somebody misses; a {{volleyball}} hall, where the rule is that nobody may hold the ball and everybody must shout; and, upstairs behind a rope, three {{billiards}} tables — the green cloth, the long slow maths, the clicking of balls into pockets — where the oldest members spent the whole week and were suspected, some days, of sleeping. The quiet room at the end of the corridor held the {{chess}} club: sixteen boards, no noise, and the only {{competition}} in the building that nobody could watch without playing. The {{gym}} filled the basement: weights, mats, machines, and a mirrored wall for watching yourself suffer. Outdoors, the grass was booked by season: the {{cricket}} — cricket being the slow summer game of bat and ball, the one that takes a whole afternoon and a week of talk — square in the warm months, and mud for the rest.

"This is where {{exercise}} becomes a {{training}} plan," said Damaris, the instructor, handing him a card. "Exercise is any movement that does you good — a walk counts. Training is exercise with a date attached: you are preparing for something. Decide what, and the plan writes itself."

The {{outdoor}} games wrapped the building in green. On the main {{pitch}} — the marked field on which football and hockey are played — a schools' {{soccer}} league trained on Tuesdays, and Damaris made Kofi learn the whole vocabulary in one lesson: you {{kick}} the ball with your foot; you {{throw}} it in from the line with both hands behind your head; you {{toss}} a coin gently into the air to decide which team attacks first; and you score a {{goal}} — the ball into the net, and also, in life, the thing you were aiming at. On the sand pitch beside it, the {{hockey}} players learned to {{knock}} the ball with the flat side of the stick only, which is the sport's whole moral system. The {{tennis}} courts were being resurfaced, so the coach lent out rackets in the car park and explained the equipment rule from a bench: "A {{racket}} has strings and hits balls that fly; a {{bat}} is solid wood and hits balls that sit still — cricket, rounders, baseball. Get this wrong in a shop and you will be sold the wrong childhood."

Behind the car park, the manager had laid six holes of crazy {{golf}}, on the grounds, he said, "that {{golf}} ruins a walk pleasantly" — golf being the sport of hitting a small ball across country into a series of holes with the fewest strokes.

On Saturday the centre held its first {{tournament}}: a competition played in rounds, losers leaving, until one winner remains. A {{competition}}, Damaris explained, is any contest in which people try to beat each other — a tournament is a competition shaped like a tree, drawn on paper, each branch ending one player's afternoon. The winner, a dental nurse with a flat smash, was crowned {{champion}} — the person who ends the competition holding the title, for exactly one year. Kofi entered the badminton tournament, lost in the first round, and stayed till evening as a {{spectator}} — a person who watches — which he found, to his surprise, was its own skill. "Every {{athlete}} in this hall," Damaris said, "every person trained to compete in sport, began as a spectator. The {{olympic}} Games are four thousand people who watched something on television and stood up. That's the entire business model of sport."

On Sunday his aunt ran the city {{marathon}} — forty-two kilometres — The route finished inside the {{stadium}} — the great concrete bowl built so that thousands can sit comfortably while a handful suffer — and the family went to cheer. A {{race}} is any competition of speed; a marathon is a race against distance, where the opponent is yourself at kilometre thirty. She had learned two words from Damaris: {{pace}} — the speed you choose at the beginning so that you still have a self left at the end — and {{stride}} — the length of one running step, the long economy of the distance runner. Kofi watched the front runners and the back markers: the ones who had gone out too fast began to {{lag}}, falling slowly behind, while one woman who had lagged at five kilometres was passing people at forty. His aunt finished {{energetic}} — still full of energy, still moving — and celebrated with a {{vigorous}} swim in the centre's pool: energetic in a forceful way, strength put openly to use.

"Next year," said Kofi, "the tournament."

"Next year," said Damaris, "the training."
tr:
河畔运动中心十月开业，第一周免费体验。十五岁的科菲周一早上就到了，带着一个计划：周日前把一切试个遍，什么都不决定，全都享受。

这栋楼按屋顶给运动分类。室内（indoor）项目——在室内进行的那些——占满温暖的场馆：六片羽毛球场（badminton），一只羽球来回争辩直到有人接不住；排球（volleyball）馆，规则是没人可以持球而人人都得喊叫；楼上绳子后面，是三张台球（billiards）桌——绿色台呢、漫长的慢算术、球进袋的咔嗒声——最年长的会员们整周待在那儿，有些日子被怀疑在睡觉。走廊尽头的安静房间属于国际象棋（chess）俱乐部：十六张棋盘，没有声音，是全楼唯一不亲自下场就看不懂的比赛（competition）。健身房（gym）占了地下室：杠铃、垫子、器械，还有一面镜墙，供你看着自己受苦。室外的草坪按季节预订：暖和的月份归板球（cricket，cricket 指那种慢悠悠的夏季球棒游戏，要占掉整个下午和随后一周的谈论）方场，其余的月份归泥浆。

“这里是锻炼（exercise）变成训练（training）计划的地方，”教练达玛丽丝递给他一张卡说，“锻炼是任何对你有好处的活动——散步也算。训练是带着日期的锻炼：你在为某个东西做准备。想清楚是什么，计划自己就写出来了。”

室外（outdoor）项目把建筑裹进绿色。主球场（pitch）——画了线的、踢足球和曲棍球的场地——周二有一支校际足球（soccer）联队训练，达玛丽丝让科菲一节课学会全部词汇：你用脚踢（kick）球；你从边线双手过头顶把球掷（throw）进场；你把硬币轻轻抛（toss）向空中决定哪队先进攻；你射进一球（goal）——球入网，也是生活中你瞄准的那个目标。旁边沙地上，曲棍球（hockey）运动员学习只用球棍的平面敲击（knock）球，这是这项运动全部的道德体系。网球场（tennis）正在翻修地面，于是教练在停车场外借出球拍，坐在长凳上讲器材规则：“球拍（racket）有弦，打会飞的球；球棒（bat）是实木，打静止的球——板球、圆场棒球、棒球。在商店里说错这个，你买到的就是错的童年。”

停车场后面，经理铺了六洞的迷你高尔夫（golf），“理由是，”他说，“高尔夫（golf）能把散步败坏得很愉快”——高尔夫就是用最少的杆数把小球打过场地打进一串洞里的运动。

周六中心举办了第一场锦标赛（tournament）：分轮进行的比赛，输者离场，直到只剩一个胜者。达玛丽丝解释说，competition（竞赛）是人们互相较量争胜的任何比赛——锦标赛是长得像一棵树的竞赛，画在纸上，每根枝条终结一个人的下午。冠军（champion）——结束比赛时头衔在握的人，任期恰好一年——是一位扣杀很平的牙科护士。科菲报了羽毛球赛，第一轮就输了，却以观众（spectator）——观看的人——的身份待到晚上，他惊讶地发现这本身就是一门技能。“这个馆里的每一个运动员（athlete）——每一个受过训练参加体育竞技的人——都始于观众。奥林匹克（olympic）运动会就是四千个在电视上看了什么然后站起来的人。这就是体育行业全部的商业模式。”

周日他姑姑跑了城市马拉松（marathon）——四十二公里——赛道终点设在体育场（stadium）里——为了几千人舒服地坐着、看少数人受苦而建的巨大混凝土碗——全家去加油。赛跑（race）是任何比速度的竞赛；马拉松是与距离的赛跑，对手是三十公里处的你自己。她从达玛丽丝那里学了两个词：配速（pace）——你在开始时选定的速度，好让你在终点还剩下自己——和步幅（stride）——一个跑步跨步的长度，长跑者的长期节约。科菲看着领跑者和落后者：出发太快的人开始落后（lag），慢慢地掉队，而一位在五公里处落后的女士正在四十公里处一个一个超人。他姑姑精力充沛（energetic）地完赛——还充满能量，还在动——然后去中心泳池痛快地游了一场激烈的泳：充满干劲、力量敞开来用的那种 energetic。 vigorous（有力的）

“明年，”科菲说，“打锦标赛。”

“明年，”达玛丽丝说，“做训练。”

quiz.q: Exercise is any movement that does you good; training is exercise with a date attached. Training is —
o: watching a tournament from the seats
any movement that does you good, like a walk
physical practice preparing for a specific event
hitting a small ball into six holes
quiz.ex: training = 训练（有目标的系统练习）。go into training 开始训练。对比 exercise（泛指锻炼）。

quiz.q: A competition played in rounds, losers leaving, until one winner remains. A tournament is —
o: a contest organised in elimination rounds
quiz.ex: tournament = 锦标赛、联赛。chess tournament 国际象棋锦标赛。对比 competition（泛指竞赛）。

quiz.q: He stayed till evening as a spectator — a person who watches. A spectator is —
o: the length of one running step
someone who lags at kilometre five
the flat side of a hockey stick
someone who watches an event without taking part
quiz.ex: spectator = 观众。spectator sport 观赏性运动。对比 participant（参与者）、athlete（运动员）。

quiz.q: Pace — the speed you choose at the beginning so that you still have a self left at the end. Pace is —
o: the speed at which something moves or is done
a coin thrown into the air
quiz.ex: pace = 速度、节奏（步速）。keep pace with 跟上。at a steady pace 以稳定的节奏。

quiz.q: A racket has strings and hits balls that fly; a bat is solid wood and hits balls that sit still. A racket is —
o: a solid wooden implement for a still ball
a strung implement for hitting a flying ball
a coin tossed to decide ends
quiz.ex: racket = （网球/羽毛球）球拍。对比 bat（板球/棒球球棒）。racket 另义：吵闹声。

quiz.q: You score a goal — the ball into the net, and also, in life, the thing you were aiming at. A goal is —
o: a score in ball games; also an aim you strive for
quiz.ex: goal = 进球、球门；目标。set a goal 设定目标。对比 aim/target（目标）。

quiz.q: The ones who had gone out too fast began to lag, falling slowly behind. To lag means —
o: to knock a ball with a flat stick
to choose your speed at the start
to pass people at kilometre forty
to fall behind, moving more slowly than others
quiz.ex: lag = 落后、滞后。lag behind 落在后面。time lag 时滞。jet lag 时差。

quiz.q: She finished energetic — still full of energy — and celebrated with a vigorous swim. Vigorous means —
quiz.ex: vigorous = 有力的、强劲的。a vigorous debate 激烈的辩论。名词 vigour 活力。对比 energetic（精力充沛的）。

title: The Movement Lesson
text:
On Saturday mornings Miss Adeyemi teaches {{movement}} — the general name for every change of position a body can make — in a mirrored studio above the butcher's shop, to anyone between eight and eighty. The physicists call the same thing {{motion}} — motion being the fact of moving itself, the change of place considered on its own, without asking why—; Miss Adeyemi calls it Saturday.

"Every verb I give you today," she began, "is a way of moving, and each one has a personality. Learn the personality, and the word will keep itself."

She started at the bottom. "{{Step}}: one foot, then the other. The neutral verb, no story attached. From it we build. {{Jog}}: running slowly and steadily, the speed of thinking. {{Jump}}: both feet leave the ground, both feet come back — the honest middle of the family. {{Leap}}: a jump with drama in it, for gaps, stages and rivers. {{Hop}}: jumping on one foot, the way you cross a hot beach. {{Spring}}: to jump as if released — sudden, elastic, coiled first, like the inside of a clock deciding. And {{bounce}}: to jump again and again, or to hit the floor and come back up — the tennis ball's verb."

The children were invited to demonstrate. One boy {{flip}}ped — jumped and turned right over in the air — and one girl {{tumble}}d — fell into a rolling shape and made it look deliberate — and both were applauded equally, which Miss Adeyemi said was the entire morality of her studio.

"Three sliding verbs, and only one of them is safe. {{Slide}}: to move smoothly along a surface, feet never leaving it — the playground verb. {{Glide}}: to slide as though gravity were only a suggestion — skaters, swans, the last stroke of a dancer. {{Slip}}: to slide by accident, uninvited; the verb that owns the ice and the bruises. Never confuse them: the first two you choose, the third one chooses you."

"Two climbing verbs and three water verbs. {{Bend}}: to curve a joint, or anything else — the body's cheapest and most useful trick. {{Climb}}: to go up using hands as well as feet — ladders, walls, mountains, ambitions. {{Dive}}: to go head-first into water, or downward as if into it. {{Plunge}}: to dive suddenly and deep — you can plunge into a pool, into a book, or into debt. {{Drift}}: to move slowly, carried rather than steering — clouds, boats, people on the last afternoon of a holiday."

Then the strength pair. "{{Pull}}: to draw something towards you. {{Drag}}: to pull something heavy that resists, along the ground — furniture, suitcases, Mondays. And the long pair: {{stretch}} — to reach a limb to its full length, breathing out; {{strain}} — to stretch too far, or try too hard, and feel the body complain. When you stretch you breathe; when you strain you stop breathing. That is the whole difference, in the body and in everything else."

At the end of the class came the floor exercise. "Now {{sprawl}}," she said, "spread yourselves loose and wide, every limb claiming floor — and then {{bow}} — bend from the waist, the shape of thanks — and we're finished."

Her oldest student, a grandmother, came for the {{yoga}} hour that followed — the Indian discipline of stretching, balance and breathing — and stayed to watch the parkour children practise their flips. In winter the studio arranged the holidays: members went north to {{ski}} — to travel over snow on long slats fixed to boots — and to {{skate}} — to move on ice, or on wheels, wearing boots instead of sense — and in the city, between lessons, everybody practised {{cycling}}, which Miss Adeyemi called "sitting down while moving, the most civilised of the verbs."

At the door, the last word. "{{Mobile}} — able to move, free to move. That is what all of this is for: not the verbs, but the freedom they name. Keep the body {{mobile}} and the verbs will look after themselves."
tr:
周六上午，阿德耶米小姐在肉铺楼上那间带镜子的工作室教动作（movement）——身体所能做出的每一种位置变化的总称——学生从八岁到八十岁都有。物理学家把同一件事叫作运动（motion，motion 指移动这一事实本身、就其自身来考虑的位置变化，不问缘由）；阿德耶米小姐则管它叫周六。

“今天给你们的每个动词，”她开场道，“都是一种移动方式，而每一个都有自己的性格。学会性格，词就自己留下了。”

她从最底下讲起。“走（step）：一只脚，再一只脚。中性动词，不带故事。由它开始搭建。慢跑（jog）：缓慢而平稳地跑，思考的速度。跳（jump）：双脚离地，双脚回落——这个家族里诚实的中间者。跃（leap）：带着戏剧性的跳，给沟壑、舞台和河流。单脚跳（hop）：用一只脚跳，你滚烫沙滩上过路的方式。弹起（spring）：像被松开一样跳起来——突然、有弹性、先蜷缩，像钟表内芯下定了决心。还有弹跳（bounce）：一跳再跳，或者落地震地板又弹回来——网球才用的动词。”

孩子们受邀示范。一个男孩做空翻（flip）——跳起并在空中整个转过去——一个女孩翻滚（tumble）——跌成一个滚动的形状，还让它显得故意——两人获得同等的掌声，阿德耶米小姐说这就是她工作室全部的道德观。

“三个滑的动词，只有一个安全。滑（slide）：沿一个表面平滑移动，脚不离地——操场动词。滑行（glide）：滑得仿佛地心引力只是个建议——滑冰者、天鹅、舞者的最后一划。打滑（slip）：意外地、不被邀请地滑；这个动词拥有冰面和淤青。永远别混淆：前两个是你选的，第三个选你。”

“弯（bend）：让关节弯成曲线，或让任何东西弯——身体最廉价也最有用的把戏。两个向上的动词，三个水里的动词。爬（climb）：手脚并用地向上——梯子、墙、山、抱负。跳水（dive）：头朝下入水，或像入水一样向下。纵身（plunge）：突然且深入地扎进去——你可以 plunge 进泳池、进一本书、或进债务里。漂流（drift）：缓慢移动，是被带着走而非掌着舵——云、船、假期最后一下午的人。”

然后是力量的一对。“拉（pull）：把东西朝自己拽。拖（drag）：拖拽抗拒你的重物，贴着地——家具、行李箱、星期一。还有长的一对：伸展（stretch）——把肢体伸到最长，同时呼气；拉伤（strain）——伸得过头，或用力过猛，让身体开始抱怨。你 stretch 的时候在呼吸；你 strain 的时候就停止了呼吸。这就是全部区别，在身体里，也在其他一切事情里。”

课程结尾是地板练习。“现在摊开（sprawl），”她说，“把自己松散地铺开，每个肢体都认领一块地板——然后鞠躬（bow）——从腰部弯下去，感谢的形状——结束。”

她最年长的学生是位祖母，来上随后的瑜伽（yoga）课——印度的伸展、平衡与呼吸的修炼——之后留下来看跑酷的孩子练空翻。冬天工作室组织度假：会员们北上滑雪（ski）——脚上固定长板在雪上滑行——和滑冰（skate）——穿冰鞋或轮鞋在冰上或轮上移动，穿的与其说是鞋不如说是胆量——而在城里，课与课之间，大家练习骑行（cycling），阿德耶米小姐称之为“坐着移动，所有动词里最文明的一个”。

门口，最后一个词。“灵活（mobile）——能够移动，自由移动。这一切就是为了这个：不是为了那些动词，而是它们命名的自由。让身体保持灵活（mobile），动词们会自己照顾自己。”

quiz.q: Leap: a jump with drama in it, for gaps, stages and rivers. To leap means —
o: to jump a long way, with force or drama
to move smoothly with feet on the floor
to fall into a rolling shape
quiz.ex: leap = 跳跃（幅度大、有力）。Look before you leap 三思而行。对比 hop（单脚小跳）、spring（弹起）。

quiz.q: Slide you choose, glide is graceful, but slip is the verb that owns the ice and the bruises. To slip means —
o: to jump and turn over in the air
to move smoothly along a surface on purpose
to slide accidentally and lose your footing
quiz.ex: slip = 滑倒、打滑（意外）。a slipping banana skin。引申：slip one's mind 忘了。对比 slide（有意滑动）。

quiz.q: Drag: to pull something heavy that resists, along the ground — furniture, suitcases, Mondays. To drag means —
o: to pull something heavy with effort along a surface
to push something gently ahead of you
to reach a limb to its full length
quiz.ex: drag = 拖、拽（费力地拉动重物）。drag one's feet 拖拖拉拉。对比 pull（拉，不强调重）。

quiz.q: When you stretch you breathe; when you strain you stop breathing — stretched too far, trying too hard. To strain means —
o: to move slowly, carried rather than steering
to bend from the waist in thanks
to injure or exhaust by over-stretching or over-trying
to applaud a tumbling girl equally
quiz.ex: strain = 拉伤；过度用力。strain a muscle 拉伤肌肉。名词：under strain 承受压力。对比 stretch（正常伸展）。

quiz.q: You can plunge into a pool, into a book, or into debt. To plunge means —
o: to dive or rush suddenly and deeply into something
to climb using hands and feet
to pull a suitcase across a floor
to jump on one foot across a hot beach
quiz.ex: plunge = 纵身跳入；骤降。take the plunge 冒险一试。prices plunge 价格骤跌。对比 dive（跳水/俯冲）。

quiz.q: Now sprawl — spread yourselves loose and wide, every limb claiming floor. To sprawl means —
o: to move on boots instead of sense
to fold yourself into a ball
to bend from the waist in thanks
to sit or lie with limbs spread loosely
quiz.ex: sprawl = 四肢摊开地坐/躺。另义：urban sprawl 城市无序扩张。

quiz.q: Drift: to move slowly, carried rather than steering — clouds, boats, people on the last afternoon of a holiday. To drift means —
o: to spring like the inside of a clock
to travel over snow on long slats
to be carried slowly, without direction
quiz.ex: drift = 漂流、缓缓移动。drift apart （关系）渐行渐远。snow drifts 雪堆（名词）。

quiz.q: Mobile — able to move, free to move; keep the body mobile and the verbs will look after themselves. Mobile means —
o: able to move or be moved easily
quiz.ex: mobile = 可移动的、流动的。mobile phone 手机；mobile library 流动图书馆。名词 mobility 移动性。反义 immobile。

title: The Week at the Lake
text:
Every August the family makes the same {{trip}} — a journey with a purpose, usually a short one, and always back — to the hills above the lake, and every year has the same argument about what to call the week.

Father, who reads American novels, calls it a {{vacation}} — the American word for a holiday, from the idea of the office being vacated. Mother, who teaches, says "holiday" and points out that vacations are what other people have. The argument is the tradition, and tradition beats vocabulary.

On the first Saturday they took the {{hike}} up the ridge — a long walk in wild country, taken seriously, in boots, with a map — because, as Grandmother put it, "a stroll is what you do to the shops; a hike is what the shops are for escaping from." Halfway up they stopped for the {{picnic}}: a meal carried in baskets and eaten on the ground, which tastes twice as good as the same food at a table, for reasons science has never properly examined. Then they walked on, and the top, when it came, was the usual mixture of wind and view.

On Sunday the minibus from the village ran its {{excursion}} to the old monastery — an excursion being a short journey made for pleasure, usually organised by someone else, often with a bus and always with a timetable. Mother preferred the hike; Father preferred the excursion; Grandmother preferred the picnic, which both contained.

By six that evening they had made {{camp}} — pitched their {{tent}} and claimed their ground — on the flat field by the north shore, where the campsite had been since 1961 and had no plans to move. Making {{camp}}, the children were told, is the second-oldest human skill: choose flat ground, keep the fire away from the canvas, and never, ever leave food where the foxes can argue about it.

On Wednesday the lake steamer ran its evening {{cruise}} — a sea-or-lake voyage taken for pleasure, without cargo, without hurry, the journey being the entire point — and the whole family rode it to the far shore and back, watching the hills do nothing beautifully.

The town on the far shore had been rebuilt, in the seventies, for {{pedestrian}}s — people on foot — and its streets were a maze of benches, fountains and shops. On holiday evenings the family {{wander}}ed through them — walking with no route at all, turning wherever a window looked interesting — and {{linger}}ed longest at the second-hand bookshop, staying well past closing time, because leaving is a decision, and nobody on holiday wanted to make one.

Uncle Theo arrived on Thursday for the birds. "I gave up the gun thirty years ago," he said, hoisting the binoculars. "Now I {{hunt}} with lenses. To hunt is to search for something and pursue it — and the birds don't mind, the bag limit is memory, and the season never closes." He was, that week, hunting one particular osprey, and by Friday he had found it, or something he was prepared to argue was it.

The last two mornings the children spent at the nature reserve on the north shore, which was run by one paid warden and forty {{volunteer}}s — people who work without payment, for the pleasure of being useful — pulling an invasive weed out of the marsh and labelling the nesting boxes. The warden paid them in biscuits and the difference between a job and a calling, which is the pay.

On Sunday they packed the tent, folded the arguments, and took the trip home — which is also a trip, because going back is also a purpose — already discussing the year after.
tr:
每年八月，这家人都要做同一趟出行（trip）——一次有目的的旅程，通常很短，而且总会回来——去湖上方的山里，而每年都要为这一周叫什么而吵同一架。

读美国小说的父亲管它叫假期（vacation）——holiday 的美式说法，来自办公室“腾空”的说法。当教师的母亲说“holiday”，并指出 vacation 是别人过的东西。这场争论就是传统，而传统胜过词汇。

第一个周六，他们徒步（hike）上了山脊——在野外认真进行的长途步行，穿着靴子，带着地图——因为正如祖母所说：“闲逛是去商店做的事；徒步（hike）是用来逃离商店的。”半山腰他们停下来野餐（picnic）：装在篮子里、坐在地上吃的一顿饭，比同样的食物端上桌好吃一倍，原因科学始终没有好好研究。然后继续走，到了山顶，照例是风和风景的混合。

周日，村里的小巴开它的短途游览（excursion）去老修道院——excursion 是为消遣而做的短途旅行，通常由别人组织，常有巴士，总有一张时间表。母亲更喜欢徒步；父亲更喜欢游览；祖母更喜欢野餐，因为两者都包含野餐。

那天傍晚六点前，他们在北岸的平地上扎营（camp）——支起帐篷（tent），认领了自己的地盘——这片营地自1961年就在这里，也没打算搬家。孩子们被告知，扎营（camp）是人类第二古老的技能：选平地，让火离帆布远点，还有永远永远别把食物留在狐狸能为之争吵的地方。

周三，湖上明轮船开它的傍晚巡游（cruise）——在海上或湖上为消遣而做的航行，没有货物，不赶时间，旅程本身就是全部意义——全家坐了个来回，看群山什么也不干、干得很美。

对岸的小镇七十年代为行人（pedestrian）——步行的人——重新规划过，街道是长椅、喷泉和商店的迷宫。假期的傍晚，一家人在里面闲逛（wander）——完全不带路线地走，哪个橱窗有意思就往哪拐——在旧书店流连（linger）最久，待到远超打烊时间，因为离开是一个决定，而假期里没人想做决定。

西奥叔叔周四为鸟而来。“我三十年前就放下猎枪了，”他架起望远镜说，“现在我打猎（hunt）只用镜头。hunt 是搜寻并追踪某物——鸟不介意，猎获上限是记忆，猎季永不关闭。”那一周他在追一只特别的鱼鹰，到周五他找到了它，或者一只他准备好坚持就是它的东西。

最后两个上午，孩子们在北岸的自然保护区度过，那里由一名领薪管理员和四十名志愿者（volunteer）——不为报酬、为了有用之乐而工作的人——运营，他们把一种入侵杂草从沼泽里拔出来，给巢箱贴标签。管理员用饼干和“一份工作与一份志业的区别”支付他们——区别就是薪水。

周日他们收起帐篷，折好争论，踏上回家的旅程——那也是一趟 trip，因为回去也是目的——并且已经在讨论下一年了。

quiz.q: A stroll is what you do to the shops; a hike is what the shops are for escaping from. A hike is —
o: a long walk in the countryside, taken seriously
quiz.ex: hike = 徒步、远足。go hiking 去远足。名词加价：a price hike（涨价）是另一义。对比 stroll（闲逛）。

quiz.q: An excursion is a short journey made for pleasure, usually organised by someone else, always with a timetable. An excursion is —
o: a long serious walk in boots
a short pleasure trip, often organised by others
quiz.ex: excursion = 短途游览、远足。go on an excursion 去游览。对比 trip（泛指出行）。

quiz.q: A meal carried in baskets and eaten on the ground, twice as good as the same food at a table. A picnic is —
o: a meal eaten outdoors, from baskets
a maze of benches and fountains
an invasive weed from the marsh
quiz.ex: picnic = 野餐。go for a picnic 去野餐。引申义：no picnic 不轻松。

quiz.q: The steamer's evening cruise — without cargo, without hurry, the journey being the entire point. A cruise is —
o: a tent pitched on flat ground
quiz.ex: cruise = 乘船游览、巡游。cruise ship 游轮。另义：出租车兜客（cruising for fares）。

quiz.q: The family wandered through the streets — walking with no route at all, turning wherever a window looked interesting. To wander means —
o: to fold the arguments and go home
to stay past closing time on purpose
to pursue an osprey with lenses
to walk around without a fixed route
quiz.ex: wander = 漫步、闲逛。wander around the old town。引申：mind wanders 走神。对比 linger（停留不走）。

quiz.q: They lingered longest at the second-hand bookshop, staying well past closing time, because leaving is a decision. To linger means —
o: to stay somewhere longer than expected
to walk with no route at all
to search for and pursue a bird
to make camp before six o'clock
quiz.ex: linger = 逗留、流连。linger over coffee 慢慢喝咖啡。近义 stay on；对比 wander（走）。

quiz.q: Now I hunt with lenses — the birds don't mind, the bag limit is memory, the season never closes. To hunt means —
o: to search for and pursue something
quiz.ex: hunt = 打猎、搜寻。hunt for a job 找工作；job-hunting 求职。名词 hunter 猎人。

quiz.q: Forty volunteers — people who work without payment, for the pleasure of being useful. A volunteer is —
o: a paid warden of a reserve
someone who works willingly without being paid
a pedestrian in a rebuilt town
quiz.ex: volunteer = 志愿者。volunteer to do sth 自愿做某事。形容词 voluntary 志愿的、自发的。

title: The Last Saturday
text:
On the last Saturday of every month, Grandmother declared war on the house, and the family reported, complaining, to the cupboard under the stairs.

The arsenal lived there. A {{broom}} — the long-handled brush for dry floors — leaned in the corner; a {{mop}} — the same idea but wet, on a head of strings — stood in its bucket; and the {{sponge}}, soft, yellow and full of holes, had absorbed so many Saturdays that nobody touched it without respect. Beside them, the chemistry shelf: a bottle of {{detergent}} — the grease-cutting chemical for dishes and floors — a dish of {{soap}} for hands, a bottle of {{shampoo}} (soap's specialist cousin, made for hair), and a small {{lotion}} for afterwards, when the war was over and the skin wanted peace.

Before any cleaning came the sorting, because Grandmother ran the house the way a city runs itself. "{{Garbage}}, {{rubbish}}, {{trash}}," she would recite — "the American word, the British word, and the word for it when you're annoyed. All three mean the same: what we have finished with." But nothing left the house in one bin. Into the {{recycle}} box went glass, paper and metal — to recycle is to send used things away to be made into new things. Onto the {{reuse}} shelf went the jam jars — to reuse is to use a thing again as itself, without remaking it: jars became pencil pots, tins became plant pots. The {{litter}} rule was absolute — litter being rubbish dropped in public places, which in Grandmother's moral system sat somewhere between theft and treason. The {{junk}} drawer, meanwhile, collected what was too broken to admire and too loved to lose — junk meaning old things of no real value — and it was opened once a year, on its birthday, and nothing in it was ever thrown away.

"And where does the rest go?" the smallest cousin once asked.

"The {{landfill}}," said Grandmother, "the great lined pit outside town where the city buries what it no longer wants. And the water — the water goes to the {{sewerage}}, the pipes and tunnels underneath that carry it all away, thank goodness, to somewhere else. Out of sight is a form of cleanliness too."

At eleven o'clock the plumber arrived, because the kitchen {{pipe}} — the tube that brings water to the tap — had been complaining since Tuesday. He worked his way through the vocabulary like a tour guide. "This is the {{tap}}," he said, turning it, "the thing you turn for water — and, as a verb, to {{tap}} a resource means to use it, the way you tap a river or an oil field. This is the {{plug}}," holding up the rubber stopper, "the thing that keeps the water in — and, as a verb, to plug in is to connect to power. Down there, if you insist, is the {{tub}}" — the basin itself, currently holding yesterday's washing-up water, gone grey and philosophical. "And this," he said, patting a length of copper, "is a {{tube}}, any long hollow pipe; in London, if you say the Tube, you mean the railway under it. Water travels by tube; people, apparently, too."

Then the floors. You {{sweep}} with the broom — long strokes, dirt travelling towards the door like a shy animal — and then you mop, and then you dry, and the {{towel}} comes off its rail for the last wipe. By four the house smelled of detergent and victory, and Grandmother sat down in the cleanest room in the district, drinking tea she had not made, looking at a floor she would not walk on until Monday.

"Dirt," she said, "is only matter in the wrong place. Which, when you think about it, is also the definition of most of the family."
tr:
每个月最后一个周六，祖母向房子宣战，全家人一边抱怨一边到楼梯下的橱柜前报到。

兵器都住在那儿。扫帚（broom）——扫干地板的长柄刷——斜靠在角落；拖把（mop）——同样的构思但带湿、装着绳头——立在水桶里；那块柔软、黄色、满是孔的海绵（sponge），已经吸饱了太多个周六，没人敢不敬地碰它。旁边是化学品架：一瓶洗涤剂（detergent）——对付盘子与地板油污的化学品——一碟洗手用肥皂（soap），一瓶洗发水（shampoo）（肥皂专门从事头发的表亲），还有一小瓶战后用的乳液（lotion），等战争结束、皮肤想要和平的时候用。

打扫之前先分拣，因为祖母管理这栋房子的方式就像一座城市管理自己。“garbage、rubbish、trash，”她会背诵道，“美式词、英式词，还有你生气时用的那个词。三个都一样：我们用完不要的东西。”但没有什么东西会混进同一个垃圾桶出门。玻璃、纸和金属进回收（recycle）箱——recycle 就是把用过的东西送去造成新的东西。果酱罐放上再利用（reuse）架——reuse 是把东西当作它本身再次使用，不用重造：罐子变笔筒，铁罐变花盆。乱扔垃圾（litter）的规则是绝对的——litter 指丢在公共场所的垃圾，在祖母的道德体系里，其罪过介于盗窃与叛国之间。与此同时，废旧杂物（junk）抽屉收集那些破得没法欣赏、又爱得没法丢弃的东西——junk 指没有真正价值的旧物——它每年在生日那天被打开一次，里面的东西一件也不会被扔掉。

“那剩下的去哪儿？”最小的表弟有一次问。

“垃圾填埋场（landfill），”祖母说，“城外那个衬了防渗层的大坑，城市把不再想要的东西埋进去。至于水——水进排水系统（sewerage），地底下把这些统统运走的管道和隧道，谢天谢地，运到别的什么地方去。眼不见，也算一种干净。”

十一点，水管工来了，因为厨房的水管（pipe）——把水送到水龙头的管子——从周二起就在抱怨。他像导游一样把词汇走了一遍。“这是水龙头（tap），”他拧开它，“拧出水的那个东西——作为动词，tap 某种资源意思是开发利用它，就像你 tap 一条河或一片油田。这是塞子（plug），”他举起橡胶塞，“留住水的东西——作为动词，plug in 是接上电源。下面那个，如果你坚持要看，是盆（tub）”——澡盆本身，此刻装着昨天的洗碗水，已经灰得很有哲学。“还有这个，”他拍拍一截铜管，“是管子（tube），任何长的中空管道；在伦敦，你说 the Tube，指的是底下的地铁。水坐管子旅行；显然，人也是。”

然后是地板。你用扫帚扫（sweep）——长长的一下一下，灰尘像害羞的动物朝门口挪——然后拖地，然后擦干，毛巾（towel）从杆上取下来做最后一道擦拭。到四点，整栋房子闻起来全是洗涤剂和胜利的味道，祖母坐在全区最干净的房间里，喝着她没泡的茶，看着一块她周一之前不会去踩的地板。

“污垢，”她说，“只是放错了位置的物质。仔细想想，这也是对家里大多数人的定义。”

quiz.q: A bottle of detergent — the grease-cutting chemical for dishes and floors. A detergent is —
o: a chemical substance used for cleaning
a soft yellow sponge full of holes
the long-handled brush for dry floors
a rubber stopper for the bath
quiz.ex: detergent = 洗涤剂、洗衣粉。washing detergent 洗涤剂。对比 soap（肥皂）。

quiz.q: Into the recycle box went glass, paper and metal — to send used things away to be made into new things. To recycle means —
o: to process used material into new products
to use a jam jar as a pencil pot
to bury waste in a lined pit
to carry water away in tunnels
quiz.ex: recycle = 回收利用。recycled paper 再生纸。对比 reuse（不加工地重复使用）。

quiz.q: Onto the reuse shelf went the jam jars — to use a thing again as itself, without remaking it. To reuse means —
o: to drop it in a public place
to send it away to become something new
to use something again without processing it
to open the drawer once a year
quiz.ex: reuse = 再使用、重复利用。reusable bags 环保袋。对比 recycle（回收再加工）。

quiz.q: Litter being rubbish dropped in public places — somewhere between theft and treason. Litter is —
o: the great lined pit outside town
old things too loved to lose
quiz.ex: litter = （公共场所的）垃圾。litter bin 废物箱；no littering 禁止乱扔垃圾。作动词：乱扔。

quiz.q: The landfill — the great lined pit outside town where the city buries what it no longer wants. A landfill is —
o: the underground pipes carrying water away
a site where waste is buried in the ground
a drawer opened once a year
quiz.ex: landfill = 垃圾填埋场。landfill site 填埋场。对比 incinerator（焚烧炉）。

quiz.q: The tap — the thing you turn for water; and, as a verb, to tap a resource means to use it. A tap is —
o: a device for turning water on and off
quiz.ex: tap = 水龙头；轻拍；开发（资源）。tap water 自来水；tap new markets 开拓新市场。

quiz.q: The plug — the thing that keeps the water in; and, as a verb, to plug in is to connect to power. A plug is —
o: a stopper that blocks a drain or hole
a shy animal travelling to the door
quiz.ex: plug = 塞子；插头。pull out the plug 拔掉塞子/插头。plug a gap 填补缺口。

quiz.q: You sweep with the broom — long strokes, dirt travelling towards the door like a shy animal. To sweep means —
o: to clean a floor with strokes of a brush
to drink tea you did not make
quiz.ex: sweep = 扫、打扫。sweep the floor 扫地。引申：A wave of reform swept the country（席卷）。

title: Moving In
text:
The flat was empty, the rent was paid, and Tomas stood in the middle of the main room with one suitcase and the strong feeling that adulthood was mostly a shopping list.

The inventory came first. A flat needs surprisingly little, once you list it honestly. {{Stuff}} — the general word for things, unnamed and unnumbered — was not on the list, because stuff was what he was trying to escape. The list wanted {{item}}s: single, countable things, each with a purpose and, ideally, a price. A bed. A lamp. A kettle.

The charity shop on the corner supplied most of it, and its owner, Mrs Farrell, supplied the vocabulary. "Everything here is second-hand {{merchandise}}," she said — merchandise being goods bought and sold — "except that shelf, which is {{souvenir}}s, and that cabinet, which is {{artifact}}s. A souvenir is a thing you keep to remember a place; an artifact is a thing made by human hands that has survived its maker — the difference is memory against history."

"And materials," said Tomas, reading a label.

"{{Material}} is what things are made of — wood, wool, glass, steel. {{Raw}} material is material as it comes from nature, unworked — the log before the table, the wool before the sweater. The opposite of refined. A {{crude}} thing, same family, means roughly made, unfinished — that chair is crude, and I love it, and it will outlive us both."

At the market he bought the sleep department: a second-hand {{mattress}} — the soft pad you sleep on — still lawful, barely; two {{sheet}}s — the large thin cloths that go between sleeper and blanket; a {{pillow}} for under his head; a thick {{blanket}} for the cold half of the year; and, from a stall run by a woman who had known his grandmother, a {{quilt}} — a padded bedcover, sewn from old clothes, warmer than anything new because of what was in it.

The floor department: one {{carpet}} — the fitted cloth that covers a whole floor, wall to wall — was beyond his budget, so he took a {{rug}} instead, a smaller piece that sits in the middle and pretends. At the door, a {{mat}} — the small rough one you wipe your feet on. On the sofa-that-was-not-yet-a-sofa, two {{cushion}}s — the soft pads that make hard seats survivable — and under the kettle, a {{pad}} of folded cloth, because the worktop was new and the kettle was old and one of them had to be protected.

The window was the last problem. One {{pane}} — the single sheet of glass in a window frame — had a crack in the corner that whistled when the wind came from the east. He hung {{curtain}}s, and learned from Mrs Farrell, who knew everything, that the whole point of curtain fabric was its {{opacity}} — the quality of not letting light through. The greater the opacity, the better the sleep. She donated the curtains herself, on the grounds that nobody in the family had ever needed them before.

On the last evening of the first week he counted what the flat contained. The bed, the quilt, the rug, the kettle. The {{necessity}}s — the things you cannot live without — came to eleven items. The rest, the lamps and the cushions and the souvenirs, were the luxuries, and he moved them around the flat for an hour, arranging, until it looked less like a warehouse and more like a home.

Downstairs, Mrs Farrell called up the stairs: "Have you got a first-aid {{kit}} anywhere? And any kitchen {{utensil}}s — the knives, the spoons, the practical things? Because a home is where the plasters and the potato peeler live, and you, my love, currently have neither."

"An {{outfit}}," she added, meaning a complete set of clothing for one purpose, "you can buy tomorrow. Tonight, borrow my plasters."
tr:
公寓是空的，房租已付，托马斯站在主屋中央，带着一只行李箱和一种强烈的感觉：成年大部分就是一张购物清单。

清单之前先盘点。一间公寓一旦诚实地列出来，需要的其实少得惊人。杂七杂八（stuff）——那些没有名字、数不清的“东西”的总称——不在清单上，因为 stuff 正是他在逃离的东西。清单要的是物件（item）：一个个可数的、各有用途、最好还有价格的东西。一张床。一盏灯。一把水壶。

街角的慈善商店供上了大部分，店主法雷尔太太供上了词汇。“这里的一切都是二手商品（merchandise），”她说——merchandise 指买卖流通的货物——“除了那层架子，那是纪念品（souvenir）；还有那个柜子，那是人工制品（artifact）。souvenir 是你留着纪念一个地方的东西；artifact 是由人手制成、活得比制造者更久的东西——区别在于记忆对历史。”

“还有材料，”托马斯读着标签说。

“材料（material）是东西的构成——木头、羊毛、玻璃、钢。原材料（raw）material 是从自然里来的、未经加工的材料——桌子之前的原木，毛衣之前的羊毛。是精加工的反面。粗糙的（crude）东西，同一家族，意思是制作简陋、未完成——那把椅子就很 crude，我爱它，它会活得比我们俩都长。”

在市场他买下了睡眠部门：一张二手床垫（mattress）——你睡在上面的软垫——勉强还合法；两条床单（sheet）——睡的人和毯子之间那层又大又薄的布；一个枕在头下的枕头（pillow）；一条过冷半年用的厚毛毯（blanket）；还有一个认识他祖母的女人摊位上的被子（quilt）——用旧衣服缝成的夹层床罩，比任何新的都暖，因为里面的东西。

地板部门：一整块地毯（carpet）——铺满整个地板、墙到墙的织物——超出预算，于是他拿了小地毯（rug），坐在中间装样子的较小一块。门口一块蹭鞋垫（mat）——粗糙的小块，用来擦脚。在那张还不是沙发的沙发上，两个靠垫（cushion）——让硬座位能活下去的软垫——水壶底下，一块折布做的垫（pad），因为台面是新的，水壶是旧的，总得有一个受保护。

窗户是最后一个问题。一块窗玻璃（pane）——窗框里的单片玻璃——角上有条裂缝，东风一来就吹口哨。他挂上窗帘（curtain），并从无所不知的法雷尔太太那里得知，窗帘布的全部意义在于它的不透明度（opacity）——不让光透过的性质。opacity 越高，睡得越好。窗帘是她自己捐的，理由是家里此前从没人需要过它们。

第一周的最后一个晚上，他清点了公寓的内容。床、被子、地毯、水壶。必需品（necessity）——没有就活不下去的东西——共十一件。其余的，灯、靠垫、纪念品，都是奢侈品，他把它们在屋里挪了一个小时，安排来安排去，直到它看起来不那么像仓库，而更像一个家。

楼下，法雷尔太太朝楼梯上喊：“你有急救箱（kit）吗？还有厨房用具（utensil）——刀、勺、那些实用的东西？因为家是创可贴和削皮器住的地方，而你，亲爱的，目前两样都没有。”

“一整套衣服（outfit），”她补充道，指为某一目的配齐的一身行头，“可以明天买。今晚，先用我的创可贴。”

quiz.q: The list wanted items: single, countable things, each with a purpose and a price. An item is —
o: a padded bedcover sewn from old clothes
the general word for unnamed things
goods bought and sold in shops
one separate object on a list
quiz.ex: item = 一件物品/项目/条目。menu items 菜单项；news items 新闻条目。对比 stuff（不可数的杂物）。

quiz.q: Second-hand merchandise — goods bought and sold. Merchandise is —
o: goods that are traded or sold
things kept to remember a place
objects made by human hands long ago
raw logs before they become tables
quiz.ex: merchandise = 商品、货品。official merchandise 正版周边。对比 goods（货物）、commodity（大宗商品）。

quiz.q: An artifact is a thing made by human hands that has survived its maker — memory against history. An artifact is —
o: a man-made object of historical interest
a thing kept to remember a holiday
a small rug pretending to be a carpet
a sheet of glass with a whistle
quiz.ex: artifact = 人工制品、文物。archaeological artifacts 考古文物。对比 souvenir（纪念品，重个人记忆）。

quiz.q: Raw material is material as it comes from nature, unworked — the log before the table. Raw means —
o: in its natural state, not processed
quiz.ex: raw = 未加工的；生的。raw materials 原材料；raw meat 生肉；raw data 原始数据。

quiz.q: A quilt — a padded bedcover, sewn from old clothes, warmer than anything new. A quilt is —
o: the cloth between sleeper and blanket
the soft pad you sleep on
the fitted carpet, wall to wall
quiz.ex: quilt = 被子（拼布缝制）。对比 blanket（毛毯）、sheet（床单）。

quiz.q: Two cushions — the soft pads that make hard seats survivable. A cushion is —
o: a small rough mat for wiping feet
a soft pad used for sitting or leaning on
a folded cloth under a kettle
a single sheet of window glass
quiz.ex: cushion = 靠垫、软垫。引申动词：cushion the blow 缓冲打击。对比 pad（各种小垫）。

quiz.q: The whole point of curtain fabric was its opacity — the quality of not letting light through. Opacity is —
o: the degree to which something blocks light
the length of a crack in a pane
the warmth of a grandmother's quilt
quiz.ex: opacity = 不透明（度）。形容词 opaque 不透明的。反义 transparency 透明度。

quiz.q: The necessities — the things you cannot live without — came to eleven items. A necessity is —
o: a padded bedcover from a market stall
a souvenir of a place you visited
a curtain donated by a neighbour
quiz.ex: necessity = 必需品；必要性。the necessities of life 生活必需品。对比 luxury（奢侈品）。

title: Bello's Hardware
text:
Bello's Hardware has sold the same four thousand objects since 1954, and Mr Bello knows the position of each one in the dark — which was lucky, because the street's electricity had died at seven that evening and the shop was lit by a single {{candle}}: wax with a burning wick through its heart, the oldest lamp in the world.

"My son," he said to Tomas at the counter, "you have come about a {{fuse}}." A fuse is the small safety part in an electrical circuit that melts and cuts the power when something goes wrong — the component whose whole career is dying usefully. "They all blow on the same night, always in winter. Bring me the old one, and take a box of {{match}}es too" — matches being the little wooden sticks with red heads that make fire on demand — "and if the lights are still dead by morning, a {{candle}} is a lamp with a salary of wax."

"Where are they?" said Tomas.

"Up the {{ladder}}," said Mr Bello — the ladder being the folding steps that lean against the shelves — "third {{shelf}} from the floor" — a shelf being the flat board that holds things up — "second {{drawer}} on the left." A drawer is the open-fronted box that slides in and out of a desk or cabinet; Mr Bello's had not closed fully since 1981.

The shop was divided, like a book, into {{section}}s — a section being one of the parts into which something larger is cut: chapters, towns, shops, oranges. "Wood is that {{section}}. Metal is here. Everything else is everywhere."

He talked the way other men breathe. "A {{nail}}" — holding one up — "is the thin metal pin you hammer into wood; a {{bolt}}" — holding up its fatter, threaded cousin — "takes a nut, and holds machines together. A nail forgives nothing; a bolt expects company. Over there, the {{razor}} — the sharp blade a man uses for {{shave|shaving}} his face — and to shave is to cut the hair off, face or wood; the plane shaves the door, the razor shaves the chin. Both, done well, count as manners."

At the counter he sorted the electricals by thickness, thickest to thinnest, like a family photo. "A {{cable}} is the heavy bundle of wires that carries power — the one that died on your street tonight. A {{cord}} is the thinner, rope-like line — a kettle cord, a curtain cord. A {{strand}} is a single thread of the many twisted together to make a rope: one strand is nothing, a hundred strands are a cable. And a man who is {{strand}}ed — verb, same word — is a man stuck somewhere without transport, which is what your street is tonight."

On the wall behind him hung the cutting tools. "{{Scissors}}" — the two-bladed cutting instrument, for paper and thread — "and {{shear}}s, their enormous cousins, for sheep and hedges. To shear a sheep is to cut its wool off once a year, and the sheep looks surprised every time, which tells you something about sheep."

"Two edge-words. The {{edge}} of a blade is the sharpened side; the edge of a table is where the table ends; and an edge in a game is an advantage — one word, three jobs. The {{rim}} is the edge of anything round — a cup, a wheel, a pair of spectacles. Never say 'the rim of the table'; the table will not understand you."

He put the kettle on the back shelf, next to the little gas ring. "Two abstract ones, before you go, because you look like a student. An {{element}} is one of the basic parts a thing is made from — the old elements were fire, water, earth and air, and the modern ones are on the chemistry wall. A {{factor}} is one of the forces that influences a result — price is a factor, weather is a factor, patience is a factor. Elements compose; factors cause. Get that right and you can pass any exam in the country."

Then he brought a small box from under the counter. "And {{staple}}s — the little metal clips that hold sheets of paper together. Also, the {{staple}} of a place is the food or product it lives on: rice is the staple of half the world, fish is the staple of this town, and gossip is the staple of the street your fuse died on."

At the door, Tomas stopped. "How much?"

"Sit on the {{stool}}," said Mr Bello, pointing at the backless wooden seat by the till, "while I write it down. And next time the lights die, don't just stand in the dark — {{lift}} the receiver and phone me. To lift is to raise; a {{lift}} is the machine that raises you between floors, or the ride in a stranger's car, or the improvement in a sad person's face. Tonight, you'll take the fuse, and your street will take the lift."
tr:
贝洛五金铺自1954年起就卖着同样的四千件东西，而贝洛先生闭着眼也知道每一件的位置——这很走运，因为那天晚上七点这条街的电断了，店铺只靠一支蜡烛（candle）照亮：中间穿一根燃烧灯芯的蜡（wax），世界上最古老的灯。

“孩子，”他对柜台前的托马斯说，“你是为保险丝来的。”fuse（保险丝）是电路里的小小安全部件，出问题时熔断、切断电流——它的整个职业生涯就是死得有用。“总在同一晚烧断，总在冬天。把旧的拿来，再拿一盒火柴（match）”——火柴是一擦就着火的红头小木棍——“要是到早上灯还不亮，一支蜡烛就是一盏以蜡为薪水的灯。”

“在哪儿？”托马斯问。

“上梯子（ladder），”贝洛先生说——梯子就是靠在货架上的折叠台阶——“从地往上第三层架（shelf）”——架是承放东西的平板——“左边第二个抽屉（drawer）。”抽屉是书桌或柜子里能推进拉出的开口盒子；贝洛先生的那个自1981年起就没完全合上过。

这家店像书一样分成了部分（section）——section 就是把较大的东西切分出的一块：章节、城区、店铺、橙子。“木头在那个 section。金属在这儿。其余的东西哪儿都是。”

他说话像别人呼吸。“钉子（nail）”——举起一枚——“是锤进木头里的细金属销；螺栓（bolt）”——举起它较粗、带螺纹的表亲——“要配螺母，把机器连在一起。钉子不原谅任何人；螺栓必须有伴。那边，剃须刀（razor）——男人刮（shave）脸用的锋利刀片——shave 就是把毛剃掉，脸上或木头上皆可；刨子给门剃，剃刀给下巴剃。两样干得好，都算教养。”

柜台边，他按粗细把电线排好，从粗到细，像全家福。“电缆（cable）是输送电力的粗线束——今晚死在你们街上那条就是。细绳（cord）是更细的、绳状的线——水壶线、窗帘绳。一股（strand）是拧成绳的许多单线中的一股：一股什么都不是，一百股就是一条电缆。而一个被困住（stranded，动词，同一个词）的人，是被卡在没交通的地方，这就是你们街今晚的样子。”

他身后墙上挂着切割工具。“剪刀（scissors）”——两片刀刃的剪切工具，剪纸和线——“还有大剪刀（shear），它们的大个子表亲，对付羊和树篱。给羊剪（shear）毛就是一年一次把羊毛剪掉，而羊每次都一脸惊讶，这多少说明了羊这种动物。”

“两个‘边’词。刀刃的刃（edge）是磨锋利的那一侧；桌子的 edge 是桌子结束的地方；比赛里的 edge 是优势——一个词，三份工作。边缘（rim）是任何圆形物的边——杯子、车轮、一副眼镜。永远别说‘桌子的 rim’；桌子会听不懂。”

他把水壶放到后架上，小煤气炉旁边。“走之前来两个抽象的，因为你看着像个学生。要素（element）是构成事物的最基本部分之一——古老的元素是火、水、土、气，现代的挂在化学墙上。因素（factor）是影响结果的诸多力量之一——价格是 factor，天气是 factor，耐心也是 factor。要素负责构成；因素负责促成。把这个弄对，全国的考试你都能过。”

然后他从柜台底下拿出一个小盒。“还有订书钉（staple）——把几张纸夹在一起的小金属夹。另外，一个地方的 staple 是它赖以为生的食物或产品：大米是半个世界的主食（staple），鱼是这座镇的主食，而闲话是你们那条街的主食——你的保险丝就死在那条街上。”

门口，托马斯停下。“多少钱？”

“坐到凳子（stool）上，”贝洛先生指着收银机旁那张无靠背的木座说，“我写下来。下次灯再灭，别光站在黑地里——拿起（lift）听筒给我打电话。lift 是抬起；电梯（lift）是在楼层之间抬升你的机器，也是陌生人汽车里的顺路一程，还是伤心人脸上的好转。今晚，你拿走保险丝，你们那条街会拿走那个 lift。”

quiz.q: A fuse is the small safety part that melts and cuts the power when something goes wrong. A fuse is —
o: a folding ladder leaning on shelves
a metal pin hammered into wood
a safety device that breaks an electrical circuit
quiz.ex: fuse = 保险丝；熔断。blow a fuse 烧断保险丝；另义：融合（fuse two ideas）。

quiz.q: A cable is the heavy bundle of wires; a cord is thinner; a strand is one thread. A cable is —
o: a single thread of a rope
a thick bundle of wires carrying power
the rope-like line of a kettle
the round edge of a wheel
quiz.ex: cable = 电缆；钢索。undersea cable 海底电缆。对比 cord（细绳）、strand（单股）。

quiz.q: Scissors — the two-bladed cutting instrument, for paper and thread. Scissors are —
o: large cousins for sheep and hedges
a cutting tool with two crossed blades
quiz.ex: scissors = 剪刀（复数形式）。a pair of scissors 一把剪刀。对比 shears（大剪刀）。

quiz.q: The edge of a blade, the edge of a table, and an edge in a game — one word, three jobs. An edge is —
o: a box that slides in and out
the flat board holding things up
the border of a surface; also an advantage
a lamp with a salary of wax
quiz.ex: edge = 边缘；刀刃；优势。on the edge of 在……边缘；competitive edge 竞争优势。

quiz.q: Elements compose; factors cause. An element is —
o: one of the basic parts something is made of
one of the forces influencing a result
the sharpened side of a blade
the wooden stick that makes fire
quiz.ex: element = 要素、元素。chemical elements 化学元素；an element of truth 一点真实成分。对比 factor（起作用的因素）。

quiz.q: Price is a factor, weather is a factor, patience is a factor. A factor is —
o: one of the basic parts of a thing
the rim of a pair of spectacles
the gas ring behind the kettle
quiz.ex: factor = 因素。key factor 关键因素。factor in 把……考虑进去。对比 element（构成要素）。

quiz.q: Staples hold sheets of paper together; rice is the staple of half the world. A staple is —
o: a component whose career is dying usefully
a thick bundle of power wires
a backless wooden seat by the till
a small metal clip; also a basic food or product
quiz.ex: staple = 订书钉；主食、主要产品。staple food 主食。

quiz.q: Sit on the stool — the backless wooden seat by the till. A stool is —
o: a drawer that will not close
a seat without a back or arms
quiz.ex: stool = 凳子。另义（医学）：stool 标本（粪便）。对比 chair（有靠背的椅子）。

title: Two Rooms Above the Bakery
text:
The office of the Devonport Review occupied two rooms above a bakery, and my first week there was an education in objects.
