The {{stationery}} cupboard — stationery being the collective noun for the writing world: paper, envelopes, pens, clips, everything written on or with — was run by Mrs Pym, who counted the paperclips the way a bank counts gold. "Your {{rubber}}," she said, handing over a small white block — the eraser that removes pencil, called a rubber in England and an eraser in America. "Your {{glue}}" — the sticky paste that joins paper to paper. "Your bottle of {{ink}}" — the coloured liquid a pen writes with. "And the box of {{tissue}}s" — soft paper for the nose — "because the window is old and the winters are long."

The copying machine in the corner was old enough to go by its brand name. "{{Xerox}} it," the editor would say, meaning: copy it — Xerox being a make of photocopier that had become the verb for copying, the way a famous vacuum brand became the verb for cleaning. To {{duplicate}} a page, to make its exact second self, was the machine's whole career, and it performed it with the noise of a small storm.

The archive held the magazine's memory. Every {{memorandum}} — the short written note passed between offices, a memo — went into a box, year by year. The very first {{pamphlet}} — a thin paper booklet, usually published to argue one thing loudly — was framed on the wall, dated 1951, arguing for a lighthouse. The back issues were stacked in {{paperback}} — books bound in flexible covers instead of hard boards — and the editor's {{portfolio}}, the large flat case for carrying photographs and drawings, doubled as his lunchbox, which explained certain stains.

"The {{cover}}," the editor said, holding up the new issue — meaning the front of the magazine — "must be striking. And note the word's other jobs: you cover a war as a reporter, the insurance covers the camera, and this lid covers the milk. One word, four careers, no complaints."

The {{phone}} on his desk — the telephone, invented, he claimed, purely so that Mrs Pym could interrupt him — sat beside the door {{bell}}, which announced visitors with one ring and the morning bread with two.

Reuben, the photographer, kept his {{camera}} in the safe and lectured on its anatomy. "The {{shutter}}" — the little door inside that opens and closes to let light in for exactly the right fraction of a second — "press the button, the shutter blinks, and your afternoon is kept forever. Photography is the art of letting light in briefly and holding it long."

The ordinary objects each had their biography. The {{bulb}} — the glass globe that gives light when electricity agrees to arrive — hung from the ceiling on its cord. The {{switch}} — the small lever that opens and closes the circuit — was wired, Reuben said, by an optimist. The {{fan}} — the machine that moves air around in summer, and, in its other life, a person devoted to something — stood unplugged from October to May. The {{vacuum}} — the machine that cleans by sucking air through itself — ran on Tuesdays and ruined two recordings. The {{refrigerator}} — known to its friends as the {{fridge}} — was the cold cupboard that kept the milk alive, and it hummed the only honest tune in the building.

"This radio," said the editor, switching it on, "is {{portable}} — light enough to carry anywhere — which means the news travels at the speed of whoever is holding it. And remember the word for what we do here: we {{spotlight}} things." A spotlight is the strong focused lamp that lights one actor and leaves the rest of the stage dark; as a verb, to spotlight something is to turn public attention onto it. "This magazine exists to spotlight what the city would rather keep unlit."

On Friday the electricity failed — the bakery below lost its ovens and we lost our light — and the archive came into its own. Mrs Pym produced a {{flashlight}} — the hand-held electric torch, in the American word — and the editor lit a {{lantern}}, the old kind of lamp with a handle, burning oil in a glass cage, the sort that hangs in stories and lighthouses. By lantern light, with the flashlight propped on a pile of back issues, we put the week's pages to bed, and I typed the last page by hand.

"Every object in this office," the editor said, hanging the lantern back on its nail, "has a story longer than yours. Be kind to them, and they'll keep you fed."
tr:
《德文波特评论》的办公室占了面包店楼上的两间屋，我在那里的第一周，是受了一番物品的教育。

文具（stationery）柜——stationery 是书写世界的总称：纸、信封、笔、回形针，一切用来写字和写在上面的东西——由皮姆太太掌管，她清点回形针的方式像银行清点黄金。“你的橡皮（rubber），”她递过来一小块白色的东西——擦掉铅笔字的东西，英国叫 rubber，美国叫 eraser。“你的胶水（glue）”——把纸和纸粘在一起的黏糊。“你的墨水（ink）”——钢笔书写用的有色液体。“还有这盒纸巾（tissue）”——擦鼻子的软纸——“因为窗户旧，冬天长。”

角落里的复印机老得可以直接用品牌称呼。“拿去 xerox（复印）一下，”主编会说，意思是：去复印——Xerox 是一个复印机品牌，已经变成了“复印”这个动词，就像某个著名的吸尘器品牌变成了“打扫”的动词一样。复印（duplicate）一页纸，造出它精确的第二个自己，是那台机器的全部职业生涯，它干这活时发出小风暴般的噪音。

档案室收藏着杂志的记忆。每一份备忘录（memorandum）——办公室之间传递的简短书面便条，即 memo——一年一年装进盒子。最早的小册子（pamphlet）——薄薄的纸制册子，通常为了大声论证一件事而出版——装裱在墙上，日期是1951年，论证的是一座灯塔。过刊堆成平装本（paperback）——用软封面而非硬纸板装订的书——而主编的作品夹（portfolio），那个装照片和 drawings 的大扁箱，兼作午餐盒，这解释了某些污渍。

“封面（cover），”主编举起新一期说——指杂志的正面——“必须抓人。注意这个词的其他工作：当记者你 cover 一场战争，保险 cover 这台相机，这个盖子 cover 牛奶。一个词，四份职业，毫无怨言。”

他桌上的电话（phone）——据他声称，电话的发明纯粹是为了让皮姆太太能打断他——旁边是门铃（bell），访客来响一声，早上的面包到响两声。

摄影师鲁本把相机（camera）锁在保险柜里，还讲它的解剖学。“快门（shutter）”——机器里面那扇小门，开合之间让光进来恰好那么一小会儿——“按下按钮，快门眨一下眼，你的下午就被永久保存了。摄影就是让光短暂进来、长久留下的艺术。”

普通物件各有各的传记。灯泡（bulb）——电力肯来时就发光的玻璃球——吊在天花板上。开关（switch）——接通和断开电路的小杆——鲁本说是被一个乐观主义者接的线。电风扇（fan）——夏天搅动空气的机器，另一辈子是个热爱某物的人——从十月到次年五月都拔着插头。真空吸尘器（vacuum）——靠往自己身体里吸气来清洁的机器——每周二运行，毁掉过两次录音。冰箱（refrigerator）——朋友们都叫它 fridge——是让牛奶活下去的冷柜子，它哼着整栋楼里唯一诚实的调子。

“这台收音机，”主编打开它，“是便携式（portable）的——轻到哪儿都能带——这意味着新闻以抱着它的人的速度传播。还要记住我们在这儿干的事的动词：我们聚焦（spotlight）。”聚光灯（spotlight）是那种只照亮一个演员、让舞台其余部分留在黑暗里的强光；作动词，spotlight 某事就是把公众注意力转向它。“这本杂志的存在，就是为了 spotlight 这座城市宁愿一直黑着的东西。”

周五停电了——楼下面包店失了炉子，我们失了光——档案室派上了用场。皮姆太太掏出一支手电筒（flashlight）——手持的电筒，美式说法——主编点起一盏提灯（lantern），那种带提手的旧式灯，玻璃罩里燃着油，故事和灯塔里挂的那种。借着提灯的光，手电筒支在一摞过刊上，我们把这周的版面付印，最后一页是我手打的。

“这间办公室里的每件东西，”主编说着，把提灯挂回钉子上，“都有比你的故事更长的故事。对它们好点，它们会养活你。”

quiz.q: Stationery — the collective noun for the writing world: paper, envelopes, pens, clips. Stationery is —
o: a large flat case for photographs
quiz.ex: stationery = 文具。注意与 stationary（静止的）拼写区分：e 是 envelope，a 是 at rest。

quiz.q: A memorandum — the short written note passed between offices, a memo. A memorandum is —
o: a thin booklet arguing one thing
a brief written message for internal use
a book with a flexible cover
the little door inside a camera
quiz.ex: memorandum = 备忘录、便函（复数 memoranda/memorandums）。缩写 memo。词根 memor（记忆）。

quiz.q: The first pamphlet — a thin paper booklet published to argue one thing loudly — argued for a lighthouse. A pamphlet is —
o: an exact copy of a page
a small thin booklet, usually on one subject
the front cover of a magazine
quiz.ex: pamphlet = 小册子。政治宣传小册。对比 paperback（平装书）。

quiz.q: The shutter — the little door inside that opens and closes to let light in for a fraction of a second. A shutter is —
o: the lever that opens a circuit
the device that opens to expose camera film
the strong lamp for one actor
quiz.ex: shutter = （相机）快门；百叶窗。另义：roll down the shutters 打烊。

quiz.q: A spotlight lights one actor and leaves the stage dark; as a verb, to turn public attention onto something. To spotlight means —
o: to focus public attention on something
to copy a page with a small storm
to keep the milk alive in winter
to interrupt the editor by telephone
quiz.ex: spotlight = 聚光灯；聚焦、使公众注意。in the spotlight 处于公众关注中。

quiz.q: This radio is portable — light enough to carry anywhere. Portable means —
o: old enough to go by brand name
quiz.ex: portable = 便携的、手提式的。portable computer 便携电脑。词根 port（携带）。

quiz.q: Mrs Pym produced a flashlight — the hand-held electric torch, in the American word. A flashlight is —
o: the glass globe hung from the ceiling
an old lamp burning oil in a glass cage
a machine that cleans by sucking air
quiz.ex: flashlight = 手电筒（美式）。英式为 torch。对比 lantern（提灯、灯笼）。

quiz.q: The editor lit a lantern — the old kind of lamp with a handle, burning oil in a glass cage. A lantern is —
o: a lamp with a handle, often oil-burning
the little door inside a camera
the cold cupboard keeping milk alive
quiz.ex: lantern = 提灯、灯笼。Chinese lantern 灯笼；lantern festival 元宵节。

title: The Valley of Mills
text:
The valley keeps three working buildings from its industrial century — a {{mill}}, a {{forge}}, and the gated entrance of a {{mine}} — and the school visits them every June, in the rain, on principle.

A {{mill}} is a building where something is ground or processed: grain into flour, mostly, powered once by water or wind. A {{forge}} is the blacksmith's workshop, built around a fire. A {{mine}} is a hole dug into the earth to bring out coal or metal ore; the miners themselves said {{pit}} — the older, darker word for the same hole — and the pit said nothing back, which everyone considered fair.

At the mill, the miller rubs the great oak gears with {{wax}} twice a year so they turn sweetly, and grinds the week's flour into paper sacks. "Wood is honest," he says, patting the {{wooden}} frame — wooden meaning made of wood — "but wood was once {{lumber}}: the sawn timber of the timber yard, before it became a mill. In America they still say lumberyard. In England we say the wood yard, because we like using two words where one would do."

Downstream stands the forge, where the blacksmith keeps four {{metal}}s and their family stories. "{{Iron}}," she says, holding up a horseshoe, "the common grey metal — strong, cheap, everywhere. {{Brass}}" — yellow, polished, on the shelf — "is copper and zinc mixed, good for instruments and doorknobs. {{Bronze}}" — its older, browner cousin — "is copper and tin: coins, statues, cannons. And {{lead}}" — soft, dull, heavy — "the metal that bends in your hand and must never go near a mouth. Any metal made by mixing metals is an {{alloy}} — a recipe, not an element. The whole of metallurgy is cookery with fireproof ingredients."

The fire is fed with coal — the {{fuel}}, the material a fire eats — and before each session she {{lubricate}}s the hammer pivot: to lubricate is to oil the moving parts so that metal slides over metal without screaming, a courtesy the machines repay in decades.

The mine is closed now. The guide, a former miner, points out the grey hill behind the fence: the {{waste}} — the left-over stone, crushed and unwanted, brought up with the coal and piled into its own landscape. "We called it the spoil heap, because everything here has two names and one of them is always sadder." The river below, he says, was {{dredge}}d last spring — dug out, the silt lifted from the bed — so the trout could come back. And the miners' lunch came down in a {{can}} — the metal container — which the pit ponies learned to open, which is why the ponies got fat and the men got thin.

Last comes the weaver's cottage, where the materials of the world hang in rows. "{{Fabric}} is the general word," says the weaver, "for any woven cloth. Every cloth begins as {{fibre}} — the thin strand of which all cloth is made. This one is {{cotton}} — the fibre of the cotton plant, soft, washable, the world's favourite. This is {{linen}} — from the flax plant, cool in summer, crisp forever. This is {{nylon}} — the synthetic fibre, invented in a laboratory, poured out of a machine like spaghetti. And this heavy one is {{canvas}} — thick cotton, for sails, tents and paintings. To {{weave}} cloth is to cross threads over and under each other; to {{knit}} is to build cloth out of a single thread and two needles, which is why knitting forgives mistakes and weaving does not."

On the top shelf sit the skins: "{{Leather}} — animal hide, tanned and cured; older than every other material on this wall and outlasting most of them." And in a box by the door, brightly, immodestly: "{{plastic}} — the modern material, moulded and synthetic, cheap, cheerful, immortal, and now filling an ocean near you. We use it for buttons. The Victorians used shell. History does not always improve."

The cottage walls themselves give the last lesson. "{{Cement}}," says the weaver, knocking the pointing, "the grey powder that, mixed with water and sand, becomes concrete — the bones of every modern building. {{Lime}} — the white powder from burnt limestone — made the mortar of these old walls, and whitewashes them still. And {{plaster}} — the smooth paste spread over interior walls, which takes your fingerprint forever if you touch it before it dries, so please don't." The school did not.

On the walk back, in the rain, the teacher asked them to name one thing from each building. "Wax," said one. "An alloy," said another. "A pit pony with a can." said a third, and everyone agreed that this was, by some distance, the best answer of the day.
tr:
这条山谷保留着工业世纪的三个仍在运转的建筑——一座磨坊（mill）、一间铁匠铺（forge）、一个装了闸门的矿井（mine）入口——每年六月，学校都本着传统冒雨前来参观。

mill 是磨碎或加工某种东西的建筑：主要是把谷物磨成面粉，从前靠水力或风力驱动。forge 是铁匠的工作坊，围着火建造。mine 是挖进地下取出煤或金属矿石的洞；矿工们自己则说 pit（矿井）——同一个洞更古老、更黑的词——而井一声不吭，大家觉得这很公平。

磨坊里，磨坊主每年给巨大的橡木齿轮上两次蜡（wax），好让它们转动得温顺，把一周的面粉磨进纸袋。“木头是诚实的，”他拍着木制（wooden）的框架说——wooden 意思是木头做的，“但木头曾经是木材（lumber）：锯木场里锯好的木料，后来才变成磨坊。美国人至今还说 lumberyard（木材场）。英国人说 wood yard，因为我们喜欢用一个词够用的地方用两个。”

下游立着铁匠铺，女铁匠保存着四种金属（metal）和它们的家族故事。“铁（iron），”她举起一只马蹄铁说，“最常见的灰色金属——结实、便宜、到处都是。黄铜（brass）”——黄色、抛光、在架子上——“是铜和锌的混合物，适合做乐器和门把手。青铜（bronze）”——它更古老、更棕的表亲——“是铜加锡：钱币、雕像、大炮。还有铅（lead）”——软、暗、沉——“一种用手就能掰弯的金属，永远不许靠近嘴。任何由混合金属制成的金属都是合金（alloy）——是一张配方，不是一种元素。整个冶金学就是用防火食材做的烹调。”

炉火吃的是煤——燃料（fuel），火所吞食的材料——每开工前她给锤轴上油润滑（lubricate）：lubricate 是给运动部件上油，让金属在金属上滑动而不尖叫，这份礼貌机器用几十年回报。

矿井如今关闭了。向导是昔日的矿工，他指着栅栏后面那座灰山：废料（waste）——和煤一起挖上来、被压碎又没人要的剩石，堆成了自己的风景。“我们管它叫矸石山，因为这里的一切都有两个名字，其中一个总是更伤心。”他说，下面的河去年春天疏浚（dredge）过——挖开河道，把淤泥从河床上吊走——好让鳟鱼回来。而矿工们的午饭装在罐头（can）——金属容器——里带下去，井下的矿马学会了开罐，所以马越来越胖，人越来越瘦。

最后是织工的小屋，全世界的材料一排排挂着。“织物（fabric）是总称，”织工说，“指任何织成的布。每块布都始于纤维（fibre）——一切布匹由以构成的细丝。这个是棉（cotton）——棉花植株的纤维，柔软、耐洗、全世界的最爱。这是亚麻（linen）——来自亚麻植物，夏凉，永远挺括。这是尼龙（nylon）——合成纤维，实验室里发明，从机器里像意面一样挤出来。这个厚的是帆布（canvas）——厚棉布，做帆、帐篷和油画布。织（weave）布是让经纬线上下交错；编（knit）是用一根线和两根针把布建起来，这就是为什么编织原谅错误，而纺织不原谅。”

顶层架子上摆着皮子：“皮革（leather）——经过鞣制的兽皮；比这面墙上任何材料都古老，也比它们大多数活得久。”门边一个盒子里，鲜亮而不知羞耻地躺着：“塑料（plastic）——现代材料，可塑、合成、便宜、快活、不朽，如今正在填满你家附近的一片海。我们用它做纽扣。维多利亚人用贝壳。历史并不总是进步。”

小屋的墙本身给出了最后一课。“水泥（cement），”织工敲着勾缝说，“灰色的粉末，和水、沙混在一起就成了混凝土——每栋现代建筑的骨头。石灰（lime）——烧石灰岩得到的白粉——砌成了这些老墙的灰浆，至今还刷白它们。还有灰泥（plaster）——抹在内墙上的光滑膏体，干燥前你一碰它就永远留下你的指纹，所以请不要。”学校没有碰。

雨中走回去的路上，老师让他们从每个建筑说出一样东西。“蜡，”一个说。“一种合金，”另一个说。“一匹拿着罐头的井马，”第三个说，所有人都同意，这是今天遥遥领先的最佳答案。

quiz.q: A forge is the blacksmith's workshop, built around a fire. A forge is —
o: a hole dug to extract coal
a building where grain is ground
a blacksmith's workshop with a furnace
a grey hill of crushed stone
quiz.ex: forge = 锻造车间；铁匠铺。作动词：伪造（forge a signature）；另义 forge ahead 稳步前进。

quiz.q: Brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin; any metal made by mixing metals is an alloy. An alloy is —
o: a pure element dug from a mine
a metal made by combining two or more metals
a synthetic fibre from a laboratory
quiz.ex: alloy = 合金。brass/bronze 都是 alloy。对比 element（元素）。

quiz.q: To lubricate is to oil the moving parts so that metal slides over metal without screaming. To lubricate means —
o: to rub oak gears with wax
to feed a fire with coal
to apply oil or grease to reduce friction
to dig silt out of a river
quiz.ex: lubricate = 润滑。lubricating oil 润滑油。名词 lubricant 润滑剂。

quiz.q: Wood was once lumber — the sawn timber of the timber yard. Lumber is —
o: timber sawn into planks for building
the grey powder mixed with water
the thin strand cloth is made from
quiz.ex: lumber = 木材（美式）。lumberjack 伐木工。英式多用 timber/wood。

quiz.q: Every cloth begins as fibre — the thin strand of which all cloth is made. A fibre is —
o: the paste spread on interior walls
the general word for woven cloth
a thin thread-like strand of material
quiz.ex: fibre = 纤维。natural/synthetic fibres 天然/合成纤维。dietary fibre 膳食纤维。

quiz.q: This heavy one is canvas — thick cotton, for sails, tents and paintings. Canvas is —
o: heavy cloth used for sails and tents
quiz.ex: canvas = 帆布、油画布。a canvas bag 帆布包。对比 linen（亚麻布）、nylon（尼龙）。

quiz.q: Plaster — the smooth paste spread over interior walls, which takes your fingerprint forever. Plaster is —
o: a lunch container opened by ponies
a soft paste spread on walls to smooth them
quiz.ex: plaster = 灰泥；（英）膏药。plaster a wall 抹墙。另义：in plaster 打着石膏。

quiz.q: The river was dredged — dug out, the silt lifted from the bed — so the trout could come back. To dredge means —
o: to clear a riverbed by lifting out mud
to pile waste into a landscape
quiz.ex: dredge = 疏浚、清淤。dredger 挖泥船。另义：dredge sth in sugar 撒上糖。

title: The Auction at the Village Hall
text:
The auction begins at ten in the morning, and by half past nine the car park is full beyond the {{fence}} — the wooden barrier that separates the field from the road, and the arriving cars from the leaving ones.

Every lot in the hall carries two pieces of paper. A {{tag}} — the small card with the lot number, tied on with string — and a {{label}} — the card telling you what the thing is and where it has been. "A {{tag}} marks," the auctioneer explains, walking the rows. "A {{label}} describes. Learn the difference and you will never be fooled at a market again." His voice is part of the stock too: it climbs through each lot by half-steps to a {{pitch}} — pitch being, of sound, the height of it, its place between the deep and the sharp; and, of a salesman, the prepared argument by which a thing is talked up — that lifts the last bid out of its chair.

On the long trestle tables: a crate of {{jar}}s — glass containers with lids, for jam and luck; a wooden {{barrel}} — the great curved cask, made of staves bound with iron hoops, once full of beer and now full of possibility; and, side by side, a {{bucket}} and a {{pail}}, which are the same object wearing two words, the {{pail}} being simply the older and more poetic of the two.

The bicycles are always popular. Lot 44 has new {{pedal}}s — the parts your feet push to make the machine go — and a horn you sound by hand, without any {{handle}} to grip, because the best horns of 1953 worked by a lever you squeezed. Lot 45, a radio, has a bakelite {{knob}} — the round control you turn to bring the world in — that turns with the sound of a small door opening.

The jewellery box is where the auction earns its reputation. The expert, Mrs Oyenekan, holds up a ring. "{{Diamond}}," she says, "the hardest natural material, carbon pressed by the earth for a geological age — and this one is glass. {{Crystal}} — clear glass, cut to catch the light — lovely in a window, fatal on a certificate. This ring is a {{counterfeit}}: an object made deliberately to deceive, a forgery with ambition. And this brooch, though honest, is {{inferior}} — of poorer quality than it pretends: thin gold, tired hinge, honest price." A thing that is a {{fake}} announces itself as something it is not; a thing that is merely inferior promises less than it costs. "The counterfeit deceives the eye," she says, "the inferior disappoints the hand. Both end up at auction, and both end up cheaper than the truth."

The front table holds the day's geography of condition. A box marked {{fragile}} — easily broken, and shipped in the hope that nobody reads — contains four glasses, of which three survived. A pair of boots marked {{durable}} — built to last, hard-wearing — has outlived both its previous owners and shows every intention of outliving the auction house. A clock no bigger than a walnut is described in the catalogue as a {{miniature}} — a very small, detailed model of a full-sized thing — and goes for the price of a full-sized thing, because smallness, done well, is expensive.

Two lots from the end comes the day's {{hurdle}} — the obstacle, the difficult jump, a word borrowed from the racing track — when two bidders fight over a brass carriage lamp and the price climbs past sense. The auctioneer, delighted, milks it. "The lamp is still {{available}}," he reminds the hall — available meaning obtainable, there for the taking, for the next ten seconds — "and going, going..."

The rain starts as the last lot falls. The hall empties into a forest of {{umbrella}}s — the folding canopy on a stick that keeps one person dry and two people arguing — and the stragglers pull on {{raincoat}}s — the coats that keep the rain off everything above the knees — and carry their jars, buckets and one honest brooch out into the weather.

At the gate, the auctioneer pins a small metal pin on the winner of the lamp: the auction house {{badge}} — the emblem, the small sign of belonging — which she will wear, he promises, to every auction for the rest of her life, or until the next brass lamp, whichever comes first.
tr:
拍卖会上午十点开始，而九点半停车场就已经满了，满过栅栏（fence）——隔开田野与道路的木制围栏，也隔开来车与去车。

会堂里每件拍品都挂着两张纸。一张标签（tag）——系着绳子、写着拍品编号的小卡片——和一张说明（label）——告诉你这东西是什么、从哪儿来的卡片。“tag 是做标记，”拍卖师在长桌之间边走边解释，“label 是做描述。学会这个区别，你在任何集市都再也不会被骗。”他的嗓音也是存货的一部分：每件拍品里它都半音半音地爬上一个音高（pitch，pitch 指声音的高低、深锐之间的位置；也指推销员那套把东西说高的说辞），把最后一口价从椅子上提起来。

长条支架桌上：一箱罐子（jar）——带盖的玻璃容器，装果酱，也装运气；一只木桶（barrel）——巨大的弧形桶，桶板箍着铁箍，曾经装满啤酒，如今装满可能性；还有并排的一只 bucket 和一只 pail（提桶），它们是同一件东西穿着两个词，pail 只是其中更古老、更有诗意的那个。

自行车总是抢手。44号拍品换了新踏板（pedal）——你的脚踩着让机器前进的部件——和一只用手按的喇叭，没有任何可握的把手（handle），因为1953年最好的喇叭靠一根你捏的杆工作。45号是一台收音机，有一个电木旋钮（knob）——转动就能把世界调进来的圆形控制器——转动时发出小门开启的声音。

首饰盒是拍卖会挣名声的地方。专家奥耶内坎太太举起一枚戒指。“钻石（diamond），”她说，“最硬的天然材料，碳被大地压了一个地质纪——而这枚是玻璃。水晶（crystal）——切割得能抓光的透明玻璃——放在窗台上可爱，放在证书上致命。这枚戒指是一件赝品（counterfeit）：刻意造出来骗人的东西，一件有野心的伪造品。而这枚胸针虽然诚实，却质量低劣（inferior）——比它假装的品质更差：金薄，铰链疲软，价格诚实。”假货（fake）是把自己说成不是的东西；单纯劣质的东西承诺的比它花的少。“赝品骗过眼睛，”她说，“劣品让手失望。两者最后都流进拍卖会，也都比真相便宜。”

前排桌子摆着当日物品状况的地理学。一只标着易碎（fragile）——容易破碎，托运时盼着没人读这两个字——的箱子里装着四只玻璃杯，幸存三只。一双标着耐用（durable）——造得耐久、经穿——的靴子已经比它前后两任主人都活得久，并且摆明打算比拍卖行也活得久。一座不比核桃大的钟，图录上写着微型（miniature）——一件小型精致的实物模型——拍出了实物的价钱，因为做得好的小，很贵。

倒数第二件拍品出现了当日难关（hurdle）——障碍、难跨的一跳，从赛跑的跨栏借来的词——两位竞买人为一盏黄铜马车灯较劲，价格爬过了理智线。拍卖师喜不自胜，慢慢榨。“这盏灯仍然可得（available），”他提醒全场——available 意思是买得到、就在那儿等着，再等十秒——“一次，两次……”

最后一件落槌时下起了雨。会堂空出来，变成一片伞（umbrella）的森林——棍子上撑开的折篷，让一个人干燥，让两个人吵架——落在后面的人套上雨衣（raincoat）——让膝盖以上不被雨淋的外套——抱着他们的罐子、提桶和一枚诚实的胸针走进雨里。

大门口，拍卖师把一枚小金属别针别在马车灯的赢家身上：拍卖行的徽章（badge）——会籍的小小标志——他保证，她余生会戴着它参加每一场拍卖会，或者直到下一盏黄铜灯出现，以先到者为准。

quiz.q: A tag marks; a label describes — it tells you what the thing is and where it has been. A label is —
o: a wooden barrier at the car park
a small card tied on with string
a piece of paper describing what something is
quiz.ex: label = 标签（说明内容）。care labels 洗涤标签。作动词：label the boxes 给箱子贴标签。对比 tag（标记）。

quiz.q: A wooden barrel — the great curved cask, made of staves bound with iron hoops. A barrel is —
o: a folding canopy on a stick
a glass jar with a lid
a small metal pin of belonging
quiz.ex: barrel = 桶；枪管。a barrel of oil 一桶油。另一习语：scrape the barrel 山穷水尽。

quiz.q: Lot 44 has new pedals — the parts your feet push to make the machine go. A pedal is —
o: the round control that brings the world in
a foot-operated lever on a machine
the horn worked by a lever
the horn you sound by hand
quiz.ex: pedal = 踏板。pedal a bicycle 蹬自行车。注意区分 peddle（叫卖）。

quiz.q: This ring is a counterfeit: an object made deliberately to deceive, a forgery with ambition. A counterfeit is —
o: a fake made to deceive people
an honest thing of poorer quality
clear glass cut to catch light
quiz.ex: counterfeit = 赝品；伪造的。counterfeit money 假币。近义 fake、forgery。对比 inferior（劣质但非故意欺骗）。

quiz.q: This brooch, though honest, is inferior — of poorer quality than it pretends. Inferior means —
quiz.ex: inferior = 较差的、次的。inferior to 比……差。反义 superior。对比 counterfeit（蓄意造假）。

quiz.q: A box marked fragile — easily broken, and shipped in the hope that nobody reads. Fragile means —
quiz.ex: fragile = 易碎的、脆弱的。fragile goods 易碎品；a fragile peace 脆弱的和平。近义 brittle。对比 durable。

quiz.q: A pair of boots marked durable has outlived both its previous owners. Durable means —
o: able to last a long time
quiz.ex: durable = 耐用的、持久的。durable goods 耐用品。名词 durability 耐久性。对比 fragile。

quiz.q: A clock no bigger than a walnut, described as a miniature — a very small, detailed model. A miniature is —
o: a very small, finely made version of something
a hurdle from the racing track
a brass lamp climbing past sense
an umbrella keeping two people arguing
quiz.ex: miniature = 微型模型；微型的。miniature painting 微型画。对比 giant。

title: The Tailor of Ropewalk Lane
text:
The tailor's shop on Ropewalk Lane is four metres wide and ninety years deep, and Mr Castellan has worked at its window for fifty of them, dressed always in the same style, which is the whole point of him.

"A {{garment}}," he says, threading a {{needle}} — the thin steel spike with a hole at one end, through which the {{thread}} passes — "is the honest word for any single piece of clothing. A {{dress}} is a garment in one piece that hangs from the shoulders. To {{clothe}} someone is to provide them with clothes — the verb of the whole industry. And a {{tailor}}, since you ask, is one who makes and repairs garments, which is me, and the verb of my existence is to {{sew}} — to join cloth with needle and thread."

He sews while he talks, and the {{stitch}} — one pass of the needle through cloth, the smallest unit of the whole art — keeps the rhythm of the sentence. Around the worktable lie his tools of temporary truth: the {{pin}} — the small sharp point that holds cloth in the shape of its future; the {{strap}} — the narrow strip of cloth that holds something up, a shoulder, a bag; the {{clasp}} — the small metal fastener joining two edges, the catch of a necklace; and the {{button}} — the disc that fastens a shirt, and, when lost, begins the day badly.

The shop's rail of example garments runs like a museum, left to right. "A {{uniform}}," he begins at the grey end, "is the clothing of an organisation — school, army, hospital — making many people look like one idea. A {{costume}} is clothing for pretending — the stage, the party, the historical drama. A {{gown}} is the long formal garment — graduates, judges, brides. A {{robe}} is the loose long garment of comfort or ceremony — bathrobes, judges again, wizards. An {{overcoat}} is the heavy coat that goes over everything in winter, which is what its name says. A {{sweater}} is the knitted garment for the top half, warm as an embrace. A {{jacket}} is the short coat, the general-purpose friend. A {{skirt}} is the garment that hangs from the waist — and also the edge of anything: the skirt of a table, the skirt of a mountain. {{Trousers}} cover the two legs separately — the British word, and the better one. {{Jeans}} are trousers of heavy cotton, American and immortal. A {{vest}} is the sleeveless top, worn under or over according to the century. A {{cloak}} is the loose outer garment of another age, fastened at the neck and moving with the weather. And {{overall}}s" — he touches a faded blue pair — "are the one-piece garments of work, worn over everything, which is exactly what the word means: over all."

His apprentice, Marta, sits at the second table with the spinning wheel — no, with the shears and the machine, and her own vocabulary to learn. "The {{spin}}ning wheel," says Mr Castellan, nodding at the old wheel in the corner, decorative now, "is what turned raw wool into thread for a thousand years — to {{spin}} is to twist fibres together into a continuous line. Every garment in this shop began as something growing, and then as something spinning."

At closing time he turns the sign and counts the day: two trousers hemmed, one cloak rescued from a moth, a wedding gown begun for March. "People think clothes are about appearance," he says, sweeping the threads into his palm. "Clothes are about armour, and memory, and the small daily ceremony of deciding who to be. The needle knows. Now go home — and tomorrow, wear something that fits."
tr:
绳道巷的裁缝铺四米宽，九十年深，卡斯特兰先生在它的橱窗前工作了其中五十年，永远穿同一种风格——这本身就是他的全部意义。

“一件衣服（garment），”他一边给针（needle）穿线一边说——针就是一端带孔的细钢刺，线（thread）从孔里穿过——“是任何单件衣物的诚实叫法。一条连衣裙（dress）是从肩部垂下的一体式衣服。给某人穿衣（clothe）是提供衣服——整个行业的动词。至于裁缝（tailor），既然你问了，就是制作和修补衣服的人，也就是我，而我存在的动词是缝（sew）——用针线把布连起来。”

他边说边缝，针脚（stitch）——针穿过布的一次穿行，这门手艺的最小单位——给句子打着节拍。工作台周围摆着他临时的真理工具：大头针（pin）——把布固定成它未来形状的尖锐小针；细带（strap）——撑住某物的窄布条，肩带、包带；搭扣（clasp）——连接两个边缘的小金属扣，项链的搭钩；还有纽扣（button）——扣住衬衫的圆片，而一旦丢了，一整天都开局不顺。

店里那排示例衣像博物馆一样从左到右挂着。“制服（uniform），”他从灰色那头开始，“是组织的衣着——学校、军队、医院——让许多人看起来像一个想法。戏服（costume）是为了假装而穿的衣服——舞台、派对、历史剧。礼服（gown）是长款的正式衣服——毕业生、法官、新娘。长袍（robe）是舒适或仪式的宽松长衣——浴袍、又是法官、巫师。大衣（overcoat）是冬天套在一切外面的厚外套，名字说的就是这个。毛衣（sweater）是针织的上半身衣服，暖得像一个拥抱。夹克（jacket）是短外套，全能的朋友。短裙（skirt）是从腰部垂下的衣服——也是任何东西的边缘：桌裙、山裙。长裤（trousers）分开包住两条腿——英式词，也是更好的那个。牛仔裤（jeans）是厚棉布裤子，美式而不朽。背心（vest）是无袖上衣，穿里穿外取决于世纪。斗篷（cloak）是另一个时代的宽松外衣，在颈间系住，随天气摆动。还有工装连体裤（overall），”——他碰了碰那条褪色的蓝的——“是干活穿的一件式衣服，套在一切外面，词义就是这样：over all，套住全部。”

他的学徒玛尔塔坐在第二张桌子旁，用剪刀和缝纫机，学她自己的词汇。“那架纺车（spinning wheel），”卡斯特兰先生朝角落里那架如今纯属装饰的旧轮子点点头，“一千年来就是把生羊毛纺成线的东西——纺（spin）就是把纤维捻在一起连成线。这店里的每一件衣服，都始于某种生长的东西，然后是某种旋转的东西。”

打烊时他翻过牌子，清点这一天：两条长裤改了裤边，一件斗篷从蛀虫嘴里救回，一件三月要穿的婚纱起了头。“人们以为衣服关乎外表，”他把线头扫进掌心说，“衣服关乎盔甲，关乎记忆，关乎每天早晨决定成为谁的这场小小仪式。针知道。回家吧——明天，穿件合身的。”

quiz.q: A garment is the honest word for any single piece of clothing. A garment is —
o: a loose garment of another age
quiz.ex: garment = （一件）衣服（正式用词）。outer garments 外衣。对比 costume（戏服）、uniform（制服）。

quiz.q: To tailor is to make and repair garments; the verb of his existence is to sew. To sew means —
o: to join cloth using a needle and thread
to fasten a shirt with a disc
to hold cloth with sharp points

quiz.q: A stitch — one pass of the needle through cloth, the smallest unit of the whole art. A stitch is —
o: the edge of a table or mountain

o: a long formal garment for brides
identical clothing worn by members of a group

quiz.q: A gown is the long formal garment — graduates, judges, brides. A gown is —
o: the garment hanging from the waist
the knitted top half of warmth
a long formal dress or robe

quiz.q: Overalls are the one-piece garments of work, worn over everything, which is what the word means. Overalls are —
o: the loose cloak of another age
a single work garment covering the body over other clothes
the sleeveless top of the century
quiz.ex: overalls = 工装裤、背带裤。作形容词 overall = 全部的：overall cost 总成本。

quiz.q: To spin is to twist fibres together into a continuous line. To spin means —
o: to join cloth with needle and thread
to twist fibres into thread or yarn
to pass a needle through cloth
to sweep threads into a palm
quiz.ex: spin = 纺纱；旋转。spin cotton into thread。另义：spin a story 编故事；head spins 头晕。

quiz.q: A cloak is the loose outer garment of another age, fastened at the neck and moving with the weather. A cloak is —
o: a disc that fastens a shirt
a metal fastener joining two edges

title: The Wardrobe Audit
text:
Every spring, Nell's grandmother takes everything out of the {{wardrobe}} — the tall cupboard where clothes hang — empties the {{laundry}} basket — the clothes waiting to be washed, and, secondly, the shop that washes them — and lays the family's entire textile life on the bed for judgement.

The audit is conducted alphabetically, more or less.

The head department: a {{hat}} is the general word for head-covering; a {{cap}} is the close-fitting one with a brim at the front or none at all; and the {{brim}} — the projecting edge round a hat's base that keeps the sun honest — is, her grandmother insists, the difference between a hat that shades you and a hat that merely sits on you. A {{scarf}} goes round the neck, for warmth or vanity. A {{handkerchief}} is the square of cloth for the nose, now largely ceremonial.

The hands department: a {{glove}} covers a hand with separate fingers; mittens keep the fingers together, warmer and less useful. A {{purse}} — in the British sense — is the small bag for money, a word that also means the money available for something: a prize purse, a shallow purse. A {{wallet}} is the flat folding case for banknotes and cards, traditionally carried in pockets rather than opinions.

The feet department: a {{sock}} is the short knitted covering for foot and ankle; a {{stocking}} is its long relation, reaching up the leg; a {{slipper}} is the soft indoor shoe; a {{boot}} is the strong shoe covering the ankle or more — and, in England, also the car's luggage space, for reasons nobody has satisfactorily explained.

The fastening department: a {{lace}} is the delicate open fabric made by looping thread — and, in another life, the cord that tightens a shoe. A {{belt}} is the strap that goes round the waist and holds things up or in. A {{chain}} is the series of linked metal rings — worn at the neck, or guarding a gate, or holding a bath plug. A {{bracelet}} goes round the wrist; a {{necklace}} goes round the neck, and is where the {{chain}} and the {{bracelet}}'s cousin, the {{bead}} — the small pierced ball of glass or stone, threaded on string — meet in the middle.

The upper-body department: the {{collar}} is the part of a garment at the neck; the {{sleeve}} is the part that covers the arm. A {{ribbon}} is the narrow decorative band — tied in hair, round a gift, on a prize. A {{stripe}} is a long band of colour on a fabric, and a garment can be striped, which is different from being ribboned, which is not a word.

And the verb for the end of the day: to {{wrap}} — to wind cloth round a thing or a person — as in shawls, parcels and cold children.

"Now," said the grandmother, surveying the bed, "the verdicts." Two hats: keep, keep. One glove, alone: the mystery of every spring. The purse and the wallet: emptied, shaken, and found to contain a bus ticket from 2019. The stockings: kept for the winter theatre of imagination. The beads: restrung, because a {{bracelet}} with a broken string is just a handful of history.

"And this?" said Nell, holding up a long length of linked silver.

"That," said her grandmother, "is a {{necklace}} that your great-grandmother wore to every wedding she attended between 1946 and 1988, and it has outlasted nine of the marriages. The {{chain}} is the strongest part of any wardrobe, in every sense. Wrap it carefully."
tr:
每年春天，内尔的祖母都会把衣柜（wardrobe）——挂衣服的高柜——里的一切都拿出来，倒空洗衣篮（laundry）——等待清洗的衣物，其次也指洗衣服的店——把全家全部的纺织生活摊在床上接受审判。

清点大致按字母顺序进行。

头部部门：帽子（hat）是头部覆盖物的总称；便帽（cap）是贴合头部、前面有檐或压根无檐的那种；而帽檐（brim）——帽子底圈外伸、让阳光变得老实的边缘——她祖母坚持认为，是一顶替你遮阳的帽子和一顶只是坐在你头上的帽子的全部区别。围巾（scarf）绕在颈间，为了保暖或为了体面。手帕（handkerchief）是擦鼻子的方巾，如今多半是仪式性的。

手部部门：手套（glove）分开包住每根手指地包住一只手；连指手套让手指们挤在一起，更暖，更没用。女用小包（purse）——英式意义上——是装钱的小包，这个词也指某事可用的钱：奖金池，瘪钱包。钱包（wallet）是装纸币和卡片的扁平折盒，传统上装在口袋而不是意见里。

脚部部门：短袜（sock）是包住脚和脚踝的针织短套；长袜（stocking）是它的长亲戚，一路到腿上；拖鞋（slipper）是室内的软鞋；靴子（boot）是包住脚踝以上的结实的鞋——在英国，也是汽车后备箱，原因没人能令人满意地解释过。

扣系部门：花边（lace）是用线圈绕出的精细镂空织物——另一辈子里，它是收紧鞋子的鞋带。腰带（belt）是绕在腰间、把东西撑住或收住的带子。链条（chain）是一串相扣的金属环——戴在颈间，或看住一扇门，或拴着浴缸的塞子。手镯（bracelet）绕手腕；项链（necklace）绕颈间，正是在这里，链子和小珠（bead）——穿了孔、用线串起的玻璃或石头小球——在中间相遇。

上身部门：衣领（collar）是衣服在颈部的部分；袖子（sleeve）是包住手臂的部分。缎带（ribbon）是窄窄的装饰带——系在头发上、礼盒上、奖品上。条纹（stripe）是织物上长长的色带，一件衣服可以是 striped（有条纹的），这与 ribboned 不同，后者不是一个词。

还有一天结束时用的动词：包裹（wrap）——把布绕在一个东西或一个人身上——如披肩、包裹和寒冷中的孩子。

“现在，”祖母审视着床说，“宣判。”两顶帽子：留，留。一只落单的手套：每年春天的悬案。小包和钱包：倒空、抖过，发现装着一张2019年的公交票。长袜：留给冬天的想象剧场。珠子：重新串过，因为一根断线的手镯只是一小把历史。

“这个呢？”内尔举起一长串相连的银链。

“那，”她祖母说，“是一条项链（necklace），你曾祖母从1946到1988年戴去参加每一场婚礼，它比其中九段婚姻都活得久。链条（chain）是任何衣柜里最结实的部分，在一切意义上。小心包好。”

o: the basket of clothes waiting to be washed
the projecting edge of a hat

a small bag for money; also available funds
the strap that goes round the waist

quiz.q: A sock is the short knitted covering for foot and ankle; a stocking is its long relation. A stocking is —
o: a close-fitting covering for the foot and leg
a shoe covering the ankle or more
a small pierced ball of glass
quiz.ex: stocking = 长袜。对比 sock（短袜）。另义：stockings 圣诞袜。

quiz.q: A lace is the delicate open fabric made by looping thread; in another life, the cord that tightens a shoe. Lace is —

a long band of colour on fabric

quiz.ex: lace = 花边、蕾丝；鞋带。a lace collar 蕾丝领。动词：lace one's shoes 系鞋带。

a band worn round the wrist
quiz.ex: bracelet = 手镯、手链。对比 necklace（项链）、anklet（脚链）。

quiz.q: A bracelet with a broken string is just a handful of history — of beads, threaded on string. A bead is —
o: the part of a garment at the neck
a small pierced ball threaded on a string
the square of cloth for the nose
quiz.ex: bead = 珠子。beads of sweat 汗珠。sweat beading on the forehead（动词）冒汗珠。

quiz.q: The verb for the end of the day: to wrap — as in shawls, parcels and cold children. To wrap means —
o: to keep the fingers together, warmer
to go round the neck for vanity
quiz.ex: wrap = 包、裹。wrap up warm 穿暖和。名词：a wrap 披肩。wrapped up in 全神贯注于。

title: The Winter Masquerade
text:
The museum's winter {{masquerade}} — the dance where everyone arrives masked, and identity becomes the evening's only mystery — required a month of preparation, and the preparations required a vocabulary.

The costume committee met on Tuesdays. "We will {{adorn}} the hall," announced Mrs Castellan, the tailor's wife — to adorn being to decorate, to add beauty to something already standing. "Ornaments first." An {{ornament}} is a decoration — a thing added not for use but for delight: baubles, figures, carved leaves. "Then we {{embellish}} the doorways" — to embellish is to decorate by adding detail, the way a sentence gains an adverb — "and the banners we will {{embroider}}: sew the museum's initials in gold thread directly onto the cloth." To embroider is to stitch a design into fabric — and, warns Mrs Castellan, also to exaggerate a story, which the committee will please not do when reporting its budget.

The masks themselves arrived from a costumier in the capital: painted leather, ribbon ties, one {{veil}} — the sheer cloth that covers the face, worn for modesty, mourning or mystery — and enough feathers to anger two continents.

The dressing rooms on the night were a laboratory. In the first, the {{hairdressing}} station — hairdressing being the art and trade of cutting and arranging hair — turned nine ordinary heads into architecture. In the second, the make-up table: {{cosmetics}} — the collective noun for the substances used to change or improve the face — and {{makeup}} — the general word for the same activity's products — lined the mirror like ammunition. The old director's wife explained the chemistry of {{pigment}} — the coloured substance itself, the powder that gives every paint and cosmetic its colour — and held up two boxes of {{dye}} — the substance used to change the colour of hair or cloth, as a verb, to dye is to apply it. "Cosmetics persuade," she said. "Dye commits."

In the third dressing room sat the museum's greatest treasure, brought up for one night only: the {{jewellery}} — the collective noun for decorative objects worn on the body — from the founder's collection. A {{jewel}} is a single such object; a {{gem}} is the precious or semi-precious stone — cut and polished — that often sits at its heart. There was a {{jade}} pendant, the green stone carved into a leaf, older than the museum and calmer than its curators.

"Is all this not rather {{extravagant}}?" asked the youngest committee member — extravagant meaning wildly excessive, spending beyond reason — "for one evening?"

"It is {{luxury}}," said the director's wife, attaching the jade with great care. "Luxury is the name for expensive comfort and beautiful unnecessary things — and one evening of them, once a year, is what makes the other three hundred and sixty-four bearable. Besides, the founders wore these. Tonight we are their {{icon}}s — not the modern kind, the small picture of a person — no, tonight we wear them like {{idol}}s: the figures people gather round and admire. For one night, the whole town is looking at us." She paused. "Which is also why," she said, "the mask."
tr:
博物馆的冬日化装舞会（masquerade）——人人戴面具到场、身份成为整晚唯一谜团的舞会——需要一个月的准备，而准备需要一套词汇。

服装委员会每逢周二开会。“我们要装饰（adorn）整个会堂，”裁缝的妻子卡斯特兰太太宣布——adorn 就是装饰，给已经立着的东西添美。“先摆饰物。”饰物（ornament）就是装饰品——不为使用、只为愉悦而添加的东西：小挂件、摆件、雕花叶片。“然后我们美化（embellish）各个门口”——embellish 是通过添加细节来修饰，就像句子加上一个副词——“横幅我们要刺绣（embroider）：用金线把博物馆的首字母直接绣在布上。”embroider 是把图案缝进织物——同时，卡斯特兰太太警告，它也指给故事添油加醋，委员会汇报预算时请不要这么做。

面具本身来自首都的一家戏服商：上了漆的皮革、缎带系绳、一整块面纱（veil）——遮住脸的轻薄织物，为了矜持、哀悼或神秘而戴——以及足以激怒两个大陆的羽毛。

当晚的化妆间像实验室。第一间是美发（hairdressing）工位——hairdressing 是修剪和造型头发的手艺与行业——把九颗平常的脑袋变成了建筑。第二间是化妆台：化妆品（cosmetics）——用于改变或美化面部的物质的总称——和 makeup（化妆用品）——同一行当产品的一般说法——像弹药一样排在镜子前。老馆长的夫人讲解颜料（pigment）的化学——颜料就是有颜色的物质本身，是赋予一切油漆和化妆品颜色的粉末——并举起两盒染剂（dye）——用来改变头发或布料颜色的物质，作动词，dye 就是使用它。“化妆品是劝说，”她说，“染剂是承诺。”

第三间化妆间坐着博物馆最大的宝藏，只为一晚取出：创始人的藏品——首饰（jewellery）——戴在身上的装饰品物的总称。一件首饰（jewel）是其中单独一件；宝石（gem）是常居其中心的、切割抛光过的珍贵或半贵重石头。有一枚玉（jade）坠，绿色的石头雕成一片叶子，比博物馆古老，比馆长们镇定。

“这一切是不是太奢侈（extravagant）了？”最年轻的委员问——extravagant 意为过分铺张、超出理智地花钱——“就为一晚上？”

“这是奢华（luxury），”馆长夫人一边极其小心地别上玉坠一边说。“luxury 是昂贵的舒适和美丽的不必要之物的名字——一年一晚的它们，正是让另外三百六十四天可以忍受的原因。再说，创始人们戴过这些。今晚我们是他们的圣像（icon）——不是现代那种、人物的小图像——不，今晚我们像偶像（idol）一样戴着它们：被人们围观和仰慕的形象。就一晚，全镇的人都在看我们。”她顿了顿。“这也正是，”她说，“面具的作用所在。”

quiz.q: The masquerade — the dance where everyone arrives masked, and identity becomes the evening's only mystery. A masquerade is —
o: the sheer cloth covering the face
a precious stone at a jewel's heart
quiz.ex: masquerade = 化装舞会；伪装。作动词：masquerade as 假扮成。词源意大利语 maschera（面具）。

quiz.q: To adorn — to decorate, to add beauty to something already standing. To adorn means —
o: to sew initials in gold thread
to decorate something with attractive things
to change the colour of cloth
quiz.ex: adorn = 装饰、佩戴。adorn oneself with jewels 佩戴珠宝。近义 decorate、ornament。

quiz.q: To embroider is to stitch a design into fabric — and also to exaggerate a story. To embroider means —
o: to add carved leaves to a hall
to sew a pattern onto cloth; also to embellish a tale
to cover the face with sheer cloth
to line cosmetics at a mirror
quiz.ex: embroider = 刺绣；添油加醋。embroidered tablecloth 绣花桌布。名词 embroidery 刺绣。

quiz.q: The pigment — the coloured substance itself, the powder that gives every paint and cosmetic its colour. A pigment is —
o: a small picture of a person
the substance that gives colour to things
a decorative object worn on the body
quiz.ex: pigment = 颜料、色素。skin pigment 皮肤色素。对比 dye（染料，改变原有色）。

quiz.q: Cosmetics persuade; dye commits — the substance used to change the colour of hair or cloth. A dye is —
o: a substance that changes the colour of things
quiz.ex: dye = 染料；染（发/布）。dye one's hair 染发。注意拼写区分 die（死亡）。

quiz.q: Jewellery — the collective noun for decorative objects worn on the body. Jewellery is —
quiz.ex: jewellery = 珠宝、首饰（总称，不可数）。a piece of jewellery 一件首饰。美式拼写 jewelry。

quiz.q: A jewel is a single such object; a gem is the precious stone at its heart. A gem is —
o: a cut and polished precious stone
the green stone carved into a leaf
the art of the dressing room
quiz.ex: gem = 宝石。引申义：a gem of an idea 绝妙的想法。对比 jewel（一件首饰/宝石）。

quiz.q: Luxury is the name for expensive comfort and beautiful unnecessary things. Luxury means —
o: a small picture of a saint
great comfort that is expensive and unnecessary
the powder that gives cosmetics colour
quiz.ex: luxury = 奢华、奢侈品。luxury goods 奢侈品。形容词 luxurious。对比 extravagance（铺张浪费）。

title: The Charity Fashion Show
text:
The sixth form organised a charity {{fashion}} show — fashion being the prevailing style of clothing, the art of what is worn now — and, because the school hall was the only venue, everything about it had to be learned quickly, including the words.

Miss Duarte, who taught textiles and ran the event like a general, opened the first rehearsal with a lecture. "A {{style}}," she said, "is a distinctive manner of doing anything — of dressing, writing, playing. {{Fashion}} is the style that currently {{prevail}}s — that wins, that holds the field — in clothing. A {{trend}} is the direction the style is moving in: this year, wide trousers, next year, who knows. A {{tendency}} is the gentler word — a general drift, an inclination to move one way, in hemlines or in history. A {{vogue}} is a fashion's period of power: the vogue for minimalism, the vogue for logos. {{Popularity}} is the state of being liked by many people, and it is the currency all the others are chasing."

"And a {{current}}?" someone asked, reading the glossary.

"Ah — the trick word. A current, noun, is a flow of water, air or electricity; a current, adjective, means happening now — the current trend, the current champion. Fashion is where the two meanings meet: it is the current that carries everyone, and it is current by definition."

The models were volunteers: tall, short, nervous, seventeen. A {{model}}, Miss Duarte explained, is a person employed to wear clothes so that people will want them — and also, in another room of the dictionary, a small copy of something built, or a person worthy of imitation. "All three meanings," she said, "walk the same runway."

The evening itself {{fascinate}}d the whole hall — to fascinate being to hold attention completely, to make looking away feel like a loss. It began with the vintage section: the garments of 1970, worn by the oldest teachers, who walked with a {{grace}} — effortless elegance of movement — that none of the seventeen-year-olds could imitate. {{Elegance}}, Miss Duarte said, is refined beauty of style — restraint made visible; {{exquisite}} is the adjective for work of extreme delicacy and beauty — an exquisite hem, an exquisite sentence; {{decent}} is the modest, respectable word — a decent coat, decent behaviour — and should never be underrated, being the standard most of the world manages.

Then the beauty thesaurus, which Miss Duarte taught as a scale rather than a ranking. A {{pretty}} face is pleasing in a delicate way; a {{beautiful}} one is the strong, complete word, the one that stops conversation; a {{charming}} person delights by manner — the charm is in the behaviour; a {{handsome}} one — usually a man, but not always, and never a vase — is striking in a strong, well-formed way. And an {{ugly}} thing, she insisted, is not the opposite of beauty but its failed attempt: ugliness is what interests the eye when beauty has stopped trying. "The thesaurus is not a competition," she said. "It is a set of instruments."

The last section was the students' own designs, and it studied the body. A {{figure}} — noun — is the shape of a human body, and also a number, and also a person of note: three meanings, one silhouette. A {{slender}} figure is gracefully thin; a {{slight}} person is small and delicate; and the difference between the two words, said Miss Duarte, is that slender is what you say with approval and slight is what you say with concern.

At the end, the audience voted with its applause, and the winner was the youngest model, whose entire {{appearance}} — the word for the way a person looks to others — consisted of her grandmother's wedding dress, cut to the knee, worn with boots, and a {{slight}} smile that suggested she knew exactly what she was doing. "That," said Miss Duarte, wiping one eye, "is how fashions actually begin. Not with a decree. With a girl, and her grandmother's dress, and a very good night."
tr:
六年级组织了一场慈善时装（fashion）秀——fashion 是当下盛行的着装风格，是“现在穿什么”的艺术——而且由于学校礼堂是唯一场地，一切都要现学，包括词汇。

教纺织课、像将军一样指挥全场的杜阿尔特小姐，在第一次排练时开了堂课。“一种风格（style），”她说，“是做任何事的独特方式——穿衣、写作、演奏。时尚（fashion）是当前盛行、占了上风（prevail）的那种风格。趋势（trend）是风格移动的方向：今年宽裤腿，明年谁知道。倾向（tendency）是更温和的词——一种大致的流向、朝某个方向移动的意向，裙摆也罢，历史也罢。盛行（vogue）是一种时尚掌权的时期：极简主义的盛行，标志图案的盛行。流行度（popularity）是被许多人喜欢的状态，而它是其他一切词都在追逐的货币。”

“那 current 呢？”有人读着词汇表问。

“啊——最刁的词。current 作名词，是水、空气或电的流；作形容词，指正在发生的——当前的趋势、现任冠军。时尚正是两个含义相遇的地方：它是裹挟所有人的电流（current），又按定义就是当下的（current）。”

模特们都是志愿者：高的、矮的、紧张的、十七岁的。杜阿尔特小姐解释说，模特（model）是受雇穿衣服、好让人们想要那些衣服的人——在词典的另一个房间里，也指某物的缩小仿制品，或值得效仿的人。“三种含义，”她说，“走的是同一条 T 台。”

晚会本身让全场着迷（fascinate）——fascinate 是完全抓住注意力，让人觉得移开视线是一种损失。开场是复古环节：1970年的衣服，由最年长的老师们穿着，他们走出一种优雅（grace）——举止间毫不费力的美感——那是所有十七岁孩子都学不来的。高雅（elegance），杜阿尔特小姐说，是风格上精致的美——看得见的克制；精美（exquisite）是形容极度细腻美丽之作的形容词——一条精美的裙边，一个精美的句子；体面（decent）是那个谦逊而值得尊敬的词——一件像样的外套，得体的举止——永远不该被低估，因为它是世界上大多数人达到的标准。

然后是美丽同义词课，杜阿尔特小姐把它当作音阶而非排名来教。一张标致（pretty）的脸是以细腻方式讨人喜欢；一张美丽（beautiful）的脸是有力的、完整的词，是让谈话停下的那个；一个迷人（charming）的人以风度取悦人——魅力在举止里；一个英俊（handsome）的人——通常是男人，但并不总是，且永远不会是花瓶——是以有力、端正的方式令人瞩目。至于丑（ugly）的东西，她坚持认为，不是美的反面，而是美的失败尝试：当美不再努力时，丑才是让眼睛感兴趣的东西。“同义词词典不是竞赛，”她说，“是一套乐器。”

最后一个环节是学生们自己的设计，研究的是身体。身材（figure）——名词——是人体的形状，也是数字，也是名人：三个含义，一个剪影。一个苗条（slender）的身材是优雅的瘦；一个瘦小（slight）的人是小而娇弱；这两个词的区别，杜阿尔特小姐说，在于 slender 是带着赞许说的，slight 是带着关切说的。

结束时，观众用掌声投票，获胜的是最年轻的模特，她的整个外表（appearance）——一个人在他人眼中的样子的那个词——由祖母的婚纱构成，剪到膝盖，配靴子穿，还有一个瘦瘦的（slight）微笑，暗示她完全清楚自己在干什么。“时尚就是这样开始的，”杜阿尔特小姐擦着一只眼睛说，“不是靠一道命令。靠一个女孩，她祖母的裙子，和一个非常好的夜晚。”

quiz.q: Fashion is the style that currently prevails — that wins, that holds the field — in clothing. Fashion is —
o: the state of being liked by many
a distinctive manner of doing anything
the direction a style is moving in
the prevailing style of dress or behaviour
quiz.ex: fashion = 时尚；方式。in fashion 流行；out of fashion 过时。对比 style（个人风格）、vogue（一时盛行）。

quiz.q: A trend is the direction the style is moving in: this year, wide trousers. A trend is —
o: a flow of water or electricity
a small copy of something built
quiz.ex: trend = 趋势。market trends 市场趋势。动词 trend：#topic 在热搜。对比 tendency（较温和的倾向）。

quiz.q: A vogue is a fashion's period of power: the vogue for minimalism. A vogue is —
o: a period of popular fashion for something
a number, a shape, a person of note
quiz.ex: vogue = 时兴、流行。in vogue 正时兴。Vogue 杂志即取此义。对比 fashion（行业整体）。

quiz.q: Fashion is the style that currently prevails — that wins, that holds the field. To prevail means —
o: to cut a wedding dress at the knee
quiz.ex: prevail = 盛行；获胜。Truth will prevail 真理必胜。prevail on sb to do 说服。

quiz.q: To fascinate is to hold attention completely, to make looking away feel like a loss. To fascinate means —
o: to organise a charity show like a general
to attract and hold intense interest
quiz.ex: fascinate = 使着迷。be fascinated by 对……着迷。形容词 fascinating 迷人的。

quiz.q: Elegance is refined beauty of style — restraint made visible. Elegance is —
quiz.ex: elegance = 高雅、典雅。形容词 elegant。对比 grace（举止的优雅）、exquisiteness（工艺的精美）。

quiz.q: Exquisite is the adjective for work of extreme delicacy and beauty — an exquisite hem. Exquisite means —
o: pleasing in a delicate way only
quiz.ex: exquisite = 精美的、精致的。exquisite craftsmanship 精湛工艺。近义 delicate、refined。

quiz.q: Slender is what you say with approval; slight is what you say with concern. Slender means —
o: striking in a strong well-formed way
quiz.ex: slender = 苗条的、纤细的（褒义）。a slender figure。另义：slender resources 微薄的资源。对比 slight（瘦小/轻微）。

title: Grandmother's Coat
text:
The coat arrived in my life the way most inheritances do: in a box, slightly too late, with a note pinned to it in handwriting that had begun to wander. "For the winter, when it comes. It is older than you and in better condition. — G."

It was a heavy {{wool}} coat — wool being the soft hair of the sheep, spun and woven into the warmest of the natural {{textile}}s, a textile being any woven fabric — the colour of a wet Highland morning, which is to say a deep {{grey}}: grey being the colour between black and white, the colour of rain, slate and grandmothers.

{{Colour}} itself, as Grandmother had taught me years before, is the general word for the quality that makes things red, blue or green — the property light plays on a surface. Her coat had once, by family report, been a proud {{purple}} — the royal colour, once more expensive than gold — and time had argued it down to grey. Things {{fade}}, she used to say — to fade being to lose colour and brightness slowly, the way afternoons do — and fading, in her view, was not decay but negotiation.

There were histories on it. A {{stain}} — a mark left where liquid has dried — on the right cuff, from a wedding in 1974: red wine, her sister, an apology never accepted. A smaller {{blot}} — a spot or smear of ink or liquid — inside the pocket, from a fountain pen that had bled to death in 1989. On the left elbow, a {{patch}} — a piece of cloth sewn over a hole to repair it — in a slightly different grey, sewn by her own hand sometime before I was born, and imperfect, and therefore the most beautiful part of the coat.

The lining was {{velvet}} — the soft thick fabric with a dense pile, the fabric of theatre curtains and crowns — worn to shine at the shoulders, and the buttons were horn, brown as strong tea. {{Brown}} being the colour of earth, wood and coffee; {{white}} the colour of snow, paper and beginnings; {{yellow}} the colour of the sun, butter and caution; {{pink}} the colour between red and white, the colour of dawn and of certain 1950s bathrooms; {{tan}} the pale brown of skin after a summer of sun — a coat, in short, carrying the whole elementary box of colours somewhere in its history.

I took it to Mr Castellan, the tailor, for cleaning and repair, and he examined it the way a doctor examines a patient of great age: with respect, and no promises.

"{{Shabby}}," he said, using the honest word for worn and threadbare — shabby being what things become when they have been loved continuously and without insurance. "But the bones are good. The {{wool}} is sound. I will clean the {{stain}} — the {{blot}}, never; that is writing, not damage. The {{patch}} stays, obviously; removing a repair is a second injury. And the pocket..." He held up a frayed edge, from which hung, miraculously, a {{string}} — a thin cord, the general word for any length of twisted fibre — that had once secured an inner purse long gone. "I will re-hem this, and the coat will be yours."

"Is it worth it?" I asked. "The repair, I mean. It is only a {{rag}} — " a rag being a scrap of old cloth, the end of the wardrobe's road — "to anyone else."

Mr Castellan looked at me the way he looks at customers who ask the price of a good button. "It is {{tight}} at the shoulders," he said — tight meaning fitting too closely — "so I will let the seams out, and it will not be. It is not {{perfect}} — perfect being without flaw, the condition nothing reaches, coats included — but it is warm, and it is a life, and it is yours to continue. Clothes are not rags until the last person who remembers them is gone. You are the last one. Wear it."

I wear it. It has faded one shade further, and the velvet shines a little more at the cuffs, and last winter a new stain arrived — coffee, mine, a Tuesday — which is, as far as I can tell, exactly how the coat prefers to grow: not by being kept, but by being used, one mark at a time.
tr:
这件大衣进入我生活的方式，和大多数遗产一样：装在盒子里，来得稍晚，别着一张字迹开始游走的字条。“留给冬天，等它来。它比你老，状况比你好。——祖母。”

这是一件厚重的羊毛（wool）大衣——wool 是羊的软毛，纺成纱、织成最暖的天然纺织品（textile），textile 指任何织造的织物——颜色是潮湿高地清晨的颜色，也就是一种深灰（grey）：grey 是黑与白之间的颜色，是雨、石板和祖母们的颜色。

颜色（colour）本身，正如祖母多年前教我的，是让东西呈现红、蓝、绿的那个性质的总称——光在表面上玩耍的属性。据家人说，这件大衣曾经是一种骄傲的紫色（purple）——王室的颜色，一度比黄金还贵——而时间把它争执成了灰色。东西会褪色（fade），她常说——fade 就是缓慢地失去颜色和光泽，像午后那样——在她看来，褪色不是衰败，而是谈判。

它身上有几段历史。右袖口有一块污渍（stain）——液体干掉后留下的痕迹——来自1974年的一场婚礼：红酒，她妹妹，一句从未被接受的道歉。口袋里有一个更小的墨点（blot）——墨水或液体的斑点——来自一支1989年寿终正寝的钢笔。左肘上有一块补丁（patch）——缝在破洞上修补的布片——灰色稍有不同，是她在某个我出生之前的时辰亲手缝的，不完美，因此是整件大衣最美的部分。

衬里是天鹅绒（velvet）——有厚密绒毛的柔软厚织物，剧院幕布和王冠的织物——肩部磨出了光泽，纽扣是牛角的，浓茶般的棕。棕色（brown）是泥土、木头和咖啡的颜色；白色（white）是雪、纸和开端的颜色；黄色（yellow）是太阳、黄油和警告的颜色；粉色（pink）是红与白之间的颜色，黎明的颜色，也是某些五十年代浴室的颜色；棕褐（tan）是皮肤晒了一个夏天之后的浅棕——总之，是一件大衣，在它的历史里某处携带着整盒基础色。

我把它拿给裁缝卡斯特兰先生清洗修补，他检查它的样子像医生检查一位高龄病人：带着敬意，不作承诺。

“破旧（shabby）了，”他用了那个诚实的词，形容磨损起毛——shabby 就是东西被持续而无保险地爱着之后变成的样子。“但骨架还好。羊毛（wool）结实。污渍（stain）我洗得掉——墨点（blot），永远不洗；那是文字，不是损伤。补丁（patch）当然留下；拆掉一次修补是第二次伤害。还有这个口袋……”他举起一个磨破的边，上面奇迹般挂着一根细绳（string）——细绳，任何一段捻过的纤维的通称——曾经系着一个早已不在的内袋。“我把边重新缝好，这件大衣就是你的了。”

“值得吗？”我问。“我是说，这修补。对别人来说它只是一块破布（rag）——”rag 是旧布碎片，衣柜之路的终点——“对任何人都是。”

卡斯特兰先生看我的眼神，像看一个问一枚好纽扣多少钱的顾客。“肩部太紧（tight），”他说——tight 是过于贴身——“我把缝放出去，就不紧了。它不完美（perfect）——perfect 是毫无瑕疵，任何东西都达不到的状态，包括大衣——但它暖，它是一段人生，而且轮到你把它继续下去了。衣服在最后一个记得它的人离开之前，都不算破布。你就是最后一个。穿上它。”

我穿着它。它又褪了一个色号，天鹅绒在袖口又亮了一点，去年冬天添了一块新污渍——咖啡，我的，一个周二——而据我所知，这正是这件大衣最喜欢的成长方式：不是被供着，而是被用着，一次一个印记。

quiz.q: Wool — the soft hair of the sheep, spun and woven into the warmest of the natural textiles. Wool is —
o: a piece of cloth sewn over a hole
the soft hair of sheep used for cloth
quiz.ex: wool = 羊毛、毛线、毛织物。pure wool 纯羊毛。pull the wool over sb's eyes 蒙蔽某人。

quiz.q: A textile being any woven fabric — the wool coat is the warmest of the natural textiles. A textile is —
o: the soft hair of a sheep
the colour between black and white
quiz.ex: textile = 纺织品。the textile industry 纺织业。词根 text（编织），同 text 课文。

quiz.q: Things fade — to lose colour and brightness slowly, the way afternoons do. To fade means —
o: to sew cloth over a hole
to leave a mark where liquid dried
to fit too closely at the shoulders
quiz.ex: fade = 褪色；逐渐消失。fade away 慢慢消失。fade-in 淡入（影视）。

quiz.q: A stain on the right cuff, from a wedding in 1974: red wine. A stain is —
o: a small spot of ink inside a pocket
a mark left where liquid has dried
a patch sewn over an elbow
quiz.ex: stain = 污渍；染色。coffee stain 咖啡渍。动词：stain the wood 给木头上色。对比 blot（墨渍小点）。

quiz.q: A smaller blot inside the pocket, from a fountain pen that had bled to death. A blot is —
o: a mark from dried red wine
a spot or smear of ink or liquid
a piece of cloth over a hole
the pale brown of summered skin
quiz.ex: blot = 墨渍、污点。blotting paper 吸墨纸。a blot on one's reputation 名誉污点。

quiz.q: On the left elbow, a patch in a slightly different grey, sewn by her own hand. A patch is —
o: the fabric of crowns and curtains
a thin cord securing a purse
a piece of cloth sewn over a hole
a scrap at the wardrobe's road-end
quiz.ex: patch = 补丁；小块土地。a vegetable patch 菜地。patchy 时好时坏的。

quiz.q: The lining was velvet — the soft thick fabric with a dense pile, of theatre curtains and crowns. Velvet is —
o: the property light plays on surfaces
soft thick fabric with a dense pile
quiz.ex: velvet = 天鹅绒。an iron fist in a velvet glove 外柔内刚。注意与 velvety（天鹅绒般柔软的）。

quiz.q: Shabby — the honest word for worn and threadbare, what things become when loved continuously without insurance. Shabby means —
o: fitting too closely at the seams
worn out and faded from long use
quiz.ex: shabby = 破旧的、褴褛的。a shabby room 破旧的房间；shabby behaviour 卑劣的行为。

title: The Wedding Banquet
text:
My cousin Adaeze was married in June, and the whole family was introduced, in one long evening, to the complete vocabulary of eating out, whether we wanted it or not.

The {{banquet}} — the grand ceremonial meal for many guests — began at seven, in a hall that could also, on other evenings, be a {{buffet}} (a meal where guests serve themselves from a long table) or a {{conference}}, depending on the arrangement of chairs. The invitations had promised "{{refreshment}}s at seven" — refreshments being the light food and drink offered at events, the polite under-promise — and by half past seven the {{hunger}} of two hundred guests, hunger being the body's demand for food, had turned the polite under-promise into a stampede of good manners.

The {{menu}} — the printed list of what a kitchen can make — had three columns, because the {{cuisine}} — the style of cooking, the tradition a kitchen belongs to — was triple: her family's, his family's, and the hotel's idea of both. The {{chef}} — the trained head cook, the general of the kitchen — had negotiated for months. The {{order}} — our choices, made to the waiters — took forty minutes, because to order is both to command a meal and to arrange a system, and my uncles were treating it as the second thing.

First came the {{appetiser}} — the small dish that opens the appetite, waking it rather than feeding it — then the long middle of the meal, then the {{supper}} dishes, supper being the evening meal, the word that country people use for what town people call dinner. Between them wandered the {{snack}} trolley — snacks being small quick eats between real meals — which the children raided with an honesty the adults envied and imitated.

My father, at the {{bar}} — the counter where drinks are served — conducted a seminar on the drinks table. "{{Juice}} for the children — the liquid of fruit. {{Soda}} for the teenagers — sweet fizzy water with a chemistry set inside. {{Coffee}} for the tired — the bean that argues with sleep and wins." He himself drank no {{alcohol}} — the general word for drinks that make you drunk — no {{liquor}} — the strong distilled sort — neither {{whisky}} — the barley one — nor {{brandy}} — the grape one — and he watched his brother-in-law progress from {{sober}} — uninfluenced, clear-headed — to {{drunk}} — past the point where the dance floor becomes a good idea — with the calm of a man watching weather.

Outside, the smokers had gathered, and the air by the fire door was grey with {{tobacco}} — the leaf that is dried, rolled and burnt for its smoke — one {{cigarette}} after another, each a small cylinder of the same leaf wrapped in paper. "Their {{appetite}} is different from ours," said my father, unkindly, and went back inside.

At midnight, the couple left, and the eating entered its final form: the {{takeaway}} — the food packed to be carried home — because a banquet properly ended is one that continues tomorrow, in other people's kitchens. The hotel had, after all, been hired to {{cater}} — to provide food and service for an event — and its final {{provision}} — its supply, what it provides — was two hundred boxes of rice and dignity.

"The {{food}} was excellent," everyone agreed on the way out, food being the general word for what keeps us alive, and what, on a night like this, briefly makes us glad to be.

"{{Delicious}}," said my grandmother — delicious meaning a pleasure to eat — and then, being grandmother, "{{Tasty}}" — full of taste — and then, being grandmother twice, "{{Yummy}}," which is what the grandchildren say, and what she had been waiting all evening to be allowed to say.
tr:
我的表姐阿达埃泽六月结婚，一整个漫长的晚上，全家人被领着学完了外出就餐的全部词汇，不管想不想学。

宴会（banquet）——为众多宾客举行的盛大仪式性正餐——七点开始，地点是一个在其他晚上还可以变成自助餐（buffet，宾客从长桌自取食物的用餐方式）或会议厅（conference，会议）的大厅，取决于椅子怎么摆。请柬上写“七点供应茶点（refreshment）”——refreshment 是活动中提供的简单饮食，一种礼貌的低承诺——到七点半，两百位宾客的饥饿（hunger）——身体对食物的索求——已经把这个礼貌的低承诺变成了一场礼数周到的踩踏。

菜单（menu）——厨房能做什么的印刷清单——有三栏，因为菜系（cuisine）——烹饪风格、厨房所属的传统——是三重的：她家的、他家的、以及酒店对两家的想象。主厨（chef）——受过训练的厨房主管、厨房的将军——为此谈判了好几个月。点单（order）——我们向服务员报出的选择——花了四十分钟，因为 order 既是点菜也是整理秩序，而我的叔叔们把它当成了后者。

先上来的是开胃菜（appetiser）——打开食欲的小碟，是唤醒食欲而非喂饱它——然后是漫长的正餐中段，然后是晚饭（supper）的菜，supper 是晚间那顿饭，乡下人对城里人叫 dinner 的东西的叫法。其间巡游着小食（snack）推车——snack 是两顿正餐之间的小快吃食——孩子们打劫它时的坦率，是成年人羡慕并模仿的东西。

我的父亲在吧台（bar）——供应酒水的柜台——办了一场关于饮料桌的研讨课。“孩子们喝果汁（juice）——水果的液体。青少年喝汽水（soda）——加了整套化学仪器的甜气泡水。疲劳的人喝咖啡（coffee）——跟睡眠吵架并且吵赢的那颗豆子。”他自己不喝任何酒（alcohol）——让人喝醉的饮料的总称——不喝烈酒（liquor）——蒸馏的烈性那种——既不喝威士忌（whisky）——大麦的那种——也不喝白兰地（brandy）——葡萄的那种——并且用一种看天气的平静，看着他内兄从清醒（sober）——不受影响、头脑清楚——走向喝醉（drunk）——过了舞池变成一个好主意的那条线。

外面，吸烟的人聚成一团，消防门边的空气被烟草（tobacco）——晒干、卷起、点燃取其烟的叶子——熏成灰色，一支接一支的香烟（cigarette）——用纸卷着同样叶子的小圆筒。“他们的胃口（appetite）跟我们不一样，”我父亲不厚道地说，回了屋里。

午夜，新人离席，宴席进入最终形态：外带（takeaway）——打包带走的食物——因为一场体面结束的宴会，是明天在别人家厨房继续的那一场。酒店毕竟是受雇来承办饮食（cater）——为活动提供餐饮服务——的，而它最后的供应（provision）——它提供的物资——是两百盒米饭和体面。

“食物（food）好极了，”出门时人人这样说，food 是让我们活着的东西的总称，也是在这样的夜晚，短暂地让我们庆幸活着的东西。

“美味（delicious），”我祖母说——delicious 意为吃起来是种享受——接着，因为是祖母，“好吃（tasty）”——充满滋味——再接着，因为是两倍的祖母，“yummy（真好吃）”，这是孙辈们说的话，也是她等了一整晚、终于被允许说的话。

quiz.q: The banquet — the grand ceremonial meal for many guests — began at seven. A banquet is —
o: the small dish that opens the appetite
a meal where guests serve themselves
a large formal meal for many people
light food and drink at events
quiz.ex: banquet = 宴会、盛宴。state banquet 国宴。对比 buffet（自助餐）、supper（晚饭）。

quiz.q: The cuisine — the style of cooking, the tradition a kitchen belongs to — was triple. A cuisine is —
o: a style or tradition of cooking
the general word for keeping alive
quiz.ex: cuisine = 菜系、烹饪风格。French cuisine 法餐。来自法语（厨房）。对比 chef（厨师）。

quiz.q: The appetiser — the small dish that opens the appetite, waking it rather than feeding it. An appetiser is —
o: the evening meal of country people
a small dish served before the meal
a sweet fizzy drink for teenagers
food packed to be carried home
quiz.ex: appetiser = 开胃菜。美式拼 appetizer。来自 appetite（食欲）。对比 dessert（甜点）。

quiz.q: The hotel had been hired to cater — to provide food and service for an event. To cater means —
o: to make the dance floor a good idea
to serve oneself from a long table
to print a list of possible dishes
to provide food and service for events
quiz.ex: cater = 承办酒席；满足需要。catering industry 餐饮业。cater for all tastes 迎合各种口味。

quiz.q: No liquor — the strong distilled sort; neither whisky, the barley one, nor brandy, the grape one. Liquor is —
o: the general word for all alcohol
the leaf that is dried and burnt
quiz.ex: liquor = 烈性酒。对比 alcohol（酒精饮料总称）。注意美式 liquor store 酒类商店。

quiz.q: He watched his brother-in-law progress from sober — uninfluenced, clear-headed — to drunk. Sober means —
o: past the point of good ideas
quiz.ex: sober = 清醒的；严肃的。sober up 醒酒。a sober assessment 冷静的评估。

quiz.q: The takeaway — the food packed to be carried home — continues tomorrow, in other people's kitchens. A takeaway is —
o: food prepared to be eaten elsewhere
a small quick eat between meals
the counter where drinks are served
quiz.ex: takeaway = 外卖（英式）。美式 takeout。另义（学术）：the takeaway from the talk 讲座的要点。

quiz.q: The invitations promised refreshments at seven — the light food and drink offered at events. Refreshments are —
o: light food and drink served at events
quiz.ex: refreshment = 茶点、点心。refreshment room （车站）茶点室。动词 refresh 使恢复精力。

title: The New Kitchen
text:
When Rosa's family moved into the flat, the kitchen came empty, and equipping it became, for one long Saturday, an education in objects and the names they answer to.

The big machines came first. The {{stove}} — the cooking surface with burners, where pans live over fire — stood against the east wall; beside it the {{oven}} — the enclosed heated box where bread becomes toast and dough becomes bread — hummed its first note. There was, confusingly, also a {{furnace}} in the building's basement — the great sealed chamber where the whole block is heated — which Rosa's father explained for the fifth time and she ignored for the fifth, and which is not, whatever it looks like on paper, a thing you can bake in.

Then the metal army. A {{kettle}} — the vessel with a spout and a handle, for boiling water, the most important machine in any household and the least replaceable. A {{pan}} — the shallow wide cooking vessel with a long handle, for frying. A {{pot}} — its deep round sibling, for soups and stews and things that simmer for hours and improve for it. Every {{lid}} — the cover that keeps the heat and the steam inside a pot — went missing within a month, as lids do, and the pots suffered openly.

The eating equipment was arranged by then and by shape. {{Cutlery}} — the collective noun for knives, forks and spoons, the tools of eating — went in the drawer by the door. A {{fork}} — the tool with prongs, for holding and lifting — lay beside a {{knife}} — the blade for cutting — and a {{spoon}} — the shallow bowl on a handle, for liquids and for soup and for the last of everything. Above them waited the plates and the vessels: a {{dish}} — the general word for a plate, and also for the food served on it; a {{bowl}} — the deep round vessel for soup and cereal; a {{saucer}} — the small flat plate that lives under a cup and catches what the cup betrays; a {{glass}} — the vessel you drink water and wine from, made of glass, transparent, breakable and honest; and a {{mug}} — the cup with a handle, thick-walled, for coffee, tea and honest work.

The materials lecture came at lunch. "This," said Rosa's mother, holding up a plate, "is {{porcelain}} — the hard white translucent ceramic, fired at the highest heat, the aristocrat of the shelf." She tapped a second plate. "And this is the broader family, {{ceramic}} — the general word for anything made from clay and fired in a kiln: plates, tiles, the bathroom's whole personality. Porcelain is a ceramic the way a duchess is a person: true, but leaving things out."

In the corner cupboard went the {{tin}}s — metal containers, sealed, keeping food alive without a fridge's opinion — and the {{tray}}s — the flat boards with edges, for carrying many things at once, the waiter's instrument and the invalid's comfort. "A tray," said her father, "is what a kitchen uses to be in two places at the same time."

By evening the kitchen was equipped, labelled and photographed for the insurance. Rosa boiled the kettle, made tea in a borrowed mug, and toasted bread in the new oven until the smoke alarm gave its opinion of the family's first night.

"Every kitchen," said her mother, opening windows, "learns its owners the same way the owners learn it. The {{stove}} is too hot, the {{oven}} too slow, and the {{kettle}} — the kettle is always right. Everything else is negotiable."
tr:
罗莎一家搬进公寓时，厨房是空的，而装备它成了漫长周六的一堂物件课，连同物件们各自应答的名字。

大机器先来。炉灶（stove）——带炉眼、锅坐在火上的烹饪台面——立在东墙边；旁边是烤箱（oven）——封闭的加热箱，面包在里面变吐司、面团在里面变面包——哼出了第一个音。令人困惑的是，楼里地下室还有一台锅炉（furnace）——给整栋楼供暖的巨大密封燃烧室——罗莎的爸爸第五次解释它，她第五次不睬，而它无论纸面上看起来如何，都不是一个能烤东西的玩意。

然后是金属军团。水壶（kettle）——带壶嘴和把手、用来烧水的容器，任何家庭里最重要也最不可替代的机器。平底锅（pan）——带长柄的浅而宽的炊具，用来煎。深锅（pot）——它深而圆的手足，用来煮汤、炖那些要咕嘟好几个小时并因此变好的东西。每一个锅盖（lid）——把热和蒸汽留在锅里的盖子——都在一个月内失踪，锅盖向来如此，锅们公开受苦。

吃饭的家伙按时间和形状摆放。餐具（cutlery）——刀、叉、勺的总称，吃饭的工具——进了门边的抽屉。叉子（fork）——带尖齿、用来叉起和舀取的工具——躺在刀（knife）——切东西的刀刃——和勺子（spoon）——柄上顶个浅碗，用来对付液体、汤和一切的最后一点——旁边。上面等着盘子和器皿：碟盘（dish）——盘子的通称，也指盛在其上的菜；碗（bowl）——盛汤和麦片的深圆器皿；茶托（saucer）——住在杯子下面、接住杯子背叛之物的小平盘；玻璃杯（glass）——你用来喝水和喝酒的器皿，玻璃制，透明，易碎而诚实；马克杯（mug）——带把的厚壁杯，装咖啡、茶和诚实的劳动。

材料课在午饭时开讲。“这个，”罗莎的妈妈举起一只盘子，“是瓷（porcelain）——坚硬、白色、半透明的陶瓷，以最高温烧成，架子上的贵族。”她敲敲第二只盘子。“而这个是更广的家族，陶瓷（ceramic）——黏土制成、窑里烧出来的一切的通称：盘子、瓷砖、浴室的全部性格。瓷是一种陶瓷，就像公爵夫人是一个人：没错，但漏了些东西。”

角落的柜子里放了罐头（tin）——密封的金属容器，不需要冰箱发表意见就让食物活着——和托盘（tray）——带边沿的平木板，一次端多件东西，服务员的乐器、病号的安慰。“托盘，”她爸爸说，“是厨房用来同时出现在两个地方的东西。”

到晚上，厨房装备完毕、贴好标签、拍了照给保险公司。罗莎烧上水壶，用借来的马克杯泡了茶，在新烤箱里烤面包，一直烤到烟雾报警器对这家的第一晚发表意见。

“每个厨房，”她妈妈一边开窗一边说，“认识主人的方式跟主人认识它一样。炉灶（stove）太烫，烤箱（oven）太慢，而水壶（kettle）——水壶永远是对的。其他一切都可以商量。”

quiz.q: The stove — the cooking surface with burners, where pans live over fire. A stove is —
o: an enclosed heated box for baking
a cooking appliance with burners on top
a vessel with a spout for boiling
a great sealed chamber for heating a block
quiz.ex: stove = 炉灶。a wood-burning stove 柴炉。对比 oven（烤箱）、furnace（锅炉）。

quiz.q: The oven — the enclosed heated box where bread becomes toast and dough becomes bread. An oven is —
o: the small flat plate under a cup
the shallow wide vessel for frying
an enclosed compartment for baking and roasting
quiz.ex: oven = 烤箱。a gas oven 燃气烤箱。习语：like an oven 热得像烤箱。

quiz.q: Cutlery — the collective noun for knives, forks and spoons, the tools of eating. Cutlery is —
quiz.ex: cutlery = 餐具（刀叉勺）。美式 silverware。不可数名词。来自 cut（切）。

quiz.q: Porcelain — the hard white translucent ceramic, fired at the highest heat, the aristocrat of the shelf. Porcelain is —
o: a deep round vessel for soup
quiz.ex: porcelain = 瓷、瓷器。a porcelain vase 瓷瓶。对比 ceramic（陶瓷总称）。

quiz.q: Ceramic — the general word for anything made from clay and fired in a kiln. Ceramics are —
quiz.ex: ceramic = 陶瓷的；陶瓷制品。ceramic tiles 瓷砖。对比 porcelain（瓷，ceramic 的一种）。

quiz.q: A tray — the flat board with edges, for carrying many things at once. A tray is —
o: the blade for cutting and lifting
the cover for a simmering pot
a flat board with raised edges for carrying
quiz.ex: tray = 托盘。a tea tray 茶盘。对比 plate（盘子）。

quiz.q: A mug — the cup with a handle, thick-walled, for coffee, tea and honest work. A mug is —
o: a large cup with a handle
quiz.ex: mug = 马克杯、大杯。另义（俚语）：a mug 容易上当的人。对比 glass（玻璃杯）。

quiz.q: The kettle — the vessel with a spout and a handle, for boiling water, the most important machine in any household. A kettle is —
o: a covered vessel for boiling water
the chamber heating the whole block
quiz.ex: kettle = 水壶。the pot calling the kettle black 五十步笑百步。英式谚语：a watched kettle never boils 心急水不开。

title: The Greengrocer's Alphabet
text:
Mr Osman's shop is seven metres of vegetables and {{fruit}} — a fruit being the sweet, seed-bearing thing a plant makes of its flower, the tree's own dessert—, and he teaches the names the way other men teach chess: patiently, and on the understanding that you will be tested by life.

"A {{vegetable}}," he begins, "is any plant grown for food — the general word, the category, the drawer everything else goes into. Now, the members."

The root family: a {{carrot}} — long, orange, sweet, the first vegetable children will eat and the last one rabbits get bored of; a {{turnip}} — the round purple-white root of winter stews; a {{radish}} — its small hot cousin, red-skinned, eaten raw and regretted politely. "Roots grow down," says Mr Osman, pointing at the earth, "and they keep the plant's food where the frost can't argue with it."

The ground family: a {{potato}} — the king of the shop, brown, reliable, the food of half of history; an {{onion}} — the layered bulb that makes cooks cry and sours... no, and sweetens everything it meets; a {{pea}} — the small green seed in a pod, eaten by the hundred and missed by the one that rolls under the fridge; a {{bean}} — the same idea in a larger body, dried or fresh, the protein of the poor and of every great cuisine; a {{cabbage}} — the great layered leaf-ball, the vegetable of winter, of shipping and of letters from the war. The strange ones: a {{cucumber}} — the long cool green fruit that thinks it is a vegetable and is not corrected; an {{eggplant}} — the heavy purple one, called aubergine by people who want it to cost more; a {{mushroom}} — which is not a plant at all but a fungus, and grows in the dark and keeps its own counsel.

The fruit shelves, where the sugar lives. A {{cherry}} — small, red, on a stem, the fruit of patience; a {{berry}} — the general word for the small soft fruits that stain; a {{grape}} — the fruit of vines, of wine, and of packing six into a bag so that the seventh falls; a {{peach}} — the velvet-skinned one, summer held in one hand; a {{pear}} — the apple's patient cousin, ripening on the windowsill; a {{plum}} — the purple one with the secret stone; an {{orange}} — the fruit that named its own colour, a rare achievement; a {{melon}} — the heavy sweet one, water in a ball; a {{lemon}} — the yellow instrument of honesty, correcting everything it touches; a {{kiwi}} — the small brown one with the green interior, the fruit of New Zealand's marketing; a {{papaya}} — the tropical one, orange inside, with seeds like small black beads.

"And now," says Mr Osman, producing a knife and an apple, "the anatomy." The {{peel}} — noun, the skin of a fruit; verb, to {{peel}} is to remove it. A {{strip}} — a long narrow piece cut or torn off anything, a strip of peel, a strip of wallpaper. The {{core}} — the central part of a fruit with its seeds, and by extension the central part of anything: the core of the argument, the core of the matter. And the {{hull}} — the outer covering of a seed or fruit, the jacket it grows in; also, in a completely different life, the body of a ship, which floats because its hull keeps the sea out, the way a peach's keeps the wasps off.

He hands the peeled apple to the smallest customer, who has been listening for twenty minutes and eating a plum throughout.

"You will forget half of this," says Mr Osman, mildly. "But the shop is open six days a week, and so is the education. Come back for the other half tomorrow."
tr:
奥斯曼先生的店有七米长的蔬菜和水果（fruit，fruit 指植物用花结出的、带籽的甜东西，树自己的甜点），他教这些名字的方式像别人教下棋：耐心地，并且默认生活会替他考试。

“蔬菜（vegetable），”他开始，“是为食用而种的任何植物——总称、类目、所有其他东西都放进的那个抽屉。现在，各位成员。”

根类家族：胡萝卜（carrot）——长、橙、甜，孩子肯吃的第一种蔬菜，兔子最后吃腻的那一种；芜菁（turnip）——冬炖菜里的紫白圆根；小萝卜（radish）——它小小的辣表亲，红皮，生吃，然后礼貌地后悔。“根往下长，”奥斯曼先生指着地说，“它们把植物的存粮放在霜争不过的地方。”

地里家族：土豆（potato）——店里的国王，棕色，可靠，半个历史的口粮；洋葱（onion）——层层包裹的鳞茎，让厨师流泪，让遇见它的一切变甜；豌豆（pea）——豆荚里的小小绿籽，论百个吃，滚到冰箱底下的那一颗会被想念；豆子（bean）——更大一号的同一构思，干吃鲜吃皆可，穷人的、也是一切伟大菜系的蛋白质；卷心菜（cabbage）——巨大的层叶球，冬天的蔬菜、海运的蔬菜、战时家信里的蔬菜。奇怪的几位：黄瓜（cucumber）——细长清凉的绿果，自以为是蔬菜，也没人纠正它；茄子（eggplant）——沉甸甸的紫色那位，被想让它们卖贵一点的人叫作 aubergine；蘑菇（mushroom）——根本不是植物而是真菌，在黑暗里生长，守着自己的秘密。

水果架，糖住的地方。樱桃（cherry）——小、红、带柄，耐心的水果；浆果（berry）——会染色的小软果的总称；葡萄（grape）——藤的水果、酒的水果，以及装六颗进袋子好让第七颗掉下去的那种水果；桃子（peach）——天鹅绒外皮的那位，单手握住的夏天；梨（pear）——苹果耐心的表亲，在窗台上慢慢熟；李子（plum）——藏着果核秘密的紫色那位；橙子（orange）——给自己的颜色命名的水果，罕见的成就；甜瓜（melon）——沉重而甜的那位，装成球的水；柠檬（lemon）——黄色的诚实工具，纠正它碰到的一切；奇异果（kiwi）——棕色小果、绿色内心，新西兰营销的果实；木瓜（papaya）——热带的那位，内心橙黄，籽像小小的黑珠子。

“现在，”奥斯曼先生拿出一把刀和一只苹果，“解剖学。”果皮（peel）——名词，水果的皮；动词，剥（peel）就是去掉它。长条（strip）——从任何东西上切下或撕下的窄长片，一条果皮、一条墙纸。果核（core）——水果带籽的中心部分，引申为任何事物的中心：论点的 core，问题的 core。还有外壳（hull）——种子或果实的外层包衣，它出生时穿的夹克；在完全另一辈子里，也是船体，它漂着，是因为 hull 把海水挡在外面，就像桃子的皮把黄蜂挡在外面。

他把削好的苹果递给最小的顾客，那孩子已经听了二十分钟，并且从头到尾吃着一个李子。

“这些你会忘掉一半，”奥斯曼先生温和地说，“但店一周开六天，教育也一周开六天。明天回来学另一半。”

quiz.q: A vegetable is any plant grown for food — the general word, the category. A vegetable is —
o: a fungus growing in the dark
the small soft fruit that stains
quiz.ex: vegetable = 蔬菜。vegetable market 菜市场。注意 mushroom 是 fungus（真菌），严格说不是 vegetable。

quiz.q: A mushroom — which is not a plant at all but a fungus, and grows in the dark and keeps its own counsel. A mushroom is —
o: a fruit with a secret stone
quiz.ex: mushroom = 蘑菇。动词引申：mushrooming 迅速增长（如雨后春笋）。

quiz.q: The peel — noun, the skin of a fruit; verb, to peel is to remove it. To peel means —
o: to keep the seeds in the centre
to cut a long narrow piece off
to remove the skin of a fruit or vegetable
to grow a jacket against wasps
quiz.ex: peel = 剥皮；果皮。peeled prawns 去壳虾仁。习语：keep your eyes peeled 睁大眼睛留意。

quiz.q: The core — the central part of a fruit with its seeds; also the core of the argument. A core is —
o: the outer covering of a seed
quiz.ex: core = 果核；核心。core values 核心价值观；to the core 彻底地。对比 peel（外皮）。

quiz.q: The hull — the outer covering of a seed; also the body of a ship, which keeps the sea out. A hull is —
o: the purple skin of an eggplant
the outer covering; also a ship's body
the layer that makes cooks cry
quiz.ex: hull = （种子）外壳；船体。hull a ship 船体。多义词，注意语境。

quiz.q: A radish — its small hot cousin, red-skinned, eaten raw and regretted politely. A radish is —
quiz.ex: radish = 小萝卜。对比 turnip（芜菁）、carrot（胡萝卜）。

quiz.q: A cabbage — the great layered leaf-ball, the vegetable of winter and of letters from the war. A cabbage is —
o: a small green seed in a pod
a large round layered leaf vegetable
a fungus keeping its own counsel
quiz.ex: cabbage = 卷心菜。cabbage head 卷心菜球。俚语：cabbage 钱（过时用法）。

quiz.q: A berry — the general word for the small soft fruits that stain. A berry is —
o: the brown fruit with a green interior
the fruit of vines and wine
quiz.ex: berry = 浆果。gooseberry 醋栗；blackberry 黑莓。动词：the two boys berrying 采浆果。

title: Harvest at Ferrow Farm
text:
The Wrens have farmed the valley for four generations, and every September the school sends a minibus of pupils to Ferrow Farm for the harvest, the vocabulary, and the sandwiches.

The fields come first. A {{crop}} — the general word for plants grown on a large scale for food — is what the farm exists to raise. This year the {{corn}} — the tall grain, the maize, the yellow towers — stood in the east field; the {{wheat}} — the winter grain that becomes bread — filled the west; and between them the {{grain}} itself was the lesson: grain being the collective word for the harvested seeds of these grasses, the small hard currency of civilisation. "To {{reap}}," says Mr Wren, standing in the dust of the combine, "is to cut and gather the crop — the old word, the scythe word. You reap what you sow, in farming and out of it, and no phrase in the language pays more interest."

In the barn, the {{flour}} — the powder of ground wheat, the beginning of bread — waits in paper sacks, and beside it a sack of {{porridge}} oats — the crushed grain that becomes the thick warm morning food — and a tub of {{paste}} — the soft wet mixture of flour and water, which is, depending on the hour, either the start of pastry or a threat to the wallpaper.

The animals hold the afternoon. {{Livestock}} — the collective word for the animals kept on a farm — live in the fields and in the vocabulary: a {{chicken}} — the bird of eggs and of Sunday; a {{turkey}} — its large dramatic cousin, the bird of one December meal and eleven months of dignity; a pig, supplying the {{pork}} — the general word for pig meat — and the {{sausage}} — the seasoned meat in a skin, the oldest way of keeping a good pig honest. The sheep give the {{mutton}} — the meat of the older sheep, the strong-flavoured word of farmyards; the cattle, the {{beef}} — the meat of the cow, the French word at the English table, ever since 1066.
