The regiment wrote to the town; the town wrote to the War Office; and in 1981 a mason cut the name into the tablet below the others, and the niece, aged ninety-one, drew back the cloth. The town owed him an {{honour}} — honour meaning the respect earned, the good name — it could no longer pay him, and paid it to the stone instead.

"Better late," she said, "than punctual and wrong."

The {{casualty}} figure — a casualty being a soldier killed, wounded or lost — stands at sixty: forty-one of the first war, nineteen of the second. The vicar, in his sermon, addresses the arithmetic. "We are asked to remember a {{victory}}" — a victory being the winning of a war or battle — "and it is right that we should. But the men whose names we have read knew mostly the other thing: {{defeat}}" — a defeat being the loss of a battle — "in the small coin — mud, boots, letters that did not arrive. Their {{triumph}}" — a triumph being a great victory, and the joy that follows one — "was coming home at all; and forty of them did not manage it."

"The posters said {{glorious}}" — glorious meaning splendid, full of glory — says Bill Skidmore afterwards, at the Legion. "We preferred cold. You went on being frightened; you {{dread}}ed — to dread meaning to fear greatly, to anticipate a thing with fear — the next day, and then the next; you put the dread in your pocket with everything else, and marched. Twice that winter we {{withdraw}}... withdrew" — to withdraw meaning to pull back, to leave the field — "and twice came forward again. The monument does not mention the withdrawals. Nobody's does. But the withdrawals are how everyone here got to be old."

"We were told we fought {{evil}}" — evil meaning profound moral wickedness — "and we did," he says, into his beer. "I saw enough to know {{hell}} — hell being the place of the damned, and no metaphor — is a place. And the {{devil}} — the devil being the supreme spirit of wickedness — held no commission on either side. He had men on both, and promoted them."

The names that could not be brought home lie abroad, mostly; to {{bury}} — to bury meaning to put a dead body into the earth, with ceremony or without — being the last service their countries can render them. A few came home in the fifties, and their {{funeral}}s — a funeral being the ceremony of burial — were the largest the town had seen in peacetime. In the churchyard stand the {{tomb}}s — a tomb being a grave built and carved above the ground — of those who made it home to die of old age instead; and the {{grave}}s of their wives beside them.

The stone where the four roads meet is the one {{comfort}} — comfort meaning consolation, the easing of grief — the town can give: everyone going anywhere passes the boys.

The statue looks towards the bakery. The mason cut it so, the story runs, because that was as far as the model's leave had taken him — four streets from the depot, and home in time for tea. On the evening of the ceremony the youngest children come up with their candles, which {{glow}} — to glow meaning to shine with a steady, warm light — in the dark, and their eyes {{twinkle}} — to twinkle meaning to shine with a flickering light — at the soldier; and the traffic, which has learned, gives the statue its three feet of pavement — the one position, the drivers agree, that he will never {{surrender}} — to surrender meaning to yield, to give up — whatever else is given away.
tr:
战争纪念碑（monument，monument 指为让记忆凝固不动而建造的东西）立在四条道路交汇的地方：一座雕像（statue，statue 指为纪念某人某事而雕刻或铸造的人像）——一个士兵，正如雕像上的士兵一贯的那样，望着的不是敌人而是面包房；他脚下是一块铭碑（tablet，tablet 指刻着文字的扁平石板），刻着四十一个名字，按它们在大战教区名册上出现（occur，occur 指发生、成为事实）的先后为序。

这项活动（event，event 指发生的事，尤指有计划、有聚会的要事）每年在离十一月十一日最近的那个星期日举行，无论天气如何；而这也是磨坊溪唯一准时、安静、全体一致的一个场合（occasion，occasion 指有仪式感的特定时日）。

老兵们（veteran，veteran 指参加过战争的人）坐在谷物交易所的门廊下：如今是八个人，当年曾是八十个。十九岁就上过萨莱诺的比尔·斯基德莫尔佩戴着他的勋章（medal，medal 指为表彰服役而颁发的小型金属十字或星章），出于原则从不擦亮。“发它们可不是为了发亮，”《信使报》来问时他这么说；而在十一月的雨里它们照样闪闪发亮（glitter，glitter 指闪耀、发出坚硬的光），比尔把这称作天气的一种好意。

名字被逐一宣读。十五岁的女号手吹响“最后一岗”；然后是两分钟的静默（pause，pause 指停顿、寂静的间隔），整个小镇停止（cease，cease 指终止、归于停止）作为一个小镇，变成一次屏住的呼吸。火车在道口停驶（halt，halt 指停下、停驻），车头低垂着。半条街外肉铺里的争论停在一句话中间，再开口时已是半句道歉。

石碑立于一九二一年，而关于第四十个名字的争执比战争又多延续了六十年。托马斯·普罗瑟一九一七年因叛国罪（treason，treason 指背叛国家的罪行）被枪决，罪名是把海岸信号出卖（betray，betray 指不忠于、把……交给敌人）给了德国；此后小镇一直管他叫叛徒（traitor，traitor 指背叛国家、朋友或所托之人的人），用的是留给天气和税收的那种口气。他家那扇每年被不明身份者打破的窗户，每年由他妹妹修好。

一九七九年档案开放，一位历史学家恰好碰上了（happen，happen 指发生、出于偶然或命运地成为事实）普罗瑟的卷宗。他原是双面间谍：让他送命的那些灯火信号，发给德国人的是假情报——由白厅办公室里的人们起草，而那些人随后弄丢了能证明这一点的文件。他的审判是一场由速记、恐慌和一份失踪证物构成的灾难（catastrophe，catastrophe 指突发的彻底灾祸）。

团里给镇上写了信；镇上给陆军部写了信；一九八一年，石匠把这个名字刻在其他人名之下，九十一岁的侄女为它揭了幕。小镇欠他一个再也还不上的荣誉（honour，honour 指挣得的敬重与好名声），便把它还给了石头。

“迟了总好过准时而错，”她说。

伤亡数字（casualty，casualty 指阵亡、负伤或失踪的士兵）如今是六十：四十一人来自第一场战争，十九人来自第二场。牧师在布道中讲这组算术。“我们要记住的是一场胜利（victory，victory 指赢得战争或战役），这没有错。但我们刚才宣读名字的那些人，最熟悉的是另一样东西：失败（defeat，defeat 指战役的失利）——以小面额支付的失败：泥泞、军靴、没能寄到的信。他们的凯旋（triumph，triumph 指大捷，以及随之而来的欢庆）是活着回了家；而他们中间有四十个没能做到。”

“海报上说光荣（glorious，glorious 指辉煌的、荣耀的），”仪式之后比尔·斯基德莫尔在老兵协会里说，“我们更愿意说'冷'。你还是害怕；你畏惧（dread，dread 指极其害怕、怀着恐惧等待某事）第二天，再畏惧再下一天；你把畏惧跟别的所有东西一起装进口袋，然后开步走。那年冬天我们撤退（withdraw，withdraw 指后退、撤离战场）过两次，又两次向前。纪念碑不提撤退。谁的纪念碑都不提。可是靠着那两次撤退，这里的每一个人才能活到年老。”

“人家告诉我们，我们打的是邪恶（evil，evil 指深重的道德败坏），我们也确实在打，”他冲着他的啤酒说。“我见过的东西足以让我知道地狱（hell，hell 指受诅咒者的居所——绝非比喻）是一个地方。而魔鬼（devil，devil 指万恶之首的邪灵）没有在任何一方持有军衔。他在两边都有人，而且给他们都升了职。”

那些没能运回家的名字大多躺在国外；安葬（bury，bury 指把遗体安放进土里）有仪式也行，没有也行——那是他们的国家能为其提供的最后一项服务。少数人五十年代运了回来，他们的葬礼（funeral，funeral 指安葬死者的仪式）是本镇和平年代规模最大的。教堂院子里立着几座坟冢（tomb，tomb 指在地上砌筑、带雕饰的坟墓），属于那些活着还乡、终老于病榻的人；旁边是他们妻子的墓穴（grave，grave 指埋葬遗体的墓穴）。

立在四条路交汇处的那块石头，是小镇所能给予的唯一安慰（comfort，comfort 指安慰、痛苦的缓解）：无论谁要去哪里，都会从这些孩子身边经过。

雕像朝着面包房的方向。据说石匠当年就是这么凿的，因为模特那次探亲假只走出兵站四条街，正赶得及回家喝茶。仪式当晚，最小的孩子们举着蜡烛上前来，烛火在黑暗中发着温暖的光（glow，glow 指发出稳定而温暖的光），他们的眼睛朝士兵一闪一闪（twinkle，twinkle 指闪烁着微光）；而已经学会规矩的车流，给雕像让出三英尺人行道——司机们一致认为，那是他永远不会让出（surrender，surrender 指让出、放弃）的阵地，无论别的什么都被让了出去。

quiz.q: The veterans sit under the porch of the corn exchange — one who has served in a war. A veteran is —
o: a grave dug in foreign earth
one awarded a medal for shining
one who has served in a war
quiz.ex: veteran = 老兵；退伍军人；老手。a veteran of two wars 打过两场战争的老兵。

quiz.q: The casualty figure stands at sixty — a soldier killed, wounded or lost. A casualty is —
o: a monument raised for the dead
a soldier killed, wounded or lost
quiz.ex: casualty = 伤亡人员。heavy casualties 重大伤亡；casualty list 伤亡名单。

quiz.q: Prosser had been shot in 1917 for treason — the crime of betraying one's country. Treason is —
o: the crime of betraying one's country
a flat stone with names on it
quiz.ex: treason = 叛国罪。commit treason 犯叛国罪。

quiz.q: Charged with betraying the coastal signals to Germany — to be false to, to hand over to the enemy. To betray is to —
o: be disloyal to, hand over to the enemy
quiz.ex: betray = 背叛；出卖；泄露。betray one's country 背叛祖国；betray a secret 泄露秘密。

quiz.q: Their triumph was coming home at all — a great victory, and the joy that follows one. A triumph is —
o: a great victory, and the joy of it
quiz.ex: triumph = 大捷；凯旋；巨大成就。in triumph 凯旋而归；triumph over adversity 战胜逆境。

quiz.q: Twice that winter we withdrew — to pull back, to leave the field. To withdraw is to —
o: give oneself up to the enemy
quiz.ex: withdraw = 撤退；撤回；取款。withdraw troops 撤军；withdraw money 取钱。

quiz.q: You dreaded the next day, and then the next — to fear greatly, to anticipate with fear. To dread is to —
quiz.ex: dread = 畏惧；担忧。dread the results 害怕结果；a dreaded disease 令人恐惧的疾病。

quiz.q: His trial had been a catastrophe of shorthand, panic and a missing exhibit — a sudden and utter disaster. A catastrophe is —
quiz.ex: catastrophe = 大灾难。a nuclear catastrophe 核灾难；catastrophic adj. 灾难性的。

title: The Siege of Millbrook Mound
text:
Miss Cawdry brings the third form up to the mound every June, sits them on the banks, and tells them the siege.

The mound stands at the north end of the town, a green pyramid with a flat top, its ditch and banks still clear: the works that {{enclose}} — to enclose meaning to shut in, to surround with a barrier — the bailey; and beyond them the old {{boundary}} — a boundary being the line that marks the edge of a possession — of the deer park, running along the hedge to the road.

"The castle is gone," she says. "The stone went to build the bridge, in 1580. But in 1349, everything you can see from here belonged to a band of soldiers who had crossed from France to {{invade}} — to invade meaning to enter a land by force, as an enemy — the valley."

They had come for the wool money, and they {{capture}}d the mill and the bridge — to capture meaning to take by force — in a single afternoon, they being soldiers and the miller being a miller. They proclaimed themselves lords of the valley, which was optimistic; and they began, with the instinct of their trade, to loot.

The people of Millbrook did what people do: they {{retreat}}ed — to retreat meaning to move back before an enemy — to the mound, with the sheep, the flour, the church plate and both dogs, and shut the gate. The band followed, looked, and settled down around it; and that was the {{siege}} — a siege being the surrounding and cutting-off of a place, to starve it into surrender — of Millbrook Mound.

"Could they not just walk away?" asks a boy, every year.

"They could have walked anywhere," says Miss Cawdry. "But not with the mill. Whoever holds the mill grinds the corn; whoever grinds the corn eats; whoever holds the bridge charges the crossing. The band had come three hundred miles for those two machines. Walking away was not in them."

There was no {{general}} — a general being an officer of the highest rank, the commander of armies — on the mound, and no plan beyond the gate. The defence was run by Walter the miller; and its {{soldier}}s — a soldier being one who serves in an army — were twelve mill-hands, a priest, a blacksmith named Hob, and the dogs.

The band {{attack}}ed — to attack meaning to set upon, to make an assault against — at dawn on the third day. The first {{assault}} — an assault being a concentrated attack, a rush upon a position — came up the north bank, where the slope is gentlest, by men with a ladder; and it failed at the top of the ladder, where Hob was waiting with his {{hammer}} — a hammer being the tool of heavy blows; to hammer, to beat as with one — and did not so much fight as work. A man who climbs a ladder towards a blacksmith, Miss Cawdry observes, has mistaken his profession.

The second assault was arrow work. The band had archers; the mound had three: the priest, who had hunted; a boy of fourteen; and Walter, whose {{bow}} — a bow being the weapon that shoots the arrow — was yew, and older than the church. For three days the {{arrow}}s — an arrow being the pointed shaft shot from a bow — came over like weather. The defenders answered with worse aim and better language.

The inventory of the defence, from the chronicle: one {{spear}} — a spear being a long shaft with a pointed head — which was a hay-fork; Hob's {{sword}} — a sword being the long-bladed weapon of the hand — with its {{blade}} — a blade being the cutting part of any edged weapon — ground thin by forty years of sharpening; the mill's {{axe}} — an axe being the tool with the heavy bladed head — ... a {{shield}} — a shield being the broad plate carried to turn a blow — cut from a boiler door; and one {{helmet}} — a helmet being armour for the head — which was a bucket, and is in the museum, labelled in the curator's hand: BUCKET (HELMET, PROBABLE).

The third assault came at night, on the west bank, and got as far as the gate. The chronicle, which was written by the priest and has opinions, says that Hob {{strike}}... struck — to strike meaning to deal a blow — the first man through with the flat of the sword; that the miller's boy {{hit}} — to hit meaning to strike a target — the second with a stone from the church; that the priest {{punch}}ed — to punch meaning to strike with the closed fist — the third, which the priest records with some surprise at himself; and that a mill-hand, pressed against the gate, took the billhook and {{chop}}ped — to chop meaning to cut with heavy downward blows — the ladder's rungs until the assault became a matter of gravity. The one wound the chronicle calls serious was a {{stab}} — a stab being a wound made with a pointed weapon — to the thigh, incurred by a defender who had tried to {{seize}} — to seize meaning to take hold of, to grab — an attacker's dagger by the interesting end.

The {{campaign}} — a campaign being a series of military operations towards one object — then settled into its long middle: three weeks of staring. Walter's {{strategy}} — strategy being the overall plan, the deep game — was patience, the well being inside the banks and the flour numbering forty sacks; his {{tactic}}s — tactics being the particular methods used in the actual fighting — were boiling water, bees, and early-morning insults; and his {{manoeuvre}}s — a manoeuvre being a planned movement of forces — were few of necessity, the top of the mound being the size of a tennis court and already full of sheep.

The band, meanwhile, made the mistake that ends sieges: they foraged wide, in parties, the valley being stripped; and so, one Tuesday, a foraging party of nine was taken at Bidgelow by a {{troop}} — a troop being a body of soldiers, especially of horse — of the sheriff's archers, who had come up from Lampford on a matter of sheep-stealing.

The end was quieter than the middle. The archers came up the valley at dusk, took the west {{guard}}s — a guard being one who keeps watch over a place — asleep, and the band, finding themselves {{surround}}ed — to surround meaning to encircle, to close round on every side — by the very tactic they had practised on others, chose the night and the north, and were gone by morning.

"They {{resist}}ed — to resist meaning to stand against, to refuse to yield — for three weeks," says Miss Cawdry, "against men whose profession it was. The mound {{withstand}}... withstood — to withstand meaning to hold out against, to bear without giving way — everything the fourteenth century could put against it, which was mostly rain. And no {{battle}} — a battle being a sustained fight between organised forces — was ever fought on it, which is why your school stands on the far side, and nobody has ever found a single arrowhead."

Then why, the children ask, do we call it the siege?

"Because the {{conquer}}or — to conquer meaning to take by force, to subdue — writes the maps," says Miss Cawdry, "and a town that neither fought a battle nor lost one must take what names it is given."

Down in the town the cows are standing on the motte, which is what the mound is for now. Every history, Miss Cawdry tells the third form, ends as a field; and the third form, being the third form, writes this down.
tr:
每年六月，考德里老师带三年级学生上土丘，让他们坐在土坡上，给他们讲围城的故事。

土丘立在镇子北端，是一座平顶的绿色金字塔，壕沟和土堤至今轮廓分明：这些工事圈围（enclose，enclose 指用屏障围合、封闭）着城场；再往外是鹿苑的旧边界（boundary，boundary 指标示属地尽头的界线），沿着树篱一直通到大路。

“城堡已经没有了，”她说。“石头在一五八〇年拿去修了桥。可是在一三四九年，你们从这里能望见的一切，都属于一伙从法兰西渡海来侵占（invade，invade 指作为敌人武力进入一片土地）这条河谷的士兵。”

他们是为羊毛钱来的，一个下午就攻占（capture，capture 指以武力夺取）了磨坊和桥——毕竟他们是士兵，而磨坊主只是磨坊主。他们自封为河谷之主，这未免过于乐观；然后凭着他们那一行的本能，开始劫掠。

磨坊溪人做了人们该做的事：带着羊、面粉、教堂银器和两条狗，退守（retreat，retreat 指在敌人面前退却）到土丘上，关上大门。那伙人跟了上来，看了看，便在四周扎了下来——这就是磨坊溪土丘围城战（siege，siege 指围困一地、断其补给以迫其投降的战法）。

“他们就不能一走了之吗？”每年都有一个男孩这么问。

“他们哪儿都能走，”考德里老师说，“就是带不走磨坊。谁占着磨坊谁磨面；谁磨面谁吃饭；谁占着桥谁收过桥钱。这伙人为这两台机器走了三百英里。一走了之这件事，不在他们的天性里。”

土丘上没有将军（general，general 指最高军衔、统率大军的军官），也没有大门以外的任何计划。防务由磨坊主沃尔特主持；他的士兵（soldier，soldier 指在军队中服役的人）是十二个磨坊工、一位神父、一个叫霍布的铁匠，还有那两条狗。

第三天拂晓，那伙人进攻（attack，attack 指攻击、冲杀上来）了。第一次突击（assault，assault 指集中兵力对一阵地的猛攻）从北坡上来——那面坡最缓——扛着梯子；它在梯子顶端失败了，霍布正提着他的铁锤（hammer，hammer 指实施沉重打击的锤子；作动词指锤打）在那里等着，与其说是打仗，不如说是干活。考德里老师评论道：顺着梯子朝一个铁匠爬上去的人，是入错了行。

第二次突击是箭的功课。那伙人有弓箭手；土丘上有三个：神父，他打过猎；一个十四岁的男孩；还有沃尔特，他的弓（bow，bow 指发射箭矢的武器）是紫杉木的，比教堂还老。一连三天，箭（arrow，arrow 指从弓上射出的带镞箭杆）像天气一样落过来。守方回敬的准头差些，词句好些。

防御工事的家底，编年史上是这么记的：一支矛（spear，spear 指装有尖头的长柄武器），其实是草叉；霍布的剑（sword，sword 指长刃的随身兵器），剑刃（blade，blade 指一切刃器的锋刃）磨了四十年、磨得薄了；磨坊的斧（axe，axe 指带重刃的斧头）；一面用锅炉门裁的盾（shield，shield 指招架打击的宽牌）；还有一顶头盔（helmet，helmet 指护头的盔）——那是一只桶，如今在博物馆里，馆长的手写标签是：桶（头盔，存疑）。

第三次突击在夜里，从西坡来，一直打到大门。编年史出自神父之手，自有立场：它说霍布用剑背击打（strike，strike 指实施一击）了第一个进门的人；磨坊主的儿子用教堂的一块石头砸中（hit，hit 指击中、命中目标）了第二个；神父一拳（punch，punch 指用握紧的拳头击打）打倒了第三个——神父记下这一笔时对自己颇有几分惊讶；一个磨坊工抵住大门，抄起长柄镰刀连劈（chop，chop 指以沉重的下劈动作砍削）梯级，直到这次突击变成一个引力问题。编年史称之为重伤的唯一一处伤，是一处刺伤（stab，stab 指尖头兵器造成的刺伤），伤在一名守军大腿上——他试图夺取（seize，seize 指抓住、攫取）一名攻击者的匕首，却抓了有刃的那一头。

此后，战役（campaign，campaign 指为同一目标展开的一连串军事行动）进入了漫长的中段：三个星期的对峙。沃尔特的战略（strategy，strategy 指全局性的总体方略）是耐心——井在堤内，面粉有四十袋；他的战术（tactic，tactics 指实际交战中使用的具体方法）是开水、蜜蜂和清晨的辱骂；至于调动（manoeuvre，manoeuvre 指部队有计划的移动），由于土丘顶只有一个网球场大、而且已经站满了羊，可做的实在有限。

与此同时，那伙人犯下了结束一切围城的那个错误：因为河谷已被搜刮一空，他们分小队四出就食；于是，某个星期二，一支九人征粮队在比奇洛被郡长的弓箭手小队（troop，troop 指一队士兵，尤指骑兵）一网成擒——那队人本是为偷羊案从兰普福德上来的。

结尾比中段安静得多。弓箭手们黄昏进谷，趁西坡的哨兵（guard，guard 指看守、警戒之人）睡熟时得了手；那伙人发现自己反倒被包围（surround，surround 指从四面围拢）了——用的正是他们施加于人的那一手——便选了夜色和北面，天亮前走得干干净净。

“他们抵抗（resist，resist 指抵挡、拒不屈服）了三个星期，”考德里老师说，“对手是以此为职业的人。这座土丘顶住了（withstand，withstand 指经受住、扛住而不垮）十四世纪所能加于它的一切——那主要是雨。而这里从来没有打过一场会战（battle，battle 指两军之间持续相接的战斗），所以你们的学校建在另一边，而且从来没人找到过一枚箭镞。”

那么，孩子们问，为什么我们管它叫围城战？

“因为征服者（conquer，conquer 指以武力攻克、降服）绘制地图，”考德里老师说，“而一个既没打过会战、也没输掉会战的镇子，只好接受人家给的名字。”

山下，母牛们正站在土丘顶上——那如今就是土丘的用途。每一部历史，考德里老师对三年级说，最后都变成一片田野；三年级因为是三年级，就把这句也记了下来。

quiz.q: That was the siege of Millbrook Mound — the surrounding and cutting-off of a place, to starve it into surrender. A siege is —
o: the overall plan of a war
a single rush upon a position
the surrounding of a place to force its surrender
a body of soldiers on horse
quiz.ex: siege = 围攻；围困。lay siege to a city 围攻一城；endure a siege of ten weeks 挨过十周围困。

quiz.q: The first assault came up the north bank by men with a ladder — a concentrated attack, a rush upon a position. An assault is —
o: a concentrated attack upon a position
an officer of the highest rank
quiz.ex: assault = 突击；袭击；攻击。an assault on the castle 强攻城堡；assault charges 袭击罪名。

quiz.q: The people retreated to the mound with the sheep and the flour — to move back before an enemy. To retreat is to —
quiz.ex: retreat = 撤退；退却。sound the retreat 鸣号收兵；beat a retreat 撤退（引申为开溜）。

quiz.q: They captured the mill and the bridge in a single afternoon — to take by force. To capture is to —
quiz.ex: capture = 攻占；俘获。capture the bridge 夺桥；captured soldiers 战俘。

quiz.q: Walter's strategy was patience, the well being inside the banks — the overall plan, the deep game. Strategy is —
o: a wound from a pointed weapon
the methods used in the actual fighting
the overall plan of a campaign
quiz.ex: strategy = 战略；策略。military strategy 军事战略；a long-term strategy 长期战略。

quiz.q: His tactics were boiling water, bees and early-morning insults — the particular methods used in fighting. Tactics are —
o: the overall plan of the war
the methods used in the actual fighting
quiz.ex: tactics = 战术；手法。delaying tactics 拖延战术；tactical adj. 战术上的。

quiz.q: His manoeuvres were few, the top of the mound being the size of a tennis court — a planned movement of forces. A manoeuvre is —
o: a flat stone with words on it
the cutting part of a sword
quiz.ex: manoeuvre = 调动；机动；演习（美式拼法 maneuver）。military manoeuvres 军事演习。

quiz.q: The mound withstood everything the fourteenth century could put against it — to hold out against, to bear without giving way. To withstand is to —
o: hold out against, bear without giving way
be taken asleep at the west bank
quiz.ex: withstand = 抵住；经受住。withstand pressure 顶住压力；withstand an attack 抗住进攻。

title: The Armoury
text:
The museum keeps its {{weapon}}s — a weapon being any instrument made for attack or defence — in the old corn store: room two, between the Roman coins and the shepherd's crooks. Mr. Pym, the curator, calls the collection his {{mission}} — a mission being the task a man sets himself, the errand of a life — and says that a small town's arms record its luck rather than its cruelty, since almost nothing in the room was ever pointed at anything but a rabbit.

The oldest piece is a {{cannon}} — a cannon being a large gun, mounted, that fires a heavy ball — dredged from the estuary in 1902 and labelled, in Mr. Pym's hand: ARMADA, PROBABLE. There is a case of duelling {{pistol}}s — a pistol being a small gun made to be held and fired in one hand — which the card says were never used, the town's gentlemen having found other ways of being wrong. There is the volunteer {{rifle}} — a rifle being a long gun with a grooved barrel, cut to spin the shot so that it flies far and true — of 1860; and set in the beam above it, visible when Mr. Pym lifts the lamp, the flattened {{bullet}} — a bullet being the small piece of metal a gun fires — of 1745, which came in at the window during the Jacobite scare, missed the miller by a coat's thickness, and has paid rent in the oak ever since. At the bottom of Pudding Lane the rifle range keeps its iron {{target}} — a target being the thing aimed at — though the volunteers are eighty years gone, and the only marksmen now are the pigeons.

The room's second subject is the powder. The {{gunpowder}} — gunpowder being the explosive mixture of the old wars, saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur — company built its mill upstream of the weir in 1832, on the sound principle that a river is a friend to a building that would rather not burn. For eleven years the only {{explosion}} — an explosion being the sudden violent bursting of a thing, with noise and force — Millbrook knew was the birthday salute; and then, on the Tuesday of the fair, the drying house went up.

A {{spark}} — a spark being the small leaping bit of fire by which a flame is begun — from a horse's shoe, the inquiry decided, though the horse was never produced; and the building {{burst}} — to burst meaning to break open, outward and all at once — like a paper bag. The {{blast}} — a blast being an explosion, and the wave of it — took every window off the bridge and most of the glass in the church. Slates came over the roofs in flights, like {{missile}}s — a missile being anything whatever, sent flying at a mark — and the schoolmaster, standing in the road with his mouth open, saw his own chimney-pot, {{deflect}}ed — to deflect meaning to turn a thing off its course — by the churchyard wall, go through the pump. The {{violence}} of the shock was felt as far as Bidgelow, where it stopped the pendulum clock, which the Bidgelow people still mention, having little else.

The {{flame}} — a flame being the burning tongue of a fire — took the malt house before the buckets were out. The brewery's fire engine, {{equip}}ped — to equip meaning to furnish with what a task needs — with buckets, ladders, a hand-pump and four men, was {{deploy}}ed — to deploy meaning to put into position for use — along the weir; the brewery's water {{tank}} — a tank being a large container for liquid — {{provide}}d — to provide meaning to supply, to furnish what is wanted — the water; and the brewery's watchman, who had {{prepare}}d — to prepare meaning to make ready beforehand — for fires all his life and never met one, {{beat}} — to beat meaning to strike again and again — the alarm on the rail with a hammer until help came up the hill. The fire was a three-day {{struggle}} — a struggle being a hard fight, against flame or anything else — and the malt house lost; but the powder in the remaining store was drowned on purpose, and the town toasted the company's discretion.

The inquest was a {{conflict}} — a conflict being a clash, of arms or of stories — of testimony: the company called the explosion an act of God, and the miller called it an act of economy; and the Mercury {{bombard}}ed — to bombard meaning to shell, and so to shower with anything at all — the directors with letters for a month. The directors {{flare}}d — to flare meaning to blaze up, to flame suddenly and briefly — with dignity, paid for the glass, and moved the works to Wales.

The last case is empty and labelled: BOMB, 1940, NOT RECOVERED. In the {{raid}} — a raid being a sudden armed attack, from sea or air — of that August, a German {{bomb}} — a bomb being a container of explosive, dropped or set to burst — came down at two in the morning into the mill pond, and sank; and the diver who went to look at it in 1948 reported that it had burst on impact, harmlessly, decades of silt ago. Mr. Pym keeps the case empty for it, he says, so that children may consider the {{enormity}} — enormity meaning the vastness and the wickedness of a thing together — of a machine built by strangers to fall on strangers, and the size of the mercy that buried it in water.
tr:
博物馆把兵器（weapon，weapon 指为攻击或防御而制的器械）存放在旧粮仓里：第二展室，在罗马钱币与牧羊人弯钩之间。馆长皮姆先生把这套收藏称为他的使命（mission，mission 指一个人给自己定下的任务、毕生的差事），并说一个小镇的兵器记录的是它的运气而非它的残忍，因为屋里几乎没有一件东西对准过兔子以外的任何目标。

最老的一件是一门炮（cannon，cannon 指架设起来发射重型炮弹的大型火炮），一九〇二年从河口捞出，皮姆先生亲手标注：无敌舰队，存疑。有一匣决斗用手枪（pistol，pistol 指单手握持发射的小型枪械），卡片上写明从未用过——本镇的绅士们自有别的认错方式。有一支一八六〇年的志愿兵步枪（rifle，rifle 指枪管刻有膛线、使弹丸旋转向前以打得又远又准的长枪）；枪上方那根梁里，皮姆先生举起灯就能看见，嵌着一七四五年那颗压扁的子弹（bullet，bullet 指枪械发射的小型金属弹头）——它在詹姆斯党恐慌期间从窗户射进来，离磨坊主只差一件外套的厚度，从此在那根橡木里交租至今。布丁巷底端的靶场还留着铁靶子（target，target 指被瞄准射击之物），尽管志愿兵们八十年前就散了，如今唯一的射手是鸽子。

这个展室的第二个主题是火药。火药（gunpowder，gunpowder 指旧日战争的黑色炸药，硝石、木炭与硫磺的混合物）公司一八三二年在堰上游建了磨坊，依据一条可靠的原理：河是一位巴不得自己不烧起来的建筑的朋友。十一年间，磨坊溪所知道的唯一一次爆炸（explosion，explosion 指事物伴随巨响与力量骤然炸裂）就是国王生日的礼炮；然后，在集市日的那个星期二，干燥房上了天。

调查认定是马掌擦出的一粒火星（spark，spark 指火焰得以开始的那种细小跳跃的火点）——虽然那匹马始终没有到案；于是那座建筑像纸袋一样炸开（burst，burst 指向外骤然破开）。爆震（blast，blast 指爆炸，及其冲击波）掀掉了桥上每一扇窗户和教堂里的大部分玻璃。石板成片飞过屋顶，像一群投掷物（missile，missile 指任何被掷向目标的飞行之物）；校长张着嘴站在路上，眼看着自家的烟囱帽被教堂墓地的墙撞偏（deflect，deflect 指使某物偏离路线），从水泵里穿了过去。震荡之猛烈（violence，violence 指伤害性的物理强力）一直传到比奇洛，震停了那座摆钟——比奇洛人至今还提这件事，他们也没有别的可提。

火舌（flame，flame 指火焰燃烧的舌尖）在水桶搬出来之前就上了麦芽房。啤酒厂的消防唧筒——配备（equip，equip 指为一项任务备齐所需之物）着水桶、梯子、一台手压泵和四个人——被部署（deploy，deploy 指布置到位以供使用）在堰边；啤酒厂的水柜（tank，tank 指盛液体的大容器）提供（provide，provide 指供应、备办所需）了水；啤酒厂的更夫一辈子都在为火灾做准备（prepare，prepare 指预先备好），却从未遇上过一场，此刻抡起锤子，在铁轨上一下一下敲（beat，beat 指反复击打）响警报，直到救兵上了山。这场火是一场三天的苦斗（struggle，struggle 指对火焰或其他任何事物的艰难搏斗），麦芽房输了；但余仓里的火药被有意淹掉，全镇举杯称赞公司的审慎。

验尸审讯是一场证词的冲突（conflict，conflict 指交锋——武力的，或说法上的）：公司称爆炸是天意，磨坊主称它是省出来的；《信使报》连着一个月向董事们狂轰（bombard，bombard 指炮击，引申为以任何东西倾泻）信件。董事们体面地发了火（flare，flare 指火苗骤然蹿起，引申为怒气上冲），赔了玻璃钱，把工厂搬去了威尔士。

最后一个展柜空着，标签是：炸弹，一九四〇，未寻获。那年八月的一次空袭（raid，raid 指自海上或空中发起的突然袭击）中，一枚德国炸弹（bomb，bomb 指内装炸药、被投掷或引爆的爆炸物）凌晨两点落进磨坊池，沉了下去；一九四八年下去查看的潜水员报告说，它在撞击时就已无害地炸开，埋在几十年的淤泥之下。皮姆先生说，他让那个柜子空着，是为了让孩子们掂量掂量这件事的骇人（enormity，enormity 指巨大与凶恶并具的性质）——一台由陌生人建造、要落到陌生人头上的机器，以及把它埋进水里的那份仁慈有多大。

quiz.q: The museum keeps its weapons in the old corn store — any instrument made for attack or defence. A weapon is —
o: a large gun mounted on a carriage
any instrument made for attack or defence
a small gun fired in one hand
quiz.ex: weapon = 武器；兵器。nuclear weapons 核武器；lethal weapons 致命武器。

quiz.q: A cannon dredged from the estuary, labelled ARMADA, PROBABLE — a large gun, mounted, that fires a heavy ball. A cannon is —
o: a small gun held in one hand
a large mounted gun firing a heavy ball
the leaping bit of fire that begins a flame
a container of explosive dropped from the air
quiz.ex: cannon = 大炮；火炮。cannon fire 炮火。

quiz.q: Slates came over the roofs in flights, like missiles — anything whatever, sent flying at a mark. A missile is —
o: a flat stone with words on it
anything sent flying at a mark
a spark from a horse's shoe
quiz.ex: missile = 导弹；投掷物。a nuclear missile 核导弹；stones used as missiles 被当作投掷物的石块。

quiz.q: The chimney-pot, deflected by the churchyard wall, went through the pump — to turn a thing off its course. To deflect is to —
o: turn a thing off its course
take every window off a bridge
pay rent in oak ever after
quiz.ex: deflect = 使偏转；使改变方向。deflect a bullet 使子弹偏转；deflect criticism 转移批评。

quiz.q: The blast took every window off the bridge — an explosion, and the wave of it. A blast is —
o: an explosion, and the wave of it
a small leaping bit of fire
quiz.ex: blast = 爆炸；冲击波；一阵狂风。a bomb blast 炸弹爆炸；the blast of the horn 号角声。

quiz.q: The brewery's engine was deployed along the weir — to put into position for use. To deploy is to —
o: break open like a paper bag
quiz.ex: deploy = 部署；调配。deploy troops 部署军队；deploy resources 调配资源。

quiz.q: The engine, equipped with buckets, ladders, a hand-pump and four men — to furnish with what a task needs. To equip is to —
o: strike the alarm on a rail
put into position along a weir
furnish with what a task needs
quiz.ex: equip = 装备；配备。be equipped with 配备有……；a well-equipped laboratory 设备精良的实验室。

quiz.q: Children may consider the enormity of a machine built by strangers to fall on strangers — the vastness and the wickedness of a thing together. Enormity is —
o: the burning tongue of a fire
the curator's set task in life
the vastness and wickedness of a thing together
an unexploded bomb in a pond
quiz.ex: enormity = （恶行的）穷凶极恶；（常误用指）巨大。the enormity of the crime 罪行之滔天。

title: The Famine Year
text:
Millbrook keeps one year in a class of its own. In 1846 the potatoes failed everywhere at once, as they failed everywhere else; the wheat came thin; and by February of 1847 the parish was looking {{famine}} — famine being a general failure of food, hunger as a public condition — in the face.

The weavers had been {{deprive}}d — to deprive meaning to strip of, to take away from — of their winter work by the failure of the Lampford bank; and families that had been poor in a manageable way became {{destitute}} — destitute meaning utterly without money, food or means — between one quarter-day and the next. Their {{plight}} — a plight being a hard and sorry condition — was considered monthly by the vestry, which wrung its hands in the minutes, and in ink.

The guardians' {{dilemma}} — a dilemma being a choice between two things, both of them bad — was the old one: feed the hungry outside the walls of the workhouse, and pauperise the rates; keep the rules, and watch the children {{starve}} — to starve meaning to suffer or die from want of food — on the main street, where consciences live. The poor law had its {{pitfall}}s — a pitfall being a hidden trap, a danger not marked on the map — and the guardians, obeying the rulebook to the letter, fell into every one of them: outdoor relief was {{prohibit}}ed — to prohibit meaning to forbid by rule or authority — to the able-bodied; charity at the gate was stopped as a corruption of the poor; and the workhouse itself was built to {{deter}} — to deter meaning to discourage, by fear of consequences — and did. The vestry had also {{forbid}}den — to forbid meaning to order a thing not to be done — baking on the Sabbath, and the bakers, who had been baking on the Sabbath all winter for the queues, were fined to a man.

By March the town had found something cheaper than bread: an explanation. A {{conspiracy}} — a conspiracy being a secret plan by several persons together to do wrong — to hold back the flour was discovered, or invented, in the tap-room of the Rising Sun. The miller was {{blame}}d — to blame meaning to fix the fault upon — for sacks that had never existed; and although no {{evidence}} — evidence being the grounds of belief, the facts offered to make a matter plain — was ever produced, and no {{proof}} — proof being evidence that settles a matter beyond argument — ever came, a hungry town does not weigh so finely. It was said besides that flour could be had under the {{counter}} — a counter being the table over which goods are sold, and under it, privately, against the rules — at the Rising Sun on Thursdays; which was news to the Rising Sun, but the flour of an imaginary sack is never sold at a real one.

What the Mercury called the bread {{revolt}} — a revolt being a rising of many against authority — began with arithmetic. On the ninth of March a weaver's wife {{challenge}}d — to challenge meaning to call in question, to put to the test — the clerk's reckoning at the corn table, aloud, before the whole market; the clerk, {{offend}}ed — to offend meaning to displease, to wound dignity — by the arithmetic, said the figure was not hers to check; and the square went from argument to crowd, and the crowd grew {{aggressive}} — aggressive meaning ready to quarrel, quick to threaten — in the way of crowds, which are hungry men multiplied. The magistrates came out onto the corn exchange steps, halved the assize price of the loaf to {{prevent}} — to prevent meaning to stop a thing before it can happen — the square filling twice, and sent for the dragoons, who arrived as a {{threat}} — a threat being a declared intention to do harm — and stayed as a decoration. Those who {{rebel}}led — to rebel meaning to rise against those in authority — were weavers, quarrymen and two sailors home from the coast; the dragoons, who had eaten, did not {{pursue}} — to pursue meaning to follow after, to chase — them far, the sergeant remarking that a man cannot be arrested for wanting his dinner.

That same winter the coverts of the Hall were {{trespass}}ed — to trespass meaning to enter another's ground without right — nightly, by men with snares; the river was netted by lamplight; the keepers, {{intrude|intruding}} — to intrude meaning to come in where one is not wanted — on the saltings at low water, found the eel-traps and mentioned them to nobody, having families; and every game law in the county was {{violate}}d — to violate meaning to break, to treat law or property with force — with a clear conscience and a quiet kitchen.

The vicar, who had {{oppose}}d — to oppose meaning to set oneself against, to resist by argument — the harsher rules since November, preached in April on the text Consider the Ravens, and told the vestry from the pulpit that the valley was being {{oppress}}ed — to oppress meaning to burden, to govern cruelly — by tolls, game laws and a poor law built for a different hunger. The ringleaders were bound over; one of them, a weaver named Hall, told the bench he was no criminal but a {{patriot}} — a patriot being one who loves his country and means to better it — which the bench found novel; the vicar, unable to let it pass entirely, {{reproach}}ed — to reproach meaning to blame, to express disappointment to a person's face — him gently for the word, and engaged him that same week to mend the church clock, at which trade he proved excellent, and was kept for forty years.

The flour never appeared under the counter, because it had never been there. In June the American wheat came in, the price fell like a barometer, and the vestry ordered the minutes of that spring rebound in leather — which the Mercury called an economy and history calls an index of shame. The famine killed no one in Millbrook, which was luck; and the memory of it kept the soup kitchen open for ninety years, which was not luck at all.
tr:
磨坊溪把一年单独归为一类。一八四六年，土豆像别处一样一齐歉收；小麦长得稀疏；到一八四七年二月，本教区已与饥荒（famine，famine 指普遍的粮食断绝、作为一种公共状态的饥饿）打了照面。

兰普福德银行的倒闭夺走了（deprive，deprive 指剥夺、夺走）织工们的冬季活计；原本以可管理的方式贫穷着的家庭，在两个季结日之间变得一贫如洗（destitute，destitute 指彻底没有钱、粮与生计）。他们的困境（plight，plight 指艰难可悲的处境）由教区委员会按月审议，并载入会议记录，墨迹分明。

济贫委员们的两难（dilemma，dilemma 指两个都很糟的选项之间的抉择）是老一套：在习艺所的墙外赈济饥民，就把税额养成了贫民；恪守规章，就看着孩子们在大街上挨饿（starve，starve 指因缺粮而受苦或死去）——而良心就住在街上。济贫法自有它的陷阱（pitfall，pitfall 指暗藏的圈套、地图上不标注的危险），委员们一字不差地照章办事，结果一个不落地全掉了进去：院外救济被禁止（prohibit，prohibit 指以规章或权力明令禁止）发给有劳力者；大门口的施舍作为对穷人的腐蚀被叫停；习艺所本身就是为威慑（deter，deter 指以对后果的恐惧加以吓阻）而建的，而且确实吓阻住了。教区委员会还曾禁止（forbid，forbid 指下令不许做某事）安息日烤面包，而面包师们整个冬天都在为门前的长队烤，于是一个不落地被罚款。

到了三月，镇上找到了比面包便宜的东西：一个解释。一桩把面粉扣下不卖的阴谋（conspiracy，conspiracy 指若干人共谋做坏事的秘密计划）在“朝阳”酒馆的雅间里被发现——或者说被发明。磨坊主被指为罪魁（blame，blame 指把过错归于），罪名是从未存在过的一袋袋面粉；尽管从没有过任何证据（evidence，evidence 指信念的依据、为讲明事情而摆出的事实），也从没有过任何证明（proof，proof 指把事情定死到无可辩驳的证据），一个饥饿的镇子是不肯如此精细地称量的。此外还有传闻说，每星期四在“朝阳”酒馆的柜台（counter，counter 指买卖货品的台面；柜台底下，即私底下、违规地）底下能买到面粉——这对“朝阳”酒馆是新闻，不过一只想象中的口袋里的面粉，从来不会在真的柜台上卖。

《信使报》所称的面包暴动（revolt，revolt 指众人对当权者的反抗）始于一道算术题。三月九日，一位织工的妻子当着整个集市，大声质疑（challenge，challenge 指提出质疑、加以检验）玉米摊上书记员的账目；书记员被这道算术冒犯了（offend，offend 指使不悦、伤尊严），说这个数字轮不到她来核；广场便从一场争论变成一群人，人群也像人群惯常的那样变得咄咄逼人（aggressive，aggressive 指好斗、动辄威胁）起来——人群无非是饥饿的人的倍数。治安官们走上谷物交易所的台阶，把法定面包价砍半，以防（prevent，prevent 指在一件事发生之前拦住它）广场第二次挤满，同时派人去请龙骑兵；龙骑兵作为一种威胁（threat，threat 指宣称要行伤害的表示）而来，作为一种摆设而留了下来。起来反抗（rebel，rebel 指奋起反抗当权者）的是织工、采石工和两个从海边回家的水手；吃过了饭的龙骑兵没有追捕（pursue，pursue 指追赶、追击）多远，中士说，一个人不能因为想吃晚饭而被捕。

同一个冬天，庄园的灌木林夜夜被人非法擅入（trespass，trespass 指无权进入他人地界）；河上有人趁灯火下网；猎场看守在退潮时闯进（intrude，intrude 指进入不受欢迎之地）盐沼，发现了鳗笼，却对谁都没有声张——他们也有家小；县里的每一条狩猎法都被违反（violate，violate 指破坏、以强力对待法律或产权），怀着清白的良心和安静的厨房。

十一月起就反对（oppose，oppose 指以言论抵制、反对）苛规的牧师，四月份以“想想乌鸦”为题讲道，从讲坛上告诉教区委员会：这条河谷正被通行税、狩猎法和一部为另一种饥荒设计的济贫法所压迫（oppress，oppress 指盘剥、苛虐地治理）。为首的人被具结开释；其中一名叫霍尔的织工对法官说，他不是罪犯，而是爱国者（patriot，patriot 指热爱并想改善其国家的人）——法官觉得这个说法很新鲜；牧师不能全然放过这句话，当面轻责（reproach，reproach 指当面责备、表示失望）了他，但当周就雇他去修教堂的大钟，这门手艺他干得出色，一留就是四十年。

面粉从未在柜台底下出现，因为它从未在那里。六月，美洲小麦运到，粮价像晴雨表一样落下来；教区委员会下令把那年春天的会议记录用皮革重新装订——《信使报》称之为节俭，历史称之为羞耻的索引。饥荒没有夺走磨坊溪一个人的性命，那是运气；对它的记忆让施粥所开了九十年，那就完全不是运气了。

quiz.q: The parish was looking famine in the face — a general failure of food, hunger as a public condition. Famine is —
o: a hidden trap in a course of action
a choice between two bad things
a secret plan by several persons
quiz.ex: famine = 饥荒。famine relief 饥荒救济；crop failure leading to famine 歉收酿成饥荒。

quiz.q: Families that had been poor in a manageable way became destitute — utterly without money, food or means. Destitute means —
o: burdened by tolls and game laws
quiz.ex: destitute = 穷困的；赤贫的。destitute families 赤贫家庭；be left destitute 变得一贫如洗。

quiz.q: The guardians' dilemma was the old one: pauperise the rates, or watch the children starve — a choice between two things, both of them bad. A dilemma is —
o: a rising of many against authority
a choice between two bad things
quiz.ex: dilemma = 困境；进退两难。face a dilemma 面临两难；an ethical dilemma 伦理困境。

quiz.q: The poor law had its pitfalls, and the guardians fell into every one — a hidden trap, a danger not marked on the map. A pitfall is —
o: a hidden trap or unsuspected danger
the assize price of a loaf
quiz.ex: pitfall = 陷阱；隐藏的危险。the pitfalls of the scheme 该计划的隐患；avoid common pitfalls 避开常见的坑。

quiz.q: A conspiracy to hold back the flour was discovered, or invented, in the tap-room — a secret plan by several persons to do wrong. A conspiracy is —
o: a secret plan by several to do wrong
the table over which goods are sold
quiz.ex: conspiracy = 阴谋；共谋。a conspiracy theory 阴谋论；conspire v. 密谋。

quiz.q: Outdoor relief was prohibited to the able-bodied — to forbid by rule or authority. To prohibit is to —
o: halve the price of a loaf
strip men of their winter work
quiz.ex: prohibit = 禁止。be prohibited from doing 被禁止做……；prohibition n. 禁令。

quiz.q: The workhouse was built to deter, and did — to discourage, by fear of consequences. To deter is to —
quiz.ex: deter = 威慑；阻止。deter crime 震慑犯罪；nuclear deterrent 核威慑力量。

quiz.q: The coverts of the Hall were trespassed nightly by men with snares — to enter another's ground without right. To trespass is to —
quiz.ex: trespass = 非法侵入。No trespassing! 禁止擅入！trespass on sb.'s time 占用他人时间（引申）。

title: The Man Who Measured the Bridge
text:
He came in the March of 1941, on the milk train, with a suitcase and a wooden box of instruments, and took a room at the Bull: a quiet man in a good coat, who said he was a surveyor and paid for a fortnight in advance. His name was Lawton; and Millbrook, being at war, was professionally interested in strangers.

The war had brought rules to the valley. There were no maps in the shop window; the signposts had come down; the camera shop was shut; and there was a {{limit}} — a limit being the line beyond which a thing may not pass — on every kind of curiosity. The Home Guard drilled on Tuesdays; the colonel, retired, of the Pudding Lane Hartes, held them on a loose {{rein}} — a rein being the strap by which a horse is governed, and so any check or control — and the colonel's daughter, who drove the ambulance, held a tighter one on the colonel. The papers that spring were full of the fifth column — saboteurs dressed as nuns, {{enemy}} — enemy meaning belonging to the other side — agents with cameras in their hatbands — and the fifth column had given the countryside a taste of {{terror}} — terror being great, mastering fear — out of all proportion to its visits, of which there had been none. It was a {{turbulent}} — turbulent meaning unquiet, stormy, disordered — year in any case; and the {{tension}} — tension being the stretched, waiting state of a thing near breaking — of the whole country settled in the smallest parishes like dust.

Mr. Lawton spent his days at the viaduct. He set up a brass instrument on a tripod; he walked the spans with a tape; he took notes in a neat book; and on the Thursday he was seen — by Mrs. Prout, from the allotment, at a range of two hundred yards, through the bean sticks — to make a drawing of the central pier. The drawing, she said, had been done with care. {{Alarm}} — alarm being fear of coming danger, and the signal of it — spread at the speed of Mrs. Prout. By Friday the town was in a {{turmoil}} — turmoil being confused trouble, everything moving and nothing settled — of rumour: that he had been signalling to the estuary with a torch; that the milk train had brought him wireless valves in his suitcase; that the guesthouse cat had taken a dislike to him, cats being notorious judges of character. The rumours were {{horrible}} — horrible meaning dreadful, exciting horror — and improved in the telling.

The colonel, {{warn}}ed — to warn meaning to give notice of danger beforehand — on the Friday evening, considered his duty until midnight. He had a {{scenario}} — a scenario being an imagined course of events, an outline of what may happen — for everything: invasion by glider, by barge, by parachutist dressed as a nun; and in none of them was there room for a man with a tripod and a fortnight's rent paid honestly. On Saturday he turned out the Home Guard in {{force}} — force being strength, numbers; in force, in numbers and strength — and Mr. Lawton was arrested at the viaduct at ten in the morning, in a {{terrific}} — terrific meaning, in the old use, terrifying; in the new use, splendid — gale, which had been {{frighten}}ing — to frighten meaning to fill with fear — the children since breakfast. The arrest itself was dignified. Mr. Lawton said he was sorry for the trouble; the colonel said the trouble would be his; and the prisoner was conducted to the police house with an escort of eight men and the entire town at the windows.

The wooden box was opened in the parlour, in the presence of the constable, the vicar and the colonel's daughter. It held: the brass instrument; the tape; a flask of tea; a roll of drawings — {{blueprint}}s — a blueprint being the engineer's drawing, white lines on blue paper — of the viaduct, every pier, every span, the abutments and the culverts; and a letter in a Ministry envelope, which nobody read, the envelope being thought the less convincing part.

The letter was the whole of it. Mr. Lawton was a civil engineer, employed by the Ministry to survey the county's bridges for demolition: so that, if the invasion came, the viaduct could be brought down before the enemy could use it. The drawings were the proof of his honesty; and the envelope, which had been opened and resealed, was the proof of nobody else's. The colonel's daughter read it aloud, twice, the second time to the colonel.

Mr. Lawton {{protest}}ed — to protest meaning to assert, to maintain publicly — that he had told no one because the scheme was secret; the Defence Regulations {{compel}}led — to compel meaning to force, to leave no choice — his silence, and the same regulations {{oblige}}d — to oblige meaning to bind by duty or law — every citizen to report strangers, so that the colonel had also been right. The vicar said the town had much to answer for; the constable said the arrest was in order; and the colonel, having said a great many things, none of them to the point, was {{order}}ed — to order meaning to command — home by his own daughter.

She it was who {{refute}}d — to refute meaning to prove wrong, to beat an argument — the rumour, publicly, on the market day: standing on the corn exchange steps with the letter and the blueprints, saying, in the voice she used for the ambulance, that the man the town had arrested had spent two weeks preparing to save it. The gale, which had {{impair}}ed — to impair meaning to weaken, to make worse — the telephones since Friday, chose that hour to drop a branch on the Bull's sign, which {{reinforce}}d — to reinforce meaning to strengthen, to add support to — nobody's argument but was taken by both sides as a sign.

The two guesthouses of Millbrook, which before the war had {{compete}}d — to compete meaning to strive against another for the same thing — for the summer visitors, and since for evacuees, put out {{rival}} notices of apology; and each landlady {{contend}}ed — to contend meaning to assert, to claim; and also, to struggle — that the other's guest had done the arresting, each being now, for the first time in memory, an honest {{competitor}} — a competitor being one who competes, a rival in trade — and meaning to be outdone by nobody in courtesy. The apology itself became, for a fortnight, a public {{contest}} — a contest being a competition, a striving for superiority — between the Mercury, which had printed the rumour, and the town council, which had enjoyed it. Mrs. Prout, who had started it all with the bean sticks, took to her room, and was brought down at last by her sister, who argued with all her {{might}} — might being strength, power — and a hot-water bottle. The vicar, hoping to {{mitigate}} — to mitigate meaning to make less severe, to soften — the town's embarrassment, preached that Sunday on the sin of suspicion; and the {{matter}} — a matter being a business, an affair, a thing requiring dealing with — was considered closed when Mr. Lawton attended evensong and sang the third verse of Onward, Christian Soldiers unaided. It had been, whatever the ending, a {{terrible}} — terrible meaning dreadful, causing great distress — fortnight.
tr:
他是一九四一年三月来的，搭早班奶火车，带着一只提箱和一木箱仪器，在“公牛”客栈要了个房间：一个穿好大衣的安静男人，自称测量员，预付了两周的房钱。他姓劳顿；而磨坊溪正处于战争中，对陌生人有着职业性的兴趣。

战争给河谷带来了规矩。橱窗里不再摆地图；指路牌拆掉了；照相馆关了门；每一种好奇心都有一条界线（limit，limit 指某事物不得逾越之线）。本土防卫军每逢周二操练；退休的上校——布丁巷哈特家的——用一根松松的缰绳（rein，rein 指驾驭马的皮带，引申为一切约束）牵着他们；而开救护车的上校之女，用更紧的一根牵着上校。那年春天，报纸上全是“第五纵队”——扮成修女的破坏者、帽带上藏相机的敌方（enemy，enemy 指属于敌对一方的）特务——而第五纵队让乡间尝到了恐惧（terror，terror 指巨大的、压倒一切的害怕）的滋味，与其来访的次数全然不成比例——它一次也没来过。无论如何，那都是个动荡（turbulent，turbulent 指不平静的、风雨飘摇的）年头；整个国家的紧张（tension，tension 指临近断裂之物的绷紧等待状态）像尘埃一样，落进了最小的教区。

劳顿先生在高架桥边度过他的白天。他在三脚架上架起一台黄铜仪器；他拿着卷尺走过一跨跨桥孔；他在一个整洁的本子上做记录；星期四，他被普劳特太太看见了——从菜地上，隔着两百码，透过豆架——正在画中间那座桥墩。她说，那张图画得很用心。惊惶（alarm，alarm 指对将至危险的恐惧，及其信号）以普劳特太太的速度传开。到星期五，全镇已陷入流言的骚乱（turmoil，turmoil 指乱作一团的麻烦，事事在动、无一落定）：说他夜里打手电朝河口发信号；说奶火车在他的提箱里给他捎来了电子管；说客栈的猫对他起了反感——猫向来是出了名的看人专家。这些流言骇人听闻（horrible，horrible 指可怕的、令人毛骨悚然的），而且越传越精。

上校在星期五晚上得到提醒（warn，warn 指预先告知危险），把他的职责考虑到了半夜。他为什么情况都备好了一套想定（scenario，scenario 指想象中的事件进程）：滑翔机入侵、驳船入侵、扮成修女的伞兵入侵；而哪一套里都容不下一个带着三脚架、老老实实预付两周房钱的人。星期六，他率本土防卫军倾巢出动（in force，force 指力量、人数；in force 即大队人马地），上午十点在高架桥逮捕了劳顿先生——正赶上一场狂风（terrific，terrific 旧义指骇人的，新义指极好的），那风从早饭起就一直在吓（frighten，frighten 指使充满恐惧）孩子们。逮捕本身是有尊严的。劳顿先生说他很抱歉添了麻烦；上校说这麻烦将会是他的；押着八名卫兵和趴满窗口的全镇人，犯人被送进了警察所。

木箱在客厅里当着警察、牧师和上校之女的面被打开。里面是：那台黄铜仪器；卷尺；一保温瓶茶；一卷图纸——蓝图（blueprint，blueprint 指工程师的白线蓝底图纸）——画着高架桥，每一座桥墩、每一跨、桥台和涵洞；还有一封装在部里信封里的信——没有人读它，因为大家觉得信封是全案最没有说服力的部分。

这封信就是全部真相。劳顿先生是一名土木工程师，受部里雇用，勘察本县的桥梁以备爆破：这样一来，一旦敌人入侵，高架桥就能赶在他们利用之前被炸掉。那些图纸是他诚实的证明；而那个被拆开又重新封上的信封，则证明不了任何别人的什么。上校之女把它大声读了两遍，第二遍是读给上校的。

劳顿先生申明（protest，protest 指公开坚称、申言）他谁也没告诉，是因为计划属于机密；《国防条例》强制（compel，compel 指强迫、令人无从选择）他保持沉默，而同一条例又要求（oblige，oblige 指以义务约束）每个公民报告形迹可疑的陌生人——所以上校也没有错。牧师说，这个镇有很多要交代的地方；警察说逮捕手续合规；上校说了许许多多话，没有一句在点子上，被自己的女儿命令（order，order 指命令）回了家。

驳倒（refute，refute 指证明其错、驳倒论点）流言的正是她，在集市日当众：她拿着那封信和蓝图站在谷物交易所的台阶上，用她喊救护车的那种嗓音说，全镇逮捕的这个人，花了两周时间准备拯救它。从星期五起就一直在损坏（impair，impair 指削弱、使变糟）电话线路的狂风，偏偏挑了那个钟点往“公牛”客栈的招牌上砸下一根树枝，什么论点也没加强（reinforce，reinforce 指加固、增援），却被双方各自认作一种征兆。

磨坊溪的两家客栈——战前为夏日游客而互相争（compete，compete 指与他人争夺同一目标）抢、此后又争抢疏散儿童的两家——各自贴出了打擂台（rival，rival 指竞争的、对着干的）式的道歉启事；两位老板娘各自坚称（contend，contend 指声称、主张，也指搏斗），动手抓人的是对方那位客人——此刻双方都是有史以来头一回成了名副其实的竞争者（competitor，competitor 指竞争之人、同行），谁也不肯在礼数上输给谁。道歉本身在两周里成了一场公开的较量（contest，contest 指竞赛、角逐）——较量的双方，一边是刊登过流言的《信使报》，一边是津津有味享受过流言的镇议会。以豆架掀起全部风波的普劳特太太闭门不出，最后是被她妹妹弄下楼来的——妹妹使出全部力气（might，might 指力量）跟她吵了两天，外加一只热水袋。牧师希望缓解（mitigate，mitigate 指减轻、使之不那么严重）全镇的难堪，那个周日以“猜疑之罪”为题讲道；而这件事（matter，matter 指一件须了结的事务）被认定为已了结，是在劳顿先生出席晚祷、独自唱完《信徒精兵歌》第三节的那一刻。无论结局如何，那都曾是可怕的（terrible，terrible 指骇人的、令人极其痛苦的）两个星期。

quiz.q: A roll of drawings — blueprints — of the viaduct: the engineer's drawing, white lines on blue paper. A blueprint is —
o: a secret plan by several persons
the strap by which a horse is governed
quiz.ex: blueprint = 蓝图；（引申）详细方案。a blueprint for reform 改革蓝图。

quiz.q: She it was who refuted the rumour — to prove wrong, to beat an argument. To refute is to —
quiz.ex: refute = 驳倒；反驳。refute an accusation 驳斥指控；refutation n. 驳斥。

quiz.q: The Defence Regulations compelled his silence — to force, to leave no choice. To compel is to —
quiz.ex: compel = 强迫；迫使。compel sb. to do 迫使某人做；compelling evidence 令人信服的证据。

quiz.q: The regulations obliged every citizen to report strangers — to bind by duty or law. To oblige is to —
o: force with no choice at all
quiz.ex: oblige = （按义务、法律）迫使；施惠。be obliged to do 不得不做；much obliged 多谢（口语）。

quiz.q: He was arrested in a terrific gale — in the old use, terrifying; in the new use, splendid. Terrific means —
quiz.ex: terrific = 极好的；（古义/严格义）可怕的。a terrific storm 可怕的暴风雨；a terrific idea 好主意。

quiz.q: The colonel held the Home Guard on a loose rein — the strap by which a horse is governed, and so any check or control. A rein is —
o: the line curiosity may not pass
the strap governing a horse; any control
a strength, a body of numbers
quiz.ex: rein = 缰绳；控制。keep a tight rein on 严加管束；rein in one's temper 克制脾气。

quiz.q: Each landlady contended that the other's guest had done the arresting — to assert, to claim; and also, to struggle. To contend is to —
quiz.ex: contend = 声称；竞争，搏斗。contend that... 坚称……；contend with difficulties 与困难搏斗。

quiz.q: The vicar, hoping to mitigate the town's embarrassment — to make less severe, to soften. To mitigate is to —
o: spread at the speed of rumour
quiz.ex: mitigate = 减轻；缓和。mitigate the effects 减轻影响；mitigating circumstances 可减轻罪行的情节。

title: The Reckoning
text:
The Mercury had called him, on the Saturday, THE SPY OF THE VIADUCT, in the way of newspapers, and sold out; and on the Monday, when the letter had been read on the corn exchange steps, it called him THE MAN WHO SAVED MILLBROOK, and sold out again. The first headline had been {{reckless}} — reckless meaning utterly careless of consequences — and the second, being equally certain, no better; and it was pointed out afterwards, chiefly by the Mercury, that the two headlines described the same gentleman in the same type, to which it was replied, chiefly by everybody else, that a paper which cannot tell a spy from an engineer should give both words a rest.

What followed the apology is the part the town preferred not to reprint. The colonel was {{humiliate}}d — to humiliate meaning to lower in dignity, to put to open shame — twice over: once by the mistake, which was public, and once by his daughter's competence, which was permanent. His letters to the Ministry were {{savage}} — savage meaning fierce and pitiless — in their defence of the arrest; the Ministry's replies were polite, and copied to his daughter, which he found {{fierce}} — fierce meaning violent, intense, of great heat — beyond bearing. The worst of the rumour had whispered {{foul}} — foul meaning wicked, unfair, against fair play — play: that the arrest was a private settling of scores with the bridge company, the colonel having old accounts there. Nothing came of it; but nothing, in the way of rumour, ever quite goes away either.

The arrest had cost more than dignity. The tripod came down badly on the wet sleepers and the brass instrument was {{damage}}d — to damage meaning to harm, to spoil the soundness of — past the county's mending. The Ministry's letter to the colonel said he had {{interfere}}d — to interfere meaning to meddle, to get in the way of what others are doing — with works of national importance, which was the kindest sentence in it. The scheme itself had been {{compromise}}d — to compromise meaning to weaken, to put at risk — by the publicity: the original drawings had to be {{discard}}ed — to discard meaning to throw away as useless — and the charges at the piers recast, and the survey {{abandon}}ed — to abandon meaning to give up, to leave a thing for good — and begun again from the far side of the valley, at night, with a different engineer; a month of dark work gone with the newspaper. The constable, it emerged, had considered charging the colonel with {{disturb}}ing — to disturb meaning to break the quiet or order of — the peace, and had decided that the peace had been disturbed quite enough already.

The town read in its Monday paper what the law kept ready for the real thing, and read it for the first time. For the real thing the law kept a real {{punishment}} — a punishment being what is imposed on the wrongdoer, the price of a wrong—: two men had been {{hang}}ed — to hang meaning, in law, to put to death by the neck — in England that year for sabotage; agents caught in the field were {{execute}}d — to execute meaning to carry out; and so, of a sentence, to put to death — within the week. The town understood, over its breakfast, what it had very nearly done to a man with a tape and a flask of tea; and the understanding sat uncomfortably all day, the way true things do. Rumour, the vicar said, had {{mislead|misled}} — to mislead meaning to lead into wrong belief — the whole county; and the {{harmful}} — harmful meaning causing harm — part of a rumour is not that it is believed but that it is half remembered. He might have added that the imagination had {{torture}}d — to torture meaning to inflict great pain upon; and by extension, to cause extreme suffering — Mr. Lawton more thoroughly in one fortnight than the enemy had managed in the whole war.

The making-up was done thoroughly, in the town's manner. The council, wishing to {{rid}} — to rid meaning to make free of, to clear away — itself of the affair, voted an address of thanks; the two guesthouses {{contribute}}d — to contribute meaning to give toward a common end — a dinner between them; the vicar, who had {{defend}}ed — to defend meaning to stand up for, to protect — Mr. Lawton from the first, gave the toast; and Mr. Lawton, who was {{owe}}d — to owe meaning to be in debt for, to have coming — more than a dinner, said the town had done what towns do, suspect in the dark and correct by daylight, and that he counted his own fortnight a small {{sacrifice}} — a sacrifice being the giving up of something valued, for a purpose — beside the work. The toast was {{interrupt}}ed — to interrupt meaning to break in upon — by the siren, which everyone present felt to be editorial. He was entitled to compensation for the instrument and chose, in writing, in four words, to {{forgo}} — to forgo meaning to do without, to give up by choice — it.

He {{devote}}d — to devote meaning to give up wholly, to dedicate — the rest of the war to the county's crossings, valley by valley, with a new tripod and the same flask; and the scheme he had begun — to {{safeguard}} — to safeguard meaning to keep safe, to protect — the valley's bridges — was finished, in the event, without ever being needed, which is the best ending such schemes have. He was seen at the Bull twice more, once settling the bill and once retrieving the flask from the dartboard; he did not {{escape}} — to escape meaning to get free of, to get clear of — the nickname, and signed the visitors' book, the one time he did, as The Spy. He {{avoid}}ed — to avoid meaning to keep away from — the town afterwards, from delicacy or self-preservation; and the town {{shrink|shrank}} — to shrink meaning to draw back; and to grow less — from him in the street, which he said he found restful. Mrs. Prout, who could no longer look a bridge in the face, {{quit}} — to quit meaning to leave, to depart from — the parish for her sister's before the beans came in.

The Reckoning is the only one of Millbrook's histories with a printed sequel: the file was opened in 1975, and the Mercury, under new management, printed the demolition scheme entire — piers, charges, the Ministry's dry little letters — and called it, on the anniversary, THE QUIETEST VICTORY THE VALLEY EVER WON. The colonel's daughter, eighty-one, wrote to the paper that her father had been a good man in a bad fortnight, which the paper printed in full; and the paper's editor, who had not been born when any of it happened, telephoned her for permission, which is the closest thing to an apology that history affords.
tr:
星期六，《信使报》以报纸的方式称他为“高架桥的间谍”，销售一空；星期一，当那封信在谷物交易所台阶上被宣读之后，它又称他为“拯救磨坊溪的人”，再度销售一空。第一条标题是不负后果的（reckless，reckless 指全然不计后果的），第二条同样言之凿凿，也好不到哪里去；事后有人指出——主要是《信使报》自己——两条标题用同一种铅字描写的是同一位绅士；得到的回答是——主要是其他所有人——一家分不清间谍和工程师的报纸，两个词都该歇歇了。

道歉之后的部分，是这个镇宁愿不再重印的。上校被羞辱（humiliate，humiliate 指使丢脸、当众折辱）了两次：一次因为那个错误，它是公开的；一次因为女儿的能干，它是永久的。他写给部里的信在为那次逮捕辩护时凶狠（savage，savage 指凶猛而不留情面的）无比；部里的回信客气有礼，且抄送了他的女儿，他觉得这比什么都火辣辣地（fierce，fierce 指激烈的、灼热的）难以忍受。流言最恶毒的一支则窃窃说着卑劣（foul，foul 指卑鄙的、违背公平竞赛的）把戏：说那次逮捕是跟桥梁公司的一笔私账，上校在那里有旧怨。什么也没查出来；但流言这种东西，从来也不会彻底走开。

逮捕的代价不止于体面。三脚架在湿漉漉的枕木上摔得不好，那台黄铜仪器损坏（damage，damage 指损害、毁坏其完好）得本县修不好了。部里给上校的信里说他妨害（interfere，interfere 指插手、妨碍他人正做的事）了具有全国重要性的工程——这已是信里最客气的一句。爆破计划本身也因这番张扬而受连累（compromise，compromise 指削弱、使陷入风险）：原有图纸只能作废（discard，discard 指当废物丢掉）销毁，桥墩上的炸药重新布设，勘察半途而废（abandon，abandon 指放弃、彻底丢下），改在夜间从河谷另一侧由另一位工程师重新开始——一个月的暗中辛苦，跟着报纸一起没了。后来才知道，警察当时考虑过以扰乱（disturb，disturb 指打破……的安静或秩序）治安罪指控上校，又觉得治安已经被扰得够多了，作罢。

小镇在星期一的报纸上读到了法律为“真货”备着的东西，而且是头一回认真读。为真货，法律备着真的惩罚（punishment，punishment 指施加于作恶者的处分、过错的代价）：那一年，英格兰已有两人因破坏罪被处以绞刑（hang，hang 在法律意义上指处以绞刑）；战场上抓获的特工在一周内被处决（execute，execute 指执行，故指执行死刑）。全镇在早餐桌上明白了，他们差一点对一个带着卷尺和一保温瓶茶的人做出什么；这份明白让人一整天都坐立不安——真话向来如此。牧师说，流言误导（mislead，mislead 指引入错误信念）了整个郡；而流言有害（harmful，harmful 指造成伤害的）之处不在于人们相信它，而在于人们半信半疑地记得它。他本可以再加一句：在两周之内，想象力对劳顿先生的拷打（torture，torture 指施以酷刑，引申为造成极大痛苦），比敌人在整场战争里做到的更彻底。

补救做得很周到，用的是这个镇的方式。镇议会想摆脱（rid，rid 指使摆脱、清除掉）这件事，表决通过了一份致敬书；两家客栈合力凑（contribute，contribute 指为共同之事出资出力）了一场晚宴；从一开始就为劳顿先生辩护（defend，defend 指维护、捍卫）的牧师致了祝酒词；而劳顿先生——全镇欠（owe，owe 指欠着、应得而未得）他的远不止一顿晚宴——说，这个镇做了镇子惯做的事：黑暗里猜疑，天亮后纠正；比起那项工程，他自己那两周不过是一次小小的牺牲（sacrifice，sacrifice 指为某一目的舍弃珍视之物）。祝酒词被警报打断（interrupt，interrupt 指打断、中途闯入）了，在场所有人都觉得这一声颇有社论意味。那台仪器他有权索赔，却用书面形式、四个词，选择放弃（forgo，forgo 指舍弃、自愿不要）了。

他把战争余下的岁月全部献给（devote，devote 指献身于、专心致志于）本县的道道桥梁，一条河谷接一条河谷，用的是新的三脚架和同一只保温瓶；他着手的那项工程——为的是保卫（safeguard，safeguard 指保护、使安全）河谷诸桥——最终完成了，却从未派上用场，这是此类工程能有的最好结局。人们又两次在“公牛”客栈见到他：一次结账，一次从飞镖盘上取回保温瓶；他没能摆脱（escape，escape 指逃脱、脱开）那个绰号，唯一一次在留言簿上签名时，写的是“间谍”。此后他避开（avoid，avoid 指躲开、避开）这个镇，出于体贴也好、自保也好；而镇上的人在街上见到他也退缩（shrink，shrink 指畏缩，也指缩小）——他说，这倒让他清静。普劳特太太再也无颜面对一座桥，豆子还没下来就离开（quit，quit 指离开、退出）本教区，投奔她妹妹去了。

“了断”是磨坊溪全部历史中唯一有印刷续篇的一件：档案一九七五年开放，《信使报》在新东家手里，把爆破计划原原本本印了出来——桥墩、炸药、部里那些干巴巴的小信——并在周年纪念日称它为“河谷赢得过的最安静的胜利”。上校的女儿八十一岁，写信告诉报社，她父亲是个好人，只是赶上了一个糟糕的两周，报纸一字未删地登了；而那位当年这一切发生时尚未出生的主编，为刊登之事打电话征得了她的同意——这是历史所能提供的最接近道歉的东西。

quiz.q: Agents caught in the field were executed within the week — to carry out; and so, of a sentence, to put to death. To execute is to —
o: carry out; of a sentence, put to death
quiz.ex: execute = 执行；处决。execute a plan 执行计划；execute sb. for treason 以叛国罪处决某人。

quiz.q: The colonel was humiliated twice over — to lower in dignity, to put to open shame. To humiliate is to —
o: give up wholly to a scheme
lower in dignity, put to open shame
quiz.ex: humiliate = 羞辱；使丢脸。a humiliating defeat 羞辱性的失败；humiliation n. 耻辱。

quiz.q: The scheme itself had been compromised by the publicity — to weaken, to put at risk. To compromise is to —
o: charge a man with the peace
quiz.ex: compromise = 使受损；妥协；折中方案。compromise security 危及安全；reach a compromise 达成妥协。

quiz.q: He chose, in writing, in four words, to forgo the compensation — to do without, to give up by choice. To forgo is to —
o: be in debt for a dinner
do without, give up by choice
quiz.ex: forgo = 放弃；弃绝（正式用语）。forgo a raise 放弃加薪；forgone conclusion（其实为 foregone）既定结局。

quiz.q: The scheme to safeguard the valley's bridges — to keep safe, to protect. To safeguard is to —
quiz.ex: safeguard = 保护；保障措施。safeguard interests 维护利益；safeguards against abuse 防止滥用的保障。

quiz.q: The original drawings had to be discarded — to throw away as useless. To discard is to —
quiz.ex: discard = 丢弃；抛弃。discard old beliefs 抛弃旧观念；discarded clothes 被丢弃的衣服。

quiz.q: The first headline had been reckless — utterly careless of consequences. Reckless means —
quiz.ex: reckless = 鲁莽的；不计后果的。reckless driving 鲁莽驾驶；recklessness n. 鲁莽。

quiz.q: Mr. Lawton, who was owed more than a dinner — to be in debt for, to have coming. To owe is to —
o: be in debt for, have coming
quiz.ex: owe = 欠（债/情）；应归功于。owe sb. an apology 欠某人一个道歉；owe much to luck 多亏运气。

title: The Heart Across the Water
text:
The estuary, which had kept its peace since the Armada cannon sank (see room two), acquired in 1962 a neighbour: a {{nuclear}} — nuclear meaning of the nucleus, the heart of the atom; and so of the power that comes out of it — power station, begun on the far marsh at Ozzleford, and visible from Millbrook church tower as a pale geometry with one white chimney.

The fishing families, whose {{fleet}} — a fleet being a number of vessels under one ownership or purpose — of oyster smacks had worked the beds for nine generations, were not converted by the brochure. They heard that the station would pour its cooling water back warm; that the chemicals would {{poison}} — to poison meaning to put poison into, to make deadly — the nursery grounds; and that the beds themselves would be {{devastate}}d — to devastate meaning to lay waste, to destroy utterly — inside a decade. The brochure said the station would be clean and kind. The fishermen observed that the brochure was printed by the company, and that herring could not read anyway; and the dispute settled into the long peace of such things: a public inquiry, a petition, a fortnight of letters in the Mercury — and work going forward all the while. The inquiry sat at Ozzleford through the spring; and while it heard the fishermen, and heard the company, the works {{proceed}}ed — to proceed meaning to go forward, to carry on — in the background of every photograph.

The {{progress}} — progress being advance, the going forward of a thing — of the works was watched from Millbrook with the ambivalence of a town within sight of money. The building men came over the bridge each morning in their hundreds; the old {{landing}} — a landing being a place where boats come ashore, a stage, a quay — at Ozzleford grew a pier of concrete; and the station's construction had a {{military}} — military meaning of soldiers, armies and war — tidiness about it: cranes, huts, a mess, a notice board with the shifts chalked on it.

That summer the Sea {{scout}}s — a scout being a member of the movement that trains boys in woodcraft and good turns; a scout also meaning one sent ahead to gather information — camped on the saltings below the works. The scoutmaster, before the first night, walked the saltings for two evenings running, {{spy}}ing — to spy meaning to watch secretly, to take note of by stealth — out the ground, as the verger said, like Joshua; and found it good, and the fish crates no obstacle at all. The troop ran its {{obstacle}} — an obstacle being a thing that stands in the way — race over the rubble and the crates; the scoutmaster taught them the channels and the one sand cliff at Cormorant Reach, which the tide undercuts, and which {{collapse}}d — to collapse meaning to fall in, to give way — that August, in the night, with no harm done and a great deal of interest. The rabbits, meanwhile, had been at the old sea wall for years: they {{burrow}} — to burrow meaning to dig a hole, to make a tunnel — into it so thoroughly that the flood of 1960 found their workings and the wall went with them; the new wall is concrete, and the rabbits, it is hoped, have retired to the golf course.

The war was still close enough to be furniture. The boatshed at the landing held, under the nets, a stack of {{camouflage}} — camouflage being the disguising of a thing, by paint or netting, so that it melts into its background — netting left from the forties, which the fishermen used for shading the oyster trays in hot weather; and the coastguard, on his evening {{patrol}} — a patrol being a regular going round, a beat — along the sea wall, still wore the manner, if not the coat, of the navy he had served in. He it was who saw the sloop.

She had come up on the afternoon tide under too much canvas, and grounded in the middle of the reach; and the wind was west and rising. The coastguard telephoned the lifeboat; the lifeboat, thirty years old and never once wanted in daylight, went out at five and was back by seven, having taken off two sailors, a dog, and the yacht's cushion. The yacht herself had been in {{peril}} — peril being grave danger — since four o'clock; the {{risk}} — risk being the chance of harm — to the crew was put at nothing by the crew and at everything by their wives, which is the custom; and the rescue was watched from the sea wall by the whole of Millbrook, and by a helicopter from the station, which came across the water and {{hover}}ed — to hover meaning to hang in the air above one place — above the mast for the better part of an hour, doing nothing whatever with great authority. It was the first helicopter most of the town had seen at close quarters, and it converted more opinions about the station than all the brochures of the company. The vicar said afterwards that mercy is the best argument for a technology, and that the oysters, given time, might come round to it too; the boys of the camp, for their part, told it ever after as an {{adventure}} — an adventure being a hazardous enterprise, an experience of risk — in which they had pulled six men from the sea, the true number being two men, a dog and a cushion.

The fishermen's fears were half fulfilled and half not: the beds thinned for three years and then held; the inquiry's conditions were kept, or broken, according to who tells it; and the station stands yet, white across the water, cooling its heart. The chief engineer at the opening ceremony was a retired {{naval}} — naval meaning of a navy — captain, who spoke of the station as a ship: steady, watchful, safe in a seaway; and the fishermen, who had come to count enemies by their grammar, found this a fair omen, ships being old friends. The county paper called the whole affair a chapter in the {{maritime}} — maritime meaning of the sea, of life and trade upon it — history of the coast; the Mercury called it THE HEART ACROSS THE WATER; and Mr. Pym, the curator, cross-referenced the clipping to the cannon in room two, which came out of the same estuary three hundred years earlier, and is the only other thing the water has ever sent the town. In between, the water has kept the peace.
tr:
河口自无敌舰队的大炮沉没以来一直保持着安宁（参见第二展室），一九六二年却得到了一位邻居：一座核（nuclear，nuclear 指原子核的，即原子之心，也指从中释放出的能量的）电站，在河对岸的奥泽尔福德滩涂上破土，从磨坊溪教堂塔上望去，是一片带着一根白烟囱的浅色几何体。

以九代人之力在牡蛎床上劳作的捕鱼人家——他们的船队（fleet，fleet 指同一船东或同一用途的一批船只）是些牡蛎单桅帆船——并没有被宣传册说服。他们听说电站会把冷却水加热后排回来；化学品会毒化（poison，poison 指把毒投入、使之含毒）育苗场；不出十年，牡蛎床本身也会被摧毁（devastate，devastate 指蹂躏、彻底毁掉）。宣传册说电站干净又和善。渔民们指出：宣传册是公司印的，何况鲱鱼反正不识字。于是这场争端落进此类事务惯有的长期和平：一场公开听证、一封请愿书、《信使报》上两周的读者来信——而工程始终照常推进。听证会整个春天都设在奥泽尔福德；它一面听取渔民的陈述，一面听取公司的陈述，而工程（proceed，proceed 指向前进行、继续下去）就在每一张照片的背景里进行着。

工程的进展（progress，progress 指推进、事物的向前行进）被磨坊溪以一种看得见钱影的小镇所特有的矛盾心态注视着。建筑工人每天清晨成百地过桥而来；奥泽尔福德的老登岸处（landing，landing 指船只靠岸的地方、码头）长出了一座混凝土栈桥；而电站的建造带着一种军事（military，military 指军人的、军队的）式的整洁：吊车、工棚、食堂，和一块用粉笔写着各班次的告示牌。

那年夏天，海童子军（scout，scout 指贝登堡创立的、训练男童野外技能与助人的那个团体的成员；也指被派在前面收集情报的人）在工地下方的盐沼上扎营。领队在第一夜之前，接连两个傍晚徒步踏勘盐沼，暗中察看（spy，spy 指暗中监视、窥探）那片地——用牧师的话说，像约书亚一样；他发现那地甚好，鱼筐也根本算不上障碍。童子军们在瓦砾和鱼筐之间进行障碍（obstacle，obstacle 指挡在路上的东西）赛跑；领队教他们认水道，认鸬鹚汊那座被潮水掏空的沙崖——那年八月它就在夜里坍塌（collapse，collapse 指塌陷、垮下）了，无人受伤，围观者众。与此同时，兔子们跟老海堤已较量多年：它们在堤里打洞（burrow，burrow 指掘穴、掏隧道）掏得太彻底，一九六〇年的洪水顺着它们的工程进了堤，海堤随之而去；新堤是混凝土的，据说兔子们已经告老，去了高尔夫球场。

战争还近得足以算作家什。登岸处的船棚里，渔网底下压着一叠四十年代剩下的伪装（camouflage，camouflage 指用涂料或网罩对事物加以掩饰，使其隐入背景）网，渔民们天热时拿它给牡蛎盘遮阳；海岸警卫队员傍晚沿着海堤例行巡逻（patrol，patrol 指按既定路线的巡视）时，身上仍带着他服役过的那支海军的做派——如果说制服已经不在了。看见那艘单桅小帆船的正是他。

她趁着午后的潮水张着过多的帆进来，在汊子中间搁了浅；风偏西，且越来越大。海岸警卫队员给救生艇打了电话；那艘服役三十年、白天从未被用过的救生艇五点出海，七点返航，救回两名水手、一条狗和那只游艇坐垫。游艇本身从四点起就一直处于险境（peril，peril 指严重的危险）；船员们把此行的风险（risk，risk 指遭受伤害的可能）说成没有，他们的妻子说成极大——这是惯例。整个磨坊溪都站在海堤上观看这次营救，电站的一架直升机也来了：它掠过水面，悬停（hover，hover 指停在空中某处上方不动）在桅杆上方足足大半个钟头，以十足的威严什么也没做。这是全镇多数人头一回近距离看见直升机，它为公司转变的舆论，比公司全部宣传册加起来还多。牧师后来说，仁慈是一项技术最好的论据，牡蛎假以时日，或许也会想通；至于露营的男孩子们，此后一直把这事讲成一场冒险（adventure，adventure 指有风险的壮举、涉险的经历）——他们从海里救起了六个人；实际数字是两个人、一条狗和一只坐垫。

渔民的担忧应验了一半，另一半没有：牡蛎床稀疏了三年，然后稳住了；听证会的条件有人遵守，有人违反——全看是谁在讲；而电站至今立在水的那一边，白白的，冷却着它的心。落成典礼上的总工程师是一位退休的海军（naval，naval 指海军的）上校，他把电站讲成一艘船：稳当、警觉、在风浪中安全；而习惯从措辞里数敌人的渔民们觉得这是个好兆头——船向来是老朋友。郡报把整件事称作海岸航海（maritime，maritime 指海的、海上生活与贸易的）史中的一章；《信使报》称之为“河对岸的那颗心”；馆长皮姆先生则把这篇剪报与第二展室的大炮做了互见索引——那门炮三百年前出自同一条河口，是这片水迄今为止送给本镇的仅有的一样别的东西。而在两者之间，这片水一直保持和平。

quiz.q: The county paper called it a chapter in the maritime history of the coast — of the sea, of life and trade upon it. Maritime means —
o: disguised to melt into the background
of the nucleus of the atom
of the sea, of life and trade upon it
quiz.ex: maritime = 海事的；航海的。maritime law 海事法；a maritime nation 海洋国家。

quiz.q: A helicopter came across the water and hovered above the mast — to hang in the air above one place. To hover is to —
o: hang in the air above one place
quiz.ex: hover = 盘旋；悬停；徘徊。a hovering helicopter 盘旋的直升机；hover between choices 犹豫不决。

quiz.q: A nuclear power station, begun on the far marsh — of the nucleus, the heart of the atom, and the power that comes out of it. Nuclear means —
o: of the atomic nucleus and its power
quiz.ex: nuclear = 核的；原子核的。nuclear power 核能；nuclear weapons 核武器。

quiz.q: The beds themselves would be devastated inside a decade — to lay waste, to destroy utterly. To devastate is to —
o: chalk the shifts on a board
quiz.ex: devastate = 毁灭；使荒废。be devastated by the flood 被洪水摧毁；devastating news 毁灭性的消息。

quiz.q: The rabbits burrow into the old sea wall — to dig a hole, to make a tunnel. To burrow is to —
o: dig a hole, make a tunnel
quiz.ex: burrow = 挖掘（地洞）；洞穴。rabbits burrowing into the bank 在堤岸里打洞的兔子；burrow into the duvet 钻进被子。

quiz.q: A stack of camouflage netting left from the forties — the disguising of a thing, by paint or netting, so that it melts into its background. Camouflage is —
o: the chance of harm to the crew
a regular going round, a beat
disguise that melts into the background
a place where boats come ashore
quiz.ex: camouflage = 伪装；迷彩。military camouflage 军事伪装；camouflaged tanks 伪装的坦克。

quiz.q: The yacht had been in peril since four o'clock — peril being grave danger. Peril is —
o: a sand cliff undercut by tide
a ship steady in a seaway
quiz.ex: peril = 严重危险。in peril of one's life 性命堪虞；perilous adj. 危险的。

quiz.q: While the inquiry heard both sides, the works proceeded — to go forward, to carry on. To proceed is to —
o: ground in the middle of the reach
keep the peace of the estuary
quiz.ex: proceed = 继续进行；着手。proceed with the plan 继续执行计划；proceedings n. 诉讼程序。

title: The Tree on the Wall
text:
The Millbrook Family History Society meets in the corn exchange on the second Thursday of the month, between the whist drive and the judo. Its president is Mrs. Vye, retired postmistress; its subject, this season, is Mrs. Vye; and its one lasting discovery is that every {{surname}} — a surname being the family name, carried after the Christian one — in the valley belongs, if you go back far enough and sideways enough, to everybody else's.

Mrs. Vye's own tree fills the back wall of her sitting room, six feet by nine, drawn in ink on lining paper. The first {{pioneer}} — a pioneer being one who goes first and opens the way for those behind — of her line was a Huguenot weaver who reached Millbrook in 1685 with a loom, a Bible and no English, and married the dyer's daughter inside a year, which is how far back the arguing goes. The second generation produced the family's permanent embarrassment: a {{prophet}} — a prophet being one who claims to speak for heaven and to foretell what is to come — who fixed the end of the world for 1743, and again for 1748, and who, when it twice failed to arrive, emigrated to Pennsylvania, where his descendants remain, cheerful and wrong. The third produced the family's only claim to ceremony: an uncle who was the town {{herald}} — a herald being, of old, an officer of arms; and by extension, one who makes announcements — and cried the fair, the assizes and the bread prices in the market square for forty years, in a voice the Mercury compared to a benevolent foghorn.

The mill passed, in the family's telling, from {{heir}} — an heir being one who inherits — to {{heir}} like a watch; though the Society's own detective work shows it more often passed sideways, so that the honest word for each holder is not heir but {{successor}} — a successor being one who follows another in a place or office, by inheritance or otherwise. It went sideways twice inside one decade: to a {{nephew}} — a nephew being the son of one's brother or sister — in 1802, and in 1809 to a {{niece}} — a niece being the daughter of one's brother or sister — who married out and took the deeds with her. Seven {{generation}}s — a generation being the span between one's birth and one's children's, roughly thirty years — of the family held it before the railway made the water wheel a curiosity. The first successor of all was the weaver's son, who married the miller's daughter and was taught the trade by his {{father-in-law}} — a father-in-law being the father of one's husband or wife — a transaction the old documents record with the warmth of a hire agreement. The {{couple}} — a couple being a pair joined, a married two — were wed in 1711, and their column of descendants runs off the bottom of the paper.

The sad pages are the honest ones. The old records set a small cross against every {{infant}} — an infant being a baby, a child in its first years — who did not see its second birthday; there are nine crosses on Mrs. Vye's wall. There is the {{orphan}} — an orphan being a child whose parents are dead — of the famine year, whom the family took in from the workhouse and kept, and whose line now flourishes in Adelaide. There are the {{twin}}s — twins being two children born of the same birth — of 1867, one of whom lived to be ninety and the other of whom is the cross third from the left; and there is the one {{juvenile}} — a juvenile being a young person, in the eyes of the law one not yet of age — who appears in the court book of 1874, fined sixpence for apples, an entry the family has decided to treat as colour.

The modern pages have caused the arguments. Two years ago the Society voted, after a debate that ran to two meetings and one apology, to add a column for {{gender}} — gender meaning the social state of being male or female — beside the old one for {{sex}} — sex meaning the biological classification into male and female — and to redraw the female line in red ink, where the old practice had followed the surname and dropped the women entire. The red ink, once it dried, showed what everyone had half known: the {{female}} — female meaning of the sex that bears children — line had been doing the inheriting all along, one daughter or daughter's daughter standing in every gap the male line left.

Cyril Vye, the president's {{cousin}}'s boy — a cousin being the child of one's uncle or aunt — came down from London with his {{husband}} — a husband being a married man — last spring. The valley had known that Cyril was {{gay}} — gay meaning attracted to persons of one's own sex — since he was sixteen, everybody having been told by everybody except Cyril; and the Society, after a moment, added the two of them to the paper as cheerfully as any {{couple}} that ever preceded them, Mrs. Vye entering Graham in the column headed {{spouse}} — a spouse being a married partner, husband or wife — which is what their certificate says, and what, she observes, the Society is for. Her {{grandfather}}'s letters, in the box beneath the tree, were written home from his years at sea; they address her grandmother as {{darling}} — a darling being a greatly loved one — in an ink that pressed through to the next page; and her grandmother's replies, written with her {{sibling}}s — siblings being brothers and sisters — shouting through the shop door, address him as Dear Fred, with the love rationed to the postscript, which the Society takes as evidence of a system.

The tree is drawn for the {{kin}} — kin meaning one's family, one's blood relations — and the {{folk}} — folk meaning one's people, in the oldest and widest sense — and it has found them everywhere: a {{relative}} — a relative being a connected by blood or marriage — in Perth who sends an annual card; an {{intimate}} — an intimate being a close, trusted friend — of the family who appears in three photographs and no document, and is marked, therefore, in pencil. The youngest {{youth}} — a youth being a young man — on the paper is apprenticed at the brewery; the youngest {{youngster}} — a youngster being a child, a young person — is four; and the newest twig of all, expected in the autumn, began as an {{embryo}} — an embryo being the first stage of a new creature, before it is born; in this case, in a dish, in a clinic in Bristol — a fact the Society recorded after a silence, and then, being the Society, with a small ceremony and tea. Mrs. Vye herself, the Society agrees, is a {{dear}} — a dear being a lovable, kindly soul — and the ink is guaranteed, the paper merchant said, for a hundred years, which should about cover it.
tr:
磨坊溪家族史学会每月第二个星期四在谷物交易所聚会，排在惠斯特牌局和柔道课之间。会长是退休的女邮政局长怀夫人；本季的研究对象，是怀夫人本人；而学会唯一经久的发现是：只要回溯得够远、旁及得够宽，河谷里每一个姓氏（surname，surname 指跟在教名之后的家族之名）都同时属于所有别的人家。

怀夫人自己的家谱占满她家客厅的一整面后墙，六英尺宽、九英尺长，用衬纸和钢笔画成。她这一脉的第一位先驱（pioneer，pioneer 指走在最前、为后来者开路的人）是个胡格诺织工，一六八五年携一台织机、一部圣经和零句英语来到磨坊溪，不出一年就娶了染匠的女儿——家里的争执，最早也就追溯到这儿。第二代出了这个家族永远的难堪：一位先知（prophet，prophet 指自称传达天意、预告未来之事的人），把世界末日先后定在一七四三年和一七四八年；末日两度爽约之后，他移民去了宾夕法尼亚，他的后裔至今还在那儿，愉快而错误着。第三代出了这个家族唯一与典礼沾边的角色：一位当过镇上传令官（herald，herald 旧义指纹章院的掌礼官，引申为发布公告之人）的叔祖，在集市广场上喊了四十年的集市、巡回审判和面包价，嗓音被《信使报》比作一具善意的雾号。

照家族自己的讲法，磨坊像一块怀表，由继承人（heir，heir 指继承者）传给继承人；但学会的侦探工作显示，它更常横着传，因此对每一位持有人，老实的说法不是继承人，而是接任者（successor，successor 指接替他人职位或产业的人，无论是否因继承）。十年之内它就横传了两次：一八〇二年传给一位侄子（nephew，nephew 指兄弟或姐妹之子），一八〇九年又传给一位侄女（niece，niece 指兄弟或姐妹之女），后者嫁出门去，把地契也一并带走了。前后七代（generation，generation 指从出生到子女出生之间的跨度，约三十年）人执掌磨坊，直到铁路把水轮变成一件古董。最早的接任者是织工之子，他娶了磨坊主的女儿，由他的岳父（father-in-law，father-in-law 指丈夫或妻子的父亲）手把手教了手艺——旧文件记下这桩交易时，笔调暖得跟一份雇佣合同差不多。这对夫妇（couple，couple 指结成一对、结了婚的两人）于一七一一年成婚，他们那一栏的后代一直排到纸的底边之外。

悲伤的那几页也是最诚实的那几页。旧记录为每一个没能过两岁生日的婴儿（infant，infant 指尚在最初几年里的孩童）画一个小十字；怀夫人的墙上有九个。有荒年那年的孤儿（orphan，orphan 指父母双亡的孩子），这一家把他从习艺所领回来养大，他这一支如今在阿德莱德枝繁叶茂。有一八六七年那对双胞胎（twin，twins 指同一次分娩生下的两个孩子），一个活到九十岁，另一个是左起第三个十字；还有唯一一个少年（juvenile，juvenile 指年轻人，法律上指尚未成年者），因偷苹果被罚六便士，记在一八七四年的法庭簿上——家族决定把这一条当作趣闻。

现代的那几页引起了争论。两年前，学会经过一场开了两次会、赔了一次不是的辩论，表决在旧有的性别（sex，sex 指男女的生物分类）一栏旁边增设社会性别（gender，gender 指作为男性或女性的社会身份）一栏，并用红墨水重画女系——旧做法只跟着姓氏走，把女性整个丢掉了。红墨水一干，就显出了大家半知半觉的事实：女（female，female 指能生育后代的性别）系一直在承担继承，男系留下的每个缺口，都站着一位女儿或外孙女。

会长表亲家的孩子西里尔·怀——表亲（cousin，cousin 指叔伯姑舅姨的子女）家的儿子——今年春天带着他的丈夫（husband，husband 指已婚的男子）从伦敦回来。西里尔是同性恋（gay，gay 指被同性吸引的）这件事，全河谷从他十六岁起就都知道了——所有人都被除了西里尔之外的所有人告知过；学会愣了片刻，便把两人写上了纸，跟前头任何一对夫妇（couple，couple 指结成一对的两人）一样兴高采烈，怀夫人在抬头为配偶（spouse，spouse 指已婚的伴侣，夫或妻）的那一栏里填上格雷厄姆——他们的证书上就是这么写的，而且，她指出，学会本来就是干这个的。她祖父（grandfather，grandfather 指父或母的父亲）的信收在谱下面的箱子里，是他出海的那些年写回家的；信里称她祖母为 darling（darling，darling 指深爱的人），墨水力透纸背；祖母的回信——写的时候，她的兄弟姐妹（sibling，siblings 指兄弟姐妹）还在店铺门外喊她——则称他为“亲爱的弗雷德”，爱意按定量配给在附言里，学会将此视为一种体制的证据。
