The vicar asked them all to {{rejoice}} — to rejoice meaning to feel joy and show it, to be glad out loud — and for once required no persuasion; the {{merry}} — merry meaning full of cheer and laughter, jolly with it — went on past midnight; every child under ten was {{thrill}}ed — a thrill being a sudden wave of feeling, excitement run through one like a current — twice by the fireworks and once by the staleness of bedtime; the county photographer {{please}}d — to please meaning to give pleasure to, to satisfy — everybody by arriving when the light did; the {{cheer}} — cheer being good spirits, and the shout that carries them — that went up when the queen cut the cake was heard at the quarry; and the Mercury's verdict, that it had been an {{agreeable}} — agreeable meaning pleasing, to the mind or the senses — day, was voted the finest understatement of the decade. As for {{pleasure}} — pleasure being the mind's enjoyment, the sweet taken in a thing — it was taken, the vicar observed, by everybody in the valley except the two organizers, whose pleasure had been spent in advance, in the getting of it.

Skidmore's summing-up, printed the following week, entered the valley's permanent stock. He conceded that the day had passed without rain, casualty or speech over eleven minutes; that the fund had closed in credit; and that his own pessimism, on this occasion, had been at fault. "But my system stands," he wrote. "The bridge is a hundred and one next year, in a manner of speaking, and I intend to be ready for it."
tr:
桥那年春天满一百岁，教区查了账，发现桥还什么都没欠它，于是决定庆祝。筹备委员会当场分成天然的两半：蒂泽德太太对天气、经费和人性——三样——都乐观（optimistic，optimistic 指倾向于看光明一面、对事情期望其好的）；比尔·斯基德莫尔对同样三样悲观（pessimistic，pessimistic 指倾向于料定最坏的；穿着雨衣的希望），同样地一以贯之。有这两位在、也多亏这两位，各项安排齐备了：她定会发生什么，他定会出什么岔子，而庆典取两者的平均数。

委员会本身就是一幅河谷性情图，《信使报》在第一次会议的报道里做了编目。有一位被动（passive，passive 指不作为而被作为的、听任事情发生而不去动手的）的委员，热情地赞同最后发言的那一位，两半都珍视他；有一位热情（enthusiastic，enthusiastic 指胸中神明充盈的、为一桩事业发热、为它燃烧的）的，主日学的老师，每会携十九条建议而来，并为落选的十八条明显神伤；有一位漠然（indifferent，indifferent 指既不偏向也不反对、对一事无兴趣亦无挂碍的）的司库，只在乎账目平衡——账目也确实平衡了；至于委员会之外，无动于衷（apathetic，apathetic 指无论哪边都没有感觉的、无意见的静默中心）的广大群众，头一个月的劳作换来的是栅栏桩一般的温度，总共募得微不足道（negligible，negligible 指小到不值一计、在算术之下的）的四镑十先令。

前一个月改变了一切，一向如此；而那一个月的活计是河谷惯常（usual，usual 指寻常所见所做的、日常的那一类）的那一套：彩旗以弗隆计量，长桌逐张摇过、报废了一张，礼拜堂与军团各自选出女王、彼此绝口不提，《信使报》把节目单登了两遍，其中一遍是对的；钱也按钱惯常的形状到账，有几笔来自从未许诺过的门户。

那一天本身归蒂泽德太太，太阳照她说的办了。桥从两岸得到了全村的幸福（happiness，happiness 指蒙福的状态、心安而且乐于此安的心境）：上午赛跑里有欢愉（delight，delight 指明亮地领受的快乐、一刻的高兴）；孩子们在哪儿，乐趣（fun，fun 指嬉戏与玩笑、引人发笑的东西）就在哪儿；主席讲了个笑话（joke，joke 指为了笑声而说或做的事，内里不带恶意），桥的岁数与他自己的各占一半——桥占了上风；到三点钟，笑声（laughter，laughter 指笑的声音与行为、身体自己的鼓掌）从茶帐一路传到河边；入夜灯亮起来时，则是更沉实的东西——喜悦（joy，joy 指深植于心的欢喜、属于整颗心而不只属于此刻的）。牧师请大家欢乐（rejoice，rejoice 指感到喜悦并且显出来、大声地高兴），这一回没用着劝；欢闹（merry，merry 指满怀欢笑兴致、乐呵呵的）一直持续过午夜；十岁以下的每个孩子都被烟花激荡（thrill，thrill 指一阵突然涌过的情绪、像电流那样穿过人的兴奋）了两次，又被“该睡了”激荡了一次；县里的摄影师赶在光线正好的时候到场，取悦（please，please 指给人以愉快、使之满意）了所有人；女王切蛋糕时响起的那阵欢呼（cheer，cheer 指高昂的情绪、以及把它喊出来的那一嗓子），采石场都听得见；《信使报》的评语——说这是宜人（agreeable，agreeable 指令人愉快的、合于心智或感官的）的一天——被公认为十年来最出色的轻描淡写。至于快乐（pleasure，pleasure 指心智的享受、从一件事里尝到的甜），牧师指出，全村人人有份，唯独两位主办人没有——他们的快乐早已预支，花在筹备它上面了。

斯基德莫尔的总结下周刊出，进了河谷的永久库存。他承认那天没有下雨、没有伤亡、没有超过十一分钟的演讲；基金有结余；他自己的悲观，这一回失算了。“不过我这套系统还立得住，”他写道，“换个说法，桥明年就一百零一岁了。我打算有所准备。”

quiz.q: Mrs. Tizzard, optimistic as to weather, funds and human nature — inclined to look on the bright side, expecting the best of a thing. Optimistic means —
quiz.ex: optimistic = 乐观的。an optimistic outlook 乐观的前景；optimism n. 乐观主义。

quiz.q: Skidmore, pessimistic on the same three subjects — inclined to expect the worst; hope wearing its waterproof. Pessimistic means —
quiz.ex: pessimistic = 悲观的。a pessimistic view 悲观的看法；pessimism n. 悲观主义。

quiz.q: The enthusiastic one brought nineteen suggestions to every meeting — full of the god within; hot for a cause, burning for it. Enthusiastic means —
quiz.ex: enthusiastic = 热情的。be enthusiastic about 对……充满热情；enthusiasm n. 热情。

quiz.q: The indifferent treasurer cared only that the books balanced — without interest or concern, neither caring for a thing nor against it. Indifferent means —
quiz.ex: indifferent = 漠不关心的。be indifferent to 对……漠不关心；indifference n. 冷漠。

quiz.q: The apathetic valley at large received the labours with the warmth of a fencepost — without feeling either way, the still centre of no opinion. Apathetic means —
quiz.ex: apathetic = 冷漠的；无动于衷的。an apathetic response 冷淡的回应；apathy n. 冷漠。

quiz.q: The first month produced a negligible sum of four pounds ten — so small it need not be counted, beneath the arithmetic. Negligible means —
quiz.ex: negligible = 可忽略不计的。a negligible amount 微不足道的量；neglect v. 忽视。

quiz.q: Laughter ran from the tea tents to the river by three o'clock — the sound and the act of laughing, the body's own applause. Laughter is —
o: a thing said to raise laughter
the sound and act of laughing
gladness deep set in the heart
a wave of feeling like current
quiz.ex: laughter = 笑；笑声。roars of laughter 哄堂大笑；laugh v. 笑。

quiz.q: The vicar asked them all to rejoice, and for once required no persuasion — to feel joy and show it, to be glad out loud. To rejoice is to —
quiz.ex: rejoice = 高兴；欢庆。rejoice at the news 为消息而欢喜；rejoicing n. 欢庆。

title: The Homecoming
text:
The letter came from Adelaide in February: Thomas Prowse, forty years gone, was coming home for his mother's ninetieth, in May, for three weeks, and would she mind. The valley, into which the letter was read before the kettle had boiled, decided at once and unanimously that she would not mind at all, having been told nothing; and the greatest conspiracy of its peacetime history began. The gift the valley settled on was the one thing money could not buy and Adelaide could not send: the {{desirable}} — desirable meaning worth having, to be wished for — element of surprise, a {{surprising}} — surprising meaning such as surprises, beyond what was looked for — return, engineered by forty co-conspirators and one absolute silence.

The machinery of it ran on neighbourliness. A {{favour}} — a favour being a kindness done or asked, a good turn between one and another — was called in at every house: the Stores held the good tea under the counter; the bus driver, {{keen}} — keen meaning eager, sharp-set upon a thing — on his own initiative, arranged to break down at the right corner; and the {{zeal}} — zeal being heat in a cause, devotion at working temperature — of the committee exceeded anything the chapel had ever raised for a roof, secrecy being the one luxury the valley had never yet afforded itself. The last week turned {{hectic}} — hectic meaning feverish with hurry, busy past the point of sense —: bunting was smuggled about in feed sacks, the cake was baked at night, and the Mercury held its front page on the editor's word, an event the county's press historians still cite as unexplained.

The day came in May, and with it the train. It had been arranged that the mother would be at the war memorial at three — the pretext, a churchyard meeting about lichen — and that Thomas should come up the lane from the station on foot, as he had left it. The {{startle}} — to startle meaning to give a sudden shock, to jump the unwary out of their wits — when she saw him was complete, and, the doctor confirmed afterwards, harmless; and the silence that followed, a full ten seconds, was more {{amazing}} — amazing meaning such as causes wonder, past the easy believing of it — to the watchers behind the wall than any sound could have been. What she said, when speech came back, was {{astound}}ing — to astound meaning to astonish utterly, to strike a person beyond words — in its plainness, and the valley has kept it as scripture since: "Well," she said. "You'll want your dinner."

The three weeks that followed were the most {{exciting}} — exciting meaning that stirs the feelings, rousing them, waking them — season the valley had had since the war: a party that filled the Corn Exchange, {{lively}} — lively meaning full of life, of quick blood and movement — past midnight; photographs in the Mercury of a mother of ninety, {{fond}} — fond meaning loving, tender, foolish in affection and wisely so — and a son of seventy, both conducting themselves like the ages they had left behind; and an evening at the Legion at which Thomas, by then {{exhilarate}}d — to exhilarate meaning to make the spirits merry, to enliven, to cheer past restraint — delivered Australia's opinion of Devon rain with such success that he was invited back the following night to repeat it. The weather stayed {{lovely}} — lovely meaning beautiful, delightful to heart and eye — for exactly the length of the visit, a fact the valley noted and did not press its luck on.

He went back in June, and the valley returned to its habits; but the conspiracy had done something to it that nobody had planned: doors stood open longer than they had, and the churchyard meeting about lichen became an annual event, nobody now remembering why. The Mercury's verdict on the whole affair — "entirely {{satisfactory}} — satisfactory meaning enough for the purpose, giving satisfaction, no more and no less —" — was, as usual with the Mercury, both the smallest and the truest word available.
tr:
信是二月从阿德莱德来的：走了四十年的托马斯·普劳斯要回家给母亲过九十大寿，五月到，住三个星期，问她介不介意。信还没等水开就在全村读过了，全村当即一致决定：她一点儿也不介意——因为她将一无所知；于是开始了河谷和平年代最大的一场密谋。河谷选定的礼物，是钱买不来、阿德莱德也寄不来的那样东西：可欲（desirable，desirable 指值得拥有的、让人盼求的）的惊奇——一次出人意料（surprising，surprising 指令人吃惊的、超出所望的）的归来，由四十名同谋和一个绝对的沉默协力完成。

这台机器靠街坊情谊运转。每一户都动用了人情（favour，favour 指所行或所求的善意、人与人之间的一桩好意）：杂货铺把好茶藏进柜台底下；公共汽车的司机热心（keen，keen 指热切的、对一件事磨快了胃口的）过头，自作主张安排在正确的街角抛锚；而委员会的热忱（zeal，zeal 指为一桩事业的热度、在工位温度上运行的奉献），超过了礼拜堂为屋顶募集过的任何一回——保密这件事，是河谷唯一从来没舍得给自己买过的奢侈品。最后一星期变成了一片忙乱（hectic，hectic 指因匆忙而发热的、忙过了头脑的那一种）：彩旗装在饲料袋里偷运，蛋糕夜里烤，《信使报》凭编辑的一句话按住头版不发——县里的报业史家至今把这件事引作无解。

五月那天到了，火车也到了。安排是让母亲三点在战争纪念碑那儿——借口是开一场关于地衣的教堂墓地会议——而托马斯从车站沿小巷步行过来，像他当年离开时那样。她看见他时的那一下惊跳（startle，startle 指给一个突然的惊吓、把无备之人吓得魂灵出窍）是完整的，而且医生事后确认无碍；随后那阵沉默，整整十秒，在墙后的目击者们看来，比任何声响都更令人惊奇（amazing，amazing 指引发惊叹的、轻易不能相信的）。她开口时说的那句话，朴素得叫人震惊（astound，astound 指使惊骇到彻底、把人打到说不出话），从此被河谷当经文收藏：“哦，”她说，“该吃饭了吧。”

随后的三个星期，是河谷自战争以来最激动人心（exciting，exciting 指搅动情绪的、令人激奋、把人唤醒的）的一季：一场坐满谷交所的聚会，热烈（lively，lively 指生机充盈的、血气与动作都快的）到过了午夜；《信使报》登出照片：九十岁的母亲，慈爱（fond，fond 指深爱的、温存的、痴于情感而痴得其所的）的七十岁的儿子，两人都做出他们落下的那个年纪的样子；还有军团的一个晚上，那时托马斯已经欢畅（exhilarate，exhilarate 指使精神高扬、使活泼、高兴得过了拘束的）到顶点，讲了澳大利亚对德文郡降雨的看法，大获成功，以致第二晚被请回去重讲一遍。天气在整个逗留期间都晴美（lovely，lovely 指美的、悦目又悦心的），河谷注意到了，没有再试运气。

六月他回去了，河谷回到各自的习性；可这场密谋给河谷留下了一样没人计划过的东西：门户比从前开得更久，而那场关于地衣的教堂墓地会议成了年年都开的例会，如今已没人记得缘起。《信使报》对全部事情的评语——“完全令人满意（satisfactory，satisfactory 指合乎目的的、给出满足的，不多也不少）”——一如《信使报》的惯例，是能找到的词里最小、也最真的一个。

quiz.q: The gift was a surprising return, beyond what was looked for — such as surprises. Surprising means —
quiz.ex: surprising = 令人惊讶的。a surprising result 意外的结果；surprise v./n. 使惊讶；惊讶。

quiz.q: A favour was called in at every house — a kindness done or asked, a good turn between one and another. A favour is —
o: the sweet taken in a thing
the still centre of no opinion
quiz.ex: favour = 恩惠；好感。do sb. a favour 帮某人一个忙；in favour of 赞成。

quiz.q: The bus driver, keen on his own initiative, arranged to break down at the right corner — eager, sharp-set upon a thing. Keen means —
o: full of life and quick movement
quiz.ex: keen = 热切的；敏锐的。be keen on 热衷于；a keen mind 敏锐的头脑。

quiz.q: The zeal of the committee exceeded anything raised for a roof — heat in a cause, devotion at working temperature. Zeal is —
quiz.ex: zeal = 热忱。revolutionary zeal 革命热忱；zealous adj. 热心的。

quiz.q: The last week turned hectic — feverish with hurry, busy past the point of sense. Hectic means —
quiz.ex: hectic = 忙乱的。a hectic schedule 紧凑的日程；a hectic day 忙乱的一天。

quiz.q: The startle when she saw him was complete, and harmless — to give a sudden shock, to jump the unwary out of their wits. To startle is to —
quiz.ex: startle = 使惊吓。be startled by a noise 被响声吓一跳；startling adj. 惊人的。

quiz.q: What she said was astounding in its plainness — to astonish utterly, to strike a person beyond words. To astound is to —
quiz.ex: astound = 使震惊。be astounded by the news 被消息惊呆；astounding adj. 令人震惊的。

quiz.q: Thomas, by then exhilarated, delivered Australia's opinion of Devon rain — to make the spirits merry, to enliven, to cheer past restraint. To exhilarate is to —
quiz.ex: exhilarate = 使振奋。an exhilarating experience 令人振奋的经历；exhilaration n. 振奋。

title: The Wedding at the Manor
text:
The engagement was announced in February and the county held its breath: the squire's daughter, and the quarry manager's son. The squire's first word, on being told, was a long one; and his second was that he was {{proud}} — proud meaning high in one's own account, holding an opinion of oneself; and of families, the same opinion carried down — of his daughter's choice, which the valley correctly translated as: he had not yet consented. The pride, at any rate, proved the workable kind, being nailed to a person and not to a name; and the name, the county pointed out, would be the last thing left wearing it once the estate was settled.

The young man himself disarmed the county inside a fortnight. He was {{frank}} — frank meaning open and unreserved, saying the thing out and not round it — to the point of indecency, by drawing-room standards; {{direct}} — direct meaning straight, going at a thing by the shortest way, in speech as in travel —; {{earnest}} — earnest meaning serious of purpose, in earnest as against in play — in the way that makes a career of farming; and his {{honesty}} — honesty being the virtue of the true word and the square dealing — had survived three generations of quarry accounts, which the squire's agent verified within the week, his enquiries being of the sort that cannot be applied for. He was {{manly}} — manly meaning having the qualities the valley credits to a man: courage, plainness, and the carrying of both — without any of the noise that usually advertises the fact; {{humble}} — humble meaning lowly in one's own eyes, holding a modest opinion of oneself — about the manor, which he had known hitherto as a place one drove past; and {{modest}} — modest meaning keeping within measure, neither overstating oneself nor one's things — about the geology degree, which the quarry had been quietly living off for two years.

The daughter had been the valley's puzzle since her schooldays, and the engagement only deepened the puzzle. She was {{curious}} — curious meaning eager to know, of the mind that must ask — about everything the county considered settled; {{daring}} — daring meaning bold, of the venturous sort, that will chance a thing — with it, in the way that had twice put her name in the Mercury and once in the county court; {{romantic}} — romantic meaning of romance, given to the heart's own view of a thing over the ledger's — in her reasons for marrying, which she declined to give the county and gave the valley instead; and {{mysterious}} — mysterious meaning keeping its own counsel, past the finding out — about the wedding itself, having planned it, it turned out, since the age of nine, in an exercise book the Mercury has since offered to buy. What she wanted from the marriage, and got, was stated in one word at the kitchen door, to her grandmother: {{freedom}} — freedom being the state of being free, ruling one's own going and doing — "the kind," she said, "you can only get by belonging to somebody."

The squire's conversion was public, complete, and the county's favourite spectacle of the decade. He turned {{liberal}} — liberal meaning open of mind and open of hand; free in thinking, and free in giving — on the subject of the marriage settlements with a speed the lawyers called imprudent; he was {{generous}} — generous meaning free in giving, noble of scale, past the expected measure — with the land, in the deed of gift that made the young couple's title to the home farm outright; and on the day itself he was {{gentle}} — gentle meaning mild, soft in manner, of the kindly handling — with everybody, including the photographer, whom the family had distrusted for thirty years. The wedding was the valley's own rather than the county's: the guests were {{polite}} — polite meaning of the polished manner, civil, doing the civil thing — to the county relations and {{friendly}} — friendly meaning of a friend's turn, kindly of disposition — to everyone else, there being no room in a barn for the other arrangement; the whole day was {{hospitable}} — hospitable meaning given to the welcoming of guests, keeping the door open and the pot on — past anything the county had seen since rationing ended; and the vicar, marrying them, was {{humorous}} — humorous meaning having the sense of the laughable, and the kindness to use it gently — in the address, of which the one line remembered is the one that ended the county's argument for good: that the valley had been marrying itself for a thousand years, and had never once yet been wrong.

The Mercury's report ran to a full page and closed on the sentence the couple had framed for the hall: "The estate gains a manager, the quarry gains a geologist, and the county gains, at no charge, a lesson."
tr:
订婚的消息是二月宣布的，全县屏住了呼吸：乡绅的女儿，和采石场经理的儿子。乡绅听说后的第一个词很长；第二个词是说，他为女儿的选择骄傲（proud，proud 指自我评价高的、对自己持有高见的；就家族而言，是把这高见传下来的那一种）——全村正确地把这句话翻译成：他还没同意。不过那份骄傲证明是好使的那种：钉在一个人身上，而不是钉在一个姓氏上；而那个姓氏，县里指出，等家产一分割，将是最后一件还戴着它的东西。

年轻人本人用两个星期缴了全县的械。他坦率（frank，frank 指公开而无保留的、把话说出来而不绕着说的）——按客厅的标准坦率到不成体统；直截（direct，direct 指直的、以最短的路直奔一事的，说话如此，行路也如此）；对待种地这门事业，是那种能把它经营成终身志业的郑重（earnest，earnest 指目的严肃的、当真的、与玩笑相对的）；而他的诚实（honesty，honesty 指真话与方正交易的品德）在采石场三代账目里活了下来——乡绅的代理人一星期内就查证了，那种查证是没法主动申请的。他有男子气概（manly，manly 指具备河谷记在男人名下的那些品质：勇气、爽直、以及把两样都端得住的），而全无通常替它做广告的那阵喧哗；对庄园谦卑（humble，humble 指自视低下的、对自己持谦卑评价的）——此前他对它的了解，仅止于“开车经过的一个地方”；对那个地质学学位也自谦（modest，modest 指守着分寸的、不夸大自己也不夸大自己之物的）——而采石场两年来一直悄悄靠它吃饭。

女儿从学生时代起就是全村的谜，订婚只是把谜加深了。她对全县认为“定案”的一切都好奇（curious，curious 指求知心切的、非问不可的那种头脑）；对它们又敢作敢为（daring，daring 指大胆的、敢于一搏的那一路），两次把名字送进《信使报》、一次送进郡法院；至于结婚的理由，她浪漫（romantic，romantic 指属于传奇的那一路、按心的看法而非账簿的看法看事的）——理由她拒绝讲给县里听，讲给了河谷；而婚礼本身神秘（mysterious，mysterious 指守着自己秘密的、查探不出的），原来她从九岁起就开始筹划，记在一个练习簿里，《信使报》后来出价想买。她要从婚姻里要的东西——也得到了——是在厨房门口用一句话说给祖母的：自由（freedom，freedom 指自由的状态、自己的来去自己做主）——“就是那种，”她说，“只有归属于某个人才拿得到的自由。”

乡绅的转变是公开的、彻底的，是县里十年间最爱看的场面。在婚产协议的题目上，他开明（liberal，liberal 指头脑与手都开放的：想得自由，给得也自由）起来的速度，被律师们称为不智；他慷慨（generous，generous 指给予大方的、超出预期分量的、有贵族气度的），一张赠与契把自耕农庄的产权整份交到年轻人手里；婚礼当天他对谁都温和（gentle，gentle 指温和的、举止柔软的、手下存着善意的），包括摄影师——这一家子不信任他有三十年了。婚礼是河谷的而不是县里的：宾客们对县里来的亲戚们客气（polite，polite 指举止有光的、客气的、行其分内礼数的），对其余所有人都友善（friendly，friendly 指朋友那一面的、性情亲切的）——谷仓里办的婚礼，另一种安排本来就无处安身；整场婚宴好客（hospitable，hospitable 指乐于迎客的、门开着、锅坐在炉上的）的程度，定量供应结束以来县里没见过；而主持婚礼的牧师风趣（humorous，humorous 指有幽默感的、识得可笑之处而且肯温厚地用它的），训辞里被记住的只有一句，就是终结了全县争论的那句：河谷自己娶自己，已经一千年了，还没有错过一回。

《信使报》的报道占了整整一版，收尾是那对新人裱起来挂在大厅的句子：“庄园得了一个管理人，采石场得了一个地质学家，县里免费上了一课。”

quiz.q: He said he was proud of his daughter's choice — high in one's own account, holding an opinion of oneself. Proud means —
quiz.ex: proud = 骄傲的；自豪的。be proud of 为……自豪；pride n. 骄傲。

quiz.q: He was frank to the point of indecency, by drawing-room standards — open and unreserved, saying the thing out and not round it. Frank means —
quiz.ex: frank = 坦率的。a frank discussion 坦率的讨论；to be frank 坦白说。

quiz.q: He was humble about the manor, which he had known as a place one drove past — lowly in one's own eyes. Humble means —
quiz.ex: humble = 谦逊的。a humble beginning 卑微的起点；humility n. 谦卑。

quiz.q: She was curious about everything the county considered settled — eager to know, of the mind that must ask. Curious means —
o: having the sense of the laughable
quiz.ex: curious = 好奇的。curious about everything 对什么都好奇；curiosity n. 好奇心。

quiz.q: She was daring with it, twice in the Mercury and once in the county court — bold, of the venturous sort, that will chance a thing. Daring means —
o: fixed and not to be moved
quiz.ex: daring = 大胆的。a daring escape 大胆的逃脱；dare v. 敢于。

quiz.q: He turned liberal on the settlements with a speed the lawyers called imprudent — open of mind and open of hand. Liberal means —
o: open of mind and open of hand
quiz.ex: liberal = 开明的；慷慨的。a liberal attitude 开明的态度；liberal arts 人文学科。

quiz.q: The whole day was hospitable past anything since rationing ended — given to the welcoming of guests, keeping the door open and the pot on. Hospitable means —
quiz.ex: hospitable = 好客的。a hospitable family 好客之家；hospitality n. 好客。

quiz.q: The vicar was humorous in the address — having the sense of the laughable, and the kindness to use it gently. Humorous means —
o: having the sense of the laughable
of the firm belief in a thing
quiz.ex: humorous = 幽默的。a humorous remark 幽默的话；humour n. 幽默。

title: The Search
text:
The boy went up after a stray ewe on the November Thursday, and the fog came down at four, as it had been {{promising}} — promising meaning giving promise, showing what is likely to come — to do all day. By six the valley was out on the hill; by seven the search had its shape, the sergeant having arrived with the Land Rover, the flask and the tact. He worked it {{careful}}ly — careful meaning taking care, exact of the small things, full of the attention — and kept it {{ready}} — ready meaning prepared, in a state of fitness for the thing when it comes —: the quarry's {{robust}} — robust meaning of oak-strength, strong and sound in the frame — men sent to the top ground, where the going was {{arduous}} — arduous meaning steep and laborious, of climbing that costs —; the farmers and their {{sturdy}} — sturdy meaning stout and solid, hard to bend and hard to tire — dogs to the lower slopes; and the rest along the wall lines, at intervals the sergeant fixed by the length of a shout.

The night did its work on everybody. The going was {{tough}} — tough meaning not easily tired or broken, of the stuff that endures —; the fog kept the {{prominent}} — prominent meaning standing out, thrusting itself upon the view — landmarks, the cairn and the wind-stunted thorn, visible for ten feet and no more; the weather, the sergeant noted, stayed {{temperate}} — temperate meaning kept within kind bounds, moderate, as weather rarely is in November and as persons may be —, for which he privately thanked the same providence the vicar was thanking on other grounds; and the hill, which is {{picturesque}} — picturesque meaning like a picture, fit to be painted — in any season by daylight, was nothing at all that night but ground to be covered. The sergeant himself never lost his {{confidence}} — confidence meaning the firm belief, the full trust reposed in a thing — and lent it out at interest, which is the art of his trade.

At the farm, the mother put the lamp in the window and the neighbours sat with her. The valley's {{tender}} — tender meaning soft of touch and of feeling, easily touched and careful of the touching — offices were all performed: the tea kept coming, the fire kept up, the bad possibilities kept out of the room. The neighbours were {{sympathetic}} — sympathetic meaning feeling with another, the sorrow shared as if it were one's own — without once saying so, which is the valley's way and the better of the two; the {{considerate}} — considerate meaning thoughtful of others, weighing their case before one's own — managed the arrival of the county relatives at the gate; the {{thoughtful}} — thoughtful meaning full of thought, mindful of what is needed — had thought of everything the sergeant would ask for before he asked for it; and when two of the younger men, done, went home at midnight, they came to the door first and {{apologise}}d — to apologise meaning to make an apology, to say the sorrow for the fault —, and their {{apology}} — an apology being the regret said aloud, the fault acknowledged — was accepted by the mother in the sentence the valley repeats still: "You'll be needed fresh at dawn; I'd sooner you slept than stood." She herself did not sit, and did not sleep: she was {{steadfast}} — steadfast meaning standing fast, fixed, not to be moved from the place or the purpose — at the window, and the lamp was the last light on the hill.

The boy was found at ten past six, in the old mine level above the reservoir, with the ewe, the ewe's new lamb, and — the sergeant's report records — a working knowledge of hypothermia acquired in the school's science room the winter before. He was {{delicate}} — delicate meaning fine and frail of make, needing the careful handling — with cold, but whole; the {{eager}} — eager meaning keen-set upon a thing, impatient of the delay — hands that carried him down the hill belonged to forty men and did no harm between them, which the doctor called the finest piece of collective surgery the county would ever see; and the dawn, coming up off the tor as they lifted him over the stile, was of the {{awesome}} — awesome meaning such as fills with awe, striking the beholder past speech — kind that makes even the Mercury's photographer late for his own wedding. The boy's {{grateful}} — grateful meaning thankful, feeling the kindness and owning it to oneself — letter to the search parties was printed entire; the family's {{gratitude}} — gratitude being the thankfulness felt and, at its best, shown — took the more durable form of a cheque to the air ambulance and a bench at the reservoir gate; and the valley, having had a long night to watch itself, was left with the feeling it always distrusts and always yields to: to {{admire}} — to admire meaning to wonder at with pleasure, to hold in esteem — its own conduct, which it does, once a decade, without shame.

The Mercury's headline called it {{remarkable}} — remarkable meaning such as calls for remark, out of the common run — and for once understated; and the boy's own comment, given the following week, entered the permanent stock: the fog had done him one favour, having taken the hill and left him the mine level, which was dry, and the company of a lamb, which was warm. "He was found," the Mercury's leader concluded, "by the whole valley, which is how anything worth finding is ever found."
tr:
男孩是十一月那个星期四上山找一只走散的母羊的，雾四点钟压了下来，像它一整天一直在许诺（promising，promising 指给出指望的、预示着要来的）的那样。六点，全村上了山；七点，搜救有了形状——警官带着路虎车、暖瓶和分寸赶到。他把行动办得仔细（careful，careful 指小心的、对细处精确的、满怀注意的），并使它常备（ready，ready 指准备好的、事情来时便处于堪用状态的）：采石场那些强壮（robust，robust 指橡树般力气的、筋骨强健结实的）汉子派上高处的地——那段路险峻（arduous，arduous 指陡而费力的、要付出代价的攀登）；农户和他们的狗——那些狗坚韧（sturdy，sturdy 指敦实坚固的、难弯折也难疲惫的）——派到低坡；其余人沿石墙线排开，间距由警官按“一嗓子的长度”核定。

黑夜对每个人都尽了自己的本分。行路艰难（tough，tough 指不轻易疲、不轻易断的、熬得住的那种料子）；雾把显著（prominent，prominent 指凸出的、硬要闯进视野的）的地标——石堆、风摧的荆棘——的能见度留在十英尺以内；天气，警官记录道，保持温和（temperate，temperate 指守在仁慈界限之内的、适中的——天气在十一月少有如此，人倒可以），他私下为此谢了天意，牧师也在为别的事谢着同一位；而这座白日里任一季节都如画（picturesque，picturesque 指如画的、配得上入画的）的山，那一夜什么也不是，只是要覆盖完的地面。警官本人从没失去过信心（confidence，confidence 指坚定的相信、对一事所寄的充分信任），而且把它放出去生息——这是他这门手艺的诀窍。

农舍这边，母亲把灯摆进窗里，邻居们陪她坐着。河谷温存（tender，tender 指触感与心情都软的、易被打动也小心去碰的）的照护全都到位：茶不断，火不熄，坏的可能不进屋。邻居们同情（sympathetic，sympathetic 指与另一人同感的、把忧苦当自己的分担的），却一次也没有说出口——这是河谷的方式，也是两种里较好的那种；体谅（considerate，considerate 指体恤他人的、先掂量别人处境再掂量自己的）的人料理了县里亲戚进门的种种；周到（thoughtful，thoughtful 指心里装着事的、惦着所需的）的人把警官要问的一切提前备齐；午夜时分两个年轻人累垮了要回家，先到门口道了歉（apologise，apologise 指致歉、为过失说出愧悔），他们的道歉（apology，apology 指说出口的愧悔、对过失的认领）被母亲用一句话收下——河谷至今还在传：“天亮还要用你们的力气，我宁可你们睡了，也别站着。”她自己没有坐，也没有睡：她在窗前坚定不移（steadfast，steadfast 指站得稳的、固定而不为所动的），那盏灯是山上最后的一盏灯。

男孩是六点过十分找到的，在水库上方旧矿井的水平巷道里，身边是那只母羊、母羊新生的羔羊，还有——警官的报告记着——前一年冬天在学校科学课上学到的低体温症知识。他冻得纤弱（delicate，delicate 指细弱纤巧的、需要小心对待的），但完好；把他抬下山的那几十双急切（eager，eager 指对一事磨尖了胃口的、等不得耽搁的）的手，属于四十个男人，彼此之间没有添一点伤——医生说这是县里能见到的最好的集体手术；他们抬他过栅栏门时，从山岗后升起来的那轮黎明，属于令人敬畏（awesome，awesome 指叫人屏息生畏的、把目击者打到说不出话的）的那一种，连《信使报》的摄影师都为它误了自己的婚礼。男孩写给各路搜救队的感谢（grateful，grateful 指心怀谢忱、并对自己承认这份善意的）信全文刊出；这家人的感激（gratitude，gratitude 指感到并——最好处——表现出来的谢意）取了更经久的形式：给空中救护队的一张支票，和水库门口的一条长凳；而熬了一整夜看顾自己的河谷，被留在它向来又警惕、又总归顺从的那种情绪里：钦佩（admire，admire 指怀着愉悦惊叹、加以敬重的）它自己的作为——它每十年这样干一回，并且不觉得羞愧。

《信使报》的标题称此事非同寻常（remarkable，remarkable 指值得注目的、出于常规之外的），这一回倒是说轻了；男孩下星期的评论进了永久库存：雾帮了他一个忙——收走了山，把矿井留给了他，那里面是干的，还有一只羊羔作伴，那是暖的。“他是被整个河谷找到的，”《信使报》的社论收尾道，“凡是值得找的东西，从来都是这么找到的。”

quiz.q: He worked it carefully — taking care, exact of the small things, full of the attention. Careful means —
quiz.ex: careful = 仔细的；小心的。a careful driver 谨慎的司机；be careful with 小心对待。

quiz.q: The quarry's robust men were sent to the top ground — of oak-strength, strong and sound in the frame. Robust means —
quiz.ex: robust = 强健的。robust health 强健的体魄；robust growth 强劲增长。

quiz.q: The top ground was where the going was arduous — steep and laborious, of climbing that costs. Arduous means —
quiz.ex: arduous = 艰巨的。an arduous task 艰巨的任务；arduous training 苦训。

quiz.q: The weather stayed temperate, for which he privately thanked providence — kept within kind bounds, moderate. Temperate means —
quiz.ex: temperate = 温和的；适度的。a temperate climate 温带气候；temperance n. 节制。

quiz.q: She was steadfast at the window, and the lamp was the last light on the hill — standing fast, fixed, not to be moved. Steadfast means —
o: standing fast, not to be moved
quiz.ex: steadfast = 坚定不移的。steadfast loyalty 坚贞的忠诚；steadfastly adv. 坚定地。

quiz.q: He was delicate with cold, but whole — fine and frail of make, needing the careful handling. Delicate means —
quiz.ex: delicate = 纤弱的；精细的。a delicate child 娇弱的孩子；delicate surgery 精细手术。

quiz.q: The family's gratitude took the durable form of a cheque and a bench — the thankfulness felt and, at its best, shown. Gratitude is —
o: the regret said for a fault
the firm belief in a thing
quiz.ex: gratitude = 感激。express one's gratitude 表达感激；grateful adj. 感激的。

quiz.q: The headline called it remarkable, and for once understated — such as calls for remark, out of the common run. Remarkable means —
o: so small it needs no counting
quiz.ex: remarkable = 非凡的。a remarkable achievement 卓越成就；remarkably adv. 显著地。

title: The Fortune-Teller
text:
The fortune-telling tent at the church fete has been kept, for twenty summers, by Mrs. Blackmore, who taught three generations of the valley their times tables and retired, at sixty, into the second of her two professions. The first had been {{strict}} — strict meaning exact in rule and in enforcement, keeping the line drawn and drawn tight —; its standards {{rigorous}} — rigorous meaning severe of standard, leaving nothing loose —; its games afternoons {{strenuous}} — strenuous meaning calling on the whole strength, of the sort that ends in mud —; and its leavers, the Mercury once observed, went out into the world knowing what a semi-colon was for, which is armour enough for most of it. The conversion had been {{enterprising}} — enterprising meaning having the eye and the nerve for an opening, ready to attempt —: the fete wanted a {{fortune}} — fortune meaning what befalls a person, the chance and the running total of a life; and by extension, the telling of it — teller, the roof wanted two hundred pounds, and she had spent forty years reading children, which is the harder discipline.

Her method, dissected afterwards at the Legion, was neither crystal ball nor cards but the oldest instrument, {{intuition}} — intuition meaning the knowing without the reasoning, the mind's short cut past its own argument —, applied with a teacher's precision. The cards were {{fancy}} — fancy being the imagination at play, the mind's pictures and its pleasure in them —; she dealt them as one deals the {{imaginary}} — imaginary meaning existing in the imagination only, having no being outside it — with the gravity of a magistrate; and the whole apparatus was, as she would have been the last to deny, an {{illusion}} — illusion meaning a false show, a thing taken for what it is not —, managed the way she had managed the school, by {{implicit}} — implicit meaning implied without being said, contained in the thing though never uttered — rules: the first, that nobody asked how it worked; the second, that she never told a fortune she could not see her way to charging for; the third, that whatever the cards said about the weather, the farmer got his half-crown's worth of hope and went home dry.

The valley's reception of her was a study in itself. The {{naive}} — naive meaning simple, wanting the world's lessons, taking things as they look — came openly and came back; the {{rational}} — rational meaning of the reason, the thinking done in order and by rule — stayed away on principle, or came only to watch the others file in; the farmers came for the weather and priced it by the acre; the young came for love, at the double rate, love being the one subject on which she charged for silence as well as speech; and the {{mundane}} — mundane meaning of the world and its ordinary business, the everyday — questions, the mare's foot, the silage, the council's drainage, outnumbered the mystical four to one, which she said was the valley all over, and the reason she trusted it. Her own part in it was honest: she was {{sincere}} — sincere meaning without pretence, meaning what one says and saying what one means — in the theatre of it, as an actress is sincere; and she was, on the evidence of forty years, {{trustworthy}} — trustworthy meaning worthy of trust, such as may be relied upon — with anything the tent was told, nothing leaving it, ever. The arrangement was {{mutual}} — mutual meaning reciprocal, done or felt by each towards the other —: the valley paid the roof fund for her theatre, and she gave the valley the one thing the church could not, a fortnight's worth of future.

Once, and once only, she broke her own rules, and the tent still collects its half-crown premium on the strength of the story. The widow Hetty came in the August her son was five months at sea, put her money down and said: "No cards, Mrs. Blackmore. The truth." And Mrs. Blackmore, who had taught the boy and marked his sums, laid her hands flat on the table — the tent, the Mercury's man reported, going suddenly {{bare}} — bare meaning uncovered, stripped, without dressing of any kind — and gave her the {{naked}} — naked meaning without cover or clothing; and of the truth, without dressing or softening — truth as she saw it: that the boy was alive; that she had known it since the Tuesday; and that the knowing had come to her unasked, as her knowing always had. It was the one reading of her career that was {{spontaneous}} — spontaneous meaning of its own accord, unforced, arising out of the moment rather than the plan — and the only one she ever refused payment for; and when the boy walked up the lane in October, the fete's takings doubled, the valley having concluded, on the evidence, that she was worth the roof and the tower both.

She gave the tent up at eighty, handing it over with the accounts to the Sunday-school teacher, and gave the Mercury the sentence that has hung in the reading room since, framed between the harvest photographs: "I never once told a fortune. I told people what they already knew, and charged the roof fund for the grammar."
tr:
教堂义卖会上的占卜帐篷，二十个夏天都由布莱克莫尔太太主持——她教了河谷三代人乘法口诀，六十岁上退休，转进了她的第二职业。头一个职业是严格的（strict，strict 指规则与执行都精确的、线画出来又拉紧的那一种），它的标准是严苛的（rigorous，rigorous 指标准苛刻、不留任何松动的），它的游戏午后是费力的（strenuous，strenuous 指需要用尽全力的、以一身泥收场的那一种），而它的毕业生——《信使报》有言——走进世界时都知道分号是干什么用的，这身盔甲应付世上的大半事都够了。改行这一步很有进取心（enterprising，enterprising 指有眼力也有胆量抓住空当、说干就干的）：义卖会缺一位算命（fortune，fortune 指落在一个人头上的东西、机遇与一生的累计总和；引申指对它的占算）先生，屋顶缺两百镑，而她读孩子的心读了四十年——那是更难的一门功夫。

她的方法，事后在军团被解剖过，既不是水晶球也不是纸牌，而是最老的仪器：直觉（intuition，intuition 指不经推理的知晓、心智绕过自身论证的近路），以教师的精度施用。牌是幻戏（fancy，fancy 指想象力的游戏、心里的图画以及看画的兴致）；她发牌，像一位治安法官在发想象（imaginary，imaginary 指仅存在于想象之中、在外面没有实体的）之物那样郑重；而整套行头——她会最后一个否认这一点——是一台幻术（illusion，illusion 指假象、被当成其所不是之物的东西），管理它的方式同她管理学校一样，靠的是默契（implicit，implicit 指不明说而暗含的、装在事里而从未出口的）规则：第一条，没人问它灵不灵；第二条，她从不给人算一个她看不出该怎么收钱的命；第三条，牌面无论怎么说天气，庄稼人都要拿到他那半克朗的指望，干干爽爽地回家去。

河谷对她的接纳，本身就是一份研究报告。天真（naive，naive 指简单的、缺着世上的功课、按事物表面接受事物的）的人坦荡地来、又坦荡地再来；讲理性（rational，rational 指出于理性的、按次序和规则进行的思考）的人原则上不来，或只来看看别人排队进去；庄稼人来问天气，按英亩论价；年轻人来问爱情，加倍收费——爱情是她唯一既收说话钱、也收沉默钱的题目；而世俗（mundane，mundane 指属于人世及其日常事务的、平常日子的）的问题——母马的蹄子、青贮、议会的排水——以四比一压倒玄学的问题，她说这就是河谷，也是她信得过它的原因。她自己的那一份是诚实的：她在戏里诚挚（sincere，sincere 指不装假的、说的是心里想的、想的也照说的），像演员在戏里诚挚一样；而凭四十年的证据，她对帐篷里听到的任何事都可托（trustworthy，trustworthy 指值得信任的、可以依靠的），什么也没有从帐篷里漏出去过，从来没有。这安排是相互的（mutual，mutual 指相互的、由每一方对另一方同样施与或感到的）：河谷为她的戏向屋顶基金付钱，她给河谷一样教堂给不了的东西——两星期长的未来。

只有一次，仅有一次，她破了自己的规矩，而帐篷至今凭这个故事多收半克朗的溢价。寡妇海蒂来的那个八月，她儿子出海五个月了；她把钱放上台面，说：“不用牌，布莱克莫尔太太。要真话。”布莱克莫尔太太教过那孩子、批过他的算术——她把双手平放在桌上，帐篷——据《信使报》的人描述——霎时空了（bare，bare 指无遮盖的、剥净了的、没有任何修饰的），她给了她赤裸的（naked，naked 指无遮无盖的；就真话而言，不加修饰也不加软化的）真相，照她所看见的：孩子活着；她从星期二就知道了；而这知晓是自己来的、无人求取，像她的知晓一向来的那样。那是她职业生涯里唯一一场自发的（spontaneous，spontaneous 指出于本心的、不受强迫的、从当下而非计划里长出来的）占算，也是她唯一一次拒绝收钱的一回；十月那孩子走上小巷回家时，义卖会的进账翻了一倍——河谷依据证据断定：她值一座屋顶，外带一座钟塔。

八十岁上她交出了帐篷，连同账目一并交给主日学的老师，又给了《信使报》一句话，如今装在框里、挂在两幅丰收照片中间：“我从没算过一次命。我只是把人们已经知道的事告诉他们，向屋顶基金收一点语法费。”

quiz.q: Her method was the oldest instrument, intuition — the knowing without the reasoning, the mind's short cut past its own argument. Intuition is —
o: a false show taken for real
what befalls a person in life
quiz.ex: intuition = 直觉。trust one's intuition 相信直觉；intuitive adj. 直觉的。

quiz.q: The whole apparatus was, as she would be the last to deny, an illusion — a false show, a thing taken for what it is not. An illusion is —
o: a thing existing only in imagination
the mind's short cut past argument
a false show, taken for what it is not
quiz.ex: illusion = 幻觉；错觉。an optical illusion 视错觉；be under no illusion 不抱幻想。

quiz.q: The naive came openly and came back — simple, wanting the world's lessons, taking things as they look. Naive means —
o: simple, taking things as they look
quiz.ex: naive = 天真的。a naive question 天真的问题；naivety n. 天真。

quiz.q: She managed it by implicit rules — implied without being said, contained in the thing though never uttered. Implicit means —
quiz.ex: implicit = 含蓄的；不言明的。implicit agreement 默契；implicit trust 绝对信任。

quiz.q: The fete wanted a fortune-teller — fortune meaning what befalls a person, the chance and the running total of a life; and by extension, the telling of it. Fortune is —
o: what befalls a person, the total of a life
quiz.ex: fortune = 命运；财产。tell sb.'s fortune 算命；make a fortune 发财。

quiz.q: She was sincere in the theatre of it, as an actress is sincere — without pretence, meaning what one says. Sincere means —
o: having the eye for an opening
without pretence, meaning what one says
quiz.ex: sincere = 真诚的。a sincere apology 真诚的道歉；sincerity n. 诚挚。

quiz.q: It was the one reading of her career that was spontaneous — of its own accord, unforced, arising out of the moment rather than the plan. Spontaneous means —
quiz.ex: spontaneous = 自发的。spontaneous applause 自发的掌声；spontaneity n. 自发性。

quiz.q: She gave her the naked truth — without cover or clothing; and of the truth, without dressing or softening. Naked means —
quiz.ex: naked = 赤裸的；无掩饰的。the naked truth 赤裸裸的事实；naked eye 肉眼。

title: The Winter of the Bad Neighbour
text:
The cottage was sold, after the forty quiet years of the Goodacres, to a man from the city whose name the valley never learned to spell and whose car the valley learned on sight. The first fortnight supplied the whole of his character. He was a {{nuisance}} — a nuisance meaning a thing or a person that plagues the peace, the troubler of it — within a week: the church bells rang too early, the cock crowed too loud, the churchyard grass was left too long, and the Scouts' bob-a-job week was, in his letter to the Mercury, an organized intrusion. By the month's end he had graduated from {{troublesome}} — troublesome meaning giving trouble, a maker of difficulties — to something the valley needed a wider word for, and had begun, alone in its history, to supply his own. The word, when it settled, was {{mean}} — mean meaning small in spirit, ungenerous, the pocket shut and the heart with it—, a word the valley otherwise kept for cows that kick at milking.

The council received his letters on the muck-spreading, which were {{hostile}} — hostile meaning of an enemy, unfriendly in act as in mind —; the hunt, whose abolition he proposed by petition, learned him the meaning of {{radical}} — radical meaning going to the root; of change that pulls the thing up rather than prunes it — in a single afternoon; and the parish meeting, over the car parking, heard language which the minute-taker rendered as {{vulgar}} — vulgar meaning coarse, of the common and unrefined sort, wanting manners — with the offending syllables left blank, the blanks being the most eloquent entry in the book's hundred years. His plans for the cottage itself — a design of glass and steel which the planning committee, in its one moment of county fame, rejected in eleven minutes — were voted {{awful}} — awful meaning dreadful, bad past the ordinary run of bad — by everyone who saw them, including, the Mercury established, the architect's own mother.

What he did to the valley took longer to see and was worse. The lane grew {{gloomy}} — gloomy meaning dark and lowering, of weather and of spirits alike — that winter in a way nobody could charge to the season; a {{sadness}} — sadness being the mind's heaviness, the low and settled state of it — settled over it, the Goodacres' old neighbours chief under the weight; the young families were {{discourage}}d — to discourage meaning to take the courage out of, to press the spirit down — from half their ventures before they began; and the planning rows were {{frustrating}} — frustrating meaning defeating the effort, blocking the will that tries — past anything the chapel's patience had been built for. Every ruling went his way or to appeal; the winds, that spring, blew {{adverse}} — adverse meaning turned against, contrary, of winds and of fortunes — in both senses, the appeal court's and the weather's being of a piece; and the Mercury's letters page, which had weathered two wars, learned to open his contributions with the resignation of a coastguard.

Of the man himself, the valley's vocabulary kept dividing. His letters ran on {{ego}} — ego meaning the self, the I in its own estimation and at its own length —, every sentence beginning where he did; his conduct was {{selfish}} — selfish meaning of self first, one's own interest served before and against all others — with a completeness that approached a gift; the Mercury's more temperate readers held him merely {{nasty}} — nasty meaning unpleasant, of an unkind make — and its less temperate ones held him {{wicked}} — wicked meaning morally wrong, evil past the mending —, a charge the vicar declined to rule on; and the parish's final verdict, delivered at the Legion by its oldest member, was the word the county still uses for him: {{weird}} — weird meaning strange past accounting, uncanny, of a piece with nothing else in the experience —. "Sixty years I've farmed next to all sorts," he said. "That one was the only man I never once got the weather out of."

He left in the third autumn, selling at a loss to a young family who asked, before signing, for the bells' Sunday schedule and had it framed. The lane recovered the following spring, as lanes do; the two years were written off, in the Mercury's phrase, to weather; and the only permanent mark he left was on the minute book, whose blanks have been shown, at intervals ever since, to every new arrival in the parish, as one shows a scar — not in anger, but as instruction.
tr:
科特奇小屋在古德克家安静的四十年之后，卖给了一个城里人，他的名字全村始终没学会拼写，他的车全村一见就认得。头两个星期就供出了他的全部人品。不出一星期，他就成了滋扰（nuisance，nuisance 指搅扰安宁的人或物、安宁的麻烦制造者）：教堂的钟敲得太早，公鸡叫得太响，教堂墓地的草留得太长，而童子军的“一便士打工周”，在他写给《信使报》的信里，是一场有组织的侵扰。到月底，他已从难缠（troublesome，troublesome 指制造麻烦的、惹出困难来的）升格为一个河谷需要更宽的词才放得下的人——并且，在河谷的历史上头一遭，开始自己供应这个词。这个词后来定下来了：刻薄（mean，mean 指气量小的、吝啬的，口袋闭着、心也跟着闭着）——这个词河谷往常只留给挤奶时踢桶的母牛。

议会收到了他关于撒粪肥的信，措辞充满敌意（hostile，hostile 指敌人的那种、行动上同心思上一样不友好的）；猎狐的事他一个下午之内递呈请愿提请废除，同时让人领教了激进（radical，radical 指连根去的、把整株拔起而不只修枝剪叶的那种变革）在一个农业教区是什么意思；而教区会议上，为了停车，他说了些会议记录员只能记作粗俗（vulgar，vulgar 指粗鄙的、市井而不加修琢的、缺着体面的）的话——犯忌的音节留了空白，那些空白是这本册子一百年里最有雄辩力的一页。至于小屋本身的计划——一套玻璃与钢的设计，规划委员会在它唯一一次名扬全县的时刻里，用十一分钟否掉了——凡见过的人一致评为糟糕（awful，awful 指糟糕透顶的、坏过了平常坏法的），《信使报》查明，其中一票来自建筑师自己的母亲。

他对河谷做的事，要看清需时更久，也更坏。那年冬天那条巷子阴郁（gloomy，gloomy 指昏暗低沉的，天气如此，心气也如此）下来，没法把账记在季节头上；一种忧伤（sadness，sadness 指心的沉重、那低落而落定的状态）罩住了它，古德克家的老邻居首当其冲；年轻人家一半的营生还没开始，就先被泼了气（discourage，discourage 指把勇气从人身上拿走、把心气压下去的）；而规划上的那些拉锯，令人丧气（frustrating，frustrating 指挫败努力的、把试着干成事的意志堵住的）到礼拜堂的耐心都不曾为此设计过。每一条裁决不是顺了他就是进了上诉；那年春天的风逆着（adverse，adverse 指转过来作对的、相反的，风向如此，运道也如此）吹——两种意义上的，上诉法院的和天气的正好是一对；《信使报》的读者来信版熬过两场战争，如今学会用海岸警卫队的坚忍翻开他的来稿。

至于这个人本身，河谷的词汇一直在分裂。他的信篇篇以自我（ego，ego 指自我、以自己的估量处着的那个“我”）开路，每个句子都从他开始；他的行事自私（selfish，selfish 指自己优先的、把自身利益置于所有人之前、且与之作对的），彻底得近乎一种天赋；《信使报》温和些的读者只认他讨厌（nasty，nasty 指叫人不快的、心肠不善的那一路），不温和的那些认他邪恶（wicked，wicked 指道德上错了的、坏到没法补的），这项指控牧师拒绝裁定；而教区的终审判决，由军团里最老的会员宣读，是全县至今用来指他的那个词：怪（weird，weird 指怪得没账可算的、蹊跷的、与全部经验都对不上号的）。“六十年，我什么样的邻居都种过地挨过，”他说，“就这一个，我连天气都没跟他聊成过一句。”

第三个秋天他走了，亏本卖给一户年轻人家——签约前先要了教堂周日的鸣钟时刻表，还装了框。第二年春天巷子缓过来了，巷子向来如此；那两年，按《信使报》的说法，记在了天气账上；而他留下的唯一永久痕迹，在会议记录簿上——那些空白，从此隔三差五地展示给教区每一个新来的人看，像给人看一道疤：不是出于愤怒，是作为教材。

quiz.q: He was a nuisance within a week — a thing or person that plagues the peace, the troubler of it. A nuisance is —
quiz.ex: nuisance = 讨厌的人（或物）。make a nuisance of oneself 惹人讨厌；public nuisance 公害。

quiz.q: His letters on the muck-spreading were hostile — of an enemy, unfriendly in act as in mind. Hostile means —
o: of an enemy, unfriendly in act
quiz.ex: hostile = 敌对的。a hostile reception 不友好的接待；hostility n. 敌意。

quiz.q: The hunt learned him the meaning of radical in a single afternoon — going to the root; of change that pulls the thing up rather than prunes it. Radical means —
o: going to the root, pulling up
quiz.ex: radical = 激进的；根本的。radical change 根本变革；radicalism n. 激进主义。

quiz.q: The meeting heard language the minute-taker rendered as vulgar — coarse, of the common and unrefined sort, wanting manners. Vulgar means —
quiz.ex: vulgar = 粗俗的。vulgar language 粗话；vulgarity n. 粗俗。

quiz.q: The lane grew gloomy that winter, of weather and of spirits alike — dark and lowering. Gloomy means —
quiz.ex: gloomy = 阴暗的；忧郁的。a gloomy day 阴天；feel gloomy 感到沮丧。

quiz.q: The young families were discouraged from half their ventures — to take the courage out of, to press the spirit down. To discourage is to —
quiz.ex: discourage = 使泄气。discourage sb. from doing sth. 使某人不敢做某事；encourage 反义词。

quiz.q: The winds that spring blew adverse in both senses — turned against, contrary, of winds and of fortunes. Adverse means —
quiz.ex: adverse = 不利的；相反的。adverse weather 恶劣天气；adverse effects 不良反应。

quiz.q: His conduct was selfish with a completeness that approached a gift — of self first, one's own interest served before and against all others. Selfish means —
o: of self first, before all others
quiz.ex: selfish = 自私的。a selfish act 自私行为；selfishness n. 自私。

title: The Beast
text:
The scare began, as scares do, with a photograph: a blur in the top field at dusk, taken by the Mercury's photographer for the harvest supplement and printed, by an editor with an eye for a quiet week, across five columns. Within a day the county had decided the blur was a big cat, escaped from a private zoo two counties off; the vet, asked to guess at the shape of it, gave it as his opinion that a {{bear}} — a bear being the big, thick-furred, short-tailed beast that walks flat-footed and stands up like a fat man reading a poster — was the likelier animal, big cats being unwilling to sit still for photographers; within two, {{suspicion}} — suspicion being the mistrust that arrives before the evidence does — had fixed on every rustle in the valley; and by the week's end the valley was living under a {{fear}} — fear being the mind's alarm, the shrinking from a thing looked for — that nobody had seen, everybody believed in, and no one could price. The parish divided along its usual seam: the {{sceptical}} — sceptical meaning given to doubting, withholding belief until it is shown —, led by the doctor and the vet, who pointed out that the blur, on close inspection, wore a collar; and the certain, led by everyone whose sheep had died of anything that winter, who pointed out that a collar was exactly the first thing an escaped beast would shake off.

The nights were the testing of it. An {{anxiety}} — anxiety being the fear that has no object, worry in the abstract, the alarm rung at nothing — went house to house like a second postman; the dogs, the valley's whole early-warning system, were {{restless}} — restless meaning without rest, unable to settle, of sleep and of legs alike — from dusk; the {{uneasy}} — uneasy meaning not at ease, ill-settled in the mind, the comfort gone out of the chair — sat up with lamps; and the {{timid}} — timid meaning wanting in courage, shy of the dark and of most other things — kept to the house after four, a list the valley was surprised to find included two farm dogs and the churchwarden. The {{doubt}} — doubt meaning the mind held between yes and no, the believing suspended — did its honest work at the Legion every night, and was voted down every night, which is also the Legion's way with weather.

The fuss outgrew the beast within the fortnight. The {{fuss}} — a fuss meaning a bustle over a matter, the noise and the running of the troubled — filled the Mercury for two editions; the search parties turned out on three evenings with {{unsuitable}} — unsuitable meaning not suited, unfit for the use or the occasion — equipment, of which the county paper printed a study: golf clubs, a wartime helmet, one boar spear from the museum, and a motor horn; the {{unwilling}} — unwilling meaning not willing, against the doing of the thing — stood at the edges and pointed; the {{reluctant}} — reluctant meaning drawing back, loath, consenting with the feet dragging — followed at a distance that kept the party always ahead of them; and the whole expedition {{hesitate}}d — to hesitate meaning to hold between choices, to stop before the step — at the first dark hedge, and went home by the road.

The county sent its expert, a mammal officer with slides, and the occasion crowned the scare. His investigation, he told the Legion, was {{unsatisfactory}} — unsatisfactory meaning not enough to satisfy, falling short of what was wanted — on the side of evidence; his explanations, delivered with the slides, left the room {{confuse}}d — to confuse meaning to mix together in the mind, to throw the understanding into disorder — as to whether the beast was a panther, a dog, or a large cat of the ordinary kind seen at an angle; and the evening ended in the {{embarrass}}ment — to embarrass meaning to put out of countenance, to discomfort before company — of the whole parish, the ninth slide having proved, under the Legion's own lamp, to be the print of the churchwarden's boot, size eleven, taken at the reservoir by the churchwarden himself on the Tuesday. The valley was {{ashamed}} — ashamed meaning feeling shame, sorry before others for oneself or one's doings — for a fortnight, and quiet for a week after that.

The beast was never found, having never, on the balance of the evidence, been; the blur was eventually identified, by the photographer's own mother, as the Stores' tomcat, an animal of ambitious stride and no fixed bedtime; and the scare closed with the {{sigh}} — a sigh being the breath let out slow, the body's own commentary on the mind's news — that went round the harvest supper, and with the vicar's harvest sermon, which the Mercury printed in full: a valley, he said, that had faced two wars, one flood, one fire and one bad neighbour, had gone indoors at dusk for a month over a tomcat with a walk; and if that was the worst of its fears, then the year, on balance, had been a good one, and it might let itself out to play.
tr:
这场恐慌像所有恐慌一样，从一张照片开始：黄昏时分上田里的一团模糊，是《信使报》的摄影师为丰收副刊拍的，让一位正愁版面的编辑用五个栏宽登了出来。不出一天，县里断定那团模糊是一头大猫，从两个郡之外一家私人动物园跑出来的；兽医被请去猜那形状，给出的意见是熊（bear，bear 指那种大个、厚毛、短尾、平脚走路、站起来像个读海报的胖子的野兽）更像些——大猫可不肯为摄影师安坐不动；不出两天，猜疑（suspicion，suspicion 指赶在证据之前先到的那种不信任）已经落在河谷的每一阵窸窣上；到周末，全村已经活在一种恐惧（fear，fear 指心里的警报、对所搜寻之物的畏缩）里——没人见过它，人人相信它，谁也给它估不出价。教区沿着惯常的裂缝分了阵营：怀疑派（sceptical，sceptical 指惯于存疑的、不见实证不交出相信的）以医生和兽医为首，他们指出细看之下那团模糊戴着项圈；笃信派以那年冬天自家死过羊的人为首，他们指出项圈恰恰是逃走的猛兽头一件要甩掉的东西。

夜晚是真正的考场。一种焦虑（anxiety，anxiety 指没有对象的恐惧、抽象的担忧、对空无敲响的警钟）像第二位邮差挨家挨户地走；狗——全村整套预警系统——从黄昏起就躁动（restless，restless 指不得安息的、安定不下来的，睡眠如此，两条腿也如此）；心神不宁（uneasy，uneasy 指不得安宁的、心里安放不平的、椅子上那份自在没了的）的人点着灯枯坐；胆怯（timid，timid 指缺乏勇气的、怕黑也怕其余一切的）的人四点以后闭门不出——这份名单里居然有两条农家的狗和教堂执事，全村自己都吃了一惊。怀疑（doubt，doubt 指悬在是与非之间的心、悬置起来的相信）每天晚上在军团里尽它诚实的本分，每晚都被投票否决——这也是军团对待天气的一贯方式。

两个星期不到，这场喧闹（fuss，fuss 指为一件事情掀起的大惊小怪、被搅扰者的动静与奔走）就长过了怪兽本身，占了《信使报》两期；搜救队出动了三个晚上，装备不合用（unsuitable，unsuitable 指不合适的、不堪此用或不当此景的）到县报专门为它拍了一版：高尔夫球杆、一顶战时头盔、一杆博物馆的猎野猪矛，还有一只汽车喇叭；不情愿（unwilling，unwilling 指不愿意的、对这件事持反对态度的）的人站在边上负责指；勉强（reluctant，reluctant 指缩着的、不乐意的、人已应允而脚还在拖的）的人隔着一截路跟着，那距离永远让队伍走在他们前头；而整支远征队在第一道黑树篱前迟疑（hesitate，hesitate 指悬在两种选择之间、迈步之前先停下）了，然后沿大路回家了。

县里派来了专家，一位带幻灯片的哺乳动物官员，这场合给恐慌加了冕。他告诉军团，他的调查在证据一面不能令人满意（unsatisfactory，unsatisfactory 指不足以令人满意的、够不上所求的）；他配着幻灯片给出的解释，让满屋子人糊涂（confuse，confuse 指在头脑里搅混、把理解力搅乱）了——那兽到底是黑豹、是狗，还是一只角度照坏了的寻常大猫；而这晚以全教区的难堪（embarrass，embarrass 指使人当众失态、在人前弄得人下不来台的）收场：第九张幻灯片在军团自家的灯下被证明是教堂执事的靴印，十一码，星期二他本人在水库边踩下的。全村羞愧（ashamed，ashamed 指感到羞耻的、为自身或自身所为在他人面前抱愧的）了两个星期，之后又静默了一星期。

怪兽始终没有找到，因为按证据的天平，它从来就没有存在过；那团模糊最终由摄影师自己的母亲鉴定为杂货铺的公猫——一只步子迈得雄心勃勃、作息毫无定规的猫。恐慌以丰收宴上此起彼伏的一声叹息（sigh，sigh 指缓缓吐出的那口气、身体对心之新闻的自行评论）收场，以牧师的丰收布道收场——《信使报》全文登了：一个扛过两场战争、一场洪水、一场大火和一个恶邻的河谷，为了一只会走路的公猫，黄昏闭门了一个月；倘若这就是它最坏的恐惧，那么这一年总体上算好年头，它可以放自己出去玩了。

quiz.q: Suspicion had fixed on every rustle in the valley — the mistrust that arrives before the evidence does. Suspicion is —
o: the mind's alarm at a thing
the believing held between yes and no
the fear that has no object
quiz.ex: suspicion = 猜疑。under suspicion 受到怀疑；suspicious adj. 可疑的。

quiz.q: The sceptical, led by the doctor and the vet, pointed out the collar — given to doubting, withholding belief until it is shown. Sceptical means —
quiz.ex: sceptical = 怀疑的。be sceptical about 对……持怀疑态度；scepticism n. 怀疑论。

quiz.q: An anxiety went house to house like a second postman — the fear that has no object, worry in the abstract. Anxiety is —
o: the shrinking from a thing looked for
fear with no object, in the abstract
the bustle over a small matter
quiz.ex: anxiety = 焦虑。feelings of anxiety 焦虑感；anxious adj. 焦虑的。

quiz.q: The timid kept to the house after four, a list including two farm dogs — wanting in courage, shy of the dark and of most other things. Timid means —
quiz.ex: timid = 胆怯的。a timid child 胆小的孩子；timidity n. 胆怯。

quiz.q: The fuss outgrew the beast within the fortnight — a bustle over a matter, the noise and running of the troubled. A fuss is —
quiz.ex: fuss = 大惊小怪。make a fuss 小题大做；fussy adj. 紧张不安的。

quiz.q: The reluctant followed at a distance that kept the party always ahead — drawing back, loath, consenting with the feet dragging. Reluctant means —
quiz.ex: reluctant = 不情愿的。be reluctant to do 不愿做；reluctance n. 勉强。

quiz.q: The whole expedition hesitated at the first dark hedge — to hold between choices, to stop before the step. To hesitate is to —
quiz.ex: hesitate = 犹豫。hesitate to do sth. 犹豫做某事；hesitation n. 犹豫。

quiz.q: The evening ended in the embarrassment of the whole parish — to put out of countenance, to discomfort before company. To embarrass is to —
quiz.ex: embarrass = 使尴尬。an embarrassing moment 尴尬时刻；embarrassment n. 尴尬。

title: The Reports
text:
The character reports were the school's oldest institution after the bell: one page a child, written at the end of every summer term in the headmaster's own hand, read aloud at prize day, and kept, by families that threw nothing out, in boxes with the christening gowns. Their author for forty years had been the old headmaster, a {{stern}} — stern meaning strict and severe, of faces and of standards, and, the dictionary insists, also the back of a ship — man whose reports were the valley's second literature after the Mercury; and his successor, inheriting the tradition with the desk, found in the drawer the instruction the old man had left himself, one line in a July hand: "Write of the child, not of the type."

The reports themselves were the valley's whole childhood, catalogued. There was the {{naughty}} — naughty meaning mischievous, given to small disobediences, of the kind that costs a school its chalk — boy, three generations of whose family had held the same paragraph; the {{clumsy}} — clumsy meaning awkward of the hands and feet, of the dropping sort — one, whose paragraph was written round the inventory of breakage: two cups, the globe, and the cup itself, twice; the {{careless}} — careless meaning without care, the fault of the hasty rather than of the wicked — scholars, whose sums were right but for the carrying; the {{greedy}} — greedy meaning given to greed, hungry past the dinner and into anyone else's — boy, detected in the tuck shop accounts with a nose for the uncounted; the {{obtrusive}} — obtrusive meaning thrusting forward, of the sort that puts itself where it has not been asked — one, who answered every question in the room, including the ones set for homework; and the {{awkward}} — awkward meaning ill at ease, clumsy of the whole person in company — age, through which every child in the valley passed and out of which, the reports faithfully recorded, every one of them came.

The slower virtues and vices had their paragraphs too. The {{slothful}} — slothful meaning of the sloth, slow and idle by nature, the sin carried as a temperament — were reported with a kindness the parents often missed on first reading; the {{sluggish}} — sluggish meaning slow-moving, of the snail's pace, of blood and of morning alike — were marked present at a quarter past nine and counselled about breakfast; the {{rigid}} — rigid meaning stiff and unbending, of rules, and of minds that keep them past the sense — one was praised for the quality and cautioned against it in the same sentence, which the old headmaster considered the whole art of the report; the {{stubborn}} — stubborn meaning fixed in the course, not to be turned, the Tregose inheritance being the standing example — were reported as a strength awaiting its subject; and the {{oblivious}} — oblivious meaning unaware, forgetting or never noticing what is going forward around one — got the valley's favourite line of all: "content, and the cause of contentment in others."

The temptations of the writing itself were the report's real subject, and the old man's margin notes fought them all his life. The {{arbitrary}} — arbitrary meaning by will rather than reason, decided on no principle, the ruler's whim — mark, given by mood instead of measure, was the first temptation, and was fought with a rule: never to mark before breakfast. The {{ridiculous}} — ridiculous meaning fit for laughter, such as deserves to be laughed at — was the second: the nativity donkey, who sat down in the manger, was reported anyway, the ridiculous being half of childhood and all of its best photographs. The third was the {{ignorant}} — ignorant meaning without knowledge, not knowing — error, the writer's own: the report that assumed the child of the second house kept a pony, the writer keeping one himself; it was corrected in the following year's edition, which the family keeps framed. The word {{stupid}} — stupid meaning wanting in sense or quickness; the word the old man forbade, on the grounds that it describes the reporter — never once appeared in forty years, an achievement the valley ranks above its attendance record. And the fourth and greatest temptation was the {{stereotype}} — a stereotype meaning the fixed and printed idea, the type cast once and applied to everyone it nearly fits —: the farmer's son reported dull because his father is silent, the parson's daughter reported saintly because her mother is; against which the one-line instruction in the drawer was the whole defence, and is now the whole tradition.

The new headmaster wrote his first set that July, in the same July hand, and read them at prize day with the same ceremony; and he ended the reading, as the old man had ended forty years of them, with the school's one standing rule, which the valley believes it wrote and the drawer knows better: that the reports are held together by nothing but {{tolerance}} — tolerance meaning the bearing and the allowing, the patient suffering of what differs — for every make of child, the naughty and the sluggish and the rigid and the stubborn alike, every one of them being, as the old man's final report had said, somebody's whole hope, and most of them, on the valley's record, somebody's future paragraph.
tr:
品行评语是这所学校仅次于校钟的最老机构：每个孩子一页，每学年末由校长亲笔写就，颁奖日当众宣读，还被人舍不得扔的家庭同受洗礼的长衫一起收在箱子里。执笔四十年的，是老校长——一位严厉（stern，stern 指面孔和标准上的严格苛刻；词典还坚持说它也是船尾）的人——他的评语是河谷排在《信使报》之后的第二种文学；接班人连同书桌一起继承了这门传统，在抽屉里发现老先生留给自己的指示，一行七月的笔迹：“写这个孩子，不写这一类。”

评语本身，就是被编了目的河谷整个的童年。有淘气（naughty，naughty 指顽皮的、犯些小小不驯的、那种要叫一所学校赔掉粉笔的）的男孩——他家三代人占着同一段落；有笨拙（clumsy，clumsy 指手脚不灵的、属于打碎东西那一派的）的孩子，他的段落围着一份破损清单写成：两只茶杯、一只地球仪，以及奖杯本身，两回；有粗心（careless，careless 指不细心的、性急者之过而非恶意者之过的）的学子，算术全对，只错在进位；有贪嘴（greedy，greedy 指贪的、过了正餐还要伸进别人碗里的）的男孩，在小吃部的账目里人赃并获——鼻子专挑没数过的那一堆；有爱出头（obtrusive，obtrusive 指硬往前挤的、把自己放到没被邀请之处的）的孩子，屋里每个问题都答，包括留作家庭作业的那些；还有局促（awkward，awkward 指浑身不得劲的、在人前整个人都笨拙起来的）的那段年纪——河谷每个孩子都从里面过，而评语忠实地记录，每一个也都从里面出来了。

慢一些的德行与毛病，也各有各的段落。怠惰（slothful，slothful 指懒怠成性的、把懒当作禀性随身携带的那种慢与闲）的孩子的评语写得温厚，家长头一遍常读不出来；迟缓（sluggish，sluggish 指行动迟缓的、蜗牛步的，血流如此，早晨也如此）的孩子被记为九点一刻到校，并被劝告要吃早饭；刻板（rigid，rigid 指僵直不弯的，规则如此，把规则守过了头的心智也如此）的孩子在同一句话里先受夸赞再受告诫——老校长认为这就是评语写作的全部艺术；倔强（stubborn，stubborn 指认定一条道不回头的、劝不转的，特雷戈斯家的遗传是常年例证）的孩子被写成“一股在等它主人的力量”；而浑然不觉（oblivious，oblivious 指无所察觉的、忘掉或从未留意周围正发生什么的）的孩子得到了河谷最心爱的那句评语：“自得，且为他人自得之因。”

写作本身的诱惑，才是评语真正的题目，老先生的页边批注同它们搏斗了一辈子。凭喜怒而非凭度量打出的武断（arbitrary，arbitrary 指出于意志而非道理的、不依任何原则定夺的、掌权者随兴的）分数，是第一重诱惑，对策立了一条规矩：早饭之前不打分。荒唐（ridiculous，ridiculous 指可笑的、配得上被人笑一场的）是第二重：圣诞剧里在马槽里坐下的那头驴，照样写进去——荒唐占童年的一半，也占童年好照片的全部。第三重是无知（ignorant，ignorant 指没有知识的、不知道的）之误，写作者自己的：那份评语想当然地以为第二户人家的孩子养着小马，因为执笔者自己养着；次年那一版作了更正，那家人裱起来挂着。愚蠢（stupid，stupid 指缺心眼缺灵光的；老先生禁用的词，理由是它描写的是写评语的人）这个词，四十年来一次也没出现过——这项成就，河谷把它排在出勤记录之上。第四重也最重的一重，是刻板印象（stereotype，stereotype 指浇铸定型了的成见、翻印一次便套用于一切沾边之人的那类脸谱）：庄稼人的儿子因为父亲沉默就被写成迟钝，牧师的女儿因为母亲体面就被写成圣洁——抽屉里那行指示是针对它的全部防线，如今成了这门传统的全部。

新校长那个七月用同样的手写出了他的第一批，在颁奖日以同样的仪轨宣读；宣读的收尾，同老先生四十年来的收尾一样，是学校那条一成不变的规矩——河谷相信规矩是它自己立的，抽屉知道得更清楚：这些评语全靠一样东西才拢得住——宽容（tolerance，tolerance 指容让与宽忍、对与自己不同者的耐心承受）——对每一种做法的孩子：淘气的、迟缓的、刻板的、倔的，一视同仁；老先生最后一份评语说过，他们每一个，都是某个人的全部指望，而且照河谷的记录，多半也是某个人将来的某一段落。

quiz.q: The naughty boy's family had held the same paragraph for three generations — mischievous, given to small disobediences. Naughty means —
quiz.ex: naughty = 淘气的。a naughty child 淘气孩子；naughtiness n. 顽皮。

quiz.q: The clumsy one's paragraph was written round the inventory of breakage — awkward of the hands and feet, of the dropping sort. Clumsy means —
quiz.ex: clumsy = 笨拙的。clumsy fingers 笨拙的手指；a clumsy apology 生硬的道歉。

quiz.q: The careless scholars' sums were right but for the carrying — without care, the fault of the hasty rather than of the wicked. Careless means —
quiz.ex: careless = 粗心的。a careless mistake 粗心的错误；care n. 小心。

quiz.q: The sluggish were marked present at a quarter past nine — slow-moving, of the snail's pace, of blood and of morning alike. Sluggish means —
quiz.ex: sluggish = 迟缓的。a sluggish economy 呆滞的经济；sluggishly adv. 缓慢地。

quiz.q: The rigid one was praised for the quality and cautioned against it in the same sentence — stiff and unbending, of rules and of minds. Rigid means —
quiz.ex: rigid = 严格的；僵硬的。rigid rules 死板的规定；rigidity n. 僵硬。

quiz.q: The oblivious got the valley's favourite line of all — unaware, forgetting or never noticing what is going forward around one. Oblivious means —
quiz.ex: oblivious = 未察觉的。be oblivious to danger 浑然不觉危险；oblivion n. 遗忘。

quiz.q: The greatest temptation was the stereotype — the fixed and printed idea, the type cast once and applied to everyone it nearly fits. A stereotype is —
o: a fixed idea applied to all who fit
quiz.ex: stereotype = 刻板印象。gender stereotypes 性别刻板印象；stereotypical adj. 老套的。

quiz.q: The reports are held together by nothing but tolerance — the bearing and the allowing, the patient suffering of what differs. Tolerance is —
o: the fixed course not to be turned
the patient bearing of what differs
quiz.ex: tolerance = 宽容。religious tolerance 宗教宽容；tolerate v. 容忍。

title: The Century's Clock
text:
The church clock stopped on the last {{night}} — a night being the dark hours between one day and the next, when the valley keeps its own counsel — of the old year, at four minutes to {{midnight}} — midnight being the middle of the night, the twelfth stroke, the top of the dark, at which one day hands the next its keys—, and the valley crossed into the new {{century}} — a century being a hundred years, time enough for a fashion to be born, to die, and to come back as an antique — to no chime at all. The silence had settled {{overnight}} — overnight meaning through the night; and by extension, suddenly, in the manner of snow and of reputations — and nobody had heard it come, the houses being asleep and the dogs, on this one night of the year, forgiven. The {{first}} — first meaning before all others in order or in time, the one from which the rest are counted — chime of the new century was therefore nobody's to hear; the valley crossed, as it had crossed into every century before it, on faith.

The clock was the parish's senior officer after the tower. The tower was {{medieval}} — medieval meaning of the Middle Ages, the thousand years between Rome and the printing press, when men built as if their grandsons would be the judges—; the clock itself was a newcomer of 1750, {{contemporary}} — contemporary meaning of the same age, living or made at one time; the word that spares two old things the argument about which is the older — with the second bridge, the squire's family, and the first Tizzard to keep the Stores: brass in the face, single in the hand, and wound by whoever of the parish council could still be trusted with the stairs.

The stopping was found at {{dawn}} — dawn being the first grey of the morning, the light that arrives before the sun, as news arrives before the newspaper — by the Marsh Farm milker, whose cows had voted against the whole celebration and wanted the old year's hours back; and it was confirmed at {{midday}} — midday being noon, the top of the day, the sun's own summit — by the congregation of a funeral, the deceased having been a punctual man and lying now in the churchyard on the stroke of nothing at all. The Mercury's headline that Thursday ran: CENTURY LATE, SAYS CHURCH CLOCK.

The argument that followed was the valley's true festivity. The schoolmaster held that the {{millennium}} — a millennium being a thousand years; and by the calendar's own arithmetic, two thousand of them since the numbering began — had not begun at all, no span of years having ever started with a year nought; the vicar held that a parish which had missed two coronations and one eclipse through committee could not afford to be right twice; and the Stores opened a book on the question, wagers payable in eggs at a {{dozen}} — a dozen being twelve, the old English number of counting, of hens' eggs and of apostles, who managed without a spare — a side. The county council, petitioned for a grant, replied with figures instead of money: the tower alone, said the letter, would consume some three hundred thousand of the council's {{million}} — a million being a thousand thousands; the number at which counting stops being a household skill and becomes a profession—, the roads budget standing at fourteen of them; and the nation, the schoolmaster read out, was spending upwards of a {{billion}} — a billion being a thousand millions; the number at which even the profession begins to round — on a great dome by the river, to celebrate the date; which lent the valley's quarrel about the date a chastening proportion.

The mending fell to Mr. Hembrow, the horologist of Lampford, whose family had held the keeping of the clock since before the railways took the trade away. He climbed on the Monday, pronounced the escapement honest and the century guilty, and stayed three days; and at the Legion afterwards he set out the whole liturgy of the keeping, which is a calendar worn as a habit: the {{daily}} — daily meaning every day, once a day; the adverb of things that will not keep, like milk and newspapers — winding; the {{monthly}} — monthly meaning once a month, every month, of wages, of magazines, and of the moon's own accounts — oiling; the {{quarterly}} — quarterly meaning once in every three months, by the quarters into which the year, the company and the school term are all divided — inspection of the bearings; the {{annual}} — annual meaning yearly, once a year, of things that return like relations; the word the seed catalogue is written in — cleaning of the works; and the {{yearly}} — yearly meaning of, or once in, every year; the plainer brother of annual, and the word the valley itself uses — visit of the man himself, with lamp, oil and opinions. None of it, he said, had been done for three years, the keeper's hip being the {{recent}} — recent meaning of the near past, lately done or lately happened, within the memory of the living — misfortune of the parish; and a clock so served does what any servant so served does: it stops, and is then famously right, twice a day.

The county's offer of an electric replacement — radio-set, self-correcting, kept true to Greenwich, in every particular {{up-to-date}} — up-to-date meaning brought level with the present date, abreast of the newest make — was declined by the parish in under ten minutes, the valley having already watched the exchange, the milking parlour and the school boiler go over to the {{modern}} — modern meaning of the present day or the near past; of the new make and the new manner; the word the past uses when it means to accuse—, and having drawn its one line at the clock. The clock went again on the Friday, four minutes fast, the four minutes being allowed to stand as interest. That summer came its two hundred and fiftieth {{anniversary}} — an anniversary being the yearly return of the day of a thing, the date kept because memory keeps accounts—, which the parish observed with tea in the tower and a hymn to the {{era}} — an era being a stretch of history with one weather of its own: the era of the horse, the era of steam, and the era the valley was then entering and could not yet name — that had received it; and the {{present}} — the present meaning the time now going, this very passing minute; the only tense the living occupy — having arrived four minutes late, the valley, upon the whole, forgave it.
tr:
教区大钟停在旧年最后一夜（night，night 指一天与下一天之间的黑暗时辰、河谷守口如瓶的那段时间）的午夜（midnight，midnight 指夜的正中、第十二响、黑暗的顶端，一个日子在此把钥匙交给下一个）前四分钟，于是全村跨进新世纪（century，century 指一百年，足够一种时兴出生、死透、再作为古董还魂的工夫）时没有听见钟声，只听见寂静。寂静是夜里（overnight，overnight 指一夜之间地；引申为突然地，下雪和变名声都是这个路数）落定的，没人听见它来——家家的屋子都睡着，狗在这一年独此一夜得了赦免。于是新世纪的头一响（first，first 指顺序或时间上在一切之前的那个、其余都从它数起的那个）钟声谁也无缘听见；全村跨进新世纪，像跨进之前的每个世纪一样，凭的是信心。

这座钟是教区里仅次于钟塔的资深要员。塔是中世纪（medieval，medieval 指中世纪的，罗马与印刷术之间那一千年，人们盖房盖得像等着孙子来验收）的，钟本身却是1750年的新贵，与第二座桥、乡绅家和头一个开杂货铺的蒂泽德同代（contemporary，contemporary 指同一年代的、同时存在或同时制成的；正是那个让两件老东西免于争论谁更老的词）：黄铜面盘，独针，靠手上弦，上弦的差事归教区议事会里还信得过楼梯的随便哪一位。

停摆是黎明（dawn，dawn 指清晨头一线灰白、赶在太阳之前到的光，正如消息赶在报纸之前到）时被沼泽农场的挤奶工发现的，他那群奶牛已经投票否决了整场庆典，要把旧年的钟点讨回去；正午（midday，midday 指中午、白昼的顶点、太阳自己的峰顶）由一场葬礼的会众确认——故人生前是个守时的人，如今躺在墓园里，等着一记根本不响的第四响。那周四《信使报》的标题是：教区大钟宣布，世纪迟到。

接下来的那场争论才是河谷真正的庆典。校长主张，千禧年（millennium，millennium 指一千年；按日历自家的算术，纪年开始以来恰是两千个）压根还没开始——任何一段年数都不曾从“零年”起算；牧师主张，一个靠开会错过了两次加冕礼和一次日食的教区，可经不起再对第二回了；杂货铺就此开了赌局，赌注以鸡蛋结算，一打（dozen，dozen 指十二、老英格兰的计数单位，母鸡的蛋和使徒都按它数，使徒们连个替补都没配）起。县议会收到请愿，回的是数字而不是钱：信上说，光塔一项就要吃掉县里那笔百万（million，million 指一千个一千；数数数到这里就不再是持家的本事，而成了一门职业）预算中的三十万上下，道路预算统共才十四个百万；而全国——校长照着报纸念——正花十亿（billion，billion 指一千个百万；连职业数数的到这个数也开始四舍五入）出头，在河边造一座大穹顶，就为庆祝这个日子；这让河谷关于日子的争吵显得很受教。

修理落到了兰普福德的钟表匠亨布罗先生头上，他们家自铁路把这门生意抢走之前就执掌这座钟的保养。他周一上塔，判定擒纵机构无罪、世纪有罪，一待三天；随后在军团里，他把保养的整套仪轨摆了出来——那是一部当日历穿戴的规程：每日（daily，daily 指每天一次的；牛奶和报纸这类存不住的东西用的副词）上弦；每月（monthly，monthly 指每月一次的，工资、杂志、月亮自己的账目都用它）上油；每季（quarterly，quarterly 指每三个月一次的，按年、公司和学期通用的那个“季”来分）查验轴承；每年（annual，annual 指一年一度的、指像亲戚一样回访的事物；种籽目录就是用它写的）清洗机芯；还有一年一回（yearly，yearly 指每年的、每一年一回的；annual 的老实兄弟，也是河谷自己爱用的词）他本人带着灯、油和高见亲临。这些，他说，三年没做了——管钟人的胯骨是教区新近（recent，recent 指近来的、不久前发生或做下的、活人还记得住的）的不幸；而一座被这样使唤的钟，同任何被这样使唤的仆人一样：它停下来，然后出了名地一天对两次。

县里提出换一座电动钟——无线电校准、自动纠偏、与格林尼治保持一致，样样都最新（up-to-date，up-to-date 指与当前日期拉平的、跟上最新款式的）——教区不到十分钟就回绝了；电话局、挤奶厅、学校锅炉已经相继投奔了现代（modern，modern 指当代或近世的、新做法新款式；过去想指摘现在时用的词），河谷把自己的底线画在了钟这里。周五钟重新走起来，快了四分钟，这四分钟被当作利息留着。那年夏天迎来它落成二百五十周年（anniversary，anniversary 指一件事情的日子一年一度地回来、因记忆记账而被守着的那个日期），教区在塔里办了茶会，为接纳它的那个时代（era，era 指自带一种天气的一段历史：马的时代、蒸汽的时代，以及河谷当时正走进去还叫不出名字的那个时代）唱了首赞美诗；而当下（present，present 指正在过去的此时此刻、活人所占据的唯一时态）既然迟到了四分钟才到，河谷总体上是原谅它了。

quiz.q: The clock stopped at four minutes to midnight — the middle of the night, the twelfth stroke, the top of the dark. Midnight is —
o: the first grey of the morning
the middle of the night, the twelfth stroke
the top of the day, noon
a stretch of a hundred years
quiz.ex: midnight = 午夜。at midnight 在午夜；burn the midnight oil 开夜车。

quiz.q: The silence had settled overnight — through the night; and by extension, suddenly. Overnight means —
o: through the night; by extension, suddenly
brought level with the newest date
quiz.ex: overnight = 一夜之间；突然。an overnight success 一夜成名；stay overnight 过夜。

quiz.q: The tower was medieval — of the Middle Ages, between Rome and the printing press. Medieval means —
o: of the same age as another
quiz.ex: medieval = 中世纪的。medieval castles 中世纪城堡；the medieval period 中世纪时期。

quiz.q: The stopping was found at dawn — the first grey of the morning, the light that arrives before the sun. Dawn is —
o: the first grey of the morning
the yearly return of a date
a period of a thousand years
quiz.ex: dawn = 黎明。at dawn 在黎明时分；dawn on sb. 某人恍然大悟。

quiz.q: Wagers were payable in eggs at a dozen a side — twelve, the old English number of counting. A dozen is —
quiz.ex: dozen = 一打。eggs by the dozen 成打地买蛋；dozens of 许多。

quiz.q: Some three hundred thousand of the council's million — a thousand thousands; where counting becomes a profession. A million is —
quiz.ex: million = 百万。millions of 数百万；one in a million 万里挑一。

quiz.q: The annual cleaning of the works — yearly, once a year, of things that return like relations. Annual means —
quiz.ex: annual = 年度的。annual report 年度报告；annually adv. 每年。

quiz.q: A hymn to the era that had received the clock — a stretch of history with one weather of its own. An era is —
o: the yearly return of a date
a stretch of history with one weather of its own
quiz.ex: era = 时代。a new era 新时代；the era of steam 蒸汽时代。

title: The Last Stationmaster
text:
The line came up the valley in 1873, and Mr. Emmott's grandfather, then nine years old, was held up on a milestone to watch the {{Opening}} — an opening being the formal beginning of a thing, the first day of its being open for use; and by extension, any gap, and any post left standing empty—: the first engine taking water at Millbrook, the squire in his good coat, and the company's chairman assuring the crowd that the district could no longer be described as remote, which it could, and was, and is. Sixty-eight years later, to the very month, the grandson retired from the same station — the last stationmaster, as it proved, that the valley would ever have — and the Mercury gave him a full column and a photograph, which is the nearest approach to a state funeral the valley ever issues.

His own account of his career, given in strict order, was the career in miniature. {{Initially}} — initially meaning at the first, in the beginning, before the later arrangements had altered anything — he had been a lad porter at the Lampford junction, taken on at fourteen with a barrow and a whistle; he had then worked the {{intermediate}} — intermediate meaning lying in between; of the stations that stand between the junction and the end of the line, and of any rung between the bottom and the top of a ladder — halts, one at a time, learning each one's particular ration of rain; he had been trained at Millbrook under the {{former}} — former meaning earlier, gone before; and, where two are named, the first-named of them, as the latter is the second — stationmaster, old Mr. Coombes, in the ten years {{preceding}} — preceding meaning going before, in time or in order; the word for the chapter on the page before this one — the first war; and his own appointment, on Mr. Coombes's retirement, had gone through without {{precedent}} — a precedent being an earlier case of a thing cited to justify the doing of it again; the law's memory of itself—, no Emmott having ever held the post before, and none, now that the account was closed, ever to hold it after.

Beside the column the Mercury printed his own timetable of a day, kept in pencil for forty-one years, and it read like a small liturgy. He was {{punctual}} — punctual meaning exact to the appointed time, arriving neither before the hour nor after it; from the Latin for the point, the pricking of the hour — all his life, to the {{minute}} — a minute being the sixtieth part of an hour; and, with the stress thrown forward, a word for anything so small it must be hunted with a magnifying glass—, and the valley, wanting no other clock, set its watches by his figure crossing the forecourt at five to eight. When the smoke showed at the viaduct, the up train's arrival was {{imminent}} — imminent meaning about to happen, hanging just over the moment, of things close enough to be already heard—; at that {{moment}} — a moment being a very short while, the time a thing takes between coming and having come — he took up the red disc and stood at the gate; the {{instant}} — an instant being the point of time itself, a now without any length in it; and, as an adjective, the word for what will not wait — the wheels stayed, the doors were opened, and {{immediately}} — immediately meaning with nothing in between, at once, the moment after without a gap — the parcels were weighed, the hampers handed down, and the schoolchildren marshalled back from the edge of the platform. The two ceremonies of the day were never {{simultaneous}} — simultaneous meaning happening at one and the same time, two things keeping a single step together—, the up and the down trains having been timetabled courteously apart. {{Meanwhile}} — meanwhile meaning in the time between, while the other thing told of was going on—, the fire was banked, the lamp trimmed, the ledgers squared; and in the {{meantime}} — the meantime being the time between two events, the while itself; the noun, where meanwhile is its adverb — between the last train of the day and the first of the next, the station was, he told the Mercury, the loneliest room in the parish and the most honest, a man being there in the {{midst}} — the midst being the very middle of a thing, the thick of it, where one is in the affair and not at the edge of it — of his own thoughts, with nothing whatever to recommend them.

Asked why — the Mercury asked; the valley had asked for years without an answer — he gave three reasons, counted on three fingers. Firstly, that a train is a promise made by a company to a valley, and the breaking of promises is the one extravagance the poor are never permitted; {{secondly}} — secondly meaning in the second place; the signpost word that announces that the counting has begun—, that the valley's whole day, milking, school, market, doctor and courting, hung off the two trains like washing off a line, and one late arrival would drag the lot of it into the dirt; and {{finally}} — finally meaning at the last, when all the others have been said—, that a man standing ready at the appointed hour is the one argument against disorder that the world has never yet laughed at.
